22425-stanford-achievement-test-ed-1922:
The Stanford Achievement Test, 1922 edition, measured school children's learning. It was among the first standard tests used across American schools. A sample reading item shows its simple early-grade style.

Fanny has a little red hen in the test passage. Every day the hen goes to her nest and lays an egg. Then she makes a funny noise to call Fanny. The child must supply the missing word that completes the sense. Arithmetic, spelling, and other subjects fill the rest. Educators used the results to compare pupils and schools. The booklet preserves early testing in its plainest form, hen and all.
22677-greece-and-the-allies-1914-1922:
Greece and the Allies, 1914–1922 is a history of Greece's tortured path through the First World War and its aftermath. The catalog record names no author. Greece split between king and prime minister over joining the Allies, fought at last beside them, then plunged into war with Turkey and catastrophe in Asia Minor.

The author notes an earlier book on Turkey, Greece, and the great powers. That book raised a storm: reproaches from private critics and scorn from public ones. Anonymous abuse followed, and bigots withdrew their acquaintance. Yet some readers, in a maelstrom of passion, kept their respect for facts. That embattled tone suits the subject. The book argues Greece's case from inside the quarrels that tore it, and historians still weigh it as a partisan but informed witness.
abelard-historia-calamitatum-bellows-192:
Henry Adams Bellows published his translation of Peter Abelard's Historia Calamitatum in 1922. Abelard, the great logic teacher of the 1100s, wrote the work as a letter of comfort to a friend. Its title means the story of his misfortunes, and it became the most famous medieval autobiography after Augustine's Confessions.

Abelard told of his fame in Paris, his love affair with his student Heloise, and the attack that left him castrated. He described his condemnation by church councils and his clashes with monks and rivals. Pride runs through his own account of his falls. Bellows's English lets modern readers meet a mind both brilliant and self-wounding.
achad-qbl-brides-reception-1922:
Charles Stansfeld Jones, who wrote as Frater Achad, was Crowley's prized student until he redrew the Tree of Life. Q B L, or The Bride's Reception, printed in 1922, is his first major work of Kabbalah. In it he shifts the letters and paths of the Tree to new places.

Achad held that a new age needed a new key, and he built that key from number and letter play. Crowley took the shift as error and revolt, and the two men split. The book opened a line of Thelemic Kabbalah that runs on its own track. Its claims still stir debate among students of the Tree.
ampere-recueil-electro-dynamiques-1822:
Andre-Marie Ampere gathered his electro-dynamic observations in French in 1822, within two years of Oersted's great discovery. Wires carrying current attract, repel, and turn in his delicate trials. Ampere worked out the math of how currents and magnets act on each other with stunning speed.

His papers founded the science of electrodynamics in real time. The unit of electric current now bears his name in his honor. He shows each trial plainly, then builds law upon law from the results. Readers meet electrical science at its birth, in the founder's own papers, fresh from the workbench and the lecture desk alike.
arxiv-2510-00322:
Gunter Steinke and Thomas Steinke wrote this 2025 theory paper on estimating statistics without leaking private data. Differential privacy usually adds noise scaled to how much one person's data can sway a result. For black-box statistics that sway is unknown or huge, so standard methods fail. A few known workarounds waste data badly or demand impossibly many function evaluations.

The authors present a scheme that trades off between those two costs in a controlled way. Users can spend more data to evaluate the function fewer times, or the reverse. They also prove lower bounds on what any such scheme must pay. Their method comes close to those bounds, marking it as nearly optimal. The work widens the range of statistics that can be released under a privacy guarantee. Arbitrary black-box computations are no longer out of reach for private estimation.
arxiv-2510-00522:
Md. Abdur Rahman and four colleagues published this 2025 paper on recognizing bird species from song, without piles of labeled recordings. Field audio is plentiful, but expert labels are scarce and slow. Their network, ARIONet, learns from raw sound with two self-supervised tasks at once. Augmented copies of the same clip should agree, while future audio frames should be predictable.

A transformer encoder fuses several complementary audio features into one representation. Contrastive training sharpens species signatures, and frame prediction captures how songs unfold in time. Four birdsong datasets, including large Xeno-Canto subsets, put the method through its paces. Classification accuracy ranged from about ninety-two to ninety-eight percent across them. Frame predictions tracked the true audio with cosine similarity up to ninety-five percent. The authors aim the tool at ecological monitoring and biodiversity surveys in the field.
arxiv-2510-00622:
Esser, Lambert, and Vedel study the p-spectrum of random wavelet series in this 2025 arXiv paper on multifractal analysis. That field measures how roughness varies from point to point in a function or signal. Classic tools assume the function stays locally bounded, which excludes many rough signals. The p-exponent extends the analysis to a wider class, and this paper asks how to read the resulting spectrum from wavelet coefficients.

The authors prove an upper bound for the p-spectrum based on how wavelet coefficients spread across scales. They then show the bound is sharp for random wavelet series under broad conditions on the coefficient distribution. Within families of functions sharing one prescribed wavelet statistic, the bound is attained by a prevalent set of functions. The result confirms the estimate reflects typical behaviour rather than a rare edge case.
arxiv-2510-00822:
Vatsavai and a large collaboration present CGSim at the SC Workshops in November 2025, a simulator for huge distributed computing systems such as the Worldwide LHC Computing Grid. That grid runs particle physics jobs across hundreds of sites, and testing new scheduling ideas on the real system is risky and slow. Existing simulators struggle with scale, fixed algorithms, and poor support for machine learning data.

Built on the validated SimGrid engine, CGSim adds modular plugins for custom scheduling and data movement policies. It also offers live dashboards and automatic event-level datasets for AI modelling. Using real ATLAS PanDA workloads, the team reports much better calibration accuracy across grid sites. Multi-site runs scaled near-linearly and finished about six times faster than single-site runs in their scalability tests.
arxiv-2510-00922:
Chirra, Teoh, Paruchuri, and Varakantham, at Singapore Management University, let an LLM-guided evolutionary search design reward functions for imitation learning, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Adversarial imitation learning trains a policy against a discriminator that scores how expert-like its behaviour looks. That score must be converted into a reward, and the conversion functions in use are hand-designed from divergence objectives. Almost nobody had studied how much that choice drives stability and performance.

Their framework evolves candidate reward assignment functions, judging each by the performance of the policy it produces. The winner, packaged as DAIL, is the first meta-learned adversarial imitation learning algorithm. It generalized to unseen environments and to policy optimizers, beating state-of-the-art hand-designed baselines. Analysing the discovered function explained part of the gain: its shape steadies training dynamics. The discovered reward matches no known divergence, so it carries no theoretical guarantees yet.
arxiv-2510-01022:
Johnson, Anand, Krishnaswamy, and Perlmutter introduce an equivariant geometric scattering network in this 2025 arXiv paper on graph machine learning. Their data are geometric graphs, where nodes sit in space and carry both scalar values and vectors, as with molecules or physical systems. A good model should give the same answer when the whole structure rotates or moves. Standard message-passing networks respect that symmetry only with many parameters and layers.

The authors build a scattering transform from vector diffusion wavelets that carries the symmetry by construction. They prove the method is equivariant under rigid rotations and translations. Plugged into a graph neural network, it matched the performance of leading equivariant message-passing models in their experiments. It did so with only a fraction of the parameter count, which matters for large geometric datasets.
arxiv-2510-01322:
Bhowmick and co-authors simulate the first black holes starting from unusually heavy seeds in the universe's densest neighborhoods. Telescopes now glimpse giant black holes improbably early, straining growth models that start small. The BRAHMA simulations plant seeds thousands of times heavier than a star, where gas stays dense and metal-poor.

With standard feedback in place, gas feeding is choked off early and mergers do the growing. Later, once feeding opens, permissive accretion models build billion-sun black holes on schedule. Radiative efficiency, more than accretion boost knobs, decides how fast the early giants grow. Seeding and dynamics each leave separable marks. Constrained initial conditions aim the simulation at rare overdense peaks. Lyman-Werner radiation sets the stage where heavy seeds can form. Subgrid friction handles mergers the resolution cannot follow directly. Quasars at the highest redshifts frame the observational stakes.
arxiv-2510-01622:
Ma and co-authors rebuild generative recommendation around five upgrades, from multimodal input to causal debiasing. Language-model recommenders juggle text, images, and user history while fighting inherited biases. Their framework fuses modalities early and retrieves outside knowledge to ground each suggestion.

A causal module works to strip bias out of the ranking logic itself. Explanations are generated alongside picks, and an adaptive layer keeps learning after deployment. Tests on movie, electronics, and local-business data improved accuracy, fairness, and diversity together. Gains stayed modest but consistent across all three benchmarks. MovieLens, Amazon electronics, and local reviews supplied three different recommendation worlds. Accuracy, fairness, and diversity rarely improve together, which makes the sweep notable. Retrieval augmentation grounds picks in catalog facts instead of model memory. Real-time adaptation tracks taste drift between retrains. Explanations ship with each recommendation. Modest, broad gains beat flashy narrow ones.
arxiv-2510-02322:
Buess and co-authors teach a model to match spoken radiology reports with CT scans. Their 2025 medical AI paper starts from daily practice. Radiologists mostly dictate reports aloud. Almost all medical AI, though, trains on typed text alone. The team built Speech-RATE, a large set of spoken style reports. They then trained SpeechCT-CLIP to align speech with 3D scan volumes. Plain speech training lagged behind text training at first. Borrowing knowledge from a pretrained text-image model changed that. The transfer is called knowledge distillation.

Zero-shot classification scores rose clearly after distillation. The F1 score climbed from about zero point six two to zero point seven one. That gain recovered most of the gap to text models. Retrieval tests also performed strongly without any transcripts. Skipping transcription avoids recognition errors entirely. Dictated doubt and tone survive as useful signal.
arxiv-2510-02422:
Xiu and co-authors make jailbreak attacks faster by letting the target model pick the target. Their 2025 security paper studies attacks on safety aligned chatbots. Classic attacks force one fixed cheerful reply from the model. That reply sits far from anything the model would say. Optimization then grinds through many rounds and often fails. Dynamic Target Attack samples real replies from the model instead. Each round picks the most harmful sampled reply as a temporary goal. The prompt then optimizes toward that nearby goal. Rounds repeat until the attack prompt works reliably.

Experiments spanned leading safety aligned models and standard jailbreak benchmarks. The method worked in both white-box and black-box settings. It beat state-of-the-art attack baselines consistently. Convergence came faster thanks to the smaller target gap. Defenders learn where alignment bends most easily. Attack research of this kind stress tests safety claims.
arxiv-2510-02522:
Deg and co-authors test how reliably slow spinning galaxies can be modeled from radio data. Their 2025 astronomy paper serves the WALLABY survey. That survey maps neutral hydrogen across wide sky areas. Small, slow galaxies stress cosmological models the most. Their signals are faint, blurry, and easily misread. The team built a testing frame for kinematic modeling codes. Mock galaxies with known spins graded each code fairly. The survey proto-pipeline, WKAPP, removed many false positives. Rival codes kept more fake detections in the same tests. Inclination below about forty degrees proved dangerous for everyone.

Half the low inclination sample turned false even for WKAPP. The team then examined eleven real slow rotators. Each spun below fifty kilometers per second at peak. Trust limits for dwarf galaxy spins are now explicit. Dark matter tests at low mass depend on them. Honest error bars protect the coming statistical samples.
arxiv-2510-02822:
Kim and co-authors present FlexiQ, a way to shrink vision models without hurting them much. Demand for those chips swings up and down during the day. Quantization lowers the number of bits used for each value. FlexiQ applies low-bit math only to channels with small value ranges. It also lowers bit width in a way that limits new errors.

FlexiQ can change its mix of low-bit channels in real time. That lets one model trade accuracy for speed as load shifts. The team tested eleven vision models, both classic and transformer based. Four-bit models with fine-tuning gained clear accuracy over rival methods. A half low-bit model lost almost no accuracy at all. It still captured a good share of the full speed gain. Runtime costs on their own chip and on GPUs stayed minimal.
arxiv-2510-02922:
Tsolissou and co-authors test vision-language models on carotid artery risk. Plaques in the neck arteries can lead to stroke. Judging their risk needs images plus clinical facts. The team fed ultrasound images with lab and demographic data to open models. An interview-style question chain mimicked a real workup. Their zero-shot results exposed sharp limits.

Some models named the imaging type and anatomy well. All of them failed at the actual risk grading. The team then adapted one model, LLaVa-NeXT-Vicuna, to ultrasound. A light method called LoRA handled the tuning. Adding the clinical table as text helped further. Specificity and balanced accuracy both rose a lot. The tuned model matched older image-only networks on the same data. The authors stress that calibration and domain tuning are vital. Raw large models are not ready for this clinical task alone.
arxiv-2510-03022:
Zhong and co-authors attack the data shortage in humanoid robotics. Teaching a humanoid needs many real demonstrations. Real demos are slow and costly to collect. Simulations and web videos carry a mismatch with real bodies. Their answer is a wearable exoskeleton called HumanoidExo. A person wears it and performs the task by hand. The suit records whole-body motion in robot-ready form.

Three hard tasks tested the idea in the real world. They covered tabletop work, work mixed with standing and squatting, and full-body tasks. Policies trained with suit data generalized to new rooms. Complex skills took hold from just five real robot demos. Walking emerged from suit data alone, with no robot trials. The suit shrinks the gap between human and robot bodies. Data grows faster and covers more varied scenes. That scale is what general-purpose humanoids have been missing.
arxiv-2510-03122:
Zhang and co-authors rebuild pictures a person saw from their brain scans. Functional MRI records which brain areas stir during viewing. The visual cortex handles form and meaning in partly split streams. Their model, HAVIR, mirrors that split in its design. One module reads voxels tied to spatial processing. It turns them into structural priors for a diffusion generator. A second module reads the semantic stream of voxels.

That module renders meaning as CLIP embeddings, a shared text-image code. A versatile diffusion model then fuses structure and meaning. The fused inputs guide the final image synthesis. Tests on complex natural scenes favored the split design. Reconstructions beat prior models on structure and semantics alike. Earlier systems often kept one at the cost of the other. Complex scenes had exposed that weakness most clearly. Brain-computer interfaces stand to gain from richer decoding.
arxiv-2510-03422:
Hong and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on how pandemic mobility limits changed household spending in India. The team used scanner data from a major retail chain plus Google mobility records. Spending data are hard to model because many households spend nothing in a given week, outcomes move together, and confounders shift over time. Their causal model handles all three problems at once. It pairs a structural nested mean model with weights that correct for uneven visit timing.

The estimator stays doubly robust, so it tolerates some mistakes in its flexible parts. Simulations confirmed the method behaves as theory promises. Applied to the Indian data, it showed that the sharp drop in mobility had a significant effect on fresh food spending in particular. Such category level findings help governments weigh health rules against household costs. Blanket claims about total spending can hide where families truly cut back.
arxiv-2510-03922:
Gallo wrote this 2025 arXiv paper in probability theory, on when a random network on a tree connects at large scales. The model places edges on a rooted tree, linking each vertex to descendants several generations below. Each edge length is kept with its own probability, chosen independently. Percolation occurs when an endless connected cluster forms, and the boundary of that regime is the critical curve.

Gallo finds the critical surface exactly, as the zero set of one polynomial whose coefficients depend explicitly on the edge lengths and branching degree. For two edge lengths, he derives new bounds on the critical probabilities. He also proves the curve is monotone and continuous, with partial results on convexity. The proofs run through a Markov chain tracking how far an open path has progressed. Exact critical surfaces are rare in percolation, so this tractable model is a useful test bed.
arxiv-2510-04022:
Wang and a large team present this 2025 arXiv paper on answering questions about long videos without wasting the model's budget. Video models receive a fixed number of tokens, and uniform sampling spends most of them on background scenes. The brief moments that answer the question get too few frames to read clearly. The authors split the job into finding the right moments first, then answering from them.

Their framework, Video-in-the-Loop, skims the video at low frame rate to localize the spans a question needs. It then re-encodes only those spans at higher fidelity and answers, citing the spans it used. Training couples span accuracy with answer correctness in one objective, so credit flows back to localization. Under fixed budgets, the method gained several points while using half the frame input of rivals. Span-aware allocation beat uniform sampling in every ablation.
arxiv-2510-04322:
Srinivasan and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on pricing options by solving financial partial differential equations with physics-informed extreme learning machines. PDE solvers underpin option pricing and risk evaluation, and physics-informed neural networks can solve them without meshes. Those networks train by slow iterative gradient descent and scale poorly, which hurts in time-sensitive trading applications. Extreme learning machines instead fix random hidden weights and solve for output weights in one least-squares step.

The authors benchmark the physics-informed variant on the Black-Scholes and Heston-Hull-White models for forward option pricing. Accuracy matched physics-informed neural networks while running as much as thirty times faster in their experiments. The method also handled the inverse problem, recovering volatility and interest rate parameters from noisy observations for model calibration. Fast, reliable PDE solvers matter most when markets move and prices must refresh in real time.
arxiv-2510-04422:
Sungwoo Jeong wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on the smallest values in random matrix models. Two families, the beta Laguerre and beta Jacobi ensembles, model random data in statistics and physics. Jeong studied the distribution of the smallest eigenvalue in each family, for any value of beta. His tool is an integral formula due to Kaneko. The results are written in terms of polynomials in many variables.

He shows that the density and distribution of the smallest eigenvalue equal those polynomials evaluated at a scaled identity matrix. The formulas hold when a weight exponent is a whole number. Existing computer algebra methods can then compute the values in explicit form. From the same formulas, he derives new differentiation rules for the multivariate polynomials. He also solves two differential equations, Painlevé V and Painlevé VI. The work links random matrix theory, special functions, and differential equations in one frame.
arxiv-2510-04522:
Yisen Gao and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on learning from graph data with geometry aware diffusion. Graph data, from molecules to social networks, does not live in flat space. Features at node, edge, and whole graph levels carry different kinds of curvature. Standard graph diffusion stuffs all of them into one flat latent space, where their geometry blurs. The team built GeoMancer, a framework that gives each level a curved home.

GeoMancer replaces a numerically touchy exponential map with a stable gyrokernel that respects the geometry. Features split across task specific manifolds, so each keeps its signature while learning. A constrained diffusion process then keeps its outputs on the right manifold instead of drifting off it. A self guided step supports generation with no condition attached. One framework thus serves both prediction tasks, such as classification and regression, and generation. Wide tests across many tasks beat earlier approaches.
arxiv-2510-04622:
Youngjoon Lee and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on making synthetic biomedical data with forecasting models. Signals such as brain and muscle recordings are scarce, since privacy rules and cost limit sharing. AI tools for medicine starve without such data. The team proposes to grow data from forecasting models trained on series. A good forecaster has learned the rhythms of the signal, so its rollouts can pass as recordings.

Their series kept the time and frequency traits of real brain and muscle signals. Tests across subjects showed the data could stand in for real data in analysis. Classifiers trained with synthetic help also scored better than those trained on real data alone. The samples filled thin regions of the data map, where rare patterns live. Because no patient data leaves the lab, the sets can be shared in repositories. The authors post their data to hubs for other teams.
arxiv-2510-04722:
Kolomiecas, Kučinskas, Klevas, and Dobrovolskas wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on strontium in a star cluster. Globular clusters hold generations of stars with different light element mixes. The generation is rich in sodium, and its polluters remain debated. The team measured sodium and strontium in thirty one red giants of the cluster 47 Tucanae. Spectra came from the archive of a telescope in Chile. They took care with line blending and the effects of convection on the measurements.

Strontium tracked sodium weakly across the sample: sodium rich stars held slightly more strontium. An earlier study by the group found the same pattern for zirconium. Together the hints suggest the polluters made heavy elements by neutron capture. The average strontium level sat near the range seen in field stars of composition. Two kinds of stars could explain the strontium to zirconium ratio. They are low mass giants or massive stars spinning fast.
arxiv-2510-05022:
Daewoong Cheong, Thang Pham, and Dung The Tran work in harmonic analysis in this 2025 arXiv paper. The classic Loomis-Whitney inequality bounds the size of a set by the sizes of its shadows, or projections. The authors carry that idea into finite Heisenberg groups. Those groups add a twist that makes the geometry non-commutative.

For the smallest case, they find the exact range of exponents where the key estimate holds. For general dimension, they prove a multilinear estimate at the critical exponent by induction. Specializing to plain sets gives a sharp inequality that forces a large projection in every configuration. A straightening map turns these bounds into covering results. The authors also draw a new link to the orthogonal projection problem.
arxiv-2510-05222:
Hongkun Chen and four co-authors show that throwing away suspicious runs can sharply improve quantum error correction in this 2025 arXiv paper. Decoding a stabilizer code means judging which errors a syndrome pattern implies. Some syndrome patterns are exponentially unlikely yet cause most logical failures. The authors study that distribution in the toric code.

Within the coding phase, failures concentrate on those rare, unlucky syndromes. Postselecting against them suppresses the logical error rate from one power to a higher power. For the toric code with perfect measurements, the exponent reached about 3.1 in their numerics. The argument extends to general topological stabilizer codes under a large-deviation principle. Postselection thus becomes a scalable accuracy tool, not just a near-term trick.
arxiv-2510-05422:
Xiamiao Zhao and four co-authors complete an extremal problem about forbidden matchings inside hypergraphs in this 2025 arXiv paper. A Berge hypergraph encodes a graph by expanding each edge into a larger hyperedge. The Turán number counts the most hyperedges possible without containing a forbidden pattern. Kang, Ni, and Shan had settled Berge matchings except for one middle range.

The authors settle exactly that remaining case for the matching's parameters. They also prove exact and general results for matchings forbidden alongside one extra hypergraph. Similar theorems cover matchings combined with Berge bipartite graphs. A generalization extends earlier Turán results for Berge hypergraphs by Gerbner, Methuku, and Palmer. The extremal theory of Berge matchings is now essentially complete.
arxiv-2510-05522:
Koh and colleagues study projections of point sets inside finite-field spaces. A projection flattens a set onto a smaller subspace, much like a shadow. Most directions give large shadows, but some exceptional directions shrink the set badly. Their 2025 paper counts those bad directions for a restricted family of viewing lines.

The team uses discrete Fourier analysis plus estimates for cone and sphere surfaces. They obtain sharp bounds on the exceptional sets, up to constant factors. Special viewing slices need separate care, since arithmetic details change the answer. The size of the bad set depends on a quadratic character and on dimension parity. Their bounds also recover known estimates for the full family of subspaces. It complements Chen's 2018 estimates. As a payoff, large enough sets yield many directions whose dot products cover a positive share of the field.
arxiv-2510-05722:
Ye and colleagues build a training-free factory for labeled segmentation images. Pixel-wise annotation is slow and expensive, sometimes an hour per image. Diffusion models can synthesize images, but label generation usually needs training or heavy compute. Their 2025 pipeline pairs ControlNet with vision-language models instead.

A multi-way prompt generator diversifies the synthetic scenes on demand. A mask generator produces the pixel-level labels alongside each image. A selection module then filters for high-quality samples only. On PASCAL and COCO few-shot benchmarks, the synthetic data lifts one-shot segmentation. It outperforms concurrent synthesis work in their comparisons. Gains reach about two points of overlap on some folds with HDMNet. Controllable targeted classes suit narrow domains where giant open-vocabulary models stumble. Lightweight expert models also fit edge devices better than SAM.
arxiv-2510-05922:
Bezerra and colleagues test whether MFCC features secretly carry prosody. Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients are the classic handcrafted features of speech processing. Textbooks treat them as purely spectral, independent of pitch and rhythm. Their 2025 study challenges that assumption with significance testing.

Three prosodic features are tested: energy, fundamental frequency, and voicing. A null hypothesis framework assesses statistical independence from the MFCCs systematically. Independence is implausible for every one of the three features. MFCCs therefore inherently encode valuable prosodic information. The source-filter theory's clean separation does not survive the data. Neighboring-frame context might extract still more of the residual prosody. Handcrafted features remain relevant even beside end-to-end waveform models. Future models can exploit this hidden prosodic content deliberately. Speech recognition and analysis design both stand to benefit. The ear-inspired mel scaling is part of why MFCCs endure.
arxiv-2510-06322:
The XRISM Collaboration compares measured gas motions in galaxy clusters against cosmological simulations in a 2025 astrophysics paper. The hot plasma filling clusters is stirred by mergers and supermassive black hole feedback. XRISM's velocity measurements in nine clusters test whether simulations stir that plasma correctly.

The team compared observations with three leading simulation suites using different feedback models. In cool cores, real dispersions were systematically lower than predicted. All ten core measurements sat below simulated medians by a factor near one and a half, in the bottom tenth. The observed kinetic pressure share, around two percent, fell well short of the predicted five to six and a half percent. Outside cores, agreement improved, except around relaxed A2029, whose calm outskirts no simulation reproduced. Current feedback models, the authors suggest, eject energy too violently in cores.
arxiv-2510-06422:
Aravena and three co-authors model how hydro reservoirs and inverters shape frequency-safe grid operation in a 2025 power systems paper. Renewables are replacing synchronous machines with inverter-based resources. Frequency control grows harder as replacement proceeds. Hydro reservoirs offer flexible stored energy, but standard scheduling models ignore their frequency role.

The team builds a new frequency-constrained unit commitment model. It captures reservoir dynamics and their effect on frequency nadir requirements data-drivenly. Simulations cover Chile in 2024 and a carbon-free 2035 scenario. Against the industry standard, the model cut operational costs up to twenty-eight percent. Security was not compromised by those savings. Hydro reservoirs emerged as central to future frequency regulation. The authors priced grid-forming inverters and synchronous condensers for 2035 support duties. Both lowered annual running costs, but grid-forming inverters returned far more on investment.
arxiv-2510-06622:
Ni Ding and four co-authors work in information theory, on measuring how much a channel leaks about a secret. Their 2025 paper gives a new reading of a quantity called Sibson mutual information. It links that quantity to alpha-leakage, which scores what an adversary can learn from one output. The result reframes a known measure as an average of small, local gains.

The authors build the average from the adversary's relative information gain at each single output event. They extend a notion called pointwise maximal leakage to cover the full range of the order parameter. Maximizing their new leakage measure leads to the Rényi divergence. Rényi capacity then reads as the worst-case leakage over both inputs and attacker choices. The paper also derives a condition for near-exact control of leakage. It suggests adapting a classic algorithm, the generalized Blahut-Arimoto method, to compute these quantities.
arxiv-2510-06822:
Sauvik Roy, Nirmalya Ghosh, Ayan Banerjee, and Subhasish Dutta Gupta ask whether structured light beams can be absorbed perfectly. Their 2025 paper revisits critical coupling, a design trick for total absorption in layered materials. Most theory treats light as a simple scalar wave. Real beams carry polarization and sometimes a twist called orbital angular momentum.

The team rebuilt the theory with a full vector treatment of the beams. They tested Gaussian beams and twisted Laguerre-Gaussian beams on a metal-dielectric layered film. Beams arrived both straight on and at an angle. At straight incidence, reflected and transmitted light dropped sharply in their model. Angled beams absorbed less well, because the bouncing components no longer overlap properly. Complete absorption stayed out of reach in this setup, though. The study exposes a real design limit for absorbers. It also gives engineers a realistic model for structured-light devices.
arxiv-2510-07322:
Mohapatra presents AgroTrack, a low-power tracking system that keeps watch over free-range cattle where phone service is weak. The 2025 paper builds on LoRa radio, which trades speed for very long range and tiny batteries. Collars carry position, motion, and temperature sensors. Data hops to gateways and then to a cloud platform for maps, alerts, and analysis. Learning models on top flag likely illness and odd behavior, turning tracking into decision support for farmers.

A field trial ran fifteen cattle over thirty acres of grazing land. Signals traveled up to six and a half kilometers with nearly all packets arriving. Collars lasted about twenty-eight days per charge. Simulations pushed the design to hundreds of animals while keeping losses low. The system recovered most data even when four gateways failed at once. For rural herders, such cheap, sturdy monitoring could cut losses from straying and sickness.
arxiv-2510-07522:
Zhang, Gould, Barsukova, and Rechtsman observe Airy resonances inside a slab of silicon drilled with a graded pattern of holes. Their 2025 paper imports a quantum classic into photonics. Airy functions describe a bouncing quantum ball in a linear potential, and Airy light beams famously bend as they travel and heal around obstacles. The team's photonic crystal varies its hole spacing linearly across the slab. That gradient plays the role of the linear potential. The electromagnetic problem maps onto a two-dimensional Schrödinger equation with a twist the authors call a superpotential: the effective mass is complex, because light leaks out of the slab as it propagates.

That non-Hermitian twist fundamentally reshapes how the resonances respond collectively. Measurements track the bending lobes of the resonances across the crystal. The work extends Airy physics from free-space beams to resonances trapped inside a structured material.
arxiv-2510-07722:
Standish wrote this 2025 paper on how to measure the complexity of a graph. Information-based complexity scores an object by the descriptions that pick it out. For graphs, Standish built such a measure from their links, treating symmetric graphs as the same. A rival measure, star complexity, counts the union and intersection steps needed to build a graph from basic stars. He asks whether the two measures track each other.

He built graphs with ten and twenty-two vertices up to a set star complexity. A star-linked variant of his measure correlated strongly with star complexity there. He tested an upper bound for star complexity on random graphs with a thousand vertices. That bound related strongly to his information measure. The evidence suggests both measures capture the same property for most graphs. Standish speculates that other graph complexity measures may join the same family.
arxiv-2510-07822:
Agarwal, Pamnani, and Hakkani-Tur wrote this 2025 paper on machine unlearning for large language models. Models memorize sensitive text, and unlearning should erase chosen information. Standard optimizer methods forget the target but also damage general skill. The authors trace the damage to updates spread across the network. Their method, SIMU, narrows the update to only the neurons that carry the unwanted information.

SIMU first identifies the critical neurons with strong influence on the forget set. A second-order unlearning step then rewrites only those neurons. Across evaluations, SIMU matched rivals at removing targeted content. It substantially beat them at keeping the model's original knowledge and utility. The authors frame unlearning as a constrained optimization problem with a retain set and a forget set. Surgical updates, they argue, resolve the usual tug between forgetting and competence. That balance matters for privacy and copyright compliance in models.
arxiv-2510-07922:
Rangwala, Azzedin, Sinnott, and Buyya wrote this 2025 paper on protecting decentralized federated learning from malicious clients. In this training style, peers exchange model updates with neighbors and no server supervises. Byzantine clients can poison the process with corrupt updates. Standard defenses compare full model vectors between neighbors, which costs enormous bandwidth at scale. The authors propose screening neighbors with tiny sketches instead of full models.

Their framework, SketchGuard, compresses each model into a small Count Sketch fingerprint for similarity checks. Full models are fetched only from neighbors who pass the screening. Theory shows the sketching keeps resilience, with convergence guarantees. Experiments across datasets, network shapes, and attacks matched leading defenses on robustness. Error rates shifted by a fraction of a point. Computation time fell by up to eighty-two percent, and communication overhead dropped by half or more.
arxiv-2510-08322:
Chi-Kwong Li and Sushil Singla join Douglas Farenick in analyzing small operator systems through their matrix ranges in a 2025 arXiv paper. Operator systems are linear spaces of operators closed under adjoints, central to quantum theory. For a tuple of elements in a C-star algebra, they study the span of the tuple, its adjoints, and the identity. The C-star envelope is the smallest full algebra that this span generates.

The authors link operator traits of the tuple to system traits of its span. They show the matrix range of the tuple matches the matrix state space of the system. This match is a homeomorphism that respects the matrix-affine structure of both sets. Using this geometry, they study boundary representations and traits like nuclearity and lifting. The approach also clarifies the Smith-Ward property in operator theory.
arxiv-2510-08422:
Glen Kiely and co-authors add trajectory-aware energy loss to ion range simulations in a 2025 arXiv paper. Fast ions slow down in materials through nuclear and electronic interactions. In channeling geometries, where ions travel along crystal channels, stopping drops and ions dive deeper. Range predictions therefore need models that follow each ion's actual path.

The team implemented a recent electron-density-based loss model inside the MDRANGE simulation code. The model stems from real-time quantum simulations of explicit ion trajectories, compressed into a fitted function. MDRANGE runs molecular dynamics, tracking atoms as they move and collide over time. Their results show accurate trajectory-dependent range profiles can be simulated with well-fitted versions of the model. The method also lets measured ion ranges validate the fitted loss functions. Full quantum simulations could never reach those system sizes directly.
arxiv-2510-08722:
Mohammad Alkhalefi, Georgios Leontidis, and Mingjun Zhong improve self-supervised image learning with semantic pairs in a 2025 arXiv paper. Instance discrimination treats each image as its own class, training on two transformed views of the same picture. Handcrafted transformations like cropping and color jitter teach useful invariance, but cannot cover real-world variation. Models may then generalize poorly to new data sets and tasks.

Semantic pairs, two different images from the same category, expose the model to genuine scene diversity instead. The authors provide the technical foundation for using such pairs in training. They construct a new data set for the purpose and run an empirical study of the effect. Incorporating semantic pairs mitigated the limited transformation coverage problem measurably. Representations became more generalizable across unseen data and downstream tasks, they report. The work argues real variation beats synthetic augmentation variety.
arxiv-2510-09822:
Weiqing Luo, Zhen Tan, Yifan Li, Xinyu Zhao, Kwonjoon Lee, Behzad Dariush, and Tianlong Chen ask what image resolution a vision-language model actually wants in a 2025 arXiv paper. Real applications need different levels of perceptual detail, yet most models, LLaVA among them, assume one fixed input resolution for every task, which costs accuracy.

The authors first investigate the resolution preferences of many vision-language tasks. Preference correlates with image complexity and with how much the model's uncertainty varies across resolutions. From those two factors they derive an empirical formula that picks the optimal resolution for a given task. They then propose a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that stretches a pretrained model's visual input to that optimal resolution. Experiments across varied vision-language tasks validate the method. The work treats resolution as a task-dependent choice to optimise, rather than a fixed setting inherited from pretraining.
arxiv-2510-10222:
de la Casa and a large team catalog starburst galaxies in the Hydra I cluster in this 2025 arXiv paper in astronomy. Starbursts are galaxies forming stars at an intense rate. Studying how environment drives star formation and its shutdown needs large samples across a wide mass range.

The team presents a new catalog of 196 galaxies in the nearby Hydra I cluster, reaching out to about 1.75 times the cluster's characteristic radius. It combines broad-band imaging in five filters with narrowband hydrogen-alpha measurements, which trace current star formation. With masses and star formation rates for each galaxy, the catalog supports tests of how cluster life triggers or quenches bursts.
arxiv-2510-10422:
Jyotirmay Nag Setu, Kevin Desai, and John Quarles classify cybersickness severity from VR gameplay video in this 2025 arXiv paper on virtual reality. VR use is growing in healthcare, education, and entertainment, but cybersickness, a motion-sickness-like reaction, still blocks wider adoption. Measuring its severity usually needs user reports or special sensors.

The authors instead read the gameplay video itself, using transfer learning and temporal modeling. A model pretrained on general video is adapted to spot patterns linked to sickness, and temporal modeling tracks how those patterns evolve. Video-based scoring could flag sickness-inducing content automatically. Developers could then fix scenes before players feel ill, using footage they already record in testing.
arxiv-2510-10622:
Kaito Ohtani and four co-authors optimize the wall thickness pattern of an advanced heat exchanger, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The geometry is a triply periodic minimal surface, a smoothly repeating structure with continuous flow paths and a high surface area to volume ratio. Such structures promise high performance heat exchange. Letting the wall thickness vary across the structure may improve it further, but testing designs by full simulation is costly.

Their method uses an effective porous media model, based on homogenization, to predict performance accurately at far lower cost. They apply it to a gyroid two fluid heat exchanger. Full scale simulations of the optimized design then showed a 12.2 percent improvement in the performance evaluation criterion over a uniform thickness design. The gain came mainly from graded walls directing more flow toward the core ends and evening out velocities, boosting heat transfer there.
arxiv-2510-10822:
Clemence Mottez and four co-authors tackle demographic bias in AI diagnosis from chest X-rays, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Deep learning models can improve diagnostic accuracy, but performance often varies across sex, age, and race groups, risking wider healthcare disparities. The team builds a detection and mitigation framework. They extend a CNN-XGBoost pipeline to multi label classification and evaluate it across four medical conditions.

Their key move is simple: replace the neural network's final layer with a gradient boosting classifier. This improved fairness across subgroups while maintaining or improving overall predictive performance. The trick worked across different backbones, including DenseNet-121 and ResNet-50, confirming a model agnostic design. Against mitigation methods such as adversarial training, reweighting, and augmentation, it cut bias competitively at a fraction of the compute cost. Combining the adapter with active learning gave the largest bias reduction, on both the CheXpert and MIMIC datasets.
arxiv-2510-11022:
Shuren Zhou and Pengjie Zhang propose timing cosmic radio flashes to weigh gravity itself, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A key test of gravity compares the Weyl potential, which bends light, with the matter overdensity. Their ratio defines an effective gravitational constant for light. Measuring it needs an unbiased proxy for matter density, which has been missing. The team shows the dispersion measure of localized fast radio bursts can serve as that proxy, within a framework respecting the weak equivalence principle.

They design an estimator combining burst dispersion measures with galaxy weak lensing cross correlations. With a conservative scale cut, the measurement could reach roughly ten percent precision per redshift bin out to redshift one, given on the order of a hundred thousand localized bursts. The main systematic error, from how electrons cluster, sits near five percent and can shrink toward one percent at large scales.
arxiv-2510-11122:
Online shoppers often search with rare or fast-changing terms that a model cannot judge from memory alone. Tingqiao Xu and co-authors present DyKnow-RAG in this 2025 arXiv paper, a system that adds context such as reviews and product encyclopedias to e-commerce search. The catch is that this context is noisy, full of promotional wording and clutter, with no time to clean it first.

DyKnow-RAG trains the model with reinforcement learning, comparing groups of rollouts produced with and without the extra context. A scaling step reweights training by which group answered each query more correctly, teaching the model when to trust context and when to ignore it. The system needs only one pass at serving time, so it fits production latency limits. It beat supervised and other reinforcement baselines offline, improved key business metrics in A/B tests on Taobao traffic, and now serves live traffic.
arxiv-2510-11222:
Classifying the moral tone of social media posts gets harder when a model trained on one platform is used on another. Battemuulen Naranbat and co-authors study fairness in that cross-domain setting in a 2025 arXiv paper. They evaluate BERT and DistilBERT as multi-label moral sentiment classifiers on Twitter and Reddit corpora built around moral foundations theory.

Transfer proved strongly asymmetric: moving from Twitter to Reddit cut the micro-F1 score by 14.9 percent, while the reverse direction cost only 1.5 percent in the same experiments reported here. Per-label analysis exposed fairness violations hidden by the averages, worst for the authority label. The authors introduce a Moral Fairness Consistency metric that tracks how stably each moral foundation is detected across domains. The metric correlated perfectly and negatively with demographic parity difference, loyalty was the most consistent label, and authority the least.
arxiv-2510-11422:
Writing conductive structures inside diamond with ultrafast laser pulses is powerful, but checking what the laser made usually requires destroying the sample or leaving the fabrication line. Xingrui Cheng and co-authors develop a live monitoring workflow in this 2025 arXiv optics paper. Their tool is Raman microspectroscopy, which reads a material's vibrational fingerprint from scattered light without damaging it, applied while laser writing proceeds.

The workflow is designed to work for any host material: it screens candidate spectral indicators with drift-resistant, self-scaling metrics and uses label-free hyperspectral unmixing where needed. In diamond, hyperspectral maps and electrical tests showed that depletion of the diamond spectral line is a monotonic, robust predictor of the structure's electrical resistance. Against expectation, it beat the carbon-bond measures usually assumed best. A single narrowband measurement channel at that marker therefore gives real-time feedback without full spectra, enabling in-line quality control.
arxiv-2510-11522:
Languages diversify even though talk favors one shared tongue, and similar splits into distinct groups appear across culture. Riz Noronha and Kunihiko Kaneko propose a minimal mechanism for that diversification in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their agents sit on a lattice, and evolve under a fitness that rewards local cooperation but also global difference.

In the simulations, clusters of diverse communities self-organize, with fitness equalized along the boundaries between communities, and the numbers and sizes of the communities are robust to parameter changes. The system passes through successive transitions between quasi-stationary states, each triggered by a new community emerging on a boundary. The authors present the model as an abstract framework. It shows how the tension between sharing information locally and keeping it distinct globally can generate a stable diversity of groups.
arxiv-2510-11622:
How many smooth structures can one topological manifold carry? In high dimensions the answer is governed by the space TOP/O, whose homotopy groups are finite, which is why only a finite number of smoothings exist. Oliver H. Wang studies the symmetry-respecting version of that classification in this 2025 arXiv algebraic topology paper. When a compact group acts on the manifold, maps into TOP/O that respect the action sort the smoothings.

Wang computes the equivariant homotopy groups of TOP/O for the cyclic group of prime order, over the rational numbers. The nonequivariant backdrop is classical: Kirby and Siebenmann showed TOP/O sorts smooth structures, Kervaire and Milnor gave the finite count of homotopy sphere groups. The rational triviality of TOP/O implies that the rational Pontryagin classes are topological invariants. That is Novikov's theorem. Wang's result extends that picture to manifolds with a cyclic symmetry.
arxiv-2510-11722:
Haruhiko Yoshioka and three colleagues present eye2vec, a tool for studying how programmers read code. Their paper appeared at the 2025 Symposium on Eye Tracking Research and Applications in Tokyo. Eye-tracking studies usually force researchers to choose targets in advance, such as words, lines, or code blocks. Different choices change the results, and the work stays largely manual.

eye2vec instead turns each pair of consecutive fixations into a transition between syntactic elements, the grammatical parts of code. It encodes those transitions as distributed representations, meaning lists of numbers that capture meaning through context. Researchers can then measure how similar two comprehension patterns are by distance in that number space. The representations also support label prediction, such as estimating a developer's skill in a language or their level of understanding. The tool accepts only eye movement data, keeping it apart from personal information.
arxiv-2510-11822:
Suryaansh Jain and three colleagues document a flattering flaw in AI judges. Developers increasingly use large language models to grade other models, since human grading is slow and costly. The team's 2025 arXiv paper shows these judges are far too agreeable. They recognize valid outputs over ninety-six percent of the time. Yet they spot invalid outputs less than twenty-five percent of the time.

That lopsidedness inflates reliability scores, and majority voting does not fix it. The authors propose an optimal minority-veto rule, in which a minority of negative verdicts can overrule the crowd. For still higher precision, they fit a regression that models each validator's bias from a small set of human-graded examples. On a code feedback task covering 366 high-school Python programs, the regression cut the maximum error to just over one percent. That is twice as good as the best ensemble of fourteen leading models.
arxiv-2510-12022:
Liang-Liang Sun and five co-authors build tools to question quantum devices that refuse to play along. In Bell tests and prepare-and-measure tests, researchers see only correlations between settings and outcomes. Inferring what states and measurements produced them is a non-convex puzzle, the hard kind with many local traps. Their 2025 arXiv paper proposes a method built for qubit systems, the two-level workhorses of quantum information.

The heart is a test drawn from an uncertainty rule made for qubits. It captures the non-convex shape of the possible correlation set, a shape linear methods miss. Given an observed correlation, the method can refer back to candidate readings and states, at times pinning them down to one answer. The inferred information also strengthens entanglement detection in the NPA hierarchy: some local-looking correlations can certify entanglement.
arxiv-2510-12122:
Tomoki Morokuma and a large team catch a quasar in the act of starving. Comparing Sloan survey images with newer Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam data across thirty thousand quasars, they found one, at redshift one point seven six seven, fading dramatically. Their 2025 arXiv paper documents a possible shutdown of mass accretion onto its central black hole.

Follow-up imaging and spectroscopy with major telescopes, combined with seventy years of archival data, trace the decline. The active nucleus faded by a factor of about fifty from the early two-thousands to 2023. Its Eddington ratio, accretion power relative to the theoretical maximum, collapsed from about zero point four to zero point zero zero eight. Careful fitting of the energy distribution across epochs, consistent with the spectra, blames a genuine drop in accretion rate rather than passing dust. This one appears to be switching off entirely.
arxiv-2510-12422:
Zuo and a large team present VideoLucy, a framework that answers questions about very long videos by searching its memory from coarse to fine, in a 2025 arXiv computer vision paper. Agent based systems using language models can retrieve and integrate key information from long videos, but they usually reason frame by frame and sample frames sparsely, which risks missing crucial details.

VideoLucy mimics human recollection with a hierarchical memory whose levels define how much detail and how much time span each memory covers. An agent based backtracking mechanism repeatedly mines deeper, question relevant memories until enough evidence exists for a confident answer. This preserves temporal context across consecutive frames while keeping fine details reachable. The authors also introduce EgoMem, a benchmark for understanding complex events and fine grained detail in extremely long videos. Built on open source models, VideoLucy beat leading methods on several benchmarks, even surpassing recent proprietary systems.
arxiv-2510-12522:
Lins organizes the competing notions of irreducibility for topical maps and shows how to check them with SAT solvers, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics note. Topical maps are a nonlinear extension of nonnegative matrices. Several analogues of irreducibility have been proposed for these maps. Irreducibility means a matrix cannot be split into separate blocks. Each one guarantees eigenvectors with all entries positive.

The note arranges the notions in order, showing which are stronger and when types coincide. It then turns to checking. Certain of these cases can be rephrased as Boolean satisfiability problems, which SAT solvers can check. That gives a practical route to proving such eigenvectors exist when the dimension is large and checking by eye is hopeless. Examples range across game theory operators, population models, and the Sinkhorn Knopp algorithm used in balancing.
arxiv-2510-12722:
El-Naggar, Kuribayashi, and Briscoe test which made up word orders let language models generalize to longer sentences than they trained on, in a 2025 arXiv linguistics paper. Whether models carry inductive biases favoring common grammatical patterns over rare ones has been studied with made up languages. Earlier systems missed attested constructions such as unbounded dependencies.

The authors rebuild the made up languages using generalized categorial grammar, which covers mildly context aware structures found in real languages. Their evaluation targets length generalization: processing unseen, longer test sentences well. With languages that better mirror natural grammar, the results sharpen. Plausible word orders, the orders common across the world's tongues, tend to be easier for models to stretch productively. Implausible orders resist it even after similar training. The work links a model's learning biases to the same pressures thought to shape human language.
arxiv-2510-13222:
Grant and Jones forecast a rare chance to fly through an interstellar comet's tail in this 2025 arXiv paper. Comet 3I/ATLAS is only the third known interstellar object to visit the solar system. In late 2025 it passes upstream of two spacecraft, ESA's Hera and NASA's Europa Clipper. Their paths may cross its ion tail, the stream of charged particles blown away from the comet.

The authors predict Europa Clipper could be immersed in the tail for about a week spanning late October into early November 2025, with Hera possibly immersed during the preceding week. Immersion would let instruments sample an interstellar comet's ion tail directly for the first time. Characteristic solar wind changes are also expected. A magnetic draping structure wrapped around the comet may be identifiable in the measurements. The authors detail both as signatures to look for.
arxiv-2510-13622:
Thakare and Akugri try to give classic embedding methods the missing power to generate new data. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies nonlinear dimensionality reduction tools like t-SNE, Isomap, and LLE. These methods compress high-dimensional data into clear low-dimensional pictures. But the map runs one way only: nothing leads back to the original space.

The authors build neural decoders that invert embeddings from the leading methods. For the first time, those embeddings become two-way maps, they report. They also run a diffusion generative process directly inside the learned embedding spaces. Tests on the CelebA face dataset compare reconstruction and sample quality against autoencoders. The decoders do reconstruct data, yet end-to-end autoencoders still do it better. Diffusion inside the sparse embeddings produced poor samples, a warning the authors highlight.
arxiv-2510-13722:
Saccardi and a large team benchmark generative models that sharpen coarse climate data, probing whether their output respects physics. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies downscaling, which turns rough weather fields into kilometre-scale detail. Standard machine learning scores can flatter models that break basic atmospheric rules. The team adds physics-inspired diagnostics and tests travel to new regions.

Models like CorrDiff score well when trained and tested on central Europe. Moved to Iberia, Morocco, or Scandinavia, their skill drops off sharply. Derived quantities such as divergence and vorticity, computed from predicted winds, come out wrong too. Those failures appear even inside the training region, not just abroad. The problem is physical consistency, not only geographic reach, the authors conclude. A simple fix helps: a loss term matching the power spectrum of real fields. It improved generalization by forcing small-scale structure to look right.
arxiv-2510-14222:
Benjamín Castro and co-authors introduce the Information Teacher, a method for judging whether a learned regression model is truly the best possible, without knowing the ground truth, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Regression assessment is hard because the data-generating mechanism is inaccessible in practice, so ordinary test metrics cannot certify that a model has reached optimality.

Their framework estimates the Shannon mutual information, a measure of shared information, between the input variables and the model's residuals, the errors it leaves behind. If the residuals carry information about the inputs, the model has left learnable structure unexploited; if they share none, the model is optimal for a broad class of additive noise models. Experiments confirm the Information Teacher detects global optimality, agreeing with the condition of zero estimation error against the inaccessible model. The authors offer it as a principled surrogate for ground-truth assessment, replacing metrics.
arxiv-2510-14522:
In a 2025 arXiv paper, Lamprou and co-authors introduce Lexo, a tool meant to stop hidden attacks inside open source software parts. Such attacks keep a part working as users expect. Yet they add secret harmful behavior that wakes up only in a chosen target setting. Rewriting a part by hand is slow, so the authors ask whether a clean version can be rebuilt automatically.

Lexo first probes a suspect part with many inputs and records what it does. That builds a picture of its visible behavior. Guided by several large language models, plus checks for correctness and coverage, it then writes a fresh version. The new version copies the behavior without the hidden code. In tests on more than one hundred real packages, including known stealthy attacks, Lexo removed the malicious code. The packages kept working, and each rebuild took under one hundred seconds on average.
arxiv-2510-14722:
Jia and co-authors show, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a new way to detect a subtle obstruction in quantum field theory called the 't Hooft anomaly. The anomaly concerns continuous flavor symmetries, the symmetries that rotate one particle type into another. Its presence decides, among other things, whether the symmetry can be gauged. The authors detect it not from fields directly, but from networks of topological defects, the lines and surfaces that implement the symmetry inside the theory.

Rearranging these defect webs turns out to expose the anomaly. In two dimensions the relevant moves are the F-moves of defect lines. By trading the defects for flat background gauge fields, the authors characterize the anomaly with cohomological data of the symmetry group. The cohomology of Lie groups with discrete topology plays the central role. A surprise falls out: for flat gauging, the mathematics naturally produces an extra dimension.
arxiv-2510-14922:
Nurfidausi, Mancini, and Torroni present TRI-DEP, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a study comparing ways to detect depression from three signals: brain waves, speech, and text. Depression is common, yet automatic detection stays hard. Multimodal systems promise more than any single signal, but earlier studies compared choices inconsistently and evaluated them under mismatched protocols, so their lessons were murky.

The team explored design choices across EEG recordings, speech, and text. They weighed handcrafted features against pre-trained embeddings. They tested different neural encoders. And they ran single-signal, paired, and three-signal configurations, all under subject-independent splits, so no person appears in both training and test data. Three findings stood out. Using all three together improved accuracy. Pre-trained embeddings beat handcrafted features. And well-designed trimodal models reached state-of-the-art performance. The authors frame the study as groundwork for future research in this area.
arxiv-2510-15122:
François Ezard, Can Umut Ileri, and Jérémie Decouchant target a bottleneck that slows busy blockchains in their 2025 arXiv paper. Once consensus got faster, executing transactions became the limiting step, especially when many transactions touch the same data. Existing parallel engines, whether optimistic or pessimistic about conflicts, lose speed badly under that heavy contention.

Their engine, NEMO, blends optimistic execution with an object-based data model and four targeted improvements. A greedy commit rule fast-tracks transactions that use only their own objects, while partial read and write hints steer scheduling before conflicts happen. A priority scheduler also favors transactions that unblock others waiting behind them. In simulated runs with sixteen workers, NEMO's throughput beat the leading optimistic system by up to 42 percent and the pessimistic baseline by up to 61 percent.
arxiv-2510-15222:
Gabriel Nixon studies how a learner should keep making good choices while the world keeps changing underneath it, in this solo 2025 arXiv paper. The setting is sequential decision-making under distribution drift, where each round's data comes from a slowly shifting source. Nixon adds stress awareness: updates lean defensively against plausible bad shifts, with that caution fading or growing as conditions demand.

His method, built on mirror descent, a standard online optimization algorithm, tilts both belief updates and decisions by the same exponential factor, which he proves are two views of one operation. He defines measures of fragility, meaning worst-case extra loss within a bounded shift, and proves regret bounds at a square-root rate over time. A self-tuning version adjusts to unknown drift without set parameters.
arxiv-2510-15622:
Getting light from a fiber into a photonic chip efficiently is a basic bottleneck for optical computing. Shiang-Yu Huang and four colleagues design ultra-small couplers in this 2025 arXiv paper. They use topology optimization, letting algorithms shape the coupler freely, and add a bottom reflector underneath. Both a single-polarization and a dual-polarization grating coupler fit in fourteen micrometres square. The devices are built on silicon-on-insulator and accept standard fibers at normal incidence.

Measured peak efficiency reaches about minus zero point nine decibels for both coupler types. That sub-decibel loss sits in the telecom C-band used by fiber networks. Such compact, efficient couplers suit dense photonic circuits and quantum technologies.
arxiv-2510-15822:
Leah Bigwood and colleagues propose a benchmark in a 2025 paper. It tests how simulations model feedback from active galactic nuclei. These are the energetic black holes at galaxy centres. Feedback is a large uncertainty in cosmological simulations. Different recipes eject very different amounts of gas. The gas is expelled from galaxy groups and clusters.

The test uses a subtle microwave signal. The kinetic Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect is a shift in the cosmic microwave background. Moving ionised gas causes it. The signal directly senses the expelled gas. The authors present the first systematic study of this test. They combine galaxy data from the DESI survey. Microwave maps come from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope. The simulation families are confronted with both.
arxiv-2511-00122:
Ran Xu, Yupeng Qi, and Jingsen Feng present Engineering.ai, a platform where teams of AI engineers collaborate on computational design the way human specialist teams do. Human teams divide expertise across disciplines but pay heavily in time and coordination cost. Building on their earlier autonomous fluid dynamics engineer and an end-to-end fluid mechanics research system, they generalize toward multi-agent engineering teams.

Specialized AI agents complete respective tasks while communicating results and data to one another. Engineering readers get a vision of AI teamwork mirroring professional practice. Complex products are multidisciplinary by nature, so a team structure may scale AI engineering better than a single generalist agent.
arxiv-2511-00222:
Large language models often play fake users in training and tests for therapy, teaching, and chat tools. Marwa Abdulhai and five co-authors note a flaw: the fake user drifts, forgets its role, or clashes with what it said before. The team defines three checks for this drift, covering the prompt, line-to-line flow, and answers to direct questions.

They then use the checks as rewards in multi-turn reinforcement learning, training models to stay in role as a patient, a student, or a chat partner. Inconsistency dropped by more than half in their tests. The result is simulated users that stay coherent across a full conversation.
arxiv-2511-00422:
Isabella Habereder, Thomas Kneib, Isao Echizen, and Timo Spinde review statistical models for data that vary across both space and time. Such data appear everywhere, but earlier reviews stuck to single fields or model families. Following PRISMA guidelines, the team searched two databases for work from 2021 to 2025 and kept eighty-three publications that met their criteria.

They propose a classification scheme for model structures and map where each structure is used: epidemiology, ecology, public health, economics, and criminology lead the list. Hierarchical models dominate, and most models add components to capture space-time dependence, though preferred shapes differ by field. Research clusters in a few disciplines despite wider relevance, and reproducibility stays limited. The review invites cross-field comparison and more transparent practice.
arxiv-2511-00822:
Masroor Bashir, Pravabati Chingangbam, and Stephen Appleby recheck a claimed anomaly in the large scale structure of the universe. A standard test compares the motion implied by the cosmic microwave background with the uneven sky counts of distant quasars. An earlier study of the CatWISE2020 quasar catalog found a mismatch at very high significance.

The team reruns the test with careful simulations that include quasar clustering, the survey's depth pattern, and its exact sky coverage. The mismatch shrinks but does not vanish, landing near three and a half sigma rather than the earlier claim. They also show that fitting extra multipoles on a partial sky can bias the dipole estimate upward, a caution for future surveys.
arxiv-2511-01222:
Mengchu Zheng, Matteo Bonvini, and Zijian Guo relax a key assumption behind double machine learning. That is a popular method for estimating a low dimensional effect while flexible machine learning handles high dimensional nuisance parts. Textbook inference needs those nuisance estimates to converge fast enough that their error becomes negligible, which can be restrictive in nonparametric settings.

Their perturbed version injects randomness into the nuisance step, producing many perturbed models, each with its own estimate and confidence interval for the target. Perturbations that stray too far from the original estimate are filtered out, and the union of the retained intervals is reported. For Lasso based learners they show at least one perturbation lands close enough to the truth with high probability, giving valid coverage even when convergence is slower than the classical requirement.
arxiv-2511-01522:
Sophie Rosu reviews a precision tool for weighing what goes on inside massive stars: apsidal motion, the slow swivel of an eccentric binary orbit's long axis. The swivel rate depends on how each star's mass is spread between core and envelope. So measuring it over years of radial velocity and light curve data reveals a star's inner density profile.

Comparing measurements with standard models shows a stubborn gap: real stars look more centrally concentrated than models predict, though adding extra internal mixing closes much of the difference. Rosu also reports checks with the non-perturbative MoBiDiCT code. Those checks show the usual perturbative shortcut underestimates the motion in strongly distorted stars. That makes the need for enhanced mixing sharper still.
arxiv-2511-01622:
Anirban Bhaduri, Timothy De Deyn, Michal Hrbek, Pat Lank, and Kabeer Manali-Rahul report a negative result in homological algebra. That field studies derived categories. These package a geometric space's sheaves into a single algebraic object. Inside such a category, a t-structure is a way of splitting objects into positive and negative parts, much like truncating a sequence.

A t-structure is singly compactly generated when one compact object controls the whole splitting, a strong finiteness property often assumed or hoped for. The authors exhibit the first schemes, geometric spaces in algebraic geometry, whose standard t-structure on the derived category of quasi-coherent sheaves lacks this property. The counterexamples close off a plausible general expectation and mark where the theory's finiteness ends.
arxiv-2511-02122:
Xinyuan Song and Ziye Ma ask whether swapping the loss function can make a machine learning method tougher against bad noise. Their test problem is matrix sensing, recovering a matrix from incomplete measurements, where the standard mean squared error loss misbehaves under heavy-tailed or non-Gaussian noise. Their alternative loss comes from nonparametric regression: it estimates the density of the residuals with a kernel and maximises the estimated log-likelihood, coinciding with the usual loss when the noise is Gaussian.

The authors analyse how the new loss reshapes the optimisation landscape, bounding the restricted isometry constants at which spurious local minima vanish. Theory and experiments agree that the robust loss handles large noise well and stays stable across many noise distributions. The broader message is that robustness can sometimes be bought by changing the loss alone.
arxiv-2511-02222:
The Super-Kamiokande Collaboration, listing 248 authors, reports a hunt for the faint glow of neutrinos left over from every supernova that has ever exploded in the observable universe. This diffuse background has never been directly detected. The search uses the giant underground water detector in Japan. Since 2020 it has been loaded with small amounts of gadolinium to make neutron captures, the signature of the target neutrinos, easier to spot.

Combining 552 days of the first gadolinium phase with 404 days of the second, the analysis looks at neutrino energies above 9.3 MeV (million electron volts) and adds new machine-learning neutron detectors plus better background rejection. No notable excess over background appeared in the model-independent search, so the team set upper limits on the flux at ninety percent confidence. A spectral fit showed only a mild, roughly 1.2 standard deviation, tension with the no-signal hypothesis.
arxiv-2511-02922:
Yunhan Qiao, Md Istiak Hossain Shihab, Summit Haque, and Christopher Hundhausen ask whether an AI coding helper makes students faster without making them wiser. Fifteen graduate students did feature work in an unfamiliar codebase, with and without GitHub Copilot, in a within-subjects design. Their 2025 study separates task success from code comprehension, two things courses often treat as one.

With Copilot, students finished faster and more correctly, yet their overall comprehension did not improve, and speed gains did not track understanding gains. Students who understood more did behave differently: they checked and revised code in loops, moving from writing to viewing far more often. The authors urge courses to grade comprehension apart from correctness, and to teach students to inspect AI-written code closely.
arxiv-2511-03222:
Duncan Rocha and Isaac R Wang ask what else the planned MUonE experiment could find besides its main target. MUonE will scatter muons off electrons to measure a key constant with great care, hoping to clarify a puzzle about the muon. The same setup, the authors note, could also spot a new kind of light particle that lives briefly before decaying.

Such particles could appear in muon collisions and decay a few centimeters away into an electron pair, leaving a displaced point that MUonE tracks well. That reach covers ground that colliders and dump experiments have missed. The study maps the masses MUonE could probe, reaching up to roughly one hundred million electron volts in particle energy terms. It frames MUonE as a double-duty search tool.
arxiv-2511-03322: Guy Bouchitte and Minh Phan study least-area surfaces whose edges are free to slide, cast as a hard minimization task. Their aim is to certify best solutions by building a calibration field, a kind of proof-carrying flow. A Cheeger-style problem gives a natural upper bound on the best value. They solve that bound problem with a potential built from the cut locus, then compare it with the original problem in detail. Such proofs matter because they turn a guessed surface into a proven optimum.
arxiv-2511-03522:
Francois Delarue, Mattia Martini, and Giacomo Enrico Sodini build tools for equations on the space of chance laws. Such laws describe big crowds of linked parts in a mean-field limit. Their space grades smoothness with a Sobolev-style norm. That norm is tied to a Dirichlet-Ferguson law on a flat torus.

They prove that transport-diffusion and Hamilton-Jacobi equations there have one solution each. A linked particle system gives a chance-based view of those solutions. That view echoes the classic Kolmogorov link. They extend the work to semilinear cases. Mean-field control tasks are covered as well. The frame gives firm ground for work on flocking, games, and spread at crowd scale.
arxiv-2511-03722:
Penelope Azuelos shows that dropping one word, completeness, multiplies a classic uniqueness result into uncountably many counterexamples. For each branching number, exactly one complete real tree has every point branching that way. Real trees are branching spaces with a single path between any two points, used across geometry and phylogenetics.

When the branching number is at least three, Azuelos builds uncountably many uniform yet incomplete trees sharing that same branching at every point. Uniformity alone therefore cannot pin the tree down. The note is short but sharp: completeness carries the whole weight of the classic theorem.
