Such boundary cases teach mathematicians exactly which assumptions do the work.
arxiv-2511-03822:
Benjamin Braun and Antwon Park introduce graphical Hermite simplices, shapes built by perturbing a rectangular simplex under control of a directed graph. Their question concerns the Smith normal form of the matrix formed by a simplex's vertex vectors, which reveals the group structure of the associated cokernel.

Motivation comes from lattice simplices whose vertices shift slightly. Conditions on the graph and diagonal entries are given that force a single non-unit invariant factor, meaning a cyclic cokernel. Bounds on the invariant factors follow from path lengths in the directed graph. The results connect graph structure directly to algebraic invariants of these perturbed shapes.
arxiv-2511-03922:
Congzhe Yan, with Zhijun Jiang, Jinyang Ni, and Guoqing Chang listed in the arXiv record as a four-author byline in grouped form, studies chiral magnons in altermagnets at finite temperature. Magnons in these materials split by chirality even without spin-orbit coupling or an external field, a behaviour usually explained near zero temperature by alternating isotropic spin exchange.

Including magnon interactions, long-range anisotropic exchange can also create chiral splitting once temperature is finite. That second route competes with the first, strongly reshaping the splitting as temperature changes. The contest links closely to spin fluctuations and can reverse the spin current driven by band splitting, reshaping how altermagnet excitations should be understood away from zero temperature.
arxiv-2511-04122:
Adiba Amira Siddiqa, Sayed Shafaat Mahmud, and Cosmin Ilie train a neural network to find dark star candidates from spectroscopy, in the second part of a series on these objects. Dark stars would be early stars powered by dark matter annihilation rather than fusion, offering a rare observational handle on dark matter itself.

A feedforward network learned from synthetic dark star spectra targets data from the James Webb Space Telescope's NIRSpec instrument. Applied to real data, the network reconfirmed four recently proposed supermassive dark star candidates, whose spectra matched the synthetic type. Compared with Monte Carlo parameter estimation, the network approach promises far faster screening of large spectroscopic datasets for these rare candidates.
arxiv-2511-04522:
Daniel Mayfrank and four colleagues train Koopman models end to end for controlling an air separation unit. The plant makes nitrogen, and its demand response case tests savings under shifting needs. Only a few realistically measurable plant variables are assumed visible.

Reinforcement learning tunes the surrogate model for control performance directly. A model trained by plain identification saved a little money but often broke constraints. The new method delivers similar savings while respecting the limits far better. Scaling the approach from a small test to a large plant model suggests it can serve real process control.
arxiv-2511-04722:
Qianyang Li leads six authors with AWEMixer, a network for long-term forecasting in sensor networks. Internet-of-things signals shift over time and carry patterns at many scales. Errors also pile up as forecasts reach farther ahead.

Plain time-domain methods miss global rhythm, while Fourier views can blur brief events. AWEMixer's Frequency Router uses global periodicity to weight local wavelet bands adaptively. A Coherent Gated Fusion Block then merges those bands into the forecast. Mixing global rhythm with local detail targets sensor streams where both slow cycles and sudden spikes matter for planning.
arxiv-2511-05022:
Charles Melvin and Rich Nguyen test PriorityFresh, a cache rule for offline alert systems, inside their AWARE test setting. When links are weak or cut, an alert device must choose which warnings to keep and show first.

PriorityFresh ranks alerts by how useful they are for action, not just by age or size. Tests in the simulation show gains on that action-first score with no loss in speed or thrift. A split forecasting model only made the test alert streams; it played no part at all in cache or push choices for the live public warnings.
arxiv-2511-05222:
Kousuke Nakano, Stefano Battaglia, and Jürg Hutter speed up atomic force estimates in variational Monte Carlo, a top method for solving the many-body Schrödinger equation on parallel machines. Forces that match the energy surface are key for dynamics, but cheap, unbiased force methods were lacking.

Their Lagrangian trick gives unbiased forces at far lower cost. That opens large systems and big data sets to force-based study in this framework. The work keeps the stochastic form that makes the method scale, while it fixes a long-standing gap for motion and structure work.
arxiv-2511-05322:
Wanlin Li and co-authors prove that the Jacobians of a family of genus-four curves have basic reduction at infinitely many primes. The result extends a classic line: Elkies showed an elliptic curve over a number field with a real place has supersingular reduction at endless primes.

Baba and Granath had pushed that line to genus two with terms on the endomorphism ring. Here the curves carry a symmetry of order five. The team studies the complex uniformization of a Deligne-Mumford style space to get the result, a step for the arithmetic of higher-genus curves.
arxiv-2511-05422:
Andreas Gross and co-authors propose a tropical analogue of a reductive group, built from a Weyl group plus the tropical form of a fixed maximal torus. Tropical geometry swaps sums and products for min-plus rules, which turns curved shapes into piecewise linear ones that are easier to sort.

For the classic groups and for G2, their objects look like tropical matrix groups. With them, they define principal bundles on metric graphs and show how those bundles arise from line bundles on covers with symmetry. A main result ties the skeleton of a moduli space to that tropical picture.
arxiv-2511-05622:
Nicholas Babey and co-authors ground action recognition in the physical layout of a scene rather than surface patterns alone. Models that read plain video often learn shallow links between pixels and action labels. They then fail in cluttered scenes where people are partly hidden.

The proposed model fuses two signals. One comes from a predictive video model that captures how the world evolves. The other is explicit three-dimensional pose data that tolerates occlusion. Tested on a general action benchmark and a high-occlusion one, the fused model beat three baselines, with the clearest edge in complex, occluded scenes. The authors argue recognition needs spatial understanding, not just pattern matching.
arxiv-2511-05722:
Zheng Du and co-authors introduce OckBench, a benchmark that grades language models on how many tokens they spend, not just on whether they are right. Two models can solve the same problem with the same accuracy while one uses up to five times as many tokens. That gap drives up serving cost and wait time, yet standard tests ignore it.

OckBench measures accuracy and token efficiency together across reasoning and coding tasks. The authors find efficiency largely unoptimized in current models. Their title invokes Occam's razor: tokens, like assumptions, should not be multiplied beyond need. They argue the field should shift how it evaluates models, and they publish the benchmark for others to use.
arxiv-2511-06022:
Thomas Jannaud and Henrik Latter argue that a popular quality check for disk simulations does not prove what it claims. The magnetorotational instability drives turbulence in accretion disks and is usually studied with ideal fluid simulations. A simulation counts as converged if a quality factor, the ratio of a magnetic length to cell size, clears a threshold.

The authors test the factor on simulations known to be unconverged and find their scores pass easily. They also attack the linear theory behind the factor: it assumes a steady vertical field, while real simulations have fields that vary fast and cross zero. In such fields the instability can grow at tiny scales the factor ignores. They suggest a modified factor that fixes some flaws.
arxiv-2511-06222:
Yue Huang, Xiangqi Wang, and Xiangliang Zhang propose a stricter order of goals for aligning large language models. In sensitive areas like self-harm, law, or medicine, a model must be trustworthy before it tries to be helpful, since the two aims often clash. Their paradigm, priority alignment, makes helpfulness count only after safety thresholds are met.

Their framework, Self-Priority Alignment, needs no human labels. The model drafts varied responses, judges and refines them itself, and cleans the set with a dual-criterion filter. Ordered preference pairs then fine-tune the model with a loss that weights confident, clear-cut decisions most. Benchmarks show helpfulness gains without safety losses, ahead of strong baselines.
arxiv-2511-06322:
N. V. Peskov models how a catalyst ingredient spreads inside a porous support bead while it dries. Making supported catalysts starts by soaking a porous sphere in a solution of the active precursor, then drying it so the material precipitates onto the pore walls. Where the deposit lands, across the bead and across pore sizes, strongly affects catalyst performance and lifetime.

The paper presents a mathematical model that simulates that precipitation pattern during drying. Worked examples show how changing key parameters reshapes the distribution through the bead's volume and through pores of different sizes. Such guidance helps engineers steer deposits toward layouts that serve industrial reactors better.
arxiv-2511-06422:
Tao Liu, Kan Ren, and Qian Chen locate drones by matching their camera views against satellite imagery. Satellite navigation signals can be blocked or absent, leaving cross-view image retrieval as a fallback. Slanted drone photos and top-down satellite maps differ hugely in geometry and appearance, which makes matching them hard.

Their framework, DiffusionUavLoc, first renders fake satellite views from drone images as structural prompts, with no training needed for that step. A text-free diffusion model then fuses those cues into features that shrug off viewpoint change. On two public benchmarks the method performed competitively, standing out on the satellite-to-drone direction of one of them.
arxiv-2511-06622:
Hojin Chu, Shinya Fujita, Boram Park, and Homoon Ryu prove that highly connected triangle-free graphs can spare a copy of any small tree without losing connectivity. Mader conjectured a broad statement of this kind in 2012, and a bipartite cousin was proposed a decade later. Removing a tree's vertices usually threatens the graph's connectivity, so degree conditions must compensate.

For any tree on a given number of vertices, a sufficiently connected triangle-free graph with a stated minimum degree contains that tree while the rest stays equally connected. The degree bound given is twice the connectivity plus about three times the tree size. Sharper versions follow for bipartite graphs and for graphs whose shortest cycles run longer.
arxiv-2511-06822:
Andrea Marchese surveys recent progress on the flat chain conjecture, an open problem in geometric measure theory. The conjecture says that two ways of describing generalized surfaces in Euclidean space, metric currents and flat chains with finite mass, actually coincide. Marchese methods the question through partial differential equations.

The survey explains recent work showing the conjecture is equivalent to a Lipschitz regularity estimate for a certain equation. That equivalence matters because it turns a question about abstract geometric objects into a concrete analytic estimate that PDE methods can attack. Readers get a map of where the problem stands and which results now carry its weight.
arxiv-2511-07122:
Changyue Shi and eight co-authors reconstruct moving three-dimensional scenes from only a handful of frames. Dynamic Gaussian splatting renders photorealistic 4D scenes, but it assumes dense video; under equipment constraints, real captures are often sparse. The authors observe that current methods fail in sparse settings in both the canonical scene and its deformation over time, especially in texture-rich areas. They aim both fixes at exactly those areas.

A texture-aware deformation regularization aligns depth so Gaussians move correctly, while texture-aware canonical optimization injects texture-based noise into the fitting of the base scene. On the NeRF-Synthetic, HyperNeRF, and NeRF-DS benchmarks plus a new iPhone-4D dataset, Sparse4DGS beat current dynamic and few-shot tools when given sparse frames, opening dynamic reconstruction to casual capture conditions.
arxiv-2511-07222:
JiaKui Hu and eight co-authors build a single model that understands and generates three-dimensional scenes from multiple photographs. Omni-View tests the principle that creation facilitates understanding: a model that can synthesize new views and estimate geometry should comprehend scenes more deeply. It combines an understanding model with a texture module for appearance synthesis and a geometry module supplying explicit geometric constraints, trained in two stages.

The parts interact synergistically, so scene question answering benefits from the same representations that render novel views. On the VSI-Bench benchmark of spatial understanding, Omni-View scored 55.4, a state-of-the-art result ahead of specialized 3D understanding models, while also performing strongly at novel view synthesis and scene creation. Code and pre-trained models are open-sourced, making the unified design available for further research.
arxiv-2511-07422:
Running huge language models now costs more effort than training them, argue Madabattula Rajesh Kumar and colleagues. Their survey traces serving systems from the Transformer breakthrough to models with trillions of parameters. Memory bandwidth, speed, and delay limits now dominate design choices.

The authors explain why splitting inference into separate stages helps. The compute-heavy prefill stage, which reads the prompt, is split from the memory-heavy decode stage, which writes the reply. Each part can then scale on its own hardware. Framed as balancing delay, throughput, and cost, disaggregation becomes a classic distributed systems problem with practical payoffs.
arxiv-2511-07522:
Gökhan Yücel and colleagues calibrate a correction astronomers need to turn starlight into total star power. Bolometric corrections adjust visible brightness for light emitted outside the visible band. Their method extracts those corrections straight from sharp, high-quality spectra of one hundred twenty eight stars.

Known temperatures anchor the sample, and standard filter profiles define the visible share. Corrections come out accurate to a few thousandths of a magnitude, with filter choice shifting results only slightly. Combining measured light ratios with classical values pins down zero-point constants. Precise constants matter because stellar luminosities feed distance scales, ages, and exoplanet host studies.
arxiv-2511-07622:
William Adkisson and Omer Ben Neria probe set theory where the axiom of choice fails yet huge cardinals remain. Above a rank Berkeley cardinal, Gabriel Goldberg showed most regular cardinals carry well-founded uniform ultrafilters. What strength those ultrafilters truly witness was unclear.

Bounds on that strength are proved, and Prikry forcing is extended into this choiceless setting. Limits emerge on which cardinals such forcing can collapse or make singular. A new tensor Prikry system then builds models with fresh consistency results. The work maps how much order survives when choice, set theory usual safety net, is removed.
arxiv-2511-07722:
Peiqi Sui, Eamon Duede, and Hoyt Long ask whether model hallucinations can serve history when handled with care. Archives omit people through inequality, leaving gaps no document fills. Critical fabulation in literature answers such gaps with disciplined imagination, and the authors adapt that stance to language models.

A narrative cloze task masks events in character timelines drawn from unpublished texts, then asks models to reconstruct them. Fully open models with audited training data anchor the tests. Outputs are judged as evidence-bound reconstruction, not fact. The study probes a provocative line: invention, openly framed, might restore hidden figures without faking the record.
arxiv-2511-08322:
Simone Ricci, Niccolo Biondi, Federico Pernici, and Alberto Del Bimbo tackle negative flips, where an updated image classifier starts failing on pictures it once got right. As new classes arrive, margins between categories shrink and conflicting patterns appear, so overall progress can quietly damage older skills. Their training method preserves the margins of the original model while the new model learns.

An explicit margin calibration term on the output scores widens the gap between old and new classes in a controlled way. A double source focal distillation loss learns from both the old model and a freshly trained one, avoiding over constraint. Benchmarks show consistently lower negative flip rates with high overall accuracy.
arxiv-2511-08422:
Saeed Tafazolian and Jaap Top construct concrete sets of hyperelliptic curves over the rationals whose Jacobians have complex multiplication, a rich extra symmetry in their number. Each curve is given by a concrete equation built from a factor and a Chebyshev polynomial of chosen degree, where the degree is a power of two or an odd prime. Such concrete cases of abelian varieties with complex multiplication are valuable test cases.

The authors prove the Jacobians are simple and determine the associated CM fields exactly. Their construction exploits the interplay between Chebyshev polynomials and Galois coverings. The result supplies concrete criteria for producing further curves in these sets, rather than isolated cases found by search.
arxiv-2511-09222:
Jiarui Liu and nine co-authors ask whether language models can reason honestly, answering only when premises truly force a conclusion. In deductive tasks, honesty means deriving the entailed conclusion or abstaining when information is insufficient. Current models often guess anyway, producing unwarranted answers.

The team built two data sets from graph structures, covering linear algebra and logical inference. Half the cases were made unanswerable by perturbing one edge. Prompting and standard training, including GRPO reinforcement learning, struggled on these tasks because negative rewards can collapse training early. Their method, ACNCHOR, injects ground-truth paths into rollouts to prevent that collapse. It stabilizes learning and improves reasoning performance markedly in their tests.
arxiv-2511-09322:
James Brown, Tarini S Hardikar, Kenny Heitritter, and Kanav Setia improve how molecules are mapped onto qubits for quantum machines. Standard mappings like Jordan-Wigner turn fermionic operators into heavy qubit operators, deepening circuits and complicating readout. Earlier local mappings suit structured models but struggle with real chemistry.

Working with the Generalized Superfast Encoding, the authors add three upgrades. These are path tuning, multi-edge structures for error detection, and a stabilizer readout scheme. On small hydrogen cluster systems, the encoding gives better energy values under realistic hardware noise. A square-lattice variant halved the error for orbital rotations on IBM Kingston hardware in their tests.
arxiv-2511-09722:
Sujay Nair, Evan Coleman, Sherrie Wang, and Elsa Olivetti prospect for hidden minerals by teaching a model to fill in blanked-out maps. Finding deposits for the energy transition is costly because the minerals sit underground. Their masked mineral modeling infills masked regions of geospatial resource maps, in the style of masked language modeling.

Trained on data for the conterminous United States, their best models reach modest but real predictive scores. The resolution is one square mile on held-out test regions. A major advantage is flexibility. Auxiliary layers from geophysics and a nationwide soil survey slot in easily, even where mineral records are absent. Adding those features improved inference and allowed evaluation in regions with no recorded minerals at all.
arxiv-2511-09822:
Jun Woo Chung, Yingjie Lao, and Weijie Zhao present a watermarking approach for gradient boosting decision trees, a model family widely used on structured data. Watermarking helps prove model ownership, but most research targets neural networks, leaving tree ensembles largely unexplored. Their approach embeds a watermark by fine-tuning the model in place, aiming for marks that are hard to notice and hard to remove.

Four embedding plans are proposed, each balancing accuracy against watermark strength. Across diverse data sets, the methods achieved high embedding rates with little accuracy loss. The watermarks also resisted later fine-tuning applied after deployment. The authors describe the work as the first robust watermarking approach designed specifically for gradient boosting decision trees.
arxiv-2511-09922:
Jinliang Ren and six co-authors demonstrate quantum phase-gradient imaging built from two metasurfaces, one generating entangled photon pairs and one reading out phase information. Quantum phase imaging suits transparent samples under very low light, where thickness and refractive index changes must be measured gently. Their compact system uses a lithium niobate metasurface for photon pair generation by down-conversion, with emission angle tunable by light alone.

A silicon metasurface then differentiates the photon wave function, turning phase gradients into measurable signal with a nearly linear response. Proof-of-concept tests imaged gradients up to twenty-five radians per millimeter with eighty-nine percent similarity to reference values. The authors note that larger, higher-quality metasurfaces could raise pixel resolution greatly, toward portable sensing and microscopy tools.
arxiv-2511-10122:
Andrea Loi, Roberto Mossa, and Fabio Zuddas extend a polydisk theorem from complex geometry to a much wider class of domains. The earlier result covered classical Cartan-Hartogs domains, which are built over symmetric domains. The new version covers Hartogs domains over arbitrary bounded symmetric domains, including reducible and exceptional ones that the classical theory left out, and the authors also prove a dual counterpart.

As an application, they show that the dual of such a Hartogs domain admits no totally geodesic immersion into any compact Riemannian manifold. That broadens a rigidity phenomenon known from earlier work: these complex domains are, in a precise sense, too curved or too structured to sit flatly inside compact spaces. The paper is a pure extension-and-application result in several complex variables.
arxiv-2511-10222:
Yudong Yang and eight co-authors red-team audio-capable language models with attacks built from composed speech and sound. Their benchmark, SACRED-Bench, mixes harmful and benign content inside one auditory scene in three ways: overlapping speeches, benign speech layered with harmful non-speech audio, and multi-speaker dialogue. Questions refer to the audio only implicitly, so no harmful text appears in the prompt itself.

Even a leading proprietary model with full safety guardrails fell for about two thirds of the attacks. As a defense, the team built SALMONN-Guard, the first guard model that inspects speech, audio, and text jointly, and it cut the attack success rate to about one fifth. The results argue that multimodal safety needs audio-aware defenses, not text filters alone.
arxiv-2511-10422:
Christopher Buyalos and four co-authors study a question about groups built from two simple matrices, one fixed and one depending on a number q. Kim and Koberda conjectured that for every rational q between negative four and four, the two matrices never generate a free group. The paper builds families of rational values where the conjecture holds.

Earlier work by Smilga is extended through three different constructions. One uses Diophantine geometry on certain polynomials, one uses sums of geometric series, and one uses ratios of Pell-type sequences. The families pile up at countless points inside the interval, adding strong support for the conjecture.
arxiv-2511-10522:
Jooheon Yoo, Michael Boyle, and Nils Deppe aim to close the gap between two ways of predicting gravitational waves from merging black holes and neutron stars. Post-Newtonian formulas describe the early inspiral cheaply but fail near merger, while numerical relativity simulations are accurate yet expensive and cover limited cases.

Their physics-informed neural network learns corrections that map the post-Newtonian description onto the numerical one. Remarkably, training used only eight hybrid surrogate waveforms, with loss terms that enforce known physics such as vanishing corrections in the Newtonian limit. The learned corrections cut phase and amplitude errors through the inspiral up to about 200 times the total mass before merger. Because the model is differentiable and cheap to run, it offers a bridge toward waveform models that extrapolate more safely.
arxiv-2511-10622:
Rajiv Sambharya, Nikolai Matni, and George Pappas build a way to certify how well a workhorse optimization method actually performs. Sequential convex programming solves hard non-convex problems by tackling a chain of easier convex ones. It is used across control, signal processing, and operations research, but its guarantees are usually local and conditional.

Their verification framework poses the question as an optimization problem in its own right. The goal is to maximize a performance metric, such as suboptimality after a fixed number of iterations, over all allowed parameters and all iterate sequences the algorithm could produce. The framework covers trust-region, convex-concave, and prox-linear variants, plus rounding schemes. The authors say it delivers the first global worst-case guarantees for these algorithms in the parametric setting.
arxiv-2511-10722:
Vicente Amado Olivo and five co-authors build a tool for a bibliographic headache: telling apart researchers who share a name. Correctly grouping an author's publications matters for recognition, funding, and hiring, yet large libraries such as NASA's Astrophysics Data System often lack the affiliation and venue metadata that disambiguation methods lean on.

Their Neural Author Name Disambiguator treats the task as similarity learning, using a Siamese neural network over only names, titles, and abstracts, the metadata that is almost always present. Foundation models embed those fields into features. Evaluated on a new dataset linking publications to ORCiD records, the system reached up to 94 percent accuracy on pairwise decisions and over 95 percent F1 when clustering papers by researcher. The test dataset is released as a benchmark.
arxiv-2511-10922:
Li-Juan Cheng, Anton Thalmaier, and Feng-Yu Wang prove a boundedness result for a key operator on curved spaces with a weight. The operator, a covariant Riesz transform, acts on differential forms, the tools used to handle fields on such spaces. Their result covers the range above two in the scale that measures size and spread.

The proof uses heat flow tests that rely on local volume growth, heat bounds, and control of curvature. Under stated curvature rules, the tests apply and give boundedness for large shifts. The result settles a stated conjecture in the plain case and yields new integral bounds for weighted spaces.
arxiv-2511-11022:
Hyunchul Bae, Eunjae Lee, and their colleagues built CIVAT, a small-scale testbed for cars that drive and cooperate at one-fifteenth of real size. Cars that share data with each other and with smart road gear can drive more safely together, but no prior testbed gave the road gear full sensing and computing roles. CIVAT was built to fill that gap.

The setup pairs a scaled city map and sensor-equipped model cars with smart road units. Cars and road gear swap data over Wi-Fi through a shared publish-subscribe system. Tests on road-based sensing and crossing control show the testbed can support joint driving trials at low cost and low risk.
arxiv-2511-11122:
Yuyang Huang, Dante Kalise, and Hicham Kouhkouh recast hard global optimization, the search for the lowest point of a bumpy function, as a control problem. Gradient methods can stall at local dips and lack global promises when the function is non-convex or non-smooth. Their frame treats minimization as steering a system over an endless, discounted horizon toward the best set.

Within that frame, they prove explicit exponential convergence rates with computable constants. The value function converges, objective values converge, and optimal paths head to the set of minimizers, all under minimal assumptions. Tests on hard non-convex problems show the approach works in practice and sharpens their earlier theory.
arxiv-2511-11222:
Isael Herrera, Miguel Alonso, and Sophie Brasselet demonstrate three-dimensional Stokes polarimetric imaging at nanoscale resolution. Polarized light fields that tilt in all three dimensions appear often in microscopy and nanophotonics, yet reading their full polarization map is hard. Classic Stokes methods assume light travels in a flat, paraxial bundle, which fails for tightly focused fields.

Their setup uses an array of gold nanospheres, each acting as a tiny dipolar scatterer that probes the local 3D polarization state. A high-aperture lens gathers the scattered light, split by circular polarization, for a simple imaging chain. An algorithm extracts the field parameters across the whole view, and the method extends to single-molecule work.
arxiv-2511-11522:
Luthira Abeykoon, Ved Patel, and their colleagues present CVChess, a deep learning system that turns a photo of a physical chessboard into Forsyth-Edwards Notation, the standard text code for a chess position. Online chess has boomed, but over-the-board players lack the engine help that digital players take for granted. Feeding the coded position to an online engine closes that divide with move advice.

A phone photo is first straightened: line detection finds the board edges, a projective warp gives a top-down view, and the board is cut into sixty-four squares. A residual convolutional network then classifies each square into piece types for both colors or empty, trained on a public chess recognition data set.
arxiv-2511-11622:
Alexis Roger and four co-authors study two design choices behind time series foundation models: how raw series are tokenized into discrete units, and whether pretraining beats starting from scratch. Both choices shape forecasting quality, but their interaction is poorly understood.

Experiments plus theory show that tokenizer design mainly controls what the model can represent and how stable training is, while pretraining chiefly speeds optimization and alignment. Pretrained models exploit good tokenizers best, especially at smaller vocabulary sizes, and a mismatched tokenizer can drag down even a pretrained model. Practical guidance follows: tune the tokenizer first, because transfer learning cannot rescue a poor representation.
arxiv-2511-11922:
Karthikeyan K, Raghuveer Thirukovalluru, and David Carlson make language model predictions on clinical text explainable by construction, with a framework called CALM. Records such as admission notes split naturally into meaningful sections, yet a standard model swallows them whole and returns an opaque risk score.

CALM predicts the outcome as the plain sum of each component's contribution, so the contribution of every section is part of the computation itself, not an after-the-fact guess. Explanations stay faithful at both the section and record level. For researchers and physicians who must defend a model's signals, additive structure over semi-structured text offers interpretability without abandoning modern language models.
arxiv-2511-12222:
Hangshuo Tian investigates how two common tricks for particle filters interact. Particle filters track a hidden state from noisy data, and swarm methods based on chicken swarm behavior can refresh the particle set. Separately, a divergence-based sampling rule adjusts how many particles are used. Their combined effect had not been fully understood.

Working in a simplified model, Tian argues the swarm update acts much like a contraction in mean-square terms, making the particle set more concentrated, or more peaked in a precise sense. An inequality argument then links that concentration to the expected bin counts in adaptive sampling. Under the stated assumptions, the combined filter should need fewer particles.
arxiv-2511-12322:
Mykhailo Vorobiov and twelve co-authors introduce an all-optical method to measure electric fields inside a plasma sheath without touching the plasma. Plasma sheaths, thin layers near a surface, are hard to probe with physical instruments that disturb them. The team adds trace rubidium vapor to an argon plasma and uses a quantum optical effect tied to Rydberg atoms.

Light resonances in the rubidium respond sharply to electric fields, and collected fluorescence lets them rebuild a two-dimensional map of field strength at fine resolution. As a demonstration they track field changes in the sheath around a biased probe tip. The precision and detection limit reported suggest wide use for low-temperature plasma studies.
arxiv-2511-12522:
Songlin Lyu and four co-authors argue that chiral nuclear forces, the effective interactions between nucleons built from the symmetries of quantum chromodynamics, simplify greatly near a special limit. One-pion exchange normally generates an important tensor force in this framework. The authors show that force is suppressed by two facts together: the nucleon-nucleon scattering lengths are large, and the pion mass is small.

On that basis they propose a new scheme in which pion exchange enters only as a small perturbation, yet nucleon phase shifts are described well up to sizable momenta. The simplified leading-order force explains why several short-range forces have worked, and shares their near symmetry and closeness to the unitarity limit.
arxiv-2511-12622:
Satish Ramakrishna explores whether higher-order interactions in a scalar field can mix ultraviolet and infrared scales in a way that bears on the cosmological constant problem. The observed vacuum energy is far below field theory estimates, and a classic theorem blocks any local field from relaxing it to zero dynamically. A separate bound ties a theory's smallest length scale to its largest.

Ramakrishna's route starts with a nonlocal action that breaks the locality assumption of that theorem, then assumes a vacuum that breaks boost symmetry while keeping spatial symmetry in a preferred frame. A smooth nonlocal quartic interaction is inserted as an ansatz. The central claim is that strongly nonlinear per-mode energies reach the Planck scale at far smaller wavenumbers than linear modes.
arxiv-2511-12722:
Nakshatra Gupta, Sumanth Prabhu, Supratik Chakraborty, and R Venkatesh ask how much targeted data poisoning a training set can withstand. In such an attack, an adversary flips training labels to change how one chosen test point gets classified. Checking every label by hand is impossible at scale, so the authors instead measure a dataset's robustness directly. Their threat model is modest: the attacker can only perturb labels and knows only the model's hypothesis space, not the data itself.

Even under those limits, they prove that computing exact robustness is NP-complete, even for linear classifiers. Their answer is a technique that brackets the true value with lower and upper bounds, computed efficiently enough to run on many public datasets where earlier methods failed. Experiments show that once poisoning passes the upper bound, the target's classification does change. The bounds give dataset owners a practical audit before training begins.
arxiv-2511-12922:
Yu Hou and Won-Yong Shin unify how language-model recommenders turn items into tokens. Recommender systems built on language models must translate products, songs, or videos into discrete tokens the model can reason over. Existing tokenizers are trained per domain, so a shop and a music service each need their own, and knowledge does not carry across. UniTok instead projects items from all domains into one latent space. Then routes them through a mixture of experts: domain specialists for each field's quirks, plus a shared expert that is always on for transferable knowledge.

A calibration step keeps each domain's tokens equally informative. Across wide-ranging real datasets, UniTok improved over strong benchmarks by large margins and kept working in new domains without retraining. The design is aimed at platforms that run recommendations across many catalogs at once and cannot afford a bespoke tokenizer for each.
arxiv-2511-13022:
Eshani Patel, Yisong Yue, and Geeling Chau fix a fragility in base models for brain signals. Such models learn representations from many recording channels at once, and those codes decode downstream tasks well, until the preprocessing changes. If the time scale, how finely the signal is binned or sampled, differs between pretraining and use, scores drop. The authors show systematically that current representations are not invariant to that mismatch. Their remedy is time-scale augmented pretraining, which trains the model across varied time scales so it stops depending on the choice.

Across decoding tasks, the augmented pretraining consistently improved robustness to time-scale differences and built measurable invariance into the representation space. The broader claim: real laboratory preprocessing diversity is a variation the model must be built to absorb.
arxiv-2511-20122:
Chen, Lei, Sheng, Liu, and Gong rebuild recommender diffusion models on thermodynamic grounds. Their 2025 paper proposes TV-Diff, a tri-view diffusion framework. Diffusion models have grown popular for recommendation tasks. Prior work adopted their goals without much checking. The team first asks whether those goals suffice.

Viewed through heat physics, these models maximize energy alone. Classic systems instead work by reducing entropy. Neither view alone captures the full problem. TV-Diff maximizes Helmholtz free energy, combining both. A custom denoiser preserves anisotropy in user-item links. That unevenness measures cross-links on the two-sided graph. A sampling process called AR-GSP supplies hard negatives. Acceptance-rejection sampling ensures those rejects are informative. A Gumbel softmax step adapts the sampling over time. Experiments show clear gains in accuracy and efficiency. Theory backs the free-energy formulation as well. Sparse suggestion data motivates the whole design.
arxiv-2511-20322:
Perko's dissertation sharpens the math behind the training loop of machine learning. Submitted in 2025 at Friedrich Schiller University Jena, it studies modified equations for stochastic optimization. Gradient descent with random data shuffling drives most training. A modified equation mimics its steps with a smooth flow.

Part one covers chapters three through five. Time-varying diffusion equations get first-order weak approximation proofs. Their linear error terms are pinned down explicitly. A special family reaches second-order accuracy too. Stochastic gradient descent serves as the worked example. Linear regression is solved completely as the testbed. Two popular modified equations are compared head to head. Part two, chapters six and seven, changes tack. Finite datasets get a new diffusion approximation. Sampling without replacement is the realistic training regime. The theory links numerical analysis with stochastic calculus.
arxiv-2511-20522:
Flynn and colleagues sort seizures by the mechanism that tips the brain over. Their 2025 paper builds a sorting framework from critical transition theory. A seizure is a sudden, large change in brain state. Such tipping can arise three ways in math models. A shifting parameter, random noise, or both can force the jump.

A model was built to mimic real seizure recordings closely. Each transition type leaves distinct marks in the model's output. Those marks trained a machine learning classifier. The classifier then judged voltage traces from epileptic rodents. Noise-driven transitions formed the largest share of seizures. That challenges the usual bifurcation-first view of seizure onset. Shifts in a parameter and mixed cases made up the rest. Knowing which mechanism dominates could redirect therapy design. Blocking onset or speeding its end depends on that split. The framework fits animal and human seizures alike.
arxiv-2511-20622:
Chetyrkin extends a classic shortcut for Higgs-gluon coupling to many heavy quarks at once. His 2025 paper generalizes the low-energy theorem in QCD. When quarks far outweigh the Higgs, they can be integrated out. The Higgs then couples to gluons through an effective vertex. A theorem links that vertex to how the coupling constant decouples.

The known theorem covered simpler heavy-quark setups. The extension handles any number of heavy flavors together. Almost no new heavy computation was needed for the proof. Plugging in a known three-loop decoupling constant does the work. Out comes the four-loop effective coupling for extended models. The three-loop result with many heavy quarks is reproduced as a check. A twin theorem for light scalar quark currents extends too. Models with extra heavy quarks beyond the Standard Model benefit. One extra loop of precision arrives nearly for free.
arxiv-2511-20922:
Guilin Zhang and colleagues fix in 2025 a bottleneck that hobbles quantum machine learning. A quantum circuit may compute features, but reading them out means measuring, and that quantum-to-classical readout throws away the original input. Their fix borrows the residual connection from classical deep learning: concatenate the quantum features with the raw input, and let the classifier see both.

The bypass adds no quantum complexity, yet in tests it beat purely quantum models and prior hybrids, in centralised and federated settings where data stays spread across devices. Accuracy improved by up to 55 percent over quantum baselines. Across four benchmarks, including Wine, Breast Cancer, and subsets of Fashion-MNIST and Forest CoverType, the hybrid reached near-classical accuracy with 10 to 20 percent fewer parameters. It resisted membership inference attacks guessing which records were trained on: attack success stayed near the random-guess level, an AUC of about 0.5 on their scale.
arxiv-2511-21322:
Kirti Bhagat and five coauthors audit how well AI storytellers portray Indian cultures in 2025, and the grades are poor. Millions use chatbots for creative writing, yet judging cultural accuracy in open-ended stories is hard. The team first built TALES-Tax, a taxonomy of cultural misrepresentation, from focus groups and surveys with people who have lived experience in India, so the categories come from insiders, not outsiders.

Bhagat and her coauthors then graded stories from 6 popular models using 2,925 annotations by 108 annotators spanning 71 regions and 14 languages. A striking 88 percent of stories contained at least one cultural inaccuracy. Errors grew worse in mid- and low-resource languages and in peri-urban settings. Oddly, a follow-up quiz bank, TALES-QA, showed the models usually know the correct facts, yet still write stories that get the culture wrong.
arxiv-2511-21522:
Yanxing Huang, Zihan Tang, Zejin Lin, Peng Li, and Yang Liu make AI proof-checkers stricter to make them better, in 2025. Language models increasingly verify their own mathematical proofs, and the bottleneck is error detection: a lax checker waves flawed proofs through. Their pessimistic verification runs several independent checks of the same proof in parallel and declares the proof wrong if any single check reports an error.

Huang and his coauthors test several pessimistic variants across many math verification benchmarks and find significant gains everywhere. The simple workflow's token efficiency even beat extended long chain-of-thought reasoning in test-time scaling, doing more with less compute. Their case studies carry a warning for the field: most apparent false negatives from strong models turned out to be annotation errors in the original datasets. The method's true accuracy is therefore underestimated, and pessimistic checking looks better the cleaner the data gets.
arxiv-2511-21822:
Fernández-Ontiveros and a large collaboration present JOLINES, a catalogue of emission-line strengths for galaxies observed by the J-PAS survey and its early pathfinder surveys. Emission lines are bright spikes in a galaxy's spectrum from glowing gas, revealing star formation, gas chemistry, and black hole activity. J-PAS takes pictures through many narrow colour filters rather than full spectra, so extracting line strengths is tricky.

The team fitted model spectra to the many-filter measurements to pin down background light before measuring lines. Tests on simulated galaxies and comparisons with true spectroscopic surveys showed a tight match, with a typical scatter of about 0.3 dex and reliable results for lines stronger than about 20 angstroms in equivalent width. The current catalogue gives dependable flux measurements for roughly 13,900 galaxy sources in the hydrogen-alpha complex and 7,200 in a key oxygen line.
arxiv-2511-22322:
Li, Nasybullov, and Zadvornov, algebraists, compare the two operations living inside a skew brace, a set equipped with an addition and a multiplication that interact through one distributive-style law. Skew braces matter because they encode solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation. A conjecture of Smoktunowicz and Vendramin predicts that when the additive group of a finite skew brace is solvable. The multiplicative group must be solvable too, despite the two operations being free to differ wildly. The conjecture remains open in general.

For a characteristic subgroup of the additive group, the images of a product and a sum coincide in the quotient under stated conditions, so the operations cannot drift far apart. As a corollary, whenever the additive derived subgroup is cyclic, the multiplicative group is solvable, settling the conjecture in that case.
arxiv-2511-22622:
Valov and Meerson study rare large fluctuations in long-running random processes. Their observable is the time integral of a power of a stationary Gaussian process, whose extremes large deviation theory normally describes with exponential scaling in time. For powers above two, short-correlated Gaussian processes break that pattern: the probability density follows anomalous scaling with exponents below one, and its rate function develops a kink.

That kink is a first-order dynamical phase transition resembling condensation: extremes come from one localised burst in the process's history, an optimal path coexisting with spread-out ones. The anomaly, seen only for the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, proves generic here. For long-correlated ones the exponents also depend on correlation decay, and when correlations are long-ranged enough the transition disappears into a crossover. Replica-exchange Wang-Landau simulations probing probabilities down to ten to the minus two hundredth confirm the theory.
arxiv-2511-22922:
Wicks asks how little logic a number theory result needs. The equations ask when twice a power of two, plus or minus another power of two, plus or minus one, equals a perfect square. The classification of integer solutions to them was proved using hypergeometric results; the rest is elementary arithmetic. Wicks asks whether it can be carried out inside a deliberately weak fragment of arithmetic built around even and odd.

The base system cannot even mention exponentiation: an element counts as a power of two if all its divisors other than one are even. Wicks extends it with meaningful axioms, inequalities and assumptions making powers of two behave well, and imports the hypergeometric results. He shows the classifications for the four Diophantine equations go through in the extended theory. Far less than Peano arithmetic suffices, and the working axioms say something real about powers of two.
arxiv-2511-23422:
Bundeliya and colleagues propose unifying two puzzles, why neutrinos have mass and what drove inflation. By coupling neutrinos to the same scalar field that inflates the early universe. In their mass-varying neutrino framework the neutrino mass is a function of the scalar field, tried in power-law, exponential. And hybrid forms, and the neutrinos push back on the field through an effective potential that includes their backreaction in one model.

Working through the modified expansion equations with Fermi-Dirac integrals tracking the neutrinos' shift from relativistic to nonrelativistic behavior. They show the coupling changes the potential's slope and curvature and so alters how long inflation lasts. The neutrino contribution nearly vanishes while neutrinos are relativistic and grows once they become heavy. And among the three couplings the hybrid form proves the most flexible realization of the unified picture for model building.
arxiv-2512-00122:
National pension plans pool everyone together, which can be unfair to groups with shorter life expectancies. Moshe Milevsky, Thomas Salisbury, and Robyn Allen examine that tension in a 2025 study. They ask whether high-mortality groups might prefer pension pools aligned with their own demographics.

The authors call such arrangements equitable longevity risk sharing pools, using a First Nations pension plan as the motivating case. Joining a separate pool means giving up some guarantees and accepting more individual risk. The study weighs that trade-off, offering actuaries and policymakers a framework for fairer retirement design. Pension design rarely faces this trade-off so directly, which gives the study its force.
arxiv-2512-00422:
Generative models can design three-dimensional shapes that look plausible yet fail as real products. Yingxuan You and co-authors present PhysGen in 2025, a framework for physically grounded shape generation aimed at industrial design. For engineered shapes, realism is tied to physical properties like aerodynamic efficiency.

A car body that ignores airflow may render beautifully and still be a bad design. PhysGen couples shape generation to the underlying physics so outputs respect engineering constraints. Designers could explore more concepts automatically while keeping each candidate grounded in how the object must actually perform. Industrial design is the test case, where a pretty shape that fails physics is worthless. Automobiles are the running example, since drag decides their efficiency.
arxiv-2512-00622:
Force feedback gloves let virtual reality users feel resistance, but most designs fit one hand size and one task. Pablo Alvarez Romeo and Mehmet Ercan Altinsoy present KinesCeTI in 2025, a modular force feedback glove with interchangeable actuation for the index finger and thumb. Adaptability is the design's central claim.

Limited adaptability, simplified feedback, and fixed architectures have constrained earlier gloves. A size-adaptable exoskeleton with swappable actuators serves more users and more applications, from rehabilitation to remote operation. Better haptics close the loop between seeing a virtual object and truly handling it. Interchangeable actuation lets one glove serve gripping, therapy, and training tasks. The index and thumb do most precision work, so they are the natural focus.
arxiv-2512-00722:
Jiaming Xu and six coauthors address a cost problem in large language models in their 2025 paper, SpeContext. Reasoning models now write long step-by-step answers, which improves their work. The catch is memory: long outputs build a large key-value cache that stores past context for the model.

That cache becomes a bottleneck when such models run in real products, such as software agents. SpeContext uses speculative context sparsity, keeping only the parts of context that matter most. Guessing well about what can be thinned out could cut memory sharply. If quality holds, long reasoning becomes cheaper to serve at scale.
arxiv-2512-01022:
Yi-Lin Wei and six coauthors open a new task in robot manipulation in a 2025 paper. Many daily jobs are cyclic: shaking a bottle, knocking a nail, or stirring in rounds. The robot must repeat an action and stop at an expected terminal time, which adds a timing demand most manipulation work ignores.

Their system, CycleManip, enables cyclic task manipulation. It leans on effective historical perception and understanding, meaning the robot tracks what it has already done in the cycle. Counting repetitions from vision is easy for people and hard for machines. A robot that tracks cycles could handle chores and assembly steps more reliably.
arxiv-2512-01222:
Ching Fang and Samuel Marks probe hidden reasoning in language models in a 2025 paper. As models grow more capable, there is concern they may develop reasoning that is encoded or hidden from human oversight. Checking whether interpretability tools can penetrate such reasoning is an open safety question.

The authors build a controlled testbed for the problem. They fine-tune a reasoning model to do its chain-of-thought in ROT-13, a simple letter-shifting cipher, while keeping its final outputs in plain English. They then test unsupervised decoding methods from interpretability research. The setup shows whether today's tools can recover reasoning that a model has disguised.
arxiv-2512-01422:
Yongkun Du and co-authors bring mask diffusion models to scene text reading. Reading text in wild photos is hard. Letters bend, blur, and mix with busy scenes. Most top readers build text one letter at a time, in order.

Mask diffusion works in a distinct way. It starts with masked text and fills it in steps. That gives a good mix of speed and care. The team is the first to use it for scene text. Their model, MDiff4STR, aims for sharp reads on signs, labels, and plates in real photos.
arxiv-2512-01722:
Borsoni introduces folded optimal transport for costs defined on extreme points. Optimal transport moves mass at least cost. Costs are often known only on the boundary extremes of a convex set. The whole set still needs a cost for real tasks.

Folding extends that boundary cost to the full set by a convex route. Standard transport returns as the case where the set is a simplex. The build also serves separable quantum transport tasks. A broader frame unifies tasks in economics, imaging, and quantum information. Separable quantum costs fit the fold cleanly, which links the new build to entanglement measures that transport theory already serves.
arxiv-2512-02622:
Xuming He and nine co-authors test whether video generators follow rules, not just look pretty. New video models hold together over time and look impressive, a step toward vision foundation models. Most benchmarks grade beauty, instruction following, and smoothness, which leaves rule based reasoning unchecked.

RULER-Bench probes whether generated videos obey stated physical and logical rules. A model can look right frame by frame while breaking the rule that binds the scene. Testing rules directly helps builders find where video models merely imitate, and where they truly grasp how a scene should unfold. Rules are a stern test: a clip can look smooth and still break the one rule that counts most.
arxiv-2512-02722:
Matteo Tolloso and Davide Bacciu give graph neural networks a new way to express doubt. Such networks learn from linked data, and honest uncertainty is essential before trusting them in practice. Most current tools rely on Bayesian inference or on ensembles of models.

Their credal graph neural networks output sets of plausible predictions instead of one fixed answer. A credal set shows the range the model still finds credible. Set valued answers can warn users when a graph based system, used in science or medicine, is guessing beyond its evidence. A set of live picks is a more honest brief than one pick dressed up as sure fact for a board.
arxiv-2512-03022:
Ranadeep Roy and Wei Chen compute a topological marker in three dimensions without the usual crushing cost. A universal topological marker measures how disorder affects topological order at the atomic scale. In higher dimensions, direct calculation of the marker becomes numerically very costly.

Their method applies the kernel polynomial method, which expands the needed quantities in fast polynomial series. They argue it works efficiently for any symmetry class in higher dimensions. Cheap markers let researchers screen disordered topological materials on a computer before growing crystals in a lab. Cheap marks let teams scan whole fields of stuff for the rare good one. Hand work can not do that at the scale new finds now demand of them in the lab.
arxiv-2512-03122:
Fitting math models of living systems to data is a hard task. Piotr Gwiazda, Alexey Kazarnikov, Anna Marciniak-Czochra, and Zuzanna Szymańska survey ways to do it in this 2025 work. Good fits are key for sound forecasts and for insight into how life works.

Data are often scarce and noisy, and living systems vary a lot. The models, based on partial differential equations, are also costly to run. The authors go beyond standard Bayesian methods and test a new likelihood framework with gradient flow tools. Their guide helps modelers pick methods for real biological problems. Their framework serves PDE models in biology, where data limits rule out many classic methods.
arxiv-2512-03322:
Learning from partly labeled data is common in real studies. Geoffrey McLachlan and Jinran Wu present an R package for that task in this 2025 work. Labels often need expert judgment or costly hand work, so most data stay unlabeled.

Their package, SSLfmm, works with finite mixture models, which view data as blends of groups. It also handles data missing in mixed ways. Semi-supervised methods that use unlabeled cases can sharpen classifiers a lot. A ready R package puts those methods in reach of working statisticians. Mixture models suit partly labeled data, since groups can absorb unlabeled cases naturally.
arxiv-2512-04322:
Om Tailor uses quantum computing methods to probe why asphalt ages. The study appeared on arXiv in 2025. It centers on dibenzothiophene, a sulfur-bearing compound in road binder. Sulfur chemistry plays a key part in how binder breaks down. Air and sun wear the binder down over years of road use. A single clear test compound helps isolate that decay.

Tailor runs a full quantum chemistry pipeline on the compound. The pipeline hunts for the lowest energy state of the molecule. It uses trial wave designs that adapt as the search proceeds. The runs reached a ground state energy the author reports as highly exact. The setup also handled strongly linked electron behavior well. Beyond this one compound, the work sets out a frame for new binder mixes. Such mixes could resist aging and last longer on real roads.
arxiv-2512-04422:
Sam Looi and David Sher study how heat spreads in flat shapes whose borders bend and meet at corners. The heat trace sums how a domain's vibrations decay, and its small-time expansion reveals shape data term by term. For straight polygons, corner terms depend only on the opening angles. For smooth domains, terms follow the border's curvature. In curvy-cornered domains the two effects had not been tracked together. Their 2025 arXiv paper finds where they first meet.

The meeting point arrives at the half-power term of the expansion. Looi and Sher compute this first joint term for both fixed and free border conditions. Each corner's share depends only on its inner angle and the one-sided curvatures of the arcs that meet there. A sharp sign law holds: the sign is set purely by whether the corner is convex or reflex. Such laws help read shape from spectra.
arxiv-2512-05722:
Théo Neukomm, Zlatko Jončev, and Philippe Schwaller teach language models to explain chemical reactions the way chemists do: by pushing arrows. Arrow pushing is a century old notation that tracks electrons as bonds break and form, while keeping mass and charge balanced. Their 2025 framework makes models predict the mechanism itself, written in a compact text format called MechSMILES, which encodes structure and electron flow with three kinds of arrow.

A Python environment checks every step against conservation laws, so models cannot invent or lose atoms. The models were tested on four tasks of rising difficulty. On the hardest task, they found the right path in over nine of ten cases on one dataset, and about three in four on another. New reaction families were learned fast: strong results on ozonolysis and Suzuki coupling came from only forty examples each.
arxiv-2512-05822:
Ji Wang and Miroslav Krstic design a controller that not only steers a system to its target but keeps it safe on the way. The systems couple wave-like equations to ordinary ones, hit by disturbances everywhere. The output to be regulated sits at the far end from the control input. Their controller uses nonovershooting backstepping, built step by step from the far end.

An extended observer estimates unmeasured states and disturbances, with explicit error bounds feeding the safety margin. Four guarantees follow. An output starting safe stays safe, and one starting unsafe is rescued into the safe region within a set time. Tracking error fades to zero. Observer errors shrink exponentially to zero. The method is demonstrated on a drone delivering a payload hung from a cable: the load follows a reference path while avoiding barriers. The design is a safety certificate, not just a steering law.
arxiv-2512-06122:
Édney Freitas and six co-authors run a fair race between open source chip design tools and a commercial suite, on the kind of circuits particle physics actually needs. High energy physics builds custom ASICs for its detectors. Three test blocks were built both ways in an open process. Effort, area, power, and timing were measured.

The open flow's state machine used half again the area and double the power. Open tools proved viable for prototyping, training, and collaboration. Commercial tools win on strict targets. Such comparisons let laboratories budget honestly. What collaborations need is block by block numbers.
arxiv-2512-06222:
Yinjian Zhao and Kunpeng Zhong use computer simulations to study how electrons drift inside Hall thrusters, a type of electric engine for spacecraft. In these engines, a magnetic field traps electrons while ions are pushed out to make thrust. Waves that grow in the trapped electron cloud can shove electrons across the field, which cuts the engine's efficiency, and the shape of the field may matter a lot.

The team runs full three dimensional particle simulations and compares a simple field shape with a more real one. They find that where the field weakens, electron flow grows uneven and stronger, a pattern the simple model misses. Their worked out rates for electron flow match what the simulations show up close. The maps they produce can help builders make leaner models that still capture how these engines behave.
arxiv-2512-06322:
Sogen Ikegami, Kiyu Fukui, Rico Pohle, and Yukitoshi Motome study a quantum magnet that sits between two famous states of disorder. Their stage is a honeycomb grid of spins, each larger than the simplest kind. At one end of a dial sits the Kitaev spin liquid, a state with no fixed spin pattern but rich links between distant spins. At the other end sits a bond solid state of the AKLT type, where spins pair up in a neat pattern.

By turning the dial, the authors map which state wins at each setting. Plain and semi refined methods predict crisp magnetic orders in the middle ground. Once full quantum jitter is let in, those orders melt away. What remains is a tangled state with weak spin links and high shared information. The study shows how clashing quantum disorders can birth states neither side gives alone.
arxiv-2512-06622:
Xiurui Zhao and six co authors hunt for fast flickers in the X ray glow of feeding black holes. The glow comes from a corona, a halo of hot plasma above the black hole, whose size and makeup are still debated. Using archived Chandra telescope data on thousands of broad line active galaxies picked from two big sky surveys, the team searched for large, rapid changes in brightness over spans of hours.

A small set of galaxies passed their strict test, doubling or more in brightness on those short spans with strong statistical backing. A flicker that fast caps the region's size, far below the sizes other methods infer for the whole corona. That gap suggests the corona is not a smooth halo but a patchwork of small, short lived flares. Such compact energy release fits magnetically dominated coronae.
arxiv-2512-06722:
L Soriano, S Bertaina, and their co authors use a defect as a spy inside a quantum spin chain. The chain is dimerized, its links alternating strong and weak, and at its edges sit special states protected by the chain's topology. Those edge states are shielded from much of the noise around them, which makes them candidates for quantum devices, provided their relaxation and decoherence are understood.

Resonance measurements show two regimes. At the coldest temperatures, relaxation is throttled by a phonon bottleneck, where the lattice cannot carry energy away fast enough. At high temperatures the dimerization gap takes over. The field each edge state feels from its twin is weakened by the chain's internal coupling, so coherence lasts longer than for lone ions at the same density. The authors distill design rules for materials that would keep such edge states coherent longer.
arxiv-2512-06822:
Ziqi Wang and seven co-authors study how a small flattened particle spins while carried by a sheared fluid, a flow that moves faster on one side than the other. Their particle is a mildly squashed sphere, about as heavy as the fluid around it, held inside a narrow channel. Lab experiments are matched, condition for condition, with detailed computer simulations of the moving fluid and particle together.

Older theory, built for tiny particles in open space, predicts how such a particle should settle into a steady rolling motion. Wang's team shows where that picture holds and where it breaks. Walls change the outcome a lot: confinement steadies the rolling state and slows the drift toward it. Weak inertia, the starting pose, and how long one watches also matter. Reconciling all three approaches gives a clearer guide for predicting particle motion in real, boxed-in flows.
arxiv-2512-06922:
George Mikros surveys a two-edged change that large language models bring to forensic linguistics, the study of language as legal evidence. On one side, the models are powerful new tools: they can scan huge text collections and help pin writing to an author through meaning-based measures. On the other side, they can imitate a person's style, hide authorship, and flood the world with synthetic text, shaking the field's basic assumptions.

Mikros notes that models mimic surface style well yet still differ from human writers in detectable ways. Even so, current detectors for machine text fail often. They wrongly flag many non-native English writers and can be beaten by tricks such as swapping look-alike letters. Under legal standards for expert evidence, that unreliability is a serious problem. He urges mixed human and machine workflows, clearer explanations from detectors, and bias checks across many groups of writers.
arxiv-2512-07022:
Geneviève Caumartin and Glaucia Melo ask whether a language-model agent can find the file where a bug lives faster if it first rewrites the bug report. In big software projects, locating the faulty file is slow, and classic search methods take the report as written, noise and all. Recent work showed that cleaned-up queries help search, but nobody had tested the effect inside an autonomous agent's workflow.

Their agent uses an open, off-the-shelf language model to pull identifiers and code snippets from each report and to summarize it before searching. A standard ranking method then retrieves candidate files with the sharpened queries. The best rewriting style lifted the ranking of the first correct file well above the raw-search baseline. It also improved overall file retrieval beyond a known agent system by a clear margin.
arxiv-2512-07222:
Qiwei Tian and co-authors defend vision-language models against attacks that hide in the smallest words. Adversarial inputs can flip a model's answer by exploiting cross-modal attention, and the team traces much of that weakness to function words, the grammatical glue like the, of, and is. Their defense, Function-word De-Attention, borrows the differential amplifier trick from electronics: compute the attention twice. Once normally and once attending only through function words, then subtract the second from the first.

The subtraction cancels the attack surface while leaving the content-bearing attention largely intact. Across three models, three data sets, two tasks, and six attack styles, attack success fell sharply on average, with only a whisper of performance lost, sometimes none. On visual grounding the improvement was dramatic, attack success collapsing while accuracy slightly rose.
arxiv-2512-07322: Yousra Gati and Vladimir Petrov Kostov compare two ways of spacing the landmarks of a degree-five polynomial. Take the five roots in order and form the midpoints of neighboring pairs; separately, take the four critical points, where the derivative vanishes, also in order. The question is how the gaps between consecutive midpoints compare with the gaps between consecutive critical points.
arxiv-2512-07822:
Arindam Mitra and Jatin Ghai wrote this 2025 quantum information paper on comparing noisy channels. A quantum channel carries quantum states from sender to receiver. Noise creeps in along the way, thinning the information the state holds.

Chaining one channel after another makes the result noisier still. The question is how to say, in physical terms, that one channel is worse than another. The authors use a broader family of maps for that comparison. These Hermitian-preserving, trace-preserving maps need not be positive maps. Suppose one channel's output can be picked out from another's output statistics. Then, they show, the first channel factors through the second via such a map. That factorization is not always achievable by post-processing. The relation they define forms a preorder among quantum channels. They work on characterizing that order in the paper. A quantifier called physical implementability measures how hard the conversion is.
arxiv-2512-07922:
Saeed Noori Gashti, Behnam Pourhassan, and İzzet Sakallı wrote this 2025 theoretical physics paper. Two conjectures guard the borders of quantum gravity's known lands. The Weak Gravity Conjecture demands gravity be the weakest force; cosmic censorship hides singularities.

Their stage is a charged black hole inside gravity's rainbow. Rainbow gravity lets the geometry itself depend on a probe's energy. The authors ask whether both conjectures can hold there at once. Topological methods first locate the photon spheres around the hole. Unstable light rings with the right charge sit outside the horizon throughout. That finding keeps both conjectures alive across the parameter space. Rainbow functions reshape the metric and shift the extremal limit of charge. A modified charge-to-mass bound follows from that reshaping. The authors then compute how strongly such holes bend passing light. Photons and massive particles both get second-order deflection angles.
arxiv-2512-08322:
Thanh Dao Nguyen, Ngoc Tan Nguyen, Thai Duong Nguyen, and colleagues, wireless researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is network slicing for integrated drone and satellite networks, a building block for global 6G coverage. Slicing divides one network into virtual lanes for different services, but airborne platforms have little power and fast changing conditions.

The team frames trajectory, transmission power, and spectrum choices as one joint decision problem. Their goal balances service quality, low energy use, and fairness across users, for broadband, ultra reliable, and massive device services alike. A multi agent deep reinforcement learning system solves it, trained centrally but executed by each drone on its own. A shared critic with attention, hosted at a low orbit satellite, coordinates the drone agents. In experiments, the approach beat existing methods on reward by a wide margin, with better energy efficiency and fairness at the same time.
arxiv-2512-08622:
Van Que Tran and Tzu Chiang Yuan present a model for dark matter made of heavy vector particles from a hidden sector. In their setup, a hidden gauge force is broken down to a smaller force with a massless dark photon. The dark particles gain a tiny electric charge through mixing between the hidden and normal photon fields.

The weak link to normal matter lets the dark particles build up slowly in the early universe through a freeze in process. Solving the thermal history, including decay of plasma modes, the authors find a wide range of settings that match the observed dark matter amount. The model also respects current limits from space and cosmology. Future detectors for light dark matter may be able to test this idea directly.
arxiv-2512-08922:
Jin Hyeon Kim and coauthors present UniT, a unified diffusion framework for restoring images with degraded text. Recovering readable text from low quality images is important for documents, signs, and screenshots. Diffusion models give strong priors for general restoration, but they often invent text in text focused tasks because they lack explicit language knowledge.

UniT joins three parts in an iterative loop: a diffusion transformer, a vision language model, and a text spotting module. The vision model extracts text content from the degraded image to guide restoration. The spotting module, trained on diffusion features, predicts text at each denoising step, letting the vision model refine its guidance as the image clears. The diffusion backbone then uses those cues to recover fine text detail while suppressing invented text. Tests on two benchmarks show faithful reconstruction of degraded text, far fewer hallucinations, and leading end to end detection scores for the task.
arxiv-2512-09022:
Sandra Zamora and coauthors present the first spatially resolved spectroscopy of a massive galaxy using the Webb telescope. The galaxy is notable for its high nitrogen to oxygen ratio despite low overall metal content. Its conditions reveal early galaxy feedback.

Broad emission components in hydrogen and oxygen lines are found between the two ultraviolet clumps of the galaxy and extend over a large distance. Their shape and motion indicate outflowing gas, not an active nucleus broad line region. The energy injection rate from stellar feedback exceeds the outflow rate by an order of magnitude, while radiation pressure matches the outflow momentum, suggesting stars alone can drive it. Most gas stays confined. Line ratio diagnostics support ionization by star formation and rule out an active nucleus.
arxiv-2512-09122:
Brian Jackson and coauthors develop simple metrics to plan searches for orbital precession and tidal decay in short period exoplanets. Such planets can precess for several reasons, including tides raised on the host star and pulls from other planets. Precession shows up as periodic shifts in transit timing, which precise long term timing of transits and occultations can detect.

Over short time scales, tidal orbital decay can mimic a precession signal, so telling the two apart needs careful model statistics. Occultation data can help separate them, but choosing the precision and schedule needed is complicated. Building on earlier decay search work, the authors map metrics that ease detection of precession and its separation from decay. They discuss which system properties maximize the chance of a detection. Prospects for help from citizen science observations are also considered. The aim is a practical planning guide for timing campaigns on close in planets.
arxiv-2512-09522:
Ziqi Wang, Alessandro Gabbana, and Federico Toschi watch how strangers copy each other in a crowded train station, and how that copying shapes the crowd. Pedestrian route choices matter for safety and design, but the effect of brief interactions between people who do not know each other was poorly understood. The authors use high-resolution trajectory data collected over three years at a route split in a station.

They find a pattern: people tend to take the same path as the person directly in front of them. That holds even with no social tie, and even when that path takes longer. The copying produces bursty dynamics, runs of pedestrians making identical choices in a row, which patterns the collective flow. A stochastic model including route costs, randomness, and social imitation reproduces the behavior, showing local imitation is the dominant driver. The findings carry implications for crowd management and design.
arxiv-2512-09722:
Timothy Budd, Thomas Meeusen, and Bart Zonneveld give a bijective proof of a known fact about hyperbolic surfaces. Work by Mirzakhani showed that Weil-Petersson volumes of hyperbolic surfaces are polynomial in the lengths of their boundaries. Rather than finding the volume, a bijective proof matches surfaces with simpler counted objects, here trees. The authors handle the genus zero case, where the surface is sphere like, with one marked cusp and geodesic boundaries allowed.

Their matching generalizes an earlier tree bijection by Budd and Curien. It required extending the Bowditch-Epstein-Penner spine construction to surfaces with boundaries. As a payoff, they obtain an exact formula for a three point function, a statistic comparing distances among three cusps on a random surface. They close by discussing links to topological recursion and to how such random surfaces behave as cusps multiply.
arxiv-2512-09822:
Nhat A. Nghiem and four coauthors give a quantum algorithm for estimating Ollivier-Ricci curvature. This curvature is a discrete cousin of the Ricci curvature from geometry, defined through optimal transport, the cheapest way of moving mass between distributions. On graphs and metric spaces it has proved useful in settings from spotting fragility in financial networks to combinatorial approaches to quantum gravity. The algorithm takes as input a cloud of points together with the distances between them.

For two particular classes of problem, the authors show their quantum method achieves an exponential speedup over the best known classical methods. Speedups of that size are rare and prized in quantum computing. The authors frame the work as a step toward quantum algorithms for geometry that deliver practical value while also feeding back into basic theory.
arxiv-2512-09922:
Giuseppe Congedo and Andy Taylor present a way to calibrate weak gravitational lensing measurements from the data themselves. Lensing surveys infer cosmic structure from tiny distortions in galaxy shapes, called cosmic shear.
