Reaching the accuracy that current and next generation surveys demand usually requires external simulations to correct leftover biases. Earlier methods handled the multiplicative and additive biases in separate steps. Congedo and Taylor instead infer both kinds jointly, directly from the distribution of measured galaxy shapes.

Their method uses no external simulations and does not depend on assuming a cosmology. Unknown modeling parameters are marginalized over, which softens the impact of degeneracies between bias and signal. They test the technique on a representative problem and show it recovers the biases well, even with noisy data. The authors see strong potential for current and future surveys.
arxiv-2512-10022: Jim Geelen proves a short statement in matroid theory, the combinatorics of independence and separation. A matroid element can be removed in two standard ways, by deletion or by contraction. Tangles are structures that record how a matroid hangs together at a coarse level, and removing an element risks splitting one. Geelen shows this never has to happen: for any element, at least one of the two removals can be chosen so that no tangle splits. The result is a clean tool for inductive arguments in the area.
arxiv-2512-10122:
Hannah Potgieter, Razvan C. Fetecau, and Steven J. Ruuth compute the first eigenpair of the p-Laplace operator, a nonlinear broadening of the classic vibration problem. For large exponent values, the eigenproblem links tightly to the geometry of the domain, but it also becomes numerically tricky. The authors work on both ordinary Euclidean domains and curved surfaces. Their scheme is a surface finite element method that couples a Newton inverse power iteration with a new domain rescaling plan. The rescaling is what keeps the math stable when the exponent grows large.

Tests in one dimension, on planar domains, and on surfaces embedded in three dimensional space show the method is exact and robust. The computed solutions converge toward the predicted infinite exponent limiting behavior, backing the theory where computation can check it. Nonlinear eigenvalue problems of this kind arise in image processing, data clustering, and the study of optimal shapes.
arxiv-2512-10422:
Youmin Ko, Sungjong Seo, and Hyunjoon Kim improve retrieval-augmented generation, the method that lets a language model look up documents before answering. Lookup helps fight made-up answers, but wrong retrievals and multi-step questions still trip it up. Their system, CoopRAG, accepted at NeurIPS 2025, makes the retriever and the model cooperate instead of working in sequence.

CoopRAG first unfolds a question into sub-questions and a reasoning chain with its uncertain spots masked out. It retrieves using that richer query, reranks documents by contrasting the retriever's early and late layers, then lets the model fill the masked spots to rebuild the chain. On three multi-hop question datasets and one simple one, it beat leading methods on both retrieval quality and final answers, and the code is available.
arxiv-2512-10522:
Zahra Rahiminasab, Michael Yuhas, and Arvind Easwaran shrink a reasoning model so it can run on small devices. The starting point is a variational autoencoder. Its latent space is disentangled, meaning each latent direction tracks one real factor of an image. That property is used to reason about test samples that fall outside the training distribution.

Their disentangled distilled encoder compresses that model through student-teacher distillation, written as a constrained optimisation problem that protects the disentanglement while the size drops. They prove guarantees for the distilled model using Rademacher complexity, a standard tool for bounding generalisation. Experiments deploy the compressed model on NVIDIA hardware to show it still reasons about out-of-distribution samples. The aim is trustworthy reasoning about unusual inputs on resource-limited machines, where the big teacher cannot go.
arxiv-2512-10722:
Gil Kalai, Tomer Shoham, and Carsten Voelkmann return to Google's 2019 quantum supremacy experiment with a statistician's scepticism. That experiment, run on a noisy intermediate-scale quantum device, claimed a task beyond classical reach, and the authors' earlier work questioned how well Google's own digital error model predicted the results. New, more detailed data from Google lets them push the analysis further.

The paper extends their check of the error model's key prediction formula against the fuller dataset, and adds a preliminary look at a few other experiments of the same era. The running theme is that statistical fingerprints in the output reveal how faithfully a noisy device followed its intended circuit. The thirty-page study, with nine figures and eight tables, is part of a longer public argument about what near-term quantum experiments actually demonstrate.
arxiv-2512-10922:
Max Zimmer and co-authors make pruning a large language model a matter of simple swaps. Cutting weights shrinks a model's cost, but Transformers punish crude magnitude pruning, and retraining is often unaffordable. Leading methods choose, layer by layer, the mask of weights to keep that minimises pruning error on a small calibration set, a problem solvable in theory, with a huge search space.

Their insight is to split the problem by rows: force every row to keep the same sparsity. And the best single swap, exchanging one kept weight for one pruned weight, becomes computable efficiently from the Gram matrix. The resulting SparseSwaps algorithm starts from any existing mask, runs on GPUs at language-model scale, and needs essentially no tuning. It cut per-layer pruning error by up to sixty percent against the Wanda baseline and improved perplexity and zero-shot accuracy across GPT-style architectures.
arxiv-2512-11022:
Zachary Scofield and colleagues study a distant galaxy cluster that appears to be merging while the universe was only a third of its present age. The cluster, known as XLSSC 122, holds surprisingly mature galaxies for such an early time. Using deep images from the James Webb Space Telescope, the team mapped its mass through weak gravitational lensing.

The mass peak matches both the X ray peak and the brightest cluster galaxy, and the mass estimate agrees with earlier strong lensing work. Data from X ray, radio, and microwave telescopes show the same stretched shape. A clear offset between the microwave signal and the mass peak points to active merging. The study serves as a pilot for mapping cluster mass at such distances with Webb.
arxiv-2512-11622:
Jiri Mazurek and Luis Ángel Calvo find a fresh flaw in a popular decision method. The Analytic Hierarchy Process, or AHP, ranks options by pair wise scores and is used from farming to space flight. Critics have long noted rank reversal, where adding a copy of an option can flip the ranking.

The pair name a new kind of flip. If all pair scores keep their direction but grow stronger by the same rule, the eigenvector method can still reorder the options. The geometric mean method stays safe from this flip. They show the effect on a real NASA case about ranking gear for the planned lunar Gateway station.
arxiv-2512-11922:
Muhammad Waseem and co-authors report field lessons on vibe coding, where developers describe what they want and AI writes the code. The style speeds up prototypes and small products. It also hides a flow debt trade off: smooth generation now, tangled upkeep later.

Drawing on several in house minimum viable products and industry reports, the team traces debt to architecture drift, security holes, and missing design reasons. Process habits, training data bias, and the rush for quick output all feed the problem. Limits in current models, platforms, and hardware add to it. The paper ends with concrete countermeasures for teams that want the speed of vibe coding without mortgaging their future code base.
arxiv-2512-12122:
Elynn Chen, Yuefeng Han, and Jiayu Li tackle tensor classification in a 2025 paper. Tensors are data arranged in many dimensions, now often made by neural networks. Sorting such data is hard when samples are few and dimensions are many, and older methods lack firm error bounds.

The team gives the sorting tensor a low rank CP structure, since strong signals seem to sit in a few parts. Their method starts with a random form of PCA, then refines its answer step by step. They prove it converges and reaches best possible error rates. Tests on graph data beat older tensor methods and graph neural networks.
arxiv-2512-12322:
Dongyeong Ko proves smoothness results for minimal hypersurfaces with symmetry in a 2025 math paper. A minimal hypersurface is a surface that locally minimizes area, like a soap film. Ko studies minimization problems with cohomogeneity two symmetry, where group orbits fill the space in a controlled way.

He builds a min-max theory in that symmetric setting, based on ideas from Pitts and Rubinstein in 1988. As a use case, he constructs many minimal hypersurfaces on round spheres in dimensions 4 to 7. For large genus, their first Betti numbers grow without bound, and they approach a union of a sphere and a Clifford hypersurface.
arxiv-2512-12722:
Tarik Viehmann and four co-authors bring rule based programming to robot coordination in ROS 2 in a 2025 paper. CLIPS is a rule based language for knowledge driven applications, well suited to coordinating autonomous robots, whose behavior depends on many facts and rules at once. A CLIPS executive existed before, but inside the lesser known Fawkes framework, limiting its reach.

The team integrates CLIPS into the ROS ecosystem, the standard middleware for robot software. That makes rule based executives available to the far larger ROS 2 community. They also show the setup's flexibility by integrating a planning framework based on PDDL, the standard planning description language. The paper describes both integrations and how they work together.
arxiv-2512-13122:
Vivek Alumootil and Tuan-Anh Vu present DePT3R, a system that tracks dense 3D points and rebuilds dynamic scenes in a single forward pass. Older methods process image pairs, need known camera poses, or assume frames arrive in time order. Those limits hurt use in fast-changing scenes.

DePT3R extracts deep features over space and time with a strong backbone, then predicts pixel-wise maps with dense heads. It needs no camera poses, which frees it for unposed image sets. On several hard dynamic-scene benchmarks, it performed strongly while using far less memory than prior state-of-the-art systems. Code and data are openly available.
arxiv-2512-13222:
Johannes Schottner, Qingguang Xie, Gaurav Nath, and Jens Harting simulate how filaments settle as a droplet dries on a surface. Such deposits, made of nanowires or nanotubes, underpin flexible sensors and printed electronics. Their final pattern controls how well the layer conducts electricity, yet patterns are hard to steer.

The team varied filament length, stiffness, and concentration under two evaporation regimes. Slow, reaction-limited drying suppressed the coffee-ring pileup at the edge and gave centered, conductive deposits. Filaments aligned tangentially at the rim, radially in the middle, and randomly at the center. Tuning the regime lowered the threshold for a connected conducting network.
arxiv-2512-13322:
Sakshi Shukla, Praveen Srivastava, and Kazunari Kaneko use the nuclear shell model to study mirror nuclei, pairs whose proton and neutron counts are swapped. They focus on sd-shell nuclei with isospin projection plus or minus two, across masses 20 to 36. Differences between mirrors trace a breaking of isospin symmetry.

Using two isospin non-conserving interactions, USDC and USDCm, they compute energy spectra, mirror energy differences, and transition strengths. They also work out magnetic and quadrupole moments and compare all of it with experimental data. Single-particle states receive special attention for weakly bound and unbound nuclei, above all the s-wave states, along with separation energies and occupancies.
arxiv-2512-13522:
Frédéric Blondeel, Lorenzo Pareschi, and Giovanni Samaey propose a new cooling scheme for simulated annealing, a search method that cools like a metal. Classic schemes lower the heat by a slow log rule to reach global minima. Their method, called CAST, lets a group of agents learn the cooling plan together.

In CAST, particles swap temperatures through random pairwise contacts, in a Boltzmann-type framework. Under set conditions, the mean temperature of the group falls in a steady way. Tests on hard benchmark problems with many peaks show faster convergence than classic annealing. The gain is largest where flexible search matters most.
arxiv-2512-13722:
Deepak Sah and Manoranjan P. Singh study electron-positron pair creation by trains of electric pulses with random timing. Pair creation from strong fields is a basic quantum effect, and pulse trains can shape the momentum pattern of the pairs made. They solve the quantum Vlasov equations for alternating-sign, Sauter-like pulses.

Random delays between pulses are drawn from a Gaussian spread, set by a standard deviation. As that spread grows, the fringe pattern in the momentum spectrum changes sharply. Averaged spectra take a Gaussian-like envelope with residual wiggles, strongest at the center. For 20 pulses, a spread near 31 inverse mass units, about 17% of the mean delay, raised the central peak nearly tenfold. A spread near 50 raised it to about a thousandfold.
arxiv-2512-13822:
Jinning Liang and co-authors predict galaxy disk structure from dark matter halo traits in the TNG50 simulation. This second paper in a series measures many halo properties: density structure, angular momentum, shape, assembly history, and environment. Disk sizes, scale heights, and mass fractions are measured for galaxies from redshift 0 to 4.

Random Forest regression shows halo traits alone predict disk size and thickness with high accuracy. Symbolic regression gives compact formulas with slightly lower accuracy. Disk height is easier to predict than size, and low-mass halos give better accuracy than massive ones. Halo concentration, shape, spin, and recent mass growth were the most informative traits. The authors supply formulas that map halo properties to disk structure for galaxy-halo modeling.
arxiv-2512-14722:
Gröbner bases are a central tool in computer algebra. They are used to solve systems of polynomial equations in many variables, a task with many practical uses. Transformers were first applied to computing them in recent work, and an improved approach is presented here.

The improvement uses hierarchical attention transformers, whose layered design matches the layered shape of the computation. The resulting system is called HATSolver. Faster symbolic computation would help fields from robotics to cryptography that rely on such equation systems. The work also tests how far learned models can go on exact mathematics, where answers are simply right or wrong.
arxiv-2512-14822:
L. Bisigello leads a large team that found a surprising set of dusty small galaxies in James Webb Space Telescope data. Dust usually grows with a galaxy's mass, so small galaxies should hold little of it. Yet some dwarfs show far more dimming by dust than their size predicts.

Using survey data called CEERS, the team picked out 1361 such galaxies, which they name HELM sources. Most lie at modest distances, with a typical mass of ten million times the mass of the Sun and strong dust dimming of about 2 magnitudes. Their sizes look normal, so the dimming is not a trick of viewing angle. They cluster a bit more than plain dwarfs and form stars a bit less, hinting that crowding or past encounters may explain the extra dust.
arxiv-2512-15022:
Jianhao Xu uses machine learning to spot faulty magnets inside the storage rings that feed light sources. Errors in quadrupole and sextupole magnets blur the beam and cut the brightness and stability of the light. The usual fixes work from closed orbit data and are slow.

Xu's framework predicts gradient errors and misalignments directly from beam position monitor readings and closed orbit distortion. Training data come from ELEGANT simulations of a four bend achromat ring. Four regression models are compared: linear regression, support vector machines, a radial basis function network, and a dense convolutional network. The learned models predict the magnet errors well and rebuild the ideal optics. The approach could speed up commissioning, give online diagnostics, and support live correction in next generation rings.
arxiv-2512-15822:
P. K. Kamlesh and co authors compute properties of two novel half Heusler materials, CaZnC and CaZnSi, from first principles in a 2025 paper. Half Heusler compounds are studied for energy conversion and optoelectronic uses. Predicting a new compound's structure and behavior before synthesis saves costly trial and error in the lab.

Using density functional theory in the WIEN2k package, the team optimizes structures and computes thermoelectric, optical, elastic, and thermodynamic traits. CaZnC shows a direct band gap of 1.186 electron volts, while CaZnSi shows an indirect gap of 1.067. Optical results suggest photovoltaic promise, and thermoelectric figures support energy conversion use. Elastic checks show both materials are stable and brittle.
arxiv-2512-16122:
Xiaohui Liu and four co-authors analyze flashes from deep space in a paper uploaded to arXiv in 2025, accepted by the Astrophysical Journal. Fast radio bursts are millisecond blasts of radio energy, and some sources repeat. Telescopes only catch bursts inside their listening band, which can distort the apparent spread of burst energies.

Focusing on the repeater FRB 20220912A, observed by China's FAST telescope, the team used simulations to separate real effects from selection bias. They find the true energy distribution fits a log-normal shape with a characteristic energy of 8.13 times 10 to the 37 erg, plus a power-law tail. A low-energy peak reported earlier vanishes once bias is removed, so it was an observational artifact. The two-humped pattern instead traces the burst's own radiation mechanism.
arxiv-2512-16222:
Kevin J Kelly and Mudit Rai study how to tell apart hypothetical particles in an arXiv paper published in 2025. Neutrino experiments with particle beams can also create long-lived particles with masses below a GeV, which might reveal new physics. Many competing models predict nearly identical signatures, so seeing something would not say what it is.

The authors test whether the DUNE experiment's near detectors could separate different particle classes and production mechanisms. Two features help: excellent energy resolution, and the PRISM concept, which moves the detector off the beam axis to sample different energy mixes. Together they improve discrimination between models that would otherwise look the same. The study guides how future data could pin down the nature of a discovery, not just its existence.
arxiv-2512-16522:
C Pinto leads a large team in observing a brilliant X-ray source in their arXiv paper from 2025, accepted by Astronomy and Astrophysics. NGC 55 ULX-1 is an ultraluminous X-ray source, an accreting compact object shining far beyond normal limits. Winds blown off its accretion flow may regulate how much matter it can swallow.

Across a multi-year XMM-Newton campaign, high-resolution spectra resolved the wind's emission and absorption lines at several epochs. The line patterns favor photoionized, low-to-moderate density gas of the classic disk wind kind. Emission comes from a slow, cool, variable plasma, perhaps a thermal wind. Absorption lines are shifted by about minus 0.15 times light speed, confirming powerful radiatively driven outflows. The wind answers the source's brightness changes, offering a window into its true accretion regime.
arxiv-2512-16622:
Elmar Langetepe and Florian Gans study a search task in the half-plane, where a seeker must find rays or lines with no advance word of where they lie. The task grows out of the classic cow-path problem and also models search over sloped ground.

The pair give and analyze a search plan with a worst-case score below 9.12725, meaning it never takes much more than nine times the best route. They also prove no plan can beat 8 in general, with a floor of at least 9.06357, so their plan is near best, off by less than 0.064. The same ideas sharpen older results for the ground search version.
arxiv-2512-17822:
L. Sundberg and six coauthors study how small particles twist as they sink through a still fluid. Computer models of such motion often borrow force rules fitted to simple shapes like spheres or rods. For odd shapes, modelers first need to know how a shape's symmetry limits the twist it can feel.

The team uses symmetry arguments and small step math to pin down the allowed form of that twist at low flow speeds. They check the rules against direct sums for nearly round particles, and the two agree. The result gives modelers a sound starting form before they fit numbers for real particle shapes.
arxiv-2512-18022:
Shad Durussel, Gergely Molnár, and Jean-François Molinari explain a flaw in a popular way to simulate breaking materials. The phase field method paints cracks as soft damage zones, which frees the crack path from the grid. In fast breaking, though, those zones keep growing wider than they should.

The team traces the widening to elastic waves getting trapped in the soft zone, where they cause extra damage. Their fix erodes mass in the damaged area so waves keep their true speed, and the fake spreading shrinks. With the fix, crack speeds and energy rates match classic fracture theory as the zone is made fine.
arxiv-2512-18222:
Evangelos Vlachos of the ATHENA Research Center in Patras studies drone networks that steer their beams both electronically and by turning the aircraft itself. Phased arrays scan fast, but their limited field of view forces the airframe to rotate to stay connected. His 2025 letter proposes a decentralized model predictive control framework for the whole network. It optimizes trajectory and heading together, maximizing total network capacity under safety constraints.

Fast fading channel nulls make the control unstable. Vlachos answers with a regularized surrogate cost built on discrete spatial smoothing. He proves the smoothing bounds the cost curvature and restores Lipschitz continuity. A sufficient condition links that constant to the controller gain, guaranteeing contraction and linear convergence. In simulations the algorithm balances beam tracking against flight safety, and it clearly outperforms velocity aligned baselines. The result points toward reliable high frequency links for cooperating drone fleets.
arxiv-2512-18822:
Alberto Sesana and Daniel G. Figueroa review the new nanohertz gravitational-wave sky. Pulsar timing arrays, which watch a galaxy-wide set of spinning neutron stars for tiny timing shifts, have found evidence of a background hum. Their 63-page review, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and bound for the Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics, explores what could be making it.

The leading suspect is astrophysical: countless pairs of supermassive black holes spiraling together, their signals stacked into one background. Environment effects, eccentric orbits, and sparse sampling blur predictions but also offer fingerprints to test that origin. The alternative is cosmological, a relic from inflation, phase transitions, or topological defects in the early universe. Either way, the signal probes dark matter, primordial black holes, and cosmic strings, opening a window no telescope could.
arxiv-2512-19122:
Mahir Labib Dihan, Sadif Ahmed, and Md Nafiu Rahman help programmers write code from instructions in Bangla. Bangla is a low-resource language for code generation, with few labeled datasets or tools. Their system, BanglaForge, turns Bangla function descriptions into working programs.

Two language models work as a pair: one writes a first solution, and a reviewer improves it using feedback from actually running the code. Retrieval of examples, careful prompts, and translation steps support the pair. On the BLP-2025 Bangla benchmark, BanglaForge reached a Pass@1 score the authors call competitive. The result shows collaboration plus self-revision can carry a low-resource language far.
arxiv-2512-19222:
Irfan Habib, Deniz Kus, and Chaithra Pilakkat extend root-system theory to Kac-Moody superalgebras, algebraic structures that mix even and odd symmetries. A pi-system is a chosen set of positive roots. Attaching a subalgebra to it raises a basic question: which real roots does that subalgebra actually own?

The authors show the real roots arise by applying even and odd reflections again and again to the pi-system, and that they form a closed subroot system. With that in hand, they prove a super version of Dynkin's classic bijection. Further results treat root strings, and show graded embeddings are exactly the subalgebras built from linearly independent pi-systems.
arxiv-2512-19322: Hassan Alhussein sets out constructions for the cohomology of tri-dendriform algebras, a kind of algebra with three linked operations. His approach ties that cohomology back to classical tools, so known methods can be reused. The stated payoff is simpler computation for a young algebraic structure whose invariants are otherwise hard to reach. The record gives the construction in outline form only, with applications left to the full text.
arxiv-2512-19422:
Muhammad Mansur Zubairu, Abdullahi Umar, and Fatma Salim Al-Kharousi dissect a small subsemigroup of the Schröder monoid. The monoid holds all order-preserving, order-shrinking partial maps of a finite chain. Their subfamily excludes every map whose domain contains the first element, a small cut with large algebraic effects.

They study the semigroup, its two-sided ideals cut by image size, and the matching Rees quotients. Each object proves right abundant for all sizes, yet none is left abundant once the chain has two or more points. Rank formulas follow: the quotient and its ideal share a rank given by a sum of binomial terms.
arxiv-2512-19522:
Zhuo He, Yingdong Ru, Qianying Liu, and Paul Henderson replace the usual dense neural shader with a convolutional one for physics-based rendering. Neural relighting learns the rendering equation from real photos, a boon when true material data cannot be had. Dense perceptron shaders, though, carry huge parameter counts and train slowly.

Their deferred pipeline, pbnds+, shades with convolutional networks instead, cutting parameters and lifting shading and relighting quality. An energy regularizer reins in reflections under dark lighting, where skewed training data usually misleads models. Experiments back the design, and the authors stress practical gains: cheaper training, faster rendering, and steadier behavior in dim scenes.
arxiv-2512-19922:
Ryusuke Hamazaki and three co-authors wrote a long primer on quantum systems that are watched as they run. New lab tools can track quantum dynamics with fine control. The primer lays out the basic formalism. First comes quantum measurement theory. Then come quantum trajectories. Those are the single histories a system follows, given one set record of outcomes.

Later parts turn to spectra and typical behavior. The averaged map's spectral traits govern whether paths behave typically. They bear on ergodicity and on purification. Lyapunov exponents of typical paths serve as marks of measurement-driven phase shifts. At over one hundred sixty pages, with twenty figures, the article is a door into the field. It appears in its accepted form.
arxiv-2512-20622:
Atmane Ayoub Mansour Bahar, Andrés Alayón Glazunov, and Romaric Duvignau survey the quietest kind of network attack. Passive attackers never touch the target network; they only listen, which makes them nearly impossible to detect. From the traffic they can fingerprint websites and applications, identify systems and users, and track positions.

Such attacks are well documented on Wi-Fi and, to a lesser extent, LTE. For 5G, theory says they remain possible, but directional beamforming, high-frequency propagation, and encryption constrain them severely in practice. For beyond-5G and early 6G, no public tools exist and hardware costs are prohibitive, so the attacks are currently infeasible. The survey flags a threat-model gap: future networks are being designed before their passive-attack surface is understood.
arxiv-2512-20822:
Zhan Qu and Michael Färber built MediEval to test medical language models on knowledge and patient context together. Older tests either quizzed textbook facts alone or judged bedside reasoning without checking correctness. MediEval instead links real patient records from MIMIC-IV to a knowledge base drawn from standard biomedical vocabularies.

The benchmark writes true and deliberately false medical statements inside real patient stories, then grades models on grounding and consistency together. Testing exposed dangerous failure modes, including invented support and answers that flip the truth. The authors' fine-tuning fix, CoRFu, penalizes unsafe confusions more heavily. It raised accuracy sharply and removed the truth-flipping errors entirely in their tests.
arxiv-2512-21422:
Nathan Stringham, Ana Marasović, and their co-authors investigate why teaching people about a language model's failure patterns has not yet curbed overreliance on the model. People see chatbots write poems and answer hard questions, so they wrongly assume the same systems will not stumble on simple arithmetic. Earlier work tried to find such patterns automatically and teach them.

The team first checks whether teachable failure patterns exist, grouping questions by their meta-labels in two datasets. They find sizable groups where the model is reliably error-prone, so patterns do exist. Next they test whether prompting and embedding-based tools can discover those known patterns, with mixed results. Finally they propose a better yardstick: measure whether users, once taught, can predict when the model will fail. A user study using that metric shows a positive effect from teaching. The approach could work, given better automatic discovery tools.
arxiv-2512-21522:
Alireza Sepehri and Muhammad Al-Zafar Khan rebuild a holographic cosmology idea inside a system from string theory. Padmanabhan had argued that a mismatch between surface and bulk degrees of freedom drives the expansion of the universe. The authors ask whether the same mechanism works in a BIon, two branes joined by a wormhole.

In their construction, each brane is itself assembled from lower-dimensional branes. Joining the small branes releases energy, and compactifying some dimensions releases more. Those releases create the surface-bulk gap the holographic argument needs. The gap drives the evolution of the universe living on one brane, changing quantities such as entropy and the Hubble constant. Working through the model, the authors recover the standard Hubble parameter and its dependence on redshift.
arxiv-2512-21622:
Nidhi Nidhi, Ambesh Kumar Pandey, and K. Sreenadh study normalized solutions of nonlinear equations with variable exponents. A normalized solution is one whose size, its mass, is prescribed in advance; the equation's Lagrange multiplier then becomes part of the unknown. Variable-exponent problems, where the power in the equation changes from point to point, arise in fluids and image processing.

To the authors' knowledge, normalized solutions had not been studied in the variable-exponent setting before. The standard scaling argument breaks down here, because rescaling changes the exponent structure. The team works in a constrained variational framework and proves a ground state solution exists, the lowest-energy state at the prescribed mass. They show the solution enjoys local Hölder-type regularity. They derive a Pohožaev identity adapted to variable exponents, that every solution must obey, and use it to confirm the solution is a ground state.
arxiv-2512-21822:
Judah Immanuel, Avik Mahata, and Aniruddha Maiti replace the inner loop of molecular dynamics with a learned graph neural network. Tracking atoms step by step is accurate but slow, since forces must be recomputed each step. A surrogate that jumps configurations forward in time could speed materials work greatly.

Their network turns each atom's setting into a graph. Message-passing layers with attention capture how atoms sit and interact in metallic systems. Rather than predicting forces, the model predicts how far atoms move, learning the system's evolution operator. Trained on classical simulations of bulk aluminum, it reproduces positions to sub-angstrom accuracy within its training horizon, and stays stable beyond it over short ranges. Checks agree with reference data: radial distribution functions and mean squared displacement trends match. The authors frame such surrogates as complements to traditional dynamics inside their validated regime, not wholesale replacements.
arxiv-2512-22122:
Lyu Yi, Weiqi Feng, Yuanbiao Wang, and Yuhong Kan tackle a trust problem in learned cardinality estimation, the database task of guessing how many rows a query will return. Learned estimators can beat classic methods on accuracy, yet they sometimes break monotonicity: relaxing a query should never shrink its estimated count. Such violations make production database teams wary of adopting them.

The authors propose MonoM, a metric that measures how well an estimator respects monotonicity across a workload. They also add a training system with a generator of comparable query pairs and a new regularization term in the loss. Tests show the training improves monotonicity and, by curbing overfitting, also improves accuracy over the learned estimator they studied.
arxiv-2512-22222:
Gnankan Landry Regis N'guessan introduces Müntz-Szász Networks, neural networks built for functions with sharp, fractional-power behavior. Usual networks use fixed activations like ReLU or tanh, which fit boundary layers, fracture mechanics, and corner singularities poorly. His architecture instead puts learnable fractional power terms on each connection, with exponents trained alongside the coefficients, grounded in the classic Müntz-Szász approximation theorem.

The paper proves the design keeps universal approximation and derives sharp error rates for singular targets. On regression tests with singular functions, the networks reached five to eight times lower error than standard networks while using ten times fewer parameters. On physics-informed problems, including a singular differential equation and stiff boundary layers, they improved results three to six times and learned exponents matching the known solution structure.
arxiv-2512-22322:
Shaofei Cai and eleven co-authors from the Youtu-Agent team rethink how to check whether a software agent finished its task. Verifying GUI agents today usually means a judge re-reading the whole noisy interaction history afterward, which is costly and unreliable. SmartSnap flips the job: the agent itself must gather proof while it works, in the form of a small set of decisive screenshots.

The authors call this design a Self-Verifying Agent, guided by completeness, conciseness, and creativity principles for its evidence. A general language model judge then rules using only those snapshots. On mobile tasks, training agents this way lifted performance substantially for both eight-billion and thirty-billion parameter models. The agents rivaled much larger systems while making verification cheap and scalable.
arxiv-2512-23122:
Dongmin Gang, Byoungyoon Park, and Huijoon Sohn revive and extend a bridge between knot theory and conformal field theory. In 2003, Hikami and Kirillov noticed that Kashaev invariants of torus knots match characters of the Virasoro minimal models. The work rebuilds that connection by combining the 3D-3D correspondence with a bulk-boundary correspondence from supersymmetric gauge theory.

The authors study three-dimensional gauge theories attached to torus-knot complements through the Dimofte-Gaiotto-Gukov construction and follow them to the infrared. Depending on the knot parameters, the theory flows to one of two places. It may reach a unitary topological theory whose boundary algebra reproduces the unitary minimal model. Or it may reach a rank-zero superconformal theory realizing the non-unitary minimal model after a twist. The machinery yields Nahm-sum-like formulas for characters. It gives an algorithm building rational vertex algebra characters from triangulation data.
arxiv-2512-23322:
Dhruv Nigam builds and compares techniques for cleaning room echo out of recorded speech. The goal is to enhance the spectrogram of reverberant speech until the room's smearing is removed. The work uses a single recording channel and no knowledge of the room in advance, which is what makes the task blind. The core tools are nonnegative matrix factorization and its deconvolution variant, which model the spectrogram as patterns unfolding over time.

Several variants are tried. Some factorize the speech spectrogram, or respect timing links through convolutive models and frame stacking. One novel route applies matrix factor deconvolution to the activation matrix of the reverberated spectrogram. Quality is judged on TIMIT sentences with measured room responses from the REVERB 2014 challenge, using perceptual quality and cepstral distortion. The literature's broad claims checked out, though exact numbers could not be reproduced. The novel approach improved the metrics inconsistently.
arxiv-2512-23722:
Adam Kamel, Tanish Rastogi, Michael Ma, Kailash Ranganathan, and Kevin Zhu ask what a language model secretly learns about a game it cannot fully see. In games of perfect information such as chess, models are known to build internal representations of the board. Poker is different: opponents' cards are hidden, so success requires tracking beliefs about unknown hands, not just visible state.

The team pretrained a GPT-style model on poker hand histories and probed its internal activations. Without explicit instruction, the model had learned deterministic structure, such as hand rankings, and probabilistic features, such as equity, the chance a hand ultimately wins. Nonlinear probes could decode these features, and the representations correlated with theoretical belief states. The work was presented at a NeurIPS 2025 mechanistic interpretability workshop.
arxiv-2512-23822:
Z. T. Wang and six co-authors report what happens when electrons in an ultra-clean two-dimensional system are driven faster than sound. Their sample is a two-dimensional electron gas of ultra-high mobility, cooled to millikelvin temperatures and placed in a magnetic field. A steady current drags the carriers along; at a current density of about one ampere per meter, their drift speed reaches the speed of sound in the material.

Beyond that sound barrier, very strong resonant features appear in the magnetoresistance, phonon-induced resistance oscillations with only weak temperature dependence. Below the barrier, by contrast, the resonant scattering fades as temperature drops unless another scattering channel amplifies it. Comparing with theory, the team extracted an electron-phonon coupling constant for the strongly nonlinear regime and found evidence for a predicted phase change of the oscillations exactly at the barrier crossing.
arxiv-2512-24122:
Kristóf Benedek and Géza Ódor simulate Europe's high-voltage power grid. They ask what happens when lines become direct current. Their tool is an adaptive second-order Kuramoto model. That model is the standard stand-in for coupled oscillators. The simulations keep nonlinear effects throughout. Those effects matter during disturbances and cascading blackouts.

Steadier synchronization links to the grid's scaling behavior. Smaller cascades appear under the same conditions. But upgrades cut both ways. At strong and weak couplings, power changes widened frequency spread. Braess-like effects also appeared. There, an improvement makes things worse. Three line types were compared. Adaptive direct-current lines performed best in steady state. They respond to local frequency differences. Their drawback is very long settling times.
arxiv-2512-24222:
Tuhin Subhra Mahato and Subhra Sankar Dhar make persistent homology robust. Persistent homology reads geometric features from data through its support. Outliers can distort that reading badly. They may sit outside the main data cloud. They may also hide inside it. The proposed method trims data to resist both cases.

Theory backs the trimming approach. The bottleneck distance links the robust version to its population analogue. That distance can be made arbitrarily small. A definite rate comes with a large enough sample. Practice matches the theory in tests. Simulated data of several kinds were used. Benchmark real data from cellular biology served as well. Readers in topological data analysis gain a version of homology that tolerates contaminated samples.
arxiv-2512-24422:
Vinicius Mikuni, Ibrahim Elsharkawy, and Benjamin Nachman carry a physics model across fields. Models of this kind learn features that transfer to many tasks. Their earlier model, OmniLearned, was trained on collider data. It sharpened discovery reach across collider experiments. This paper asks whether collider knowledge helps cosmology.

The answer is yes, within the tested settings. The collider-trained model improved predictions of cosmic parameters. It also predicted halo and galaxy speeds in CosmoBench datasets. Those datasets differ sharply from particle collision data. The authors stress the milestone. A model from collider physics had never been shown to work across fields of science before. Such transfer hints at shared structure in physical data.
arxiv-2512-24622:
Qingyu Xu and three colleagues build detection tools for fire rescue scenes. Commanders need object detection to make decisions during rescues. Prior work favored mountain and forest settings. Urban scenes are more frequent and more complex, yet understudied. Existing systems also detect few classes, mostly flames and smoke.

Their dataset, FireRescue, targets command needs directly. It covers urban, mountain, forest, and water scenarios. Eight key categories include fire trucks and firefighters. Nearly sixteen thousand images carry thirty-two thousand bounding boxes. An improved YOLO model accompanies the data. An attention module sharpens easily confused categories, like fire trucks against ordinary trucks. A dynamic sampler strengthens foreground features under smoke. Results improve detection across YOLO variants in these chaotic scenes.
arxiv-2512-25022:
Johanna Duntsch and Felix Gunther develop a discrete theory of real Riemann surfaces using four-sided grid splitting called quad-graphs and a linear gridding of the Cauchy-Riemann equations. A discrete antiholomorphic involution, the symmetry key a real surface, is built. Topological types of discrete real surfaces are sorted, getting back standard results on real ovals and separation.

A symplectic homology basis adapted to the involution supports a discrete period matrix with the same canonical splitting as in the smooth theory. Discrete geometry readers get a faithful discrete version of a standard subject. Keeping period structure intact is the hard part that makes the gridding useful.
arxiv-2601-06622:
P. D. Khanh and four co-authors build rough-but-sound solvers for a wide class of problems in 2026. The class is made of costs writ as a gap between two bowl-shaped costs. Such problems show up in many fields, in work with flow and heat laws too.

Their new solver lets each step be worked out in rough form. Slopes can be read with some error, and sub-steps need not be solved in full. Yet the solver still lands on a flat point, and they prove this holds. Real solvers are never exact, so this match to practice counts for a lot. The team shows the solver at work on flow-based design tasks. The proof's slack is what makes the method safe to run. It is a rare case where loose steps keep a firm pledge.
arxiv-2601-07022:
The Upstage Solar Team posted a 2026 arXiv report on a new large language model called Solar Open. Solar Open has 102 billion settings, called parameters. It works in two languages. It is built as a Mixture-of-Experts model, where each chunk of text is sent to a few expert parts, not the whole model. The report aims at languages that most models serve poorly.

The team lays out a clear method for how such a model can match strong rivals. They name three linked tasks that drive the work. The first task is data. Scant data in the target languages makes training hard. To fix that, the team made 4.5 trillion tokens of new data. The data is of high grade, tied to set fields, and shaped for later reward-based training. The report tells builders how the whole build was done.
arxiv-2601-07722:
Vishal Parmar and Ignazio Bombaci study the crust of neutron stars with Bayesian methods and a unified matter model. Neutron star crust is the solid outer layer of the densest known stars. Their framework uses a relativistic mean-field description of dense matter throughout. The analysis focuses on probability distributions for crust properties. Several kinds of evidence constrain those distributions.

The constraints come from nuclear experiments, chiral effective field theory, and multi-messenger neutron star observations. Bayesian methods let all three speak at once, with uncertainty kept visible. Crust properties affect how neutron stars cool, spin down, and emit gravitational waves. A unified model avoids stitched-together descriptions of different layers. The paper speaks to nuclear astrophysicists who need crust estimates with honest error bars.
arxiv-2601-07822:
A Cosmoglobe team builds a unified model of large-scale thermal dust emission across microwave and infrared bands. They fit a four-component dust model to COBE-DIRBE data between 3.5 and 240 micrometers. The work sits inside the global Bayesian end-to-end Cosmoglobe DR2 reanalysis. Their 2026 preprint is part seven of that series. A concordance model is the goal: one description that fits many data sets at once.

Dust emission blocks and biases views of the cosmic microwave background. A model that works from infrared to microwave frequencies helps separate dust from the primordial signal. Four components let different dust populations glow in their own ways. Bayesian end-to-end analysis keeps instrument effects inside the same fit. The paper speaks to cosmologists who clean microwave maps. It also serves scholars who study galactic dust itself.
arxiv-2601-07922:
Krystian Iłkiewicz and colleagues report a bow shock around a white dwarf that has no accretion disk. Bow shocks form when an outflow meets the interstellar medium. In white dwarfs that accrete from a companion, outflows usually come from a donor wind, the disk, or a surface explosion. A diskless accreting white dwarf should not obviously drive one. Yet the team finds a persistent bow shock around such a system. Their 2026 preprint presents the case.

Persistence matters: a steady shock needs a steady outflow to sustain it. Finding one without a disk challenges the usual list of outflow sources. Magnetism may play a role, as the system is a magnetised accretor. The result pushes astronomers to rethink how these binaries shed matter and energy. The paper serves scholars on cataclysmic variables and white dwarf binaries. It is an observational puzzle with theoretical consequences.
arxiv-2601-08122: Atefeh Termehchi, Ekram Hossain, and Isaac Woungang analyze domain generalization for recurrent neural networks. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that deep learning models often lack interpretability and fail on new data distributions. That weakness undermines trust, above all in safety-critical uses. Interest has grown in both explaining generalization and building models that hold up off-distribution. The authors give a generalization analysis and a method for a family of recurrent networks. Recurrent models process sequences, so their behavior across domains matters for speech, text, and sensor data.
arxiv-2601-08522: Louis Gaillard wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on bounds for the degree of solutions to two kinds of equations. The kinds are linear differential equations and recurrences. Such equations show much about their own solutions. They also serve as neat forms to store solutions, for sums with special functions. Gaillard finds a large class of methods that build such forms. Each method builds a linear link between steps of a basic operator called a pseudo-linear map. The bounds cap the size of what those methods produce.
arxiv-2601-08822:
D. Pauli and eight co-authors study the most huge stars and how they shed mass. Huge stars pour out light and wind. That flow shapes the space round them and once helped clear the early fog of the cosmos. Yet the life path of such stars is still not well known, so their true flow is hard to gauge.

The team looks at mass loss when a star nears its light cap. Past that cap, light push can throw off whole shells of gas at once. Such bursts can change the star mass fast and shift its whole late life. A reader in star work gets a fresh take on those bursts. They may be a main key to how huge stars end.
arxiv-2601-09522:
Badr-Eddine Marani and five co-authors work on making neural network predictions honest about doubt. Their 2026 arXiv paper adapts conformal prediction to each class separately. Deep networks often sound sure even when they are wrong, and their stated probabilities can mislead.

Conformal prediction wraps a model's output in a set with a guaranteed coverage rate. A single global rule, though, can give some classes loose sets and others tight ones. Class-adaptive training aims to even that out while learning. Fairer uncertainty matters most where a wrong, confident answer is costly, as in medical imaging.
arxiv-2601-10022:
Dilipkumar Asthagiri and Dmitry Matyushov track how water holds a twist over time. In a fluid, a twist does not fade at a flat rate. Past twists shape how the next twist fades. This drag from the past is named a memory effect. It bends the fade curve from a plain exp form.

Such memory curves had not been worked out for the spin of water. The pair now do that math. They treat one water unit on its own. They also treat the full sample as one whole. The test case is the SPC/E model of water. The curves aid work on how fluids move and react.
arxiv-2601-10122:
Ye Wang, Jiaxing Chen, and Hongjiang Xiao map the state of role play agents. These agents act as a set role in talk. They may play a guide, a peer, or a famed name. Large language models gave this field a fresh push.

The paper sorts past work in three waves. First came rule based forms with set lines. Next came style copy, where agents learned how a role talks. Last came mind copy, with traits and memory at the core. The team lists what each wave can do. They also name what still blocks the field and where it may go next.
arxiv-2601-10522:
Federico Malizia, Andrés Guzmán, Federico Battiston, and István Kiss study how nested sets speed or curb spread on a hypergraph. In such a net, a set can hold an other set in full. That nest form is named nested hyperedges. Spread here can be a germ, a tale, or a trend.

The team build a theory for spread on such nets. Nested sets help spread start at a lower point. Yet they curb the sharp jump form of spread. That jump is named explosive behavior. The twin acts were not both known till now. The work ties micro form to macro acts.
arxiv-2601-10622:
Yu-Han Ni, Chao Wu, and Jiang-Hao Yu build amplitudes for massive particles in the Standard Model. Amplitudes give the odds of particle processes. Working in the minimal helicity-chirality frame, they construct amplitudes with more legs from basic blocks. The blocks are contact amplitudes with three and four particles.

The four-point contact terms turn out to be needed. Without them, gauge invariance breaks in the broken Standard Model. That symmetry is what keeps the theory consistent. A recipe like this speeds up the math for events with heavy particles. It extends an earlier massless-massive correspondence the authors set out in part one.
arxiv-2601-10722:
Daniel Casini, Jian-Jia Chen, Jing Li, Federico Reghenzani, and Harun Teper survey real-time support in ROS 2. ROS 2 is the middleware that ties robot software parts together. It offers modular design, spread-out execution, and rich communication. Robots that must react on a strict clock need more than that: they need timing they can count on.

Over the last six years, both researchers and industry have pushed ROS 2 toward hard real-time use. The survey gathers the support, the analysis methods, and the latest advances. It maps what is proven, what is patched, and what is still missing. Teams building time-critical robots get a guide to what ROS 2 can promise today.
arxiv-2601-10822:
Jeffrey Davis and co-authors present a framework for choosing the best observables at the Large Hadron Collider. An observable is a measured pattern in collision data. Some patterns are far more sensitive to new physics than others. The team integrates analytic methods with machine learning to compute observables that are optimal for effective field theory and wider uses.

They also introduce a new metric for judging how well such methods perform. Better observables mean each collision yields more evidence. At a machine where new particles may hide in rare corners, that gain matters. The work helps collider physicists squeeze the most physics from data they already collect.
arxiv-2601-11022:
Sravan Danda, Aditya Challa, Shlok Mehendale, and Snehanshu Saha adapt models at test time by matching geometric quantiles. Test-time adaptation adjusts a classifier when test data drift from training data. Most methods tweak the model's weights, tying them to one architecture. The authors seek a method that serves transformers and convolutional networks alike.

Their approach matches high-dimensional geometric quantiles between training and test data. Quantiles summarize a distribution's shape, so matching them can realign a model without deep surgery. Drift is the norm in deployed vision: new cameras, weather, and sites all shift the data. A broad, architecture-free adapter could keep models accurate where they actually run.
arxiv-2601-11222:
Haochen Wu, Heng Wu, and Benzhuo Lu teach neural nets to solve equations. Their 2026 preprint deals with linear PDEs, a core class in applied math. For some of these, a known base solution shape exists. The team builds its whole method around that fact.

Most operator learning needs data from the full domain. Their frame trains on edge data alone, by sharp contrast. It uses the values and slopes found on the boundary. Fake data from the base solution feeds the training set. Edge integral tools add the rest of the math needed. The mix aims at fast solves that still respect the boundary.
arxiv-2601-11622:
Hassan Ugail and Newton Howard read language models as systems that change in time. Their 2026 preprint seeks working regimes inside LLMs. Text writing runs through vast inner workings in the model. How those workings unfold in time is poorly understood.

Most work on reading models stresses static states instead. Causal interventions are the other common lens in the field. Both leave temporal structure largely unexplored, they argue. The team borrows concepts from neuroscience for the task. Temporal integration and metastability mark neural organization there. They adapt those ideas to transformer models here. A combined time metric is computed from activations. It is tracked across step-by-step text writing in the model.
arxiv-2601-12022:
Amir Dalal, Vladyslav Kozii, and Jonathan Ruhman test if broken symmetry can kill a route to superconductivity. The Kohn-Luttinger route makes superconductivity from pure repulsion between electrons. Its first proof needs full rotational symmetry.

Real materials have only discrete symmetries, such as those of a crystal grid. The team ask how strong that break must be to stop the effect. If the route is robust, more plain materials could host it. Their work sets bounds on that robustness with care.  The bounds show how much break the route can stand.  If it holds, plain repulsive matter could pair in more cases than thought.
arxiv-2601-12222:
Yishan Lv, Jing Luo, Boyuan Ju, and their co-authors grade the beauty of AI-made songs. Generative AI now makes much music, so auto grades are needed. Past work deals with speech, plain audio, or singing quality, not song beauty as such.

Most tools guess one exact mean opinion score. That misses the nuance of how humans judge beauty. Their method uses multi-stem attention, which splits a song into parts, plus a model of doubt in ranks. A richer grade could guide music tools with more taste.  Doubt aware grades fit how fans judge songs too.
arxiv-2601-12422:
Jiri Blazek and five co authors work on cosmic ray air showers. When an ultra high energy cosmic ray hits the air, it spawns a vast cascade of particles. Models of how hadrons collide drive how that cascade grows. Three generic traits of those collisions matter a lot: cross section, elasticity, and multiplicity.

The team present a way to tweak those three traits on purpose. They then run full three dimensional simulations of the showers. Any observable can be checked to see how much each tweak moves it. This gives a clean test of how much model doubt flows into real data. Their work was prepared as a preprint for a leading physics journal.
arxiv-2601-12522:
Asif Mohammed Samir and Mohammad Masudur Rahman work on finding bugs in code with AI agents. Bugs cost tech firms billions of dollars each year. Developers spend roughly half of their time on bug resolution. One key step is localization: finding which parts of the code are at fault.

Older methods score each code part on its own, by how suspicious it looks. That view misses how parts connect across a codebase. A fault often makes sense only when links between methods and files are seen. The team give agents two aids: formed hypotheses and dynamic cognition. Their paper was set for a program comprehension venue in 2026. Better localization could cut a large share of debugging time.
arxiv-2601-12622:
N. J. C. Spooner and colleagues report direct measurements of thoron gas coming off detector materials. Thoron is radon 220, a radioactive gas that seeps from many solids. Radon is a major background in rare event physics, where tiny signals hide easily. Measuring how much gas a material emits is a key way to control that background.

Most past emanation work targeted radon 222, the dominant isotope for these backgrounds. Thoron has been measured far less, despite its own risks. The team measure thoron emanation inside the chamber itself, a direct approach. Rare event searches, like dark matter hunts, need such care at every step. A missed background can fake a discovery, so these checks matter.
arxiv-2601-12822:
Wenqi Zhang and five co authors defend computer use agents against malicious instructions. These agents use large foundation models to operate systems through graphical interfaces. They can perform complex tasks autonomously on a real machine. That autonomy introduces serious security risks, though. Malicious instructions or visual prompt injections can trigger unsafe reasoning.

Unsafe reasoning can lead to harmful system level actions before a human notices. Their system is called MirrorGuard. It works toward secure agents via simulation to real reasoning correction, per the title. Testing reasoning in simulation first could catch bad plans safely. The work serves the safe deployment of agents that click, type, and run commands.
arxiv-2601-13222:
Laura Dietz and co-authors fold judged facts into text that AI writes from sources. Their line of work joins auto judging into retrieval augmented generation, where a model writes with docs in hand. The aim is text that can be checked, fact by fact.

Their system is called Crucible. It builds a bank of question and answer bits, called nuggets, from the docs it pulls. Each nugget keeps a clear link to its source. The bank then guides how text is drawn out, picked, and put into a report. For teams that need sourced text, the route keeps claims tied to proof as the text is built, not just checked at the end.
arxiv-2601-13422:
Dahai Yu and co-authors guess home level energy use in a frame built for trust. Such guesses aid grid runs, build plans, and storm reply. Many deep tools for the task miss one of two needs. Some skip how homes sway each other in space. Some cannot scale to one guess per home.

Their frame is called TrustEnergy. It aims for both fine scale and sound doubt. A guess per home with a trust score fits how grid teams act, by block and by home. For firms, a fine guess they can trust beats a sharp guess they cannot check. The frame joins the two in one build.
arxiv-2601-13522:
Shuang Li speeds up low rank tensor sense for Tucker forms by a chance based step swap rule. Tensor sense works back a big multi way array from few reads. Low Tucker rank forms are prized since they hold multi mode plans in small room. Past tools project the full array at dear cost, or split it yet still sum full gradients.

Their rule is called StoTAM. It swaps steps in a round and uses chance picks in place of full sums. Each step then works on a part of the task, not the whole. For signal and learn teams with huge arrays, a cheaper step can be the gap of a run that ends and one that times out.
arxiv-2601-14122: Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul study weighted zero-sum constants for sequences over a finite field in 2026. A sequence over the field of p elements is weighted zero-sum if set weights make its weighted sum vanish. The weights here come from a set tied to the p-adic valuation. Constants in this area give the smallest length that forces such a pattern.
arxiv-2601-14222:
Tiziano Schiavone and co-authors revisit matter creation as a driver of cosmic acceleration in 2026. The persistent Hubble tension motivates alternatives to standard cosmology. So does the lack of a fundamental explanation for dark energy. Gravitationally induced particle creation is a phenomenological non-equilibrium process.

It can effectively mimic a dynamical dark-energy component in the late universe. The team places observational constraints on this matter creation process. They test it against the Hubble tension, the mismatch in expansion rate measures. A viable mimic would ease two puzzles with one mechanism. The tests use real sky data, not just toy runs. A model that fits the data and eases the tension would earn a close look.
arxiv-2601-14422:
Jackson H. O'Donnell leads a team on a strong gravitational lens in this 2026 paper. The lens is a galaxy cluster known as the Carousel lens, at redshift 0.49. Its gravity bends light from galaxies behind it. The team presents a spectroscopic survey of the field. They measured both field galaxies and lensed sources near the cluster.

Spectroscopy spreads light into a spectrum, which yields redshifts and chemical clues. This paper is the first in a series, marked by the Roman numeral in its title. Readers get the survey base for the Carousel field: who is there, at what distance, and which sources the lens magnifies.
arxiv-2601-14522:
Hunjae Lee and Corey Clark analyze how transformers move information in this 2026 paper. In decoder-only, causal transformers, the computation graph is set by causal masking. Information flows through direct-path attention. It also flows through indirect paths formed by intermediate tokens. The authors name those indirect paths runways.

They argue that certain failure modes of causal transformers trace to a misalignment. The direct and indirect modes of propagation do not line up as they should. A growing body of recent work reports the failures they study. Their title calls the effect the runway cascade. Readers get a new lens for why causal models stumble in patterned ways.
arxiv-2601-14722:
Surapon Nonesung and four co-authors present a Thai document model in this 2026 paper. Document extraction is a core component of digital workflows. Existing vision-language models predominantly favor high-resource languages. Thai presents additional challenges. Its script uses non-Latin letters, and it lacks explicit word boundaries. Real-world Thai documents are also often highly unstructured.

Those traits limit the effectiveness of current open-source models. The team's model, Typhoon OCR, is an open vision-language model for Thai document extraction. The need is wide. Thai forms run from bank slips to old state files, and most tools read them poorly. Readers get a tool built for a language most OCR systems treat as an afterthought, tested on the messy documents Thai offices actually handle.
arxiv-2601-15122:
Parviz Ahmadov and Masoud Mansoury tackle a skew in recommender systems called popularity bias. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the way a few hit items hog attention. Most items stay underexposed, which hurts both quality and fairness of exposure.

Past fixes help somewhat, but they rarely show how they work. The authors move from insight to intervention. They steer single neurons inside the model in a way that can be read and checked. That steering aims to curb the bias while keeping the system's choices open and transparent to its users.
arxiv-2601-15222:
Stavrow A. Bahnam, Robin Ferede, and a Delft team teach a drone to race at champion level with one camera. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with autonomous drone racing. The sport pushes light flying robots to their physical limits.

The onboard AI must run under tight limits on weight, power, and time. Most racing systems lean on richer sensing. MonoRace takes a robust monocular approach instead. A single camera feeds the AI that steers the drone around the track. The paper reports how this lean setup reaches true champion-level racing speed.
arxiv-2601-15722:
Xiuling Wang, Xin Huang, Haibo Hu, and Jianliang Xu cut communication costs in federated graph learning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Graph neural networks learn well from graph-structured data. Federated versions train across decentralized data holders. That setup protects privacy but creates heavy traffic. Sharing graph data or updates between sites is costly. It can also leak structure that holders want to keep.

The authors use generative diffusion modeling to ease the load. The title promises communication-efficient federated graph classification. Diffusion models can synthesize stand-in data, reducing what must be sent. Classification across graphs held by banks, hospitals, or platforms is the use case. For federated learning, communication is often the true bottleneck. Cutting it widens where the method can run.
arxiv-2601-16122:
Jörg Schröder and Maximilian Vorwerk set out a step rule for maths of small magnets. Their 2026 preprint deals with the Landau Lifshitz Gilbert maths. That maths tracks how the magnet dir shifts in time. Steps must keep the length of the magnet dir fixed. Drift in length breaks the sense of the result.

The pair use a growth based step that holds length by form. They show the step keeps the true build of the maths. It also keeps key traits like energy loss in line. A sound step lets codes run magnet acts with trust. The work serves teams who model thin magnet films and gear.
arxiv-2601-16622:
Lin Huang and coauthors build on the fly fair gaze with straight store cost. Their 2026 preprint, named E2Former-V2, deals with graph nets for 3D atom sets. Such nets must treat turns and shifts of the set as same. Past top builds make dense parts for each edge in the set. Dense parts blow up store cost as sets grow large.

On the fly gaze skips dense parts and keeps store straight. Straight store lets the net run on big atom sets. Big sets span drugs, stuff and cell parts of real worth. The work seeks scale for fair atom nets. It tests speed and grade side by side.
arxiv-2601-16722:
Martina Alutto, Qiulin Xu, Fabrizio Dabbene, Hideaki Ishii, and Chiara Ravazzi model how green habits spread. Their 2026 preprint joins two forces in one frame. One force is peer talk, which shapes what folks think. The next force is use, which grows by spread from user to user. Each force feeds back on the next.

The team then asks how to steer the spread well. A plan-ahead control picks nudges over time. The web of links has more than one layer. Such tools could help towns push clean acts. They could also warn where push plans may fail.
arxiv-2601-16822:
Andrei Antonov, Pietro Bisio, Mariangela Bondì, Andrea Celentano, Anna Marini, and Luca Marsicano build a part for a dark matter hunt. The NA64 test at CERN fires positron beams at a thick block. Dark bits, if made, would slip out unseen. The miss in energy would be the clue. Their 2026 preprint tests a gauge block named POKERINO.

The block must gauge beam energy with fine care. The team built a first model and ran beam tests. They checked its spread and drift with care. A sound gauge keeps false clues out of the hunt. It also sharpens the true miss mark if dark bits exist.
arxiv-2601-16922:
Navid Ardeshir, Samuel Deng, Daniel Hsu, and Jingwen Liu sharpen how much data group learning needs. Group learning must do well for each crowd in a pool. Crowds may overlap, and their count can be vast. Their 2026 preprint studies a case where each crowd's aim can be hit in full. In that case, less data is needed than in the loose case.

Plain risk cuts over the right class give the gain. The gain holds though crowd count is not fin. It needs just a fin gauge of crowd shape. Less data per task cuts cost in fair AI work. Such work spans loans, health, and school tools.
arxiv-2601-17222:
Jonathan Soriano and six co-authors work on redshift measures for galaxies. Redshift tells how far a galaxy is and how the cosmos has grown. Spectra give exact values, but they are slow to take. Photos give rough values fast, a method called photometric redshift. Machine learning models do much of that work today.

The catch is range. Most models train on spectra-linked sets and fit few galaxy types. The team tests ways to widen that range. They also work on honest doubt ranges for each guess. Broad, trusted redshift maps help map galaxy growth. They also sharpen tests of the cosmos as a whole.
arxiv-2601-17522:
A. Mantile and A. Posilicano study the acoustic operator with piecewise constant coefficients. The operator models sound in media split into zones. Each zone is a bounded Lipschitz domain with its own speed and density. Transmission conditions link the zones at their borders. The authors work out the resolvent and spectrum of the operator. They also study its resonances.

Resonances govern how sound rings and decays in such media. They matter for room acoustics, sonar, and medical ultrasound. A firm spectral picture guides safe simulation. It also shows where energy can trap. The work is core analysis for wave physics. Piecewise media are the rule in real materials, not the exception.
arxiv-2601-17822:
Khlood Alharthi and Paul Stevenson study ripples in the shape of atomic nuclei. Their 2026 preprint is about octupole excitations. These are states in which the nucleus wobbles in a pear-like way around its steady shape. Each wobble tests what the matter inside the nucleus is like. Shape changes probe how the matter handles squeeze, surface stretch, and shifts between proton and neutron parts.

The paper focuses on the role of surface energy in these states. The surface of a nucleus acts a bit like the skin of a drop, and its stiffness shapes the wobble. Pinning down that role helps link lab data to the physics of nuclear matter. Such links feed into models of stars and of how nuclei hold together.
arxiv-2601-18022: Tsao-Hsien Chen proves a duality result in the relative Langlands program. His 2026 preprint shows that the cotangent bundle of a quasi-split symmetric space matches a dual space. That dual is the variety of the loop symmetric space for the Langlands dual group. The result gives concrete cases of relative Langlands duality for non-split groups, a setting where such cases have been scarce.
arxiv-2601-18322:
A team of authors improves spatial audio capture for head-worn devices. Their 2026 preprint deals with neural Ambisonics encoders. Smart glasses and extended reality headsets need high-quality spatial sound from small microphone arrays worn on the head. Ambisonics is a device-agnostic format that maps array signals to spherical harmonic coefficients. In practice, accurate encoding from a compact array is hard. The authors use residual learning to help neural encoders do that mapping better.

Residual learning trains a network to fix the errors of a base estimate. Better encoding means more believable sound scenes for the wearer. Spatial audio sells immersion in calls, media, and assistive tech. The work targets a core step in that chain.
arxiv-2601-18522:
D. Alexander and four colleagues weigh how much the gas from farm stock warms the Earth. The gas, methane, leaks from the guts and dung of herd beasts. The team argue that its role in world heat is so small that it counts for next to nought. They back the claim with a thought test about the world's herd of cows.

In that test, to wipe out all cows on Earth at once would cut the gas by a share that moves world heat by a few hundredths of a degree. The team say such a small shift shows that herd gas is not a main driver of heat. The claim runs against the main view in climate work, and it is sure to draw sharp replies. Read it as one side of a live row, set out with its own sums.
arxiv-2601-18722:
Lintang Sutawika and three colleagues find a way to lift a model's thought in tongues it was barely trained on. When a hard ask comes in a rare tongue, scores drop far past the score for the same ask in English. That gap locks out much of the world from the best of these tools. The team use no fresh data in the rare tongue at all.

Their plan has the model play it-self in pairs. A judge twin, fed the English ask as a hid edge, grades pairs of tries in the rare tongue. The grades teach the model to pick its best line of thought, tongue by tongue. A lift with no new data is a prize for low-resource tongues. It could spread strong thought tools to lands they now skip.
arxiv-2601-19122:
Weiran Guo and three co-authors hunt for weak spots in how models call outside tools. Function calling lets a language model use software tools and data feeds, a key skill for agents. Ways to train that skill rest on hand labeled or model made data, which may leave blind spots.

The team uses reinforcement learning to grow attack data that exposes those blind spots. Training against its own worst cases should harden the model where it truly fails. The loop mirrors how security teams probe a system: find the break, then teach against it.
arxiv-2601-19322:
Péter Salvi designs smooth surfaces that pass through every corner of a given mesh. A closed mesh of any topology sets the corners; the surface must interpolate them all. His method blends local patches, each a multi sided quadratic piece, into quadrilateral patches that join smoothly.

Faces with other than four sides need a special parameterization built from rational curves. Triangles among the subpatches get their own handling, with alternate forms discussed. Smooth through point surfaces serve design and animation, where a cage of points must become a skin that looks unbroken.
arxiv-2601-19422:
Moses Boudourides refines a classic network measure and ties it to how disease spreads. Newman's assortativity grades whether like nodes link to like. Boudourides splits that grade by a fixed partition of the nodes. Edges are classed by whether their ends sit inside a region or on its boundary.

The split yields interior boundary assortativity profiles, a finer structural fingerprint. He shows the profiles arise naturally from epidemic dynamics of the SIS kind on the network. A finer fingerprint could predict spread better, since where an edge sits, core or border, shapes how infection crosses between regions.
arxiv-2601-19522:
Jiadong Li, Hans-Walter Rix, and a large team of astronomers count the smallest stars in the oldest parts of our galaxy. Their target is the stellar mass function, which says how many stars are born at each mass. They focus on low-mass stars in regions poor in iron and other heavy elements. No one had measured this count for such metal-poor stars before.

Stars with few heavy elements formed early, when the galaxy was young. Their mass pattern is a fossil record of that era. The team reports the first determination of this function for such stars. The result tests ideas about how star formation changes with chemical makeup. It also sharpens the story of how the Milky Way built its oldest populations.
arxiv-2601-19622:
Thomas Bömer and four colleagues automate a craft inside search algorithms. A* search finds good paths by guessing, at each step, how much cost remains. That guess is the heuristic, and its quality decides how fast the search runs. Heuristics are usually handcrafted by experts, which takes time and skill.

The authors use large language models to design heuristics inside an evolutionary loop. Their twist is prompt augmentation: the prompts guiding the model are improved in a structured way. Better prompts should yield better candidate heuristics with less waste. The work tests how far this automated design can go. If it holds up, search tools could tune themselves for new problems.
arxiv-2601-19922:
Laya Iyer, Kriti Aggarwal, and colleagues build a benchmark for emotional support conversations. Supportive dialogue needs more than fluent language. A good supporter reads emotions, adjusts tone, and handles resistance, frustration, or distress. These skills decide whether a conversation actually helps.

Their benchmark, HEART, assesses humans and language models on the same footing. Putting both through identical tests exposes where models truly lag. It also shows where human supporters vary. Emotional support is a growing use of AI, in apps and helplines alike. A shared benchmark sets a bar for safety and quality. The work gives the field a common measure for a delicate task.
arxiv-2601-20322:
Martin Markl and Dominik Trnka prove a three-way equivalence in category theory, the abstract study of structures and maps. They show that a pointed category has kernels exactly when it is a lax algebra for the arrow 2-monad. They also show this holds exactly when the category is the décalage of a supercoherent structure.

The authors then read categories with kernels as the long-sought weak version of unary operadic categories. Equivalences like this let results move between fields: a fact proved in one language becomes usable in another. The paper ties homotopy-flavored algebra to concrete categorical structure.
arxiv-2601-20422:
Yumou Liu and five colleagues study paid promotion on content platforms and find a flaw in how it interacts with recommendation. Platforms offer promotion to cure cold start, giving new content exposure through auctions. The authors' empirical analysis shows promotion rescues low-to-medium quality content but can harm high-quality content.
