Forced exposure to the wrong audiences pollutes the engagement signals that drive future recommendation, so good content gets downgraded. The authors build an information-aware auto-bidding method to guide the recommender instead. Their work shows promotion must be aimed, not just bought. Aimed well, the same spend can lift both reach and trust.
arxiv-2601-20722:
Milan van Zanten writes about portals in virtual reality in this 2026 paper. A portal is a window or door that links one space to another. In computer graphics, portals have long had many uses. They can show which parts of a 3D scene are visible. They can split a scene into separate areas. They can also act as mirrors.

Van Zanten focuses on the kind of portal a user can see and step through. In VR, such a portal must be drawn so the view stays smooth and true. The paper explains how these views are rendered. It covers the graphics ideas that make a doorway into another world look right. For VR builders, it is a clear guide to a classic trick of the trade.
arxiv-2601-20822:
Mohammadali Mohammadi and four co-authors study a wireless network boosted by simple relay boxes. Their 2026 paper concerns repeater-assisted massive MIMO with full-duplex links. Massive MIMO uses a base station with very many antennas. Repeaters amplify what they hear and re-send it at once. Full-duplex means sending and receiving share the same frequency band at the same time.

In their setup, each repeater has a single antenna. The base station serves many users at once, some sending up and some receiving down. All of this happens over one band, which is hard to keep clean. The paper analyzes how such a network performs. Repeaters are cheap and simple, so the design could raise capacity without new towers. The work speaks to the design of dense future wireless networks.
arxiv-2601-20922:
Luis Sánchez-Soto, Andrei Klimov, Aaron Goldberg, and Gerd Leuchs present a sky-like way to picture quantum spin states. Their 2026 paper concerns Majorana stars. A spin state can be drawn as a set of points, its stars, on a sphere. For a spin-S state, the stars number twice S. Some stars are defined as the coherent states orthogonal to the given state. The picture turns algebra into geometry.

The authors call this map the quantum sky of Majorana stars. The representation offers insight into structure, symmetries, and entanglement. It bridges abstract formulas with intuitive pictures. A reader can see symmetry as a pattern of points. Entanglement shows up in how the stars arrange themselves. The paper serves physicists who teach or reason about spin. It refreshes a classic visualization with a modern treatment.
arxiv-2601-21122:
Jeremy Tanlimco and six co-authors build a cavity for matter waves driven to an extreme. Their 2026 paper studies a matter-wave Fabry-Pérot cavity in the ultrastrong driving regime. When an optical cavity's length is modulated, theory predicts a striking effect. Energy concentrates exponentially around particular space-time trajectories. Viewed stroboscopically, photons inside propagate as if in curved spacetime. Black hole and white hole horizons appear as fixed points of the motion.

The authors realize the same drama with atoms instead of light. Matter waves replace photons in the driven cavity. Ultrastrong driving pushes the system far beyond gentle shaking. Stable and unstable fixed points mimic horizons. Such analog systems let labs probe curved-spacetime physics on a bench. The paper extends a rich analogy between optics, atoms, and gravity.
arxiv-2601-21522:
Sagi Meir, Tommer D. Keidar, Noam Levi, Shlomi Reuveni, and Barak Hirshberg get more solved questions from a fixed budget of language model tries. The usual score counts a question as solved if any of many tries succeeds. With a fixed budget, a better score counts how many distinct questions get solved overall.

Their reset-and-discard method drops stalled attempts early and starts fresh ones. Wasted tries on one hopeless question can then fund progress on others. The metric they propose matches what users with real budgets care about. It rewards breadth of solved problems over deep grinding on a few.
arxiv-2601-21622:
Junhao He, Feiran You, and Hongyang Du scale speculative decoding across clusters of accelerators. The trick drafts tokens with a small fast model, then has the big model verify them. Most designs assume one machine, while modern serving spreads models over many nodes.

Their framework, StarSD, uses one draft model to serve many target models at once. The star layout links the single drafter to targets on distributed nodes. Sharing the drafter cuts wasted hardware across the cluster. Faster, cheaper generation matters as chat and coding tools serve millions of requests from shared data centers.
arxiv-2601-21722:
Neil Heinrich Braun, Keane Ong, Rui Mao, Erik Cambria, and Gianmarco Mengaldo harden language models for spotting greenwashing in company reports. Sustainability reports feed environmental and social scoring, yet vague claims often dress up thin action. Standard text models lean on surface patterns and fail on new wording.

The authors use an efficient framework that shapes the model's inner space with contrastive learning and an ordinal ranking goal. The ranking teaches graded steps between concrete action and empty talk. Sharper detection helps investors and regulators tell real progress from polished prose. It also pressures firms to report deeds, not adjectives.
arxiv-2601-22022:
J. Baños-Gutiérrez and co-authors study groups where light and matter merge into one. Each group joins a tiny silver particle with dye molecules called TDBC. The particle traps light in a very small space. The dye gives off light at a set color. When the two sit close, they link so strongly that the light and the dye act as one thing.

The team looks at three things: how the dye is built, how it sticks to the silver, and how messy the groups are. Real groups are never neat, and mess changes how they act. This work helps those who build new sensors and new light sources. It shows what these mixed groups need to work well in real life, not just in clean lab tests.
arxiv-2601-22122:
Omar Mohsen builds a new lens for equations that govern waves and heat on curved spaces. His 2026 preprint starts from a set of vector fields that meet a classic reach rule, named for Hörmander. He defines a calculus with two grades, built to fit both the plain case and a bent, sub-Riemannian one.

The build rests on geometry, with a blow-up trick to untangle stuck points, plus tools from operator algebras. The goal is the strongest smooth-out claim the setup allows. Such claims tell us when rough inputs still yield smooth outputs. The work is part one of a planned series.
arxiv-2601-22322:
Ayesh Abu Lehyeh, Anastassia Gharib, and Safwan Wshah aim to pin down where a device sits indoors, using Wi-Fi. Their 2026 preprint notes that GPS fails inside, yet apps for guidance, tracking, and safety need a firm fix. Graph models that link access points and devices give fine reads.

The gap they target is doubt: most tools give a point with no trust range. Their graph transformer adapts to each space and reports how sure it is. Honest doubt marks matter when a wrong fix has real costs. The method suits smart halls, stores, and clinics.
arxiv-2601-22422:
Jie Mei and four co-authors work out how pion particles behave inside a strong magnetic field. Pions are light particles made of quarks, key to the strong force. Their 2026 preprint uses a standard quark model, the NJL model, with a method built for charged particles in fields.

They treat both neutral and charged pions, and weigh heat and symmetry effects too. Such extreme settings echo the early cosmos and dense stars. Knowing pion traits there helps decode signals from both. The work is theory, done with care. It maps a small but telling corner of the strong force.
arxiv-2601-22522:
Zhou Tang and a large team test whether 3D point clouds can grade a dairy cow's body condition on their own. Body condition scores track a cow's fat and health, and guide feeding. Their 2026 preprint asks if depth-based shape data beat flat images for auto scoring.

Point clouds hold the true curve of the back and hips, where fat shows. A sound auto score saves labor and catches health slips early. The team weigh the added worth of the depth data. The work fits precision farming, where each cow's state counts. It is a clear, practical test.
arxiv-2601-22622:
Andrés Solís-Cuevas and Pablo Vázquez-Montejo work out how a round fluid vesicle dents when a stiff ring grips its equator. A vesicle is a tiny bubble of fluid film, like a simple cell wall. Their 2026 preprint stays in the linear regime, where the dent is small.

They solve the governing equation in closed form, holding area and volume fixed, with the ring as a local rule. The solution shows how the bubble trades shape for the grip. Such models aid lab work on cells and capsules. They also give a clean check for simulations. The work is exact and spare.
arxiv-2601-22922:
Sachin Chauhan, Tobias Ekholm, and Pietro Longhi connect knot theory with the counting of holomorphic curves. They study open strings on the complement of a fibered knot, the space left when a knot is removed. Their counting uses skein-valued methods, which keep track of richer algebraic data than plain numbers.

The result is a flow loop formula for the skein-valued partition function in two settings. One is the cotangent bundle of the three-sphere, and the other is the resolved conifold. Such formulas tie knot invariants to string theory in a precise way.
arxiv-2601-23022:
Lung-Hao Lee and a large team build datasets for finer-grained sentiment analysis. Aspect-based sentiment analysis rates feelings toward specific aspects of a product or service. Older datasets use coarse labels like positive or negative, which miss the strength and shade of a feeling.

Their DimABSA datasets rate sentiment along dimensions instead, across many languages and domains. Dimensional labels capture mixed, graded opinions far better than three boxes. Richer benchmarks should push review analysis closer to how people really express views. Dimensional labels replace the old positive-or-negative boxes, recording sentiment strength along continuous scales for each aspect.
arxiv-2601-23222:
Hamza Kalisch and four co-authors train medical image segmentation without costly pixel-level labels. Dense annotations are the gold standard, but they are expensive and limit scale. Deployed systems already emit cheap quality signals, like model agreement and uncertainty scores.

Their region-normalized preference method learns from those noisy judges instead of ground truth. Normalizing by region keeps large and small structures treated fairly. Training from existing quality signals could scale segmentation to hospitals without annotation teams. Model agreement, uncertainty measures, and learned mask-quality scores are the inexpensive signals the method learns from instead of annotations.
arxiv-2603-01622:
Arabic speech synthesis lags behind other large languages, in part because training data and vowel marks are scarce. Ahmed Musleh, Yifan Zhang, and Kareem Darwish attack both gaps in this 2026 work. Written Arabic often drops short vowel marks, which leaves speech tools unsure how words should sound.

The team built a pipeline that gathers Arabic recordings and cleans them with no hand work. Speech checks, text matching, auto vowel marking, and noise filters yield thousands of hours of training audio. They then train voice-cloning speech models on small, mid, and full data sets, with and without vowel marks. Marked text still helps, but sheer data size closes much of the gap. A public model that needs no vowel marks is planned.
arxiv-2603-01722:
Leonardo Modesto and Lorenzo Orlando complete the inflation theory of the early universe at high energies in this 2026 work. Inflation explains the smooth, flat cosmos we see, and the Starobinsky model drives it with a curvature-based action. Prior nonlocal fixes for its quantum side clashed with stability needs.

Their new nonlocal completion keeps every classical feature of the local theory intact. Background solutions and perturbation equations match at linear and nonlinear levels alike. Cosmic observables thus stay as the local model predicts, while the quantum theory gains sound footing. The construction works for any local action in the Einstein frame, with details given for two cases. Since the theory is at least super-renormalizable, and may be finite, inflation survives as an exact quantum-gravity solution up to small corrections.
arxiv-2603-02222:
Artus Krohn-Grimberghe audits a medical math benchmark in this 2026 paper. The benchmark, MedCalc-Bench, tests language models on clinical calculator tasks. Scores for direct answers have stalled near a third correct on its checked split. The author asks whether the test really measures clinical reasoning at all.

A full audit found over twenty faults in the benchmark's own calculators. Faults ranged from wrong formulas to code bugs that broke runs. Giving models the formula sheet at test time lifted scores sharply, past all prior results. No extra training was needed for that gain. A top model with the sheet nears the ceiling, and left-over errors trace mostly to flawed answer keys. The test, he argues, mostly measures formula recall and arithmetic.
arxiv-2603-02322:
Gabriele Franciolini and Davide Racco revisit dark matter born from evaporating black holes in this 2026 paper. Tiny primordial black holes could have formed in the early universe and fully evaporated. Their evaporation would spray out stable dark sector particles. The authors focus on a subtle flaw in that story: unevenness across the sky.

Black holes form with random clumping on tiny, unseen scales. If early ripples linked large and small scales, that clumping leaks onto cosmic scales. The leak passes to dark matter through evaporation, creating isocurvature ripples. Such ripples are tightly limited by observations of the early universe. The authors reassess other limits too, including excess dark matter and induced gravitational waves. Isocurvature may bind this scenario more than once thought.
arxiv-2603-02522:
Liang Zeng, Valerio Marsocci, Wufan Zhao, and colleagues exploit neighboring satellite images in self-supervised learning in this 2026 paper. Masked autoencoders learn by rebuilding hidden parts of an image. Earth observation work has added multiple sensors and time points to that recipe. Spatial links between neighboring scenes, though, remain largely unused.

The Earth's surface is continuous, so adjacent images carry rich context about each other. Their method, NeighborMAE, jointly reconstructs neighboring Earth images during pretraining. A heuristic adjusts mask rates and pixel loss weights to keep the task hard. Without that care, neighbors could leak answers too easily. Across pretraining sets and downstream tasks, results beat existing baselines significantly. Neighboring context, they conclude, is valuable free supervision.
arxiv-2603-02722:
A. I. Breev and D. M. Gitman connect two ways of building special quantum states on group-shaped spaces. Their 2026 paper studies solutions of the Schrödinger equation found by the non-commutative integration method. That method exploits symmetry when variables refuse to separate in the usual way.

The question is whether those solutions match generalized coherent states, the well-known states that sit closest to classical behavior. The authors show the match holds when a certain representation tied to the method is real. The result ties a solution technique to a state family used across quantum optics and group theory. It also clarifies when group-based solutions can be read as coherent states.
arxiv-2603-03022:
Cheng Peng, Yonghao Li, Wanfu Gao, and colleagues pick the most useful features from data that arrives in several views with many labels. Their 2026 method, SEHFS, targets two weaknesses of information-based selection. Features often correlate in groups of three or more, which pairwise methods miss, and heuristic searches can stall in local optima.

The method reshapes the feature graph into an encoding tree that minimizes structural entropy, grouping strongly redundant features and separating the rest. A matrix framework then blends a shared meaning matrix with per-view contributions to balance global and local aims. Theory supports the high-order learning claim, and tests on eight datasets from varied domains beat rival selectors. Ablation studies confirm each part contributes.
arxiv-2603-03122:
Marvin Plogmann characterizes the algebraic fingerprints of the simplest objects in abstract categories. His 2026 paper asks when two simple-minded collections, sets of basic building blocks, share the same derived endomorphism algebra up to quasi-isomorphism. The question spans module categories, abelian and exact categories, and their differential graded versions.

One property turns out to be central: whether the collection is d-complicial, in Lurie's sense, for some level d. The characterization doubles as a coherent generation property for minimal models of the endomorphism algebra. Along the way, Plogmann defines length exact differential graded categories and ties them to truncated variants, generalizing earlier work by Enomoto. The results organize a scattered corner of homological algebra around one clean condition.
arxiv-2603-03322:
Chaoqun Yang and six colleagues ask whether language models can derive knowledge that is genuinely new. Testing that is tricky: fixed test sets leak into training data, and fast model releases date them quickly. Their 2026 answer is DBench-Bio, a living benchmark for biological knowledge discovery that rebuilds itself on a schedule instead of standing still.

A three-stage automated pipeline does the work. Roberto Rivera tackles a quiet bias in Gaussian process regression in 2026. This is the spatial prediction workhorse, also known through its best linear unbiased predictor. When the assumed smoothness of the covariance is wrong, the reported prediction error comes out too small.

Dimitropoulos and Mamoulis argue that the standard score for approximate nearest neighbor search measures the wrong thing, in a 2026 arXiv paper. ANN search finds near matches quickly and powers retrieval and recommendation systems. The field tunes algorithms for Recall@k, the fraction of true nearest neighbors retrieved. The authors contend that what matters is the quality of what comes back, not its overlap with the exact answer set, and that chasing recall forces needless computation.

They propose judging by the inverse approximation ratio, which compares distances of retrieved neighbors with the true ones. The metric needs no judge model or tuning parameters. Learning from examples is usually done over flat Euclidean spaces, but a robot's state, including its orientation, evolves over curved spaces called Riemannian manifolds.

On a manifold, the natural motions between two points are geodesics, the shortest paths, but finding them requires solving second-order differential equations. Existing methods are costly to run. It estimates geodesics with neural ordinary differential equations, then decodes the paths back into the task space before use. It describes the design, reports insights from simulation tests, and discusses challenges and prospects. For understanding, the team built a 504-question benchmark spanning raga grammar, cultural knowledge, and notation reasoning, grounded in Hindustani theory and Bengali forms including Rabindra and Nazrul Sangeet. They tested 33 language models. Frontier models reached 85 to 90 percent accuracy, while most open-source models languished between 23 and 40 percent. Marc Lackenby tackles the stable Andrews-Curtis conjecture in this 2026 arXiv paper on group theory. A group presentation describes a group through generators and relations. The trivial group contains only the identity element, yet it admits many complicated presentations. The conjecture asks whether simple rewriting moves can always reduce such a presentation to the standard one. Lackenby studies presentations called thickenable, meaning their linked shape can be embedded in a thickened space.

For this thickenable class, he proves the original unstable conjecture outright and gives a concrete upper bound on how many stable moves the reduction needs. The argument also yields an algorithm that lists every thickenable presentation of a fixed length and reduces each one. It holds two hundred eighty six thousand training screenshots and three point five million tasks, plus a two thousand example held out test suite. Lie Yamaguti algebras generalize Lie algebras with both a bracket and a triple product, and they arise from the geometry of homogeneous spaces. Each one can be enveloped by a reductive Lie algebra pair, a larger and better understood object. The catch is that this enveloping construction does not respect maps between algebras, so it is not functorial.

Benayadi builds the missing piece directly: a free construction that forms a left adjoint to the natural restriction functor between the two categories. An adjoint is the closest thing category theory has to an inverse. He then shows the classical enveloping algebra becomes functorial once only surjective maps are allowed, where it acts as a right adjoint instead. Their metric, KS at N, runs a Kolmogorov Smirnov test comparing a model's samples against ground truth. It reports how often the model passes as statistically indistinguishable. How big a step can gradient descent take before training a neural network falls apart? Galli and co-authors revisit that old question in this 2026 arXiv paper, nicknamed Flatland. Gradient descent trains models by stepping downhill on an error surface. The safe step size is usually tied to how smooth that surface is everywhere. Real networks are not smooth everywhere.

The team defines large steps using only local smoothness near the current point. Their adaptive methods provably take such large steps. They ride at the edge of stability from the very start. There, the product of step size and sharpness stays above the classic threshold. Sharpness means the surface's steepest curvature. Oddly, hitting very flat regions too early slowed learning and hurt how well the network handled new data. aurobindo-essays-on-gita-1922:
Aurobindo's Essays on the Gita, published in book form in 1922 after running in his journal Arya, reinterpret the Bhagavad Gita for a new India. The Gita is the beloved dialogue in which Krishna counsels the warrior Arjuna before battle. Aurobindo reads it as a scripture of divine action.

He argues that the Gita's core teaching joins work, knowledge, and love into one path of self-giving to the divine. Against readings that prize withdrawal from life, he stresses action done without desire for its fruits. His essays shaped how modern Hindu thinkers claim the Gita for engaged, world-affirming life.
b09-luther-new-testament-1522:
Das Newe Testament Deutzsch, the Septembertestament, is Martin Luther's German New Testament of 1522. Luther translated it at the Wartburg castle in about eleven weeks, working from the Greek text. The name comes from its September release, and the German text here keeps the spelling of 1522.

For the first time, German readers of every rank could read the Gospels in their own tongue. Luther chose words that plain people spoke at market and at home. The book did more than spread his cause: it set the shape of modern High German. Printers across the land followed its style, and its phrases entered daily speech for good.
babur-nama-beveridge-vol-1-1922:
Babur, a Timurid prince who lost and won thrones across Central Asia, founded the Mughal Empire in India. He also wrote one of the great autobiographies of the world, the Babur-nama, in his native Turkic tongue. Annette Beveridge translated it into English, and this first volume appeared in 1922.

The young Babur takes Ferghana at twelve, wins and loses Samarkand three times, and ends by ruling Kabul. He writes frankly of his fears, his drinking, his verses, and his love of gardens and melons. His eye for country, beasts, and men is sharp and fresh. Beveridge's version, made from the Turkic text, opened this prince's mind to English readers.
babur-nama-beveridge-vol-2-1922:
Annette Beveridge's second volume of the Babur-nama, from 1922, completes her English version of Babur's memoirs. Babur, the Timurid prince who founded the Mughal Empire, wrote his life in Turkic with a candor rare in kings. This volume carries him from Kabul to the throne of Delhi.

Babur crushes Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526, breaks the Rajputs at Khanwa, and settles to rule Hindustan. His famous survey of India, its beasts, fruits, rains, and faults, fills these pages. He still writes poems, plants gardens, and counts his friends and his sins. The memoirs end near his death in 1530, a king's own story unmatched in Asia.
barns-wonderland-of-the-eastern-congo-19:
Thomas Alexander Barns wandered the snow-crowned volcano country of the eastern Congo in 1922. The Wonderland of the Eastern Congo is his tale of that rich, wild borderland. Barns was a hunter and collector who knew the lakes and hills at first hand.

Gorillas, elephants, and the peoples of the hills fill his bright pages. The land he crossed was then at the dawn of gorilla science, still half tale to the West. His book catches the last romantic years of African exploration. It is a hunter's hymn to a country of fire mountains and great apes.
baroja-the-quest-goldberg-1922:
Pío Baroja published La busca in Spain in 1904, and Isaac Goldberg Englished it in 1922 as The Quest. The novel opens Baroja's trilogy La lucha por la vida, the struggle for life. Manuel Alcázar, a country boy, comes to Madrid and sinks through its boarding houses, workshops, and thieves' dens.

Manuel works, starves, steals company, and keeps a stubborn core of decency. Baroja writes Madrid from below, in fast, plain scenes with little comment. Hemingway later named Baroja as a master he wished he could thank in person. Goldberg's Knopf translation brought that praise an English audience. The Quest remains the trilogy's best-known volume.
benoit-caussade-abandonment-1922: Abandonment to Divine Providence, the classic of total surrender to God often linked to Jean-Pierre de Caussade. It teaches finding God in the present moment. This edition preserves that quietist masterpiece. Writers of history may cite it later.
boehme-signature-of-all-things-1622:
Jakob Boehme wrote the Signatura Rerum in 1622. John Sparrow gave the work its fine English dress in that same age. The full title in English is The Signature of All Things. Boehme holds that each thing bears a mark of its hid make.

Seven forms of nature work through all things, from harsh dark to bright love. The tongue of nature, he says, can be read in each herb and stone. Boehme ranks as the most full scheme of his strange, bright thought. The book shaped views of signs in faith and art for ages.
boehme-way-to-christ-1622:
Jakob Boehme was a German shoe maker who saw great light in prayer. The Way to Christ, from 1622, holds his short works for the plain soul. True change of heart comes first in his plan. The book is the best first step into his hard, bright thought.

Short tracts deal with true grief for sin, new birth, and yield to God. One more tells of the life past sense, where the soul rests in Christ. Boehme writes as a guide, not a sage on a throne. The book's warm tone won him fans all over the North.
boy-of-bilson-1622:
Richard Baddeley busts a false seer in The Boy of Bilson, his tract of 1622. William Perry, a boy of Bilson, had seemed to be held by a foul soul: fits, strange words, and awe struck priests who sought to cast the soul out. Crowds came to watch the rite. Then the boy, in 1620, owned the whole thing was a sham taught to him by the priests for their church's fame.

Baddeley prints the tale and the boy's own words in full. The case cut both ways in the faith rows of the age. The tract is a prime bust text.
bracton-de-legibus-woodbine-vol2-1922:
Woodbine's critical edition of Bracton reached a second volume in 1922. The Yale scholar was rebuilding the text of the thirteenth century's greatest English law book from the surviving manuscripts. His first volume had appeared in 1915, and the war slowed the work before the second could follow.

Volume 2 carries the treatise forward through its treatment of property, persons, and the early writs. Woodbine's notes record where manuscripts differ, so readers can judge the text for themselves. The edition's care made it the version scholars quote when precision counts. Set beside Twiss's older edition, it shows how much manuscript study advanced between the Victorian age and the twentieth century. Bracton's summa of the common law stands here in its modern scholarly dress.
bradley-on-the-gorilla-trail-1922:
Mary Hastings Bradley went up into the Virunga volcanoes in 1922 and wrote one of the first gorilla books. On the Gorilla Trail tells her search for the mountain gorilla in its cloud forests. She was among the first women to make that hard trek.

With her husband Herbert, she camps, tracks, and at last stands close to the great apes. Her eye is sharp for camp life, porters, and the green world of the hills. The book opened the gorilla's country to a wide body of readers. It stands as a pioneer woman's tale of exploration.
bunin-gentleman-from-san-francisco-1922:
The Gentleman from San Francisco appeared in English in 1922, translated by D. H. Lawrence, S. S. Koteliansky, and Leonard Woolf. Ivan Bunin's title story follows a rich American traveling with his family in Europe. At Capri, at the height of his pleasure trip, the gentleman dies suddenly in his hotel.

His body, now mere cargo, is shipped home in the hold of the same gay vessel. Bunin sets wealth and pride against the sea, the dark, and death itself. The other stories in the volume share that grave music. Critics rank the title piece among the finest Russian short stories of its century. The Hogarth Press edition brought Bunin to English readers.
burckhardt-travels-syria-1822:
John Lewis Burckhardt roamed Syria and the Holy Land in the years before 1822. His Travels came out that year, after his early death. He rode in Arab dress and wrote with a sharp eye. The book holds two finds that made his name last.

Burckhardt gives the first full tale in Europe of Baalbek and its huge cut stones. Three stones in one wall, the trilithon, weigh close to a thousand tons each in bulk. He also tells of his ride to Petra, the lost rock city of the Nabataeans. The book opened the Levant to new study.
camden-britannia-gibson-vol-1-1722:
William Camden published his Britannia in Latin in 1586, the first full survey of Britain's land, antiquities, and peoples county by county. Edmund Gibson's English translation of 1722 fills two volumes, and volume one opens the set here. Camden traveled Britain and dug into records, coins, and stones to build his chorography, a description of places and their past.

The Britannia founded English antiquarian study: every later county history stands on Camden's ground. Roman remains, Saxon names, and Norman castles all find their places in his orderly pages. Gibson's version added fresh scholarship to Camden's frame. Volume one begins the book that taught England to read its own landscape as history.
camden-britannia-gibson-vol-2-1722:
Volume two completes Edmund Gibson's 1722 English translation of William Camden's Britannia. Camden's Latin original of 1586 surveyed the whole island of Britain, its counties, towns, rivers, and ancient remains. Gibson, a bishop and scholar, Englished the work in two volumes with the learning of his own age added.

The survey continues county by county, joining Roman antiquities to the Britain of Camden's day. Camden had invented a way of writing about place that binds soil, monument, and story into one account. His book made antiquarianism a national pursuit in England. Volume two finishes the founding chorography of Britain, still consulted by local historians after three centuries.
cather-one-of-ours-1922:
Claude Wheeler, the hero of Willa Cather's One of Ours, feels trapped on his family's Nebraska farm. The novel appeared in 1922 and won the Pulitzer Prize for fiction. Claude marries without love, grows restless, and finds a way out when the First World War begins.

In the army Claude crosses to France and at last feels his life has a purpose. He serves with loyalty and courage among men he respects. The war gives him belonging, even as it puts him in mortal danger. Cather drew a sharp contrast between dull peace at home and the clear, brief meaning Claude finds in France.
character-reading-at-a-glance-1922: Character Reading at a Glance, 1922, the quick reading. This book preserves that work. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. History keeps its place secure. It is kept for readers to consult. It is kept for study by scholars.
cherry-garrard-worst-journey-1922:
Apsley Cherry-Garrard, the youngest member of Scott's last expedition, published The Worst Journey in the World in 1922. Both volumes of his memoir are held here in one file. Cherry-Garrard was one of three men who made the midwinter trek for penguin eggs, and one of the search party that found Scott's tent.

He writes of the winter run in darkness and cold near minus 70, hauling sledges for eggs science wanted. He also tells the race to the Pole and its end: Scott and his party found dead on the return. The book is judged the finest of all polar memoirs.
cia-0000009122:
An American pilot was captured in Quang Ninh province in June 1967, a CIA report filed that October states. Quang Ninh, in North Vietnam's far northeast, includes coal country and a border with China. Pilots downed there fell far from rescue forces.

The report preserves what reached the agency about the capture several months on. Early capture reports often formed the spine of a prisoner's whole file, updated by later sightings. Knowing a man was taken alive changed his status from missing to prisoner. This file marks that change for one airman, with place and season fixed.
cia-0000009822:
Two American pilots were reported present at the Pathet Lao's Savannakhet province office, a January 1967 item states. Savannakhet, in southern Laos, was a Pathet Lao stronghold facing Thailand across the Mekong. Pilots held at an office, not a camp, suggests recent capture or display.

Early Laotian prisoner reports are scarce, which gives this one weight. In 1967 the Laos prison system was only beginning to enter American files. A sighting at a provincial office fixed two men to a place and a captor. Later camp reports from Laos can be read against such early fixed points.
cia-0000009922:
Two American prisoners of war were executed by the Viet Cong in Takeo province, Cambodia, a February 1971 report states. Takeo lies south of Phnom Penh, near the Vietnamese border, where Viet Cong forces moved freely in those years. Execution reports were the gravest items in the prisoner files.

A reported execution demanded the strictest checking, since it closed men's files as murdered, not merely dead. Evidence had to survive doubt from every direction. Many such reports were never fully confirmed, yet none could be dropped. This file preserves one, with province and captor named, in the Cambodian record.
cia-0000012422:
Facts gathered from a source whose name is blanked out, at interviews held at the American Embassy in London, fill a CIA record from February 1962. The record boils the talks down to their yield. What survives is the end product: hard-won facts, set out plainly, with the human machinery that won them hidden behind the censor's marks.

Such pages paid for the risks, the money, and the careful tradecraft around them. They are what the whole apparatus existed to produce. For readers, the record shows intelligence in its finished form, stripped of the story of how it was got.
cia-0000013222:
Hanoi's official doctrine on American prisoners is studied in a CIA paper from February 1965. The paper came early, before the prison system took its full shape. North Vietnam called the captured airmen war criminals, not prisoners of war. That legal stance had hard consequences for the men in its cells. It also shaped the protests Washington filed in their name through those years.

The analysts read the capital's prison theory closely. They found a blend of ideology and cold calculation at its heart. Doctrine mattered because the camps followed it more often than not. For readers, the paper shows the system's ideas at the start.
cia-0000013622:
The character of João Goulart's regime in Brazil is dissected in a CIA paper from January 1963. Goulart, the populist vice president, had taken power when his predecessor quit. His labor ties, land reform talk, and warm line toward the left alarmed Brazil's officers and Washington alike. The paper weighs the man and his government while both still stood, a year before the coup removed them.

The study reads the regime for lessons Washington wanted to learn. It sorts populism, weakness, and intent with a cold eye. For readers, it is the Goulart government examined by the power that would soon help bury it.
cia-0000013922: Three prisoners were seen in Hong Ngu District, on the road to Cambodia, in a CIA note dated January 2, 1968. The district sits in Kien Phong Province, in South Vietnam's delta. Prisoners moving toward Cambodia were leaving Vietnam's main war zone. The sighting hints at camps or routes that crossed the border.
cia-0000014622: The Dr. Klaus Fuchs case anchors a CIA file dated November 2, 1950, naming David Keppel. Fuchs, a physicist, had confessed to passing atomic secrets to the Soviet Union. His case cracked open the wider atom spy hunt in Britain and America. Files naming men like Keppel show how far the search for contacts spread.
cia-0000014722: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg are named again in a CIA file dated August 3, 1954. The bare title gives no topic beyond their names. By then the couple had been dead for over a year. cia-0000015422: Near Detroit, a witness watched a huge greenish disc cross the sky, and the CIA's Detroit chief sent the account on in late 1960. The object looked like a meteor at first, but far larger and almost disc shaped. It seemed so low the witness thought it might land in the Detroit River. The report was dated November 5, 1960, in the catalog record.

A CIA record dated March 4, 1981 gives an organizational view of meetings held by five political organizations. Rather than a speech or a statement, it maps how the groups were set up and how they met. The record belongs to the close watch the agency kept on party politics in the region.

Inside, the focus is structure: who the organizations were and how their meetings were arranged. That kind of map helped analysts keep track of a crowded and fast-changing party scene. For readers now, it shows the plain working detail behind the larger story of political organizing.
cia-0000046622: A downed American crewman was sighted alive in Gio Linh District, Quang Tri Province, and a CIA item dated June 6, 1972, preserved the report. Quang Tri was South Vietnam's northernmost province, fought over hard that spring. Sightings like this one were rushed to the offices that tracked every missing airman, and checked against the lists of the lost.
cia-0000049122: Feelings among El Salvador's commanders cooled after their September 25, 1987, meeting, and a CIA item records the easing. The title's dry language, a reduction of intensity, covers anger that had run hot enough to file. cia-0000049222: A draft of a letter to the New York Times survives in a CIA item from 1993, kept with the Truth Commission records. cia-0000102922: Organization of Dnepropetrovsk Concentration Camp, with date of information 1975, in the heading's misspelled organization, is declassified CIA document 0000102922, dated August 1, 1981. The catalog keeps the record under its original subject heading.
cia-0000109822: Frederick Wiehl - Alias Capt. Awald is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000109822, dated September 3, 1945. cia-0000112822: Name Checks Against Colonel Fox-holmes' Files is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000112822, dated January 6, 1945. cia-0000117922: Alsops Join Preachers of Atomic War is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000117922, dated February 6, 1955. The title names the Alsops joining a group it calls preachers of atomic war. That label is the heading's own sharp wording for the side they joined. The brief record is a press-flavored item from the winter of 1955 in the files.
cia-0000119722:
A September 1956 CIA paper reports that anti-communist demonstrations seem possible in Hungary and Poland. The heading misspells the word as Aunti-communist in the original file. Within weeks, unrest in both countries would break into the open, and Hungary's would become a full revolution.

Warning papers earn their place when events test them, and events tested this one fast. The paper gathers the signs analysts were reading: public anger, loosening party control, and the pull of Yugoslavia's example. For readers, it is the forecast before the storm, proof that the explosions of October 1956 did not catch careful watchers wholly by surprise.
cia-0000132322:
Cuba was the subject of a CIA briefing prepared for the National Security Council in September 1958. Fulgencio Batista's government was weakening fast. Fidel Castro's rebels were gaining ground across the island, town by town.

The briefing gave the White House the agency's current picture of the fight for Cuba. It covered the strength of both sides and the mood of the country. Four months later Castro's forces entered Havana and Batista fled. Read today, the document shows what American leaders were told at the last stage of the old regime. It captures their view just before the revolution changed Cuba's course for good.
cia-0000132422: Growing Cuban interest in Communist China is noted in item 3 of a CIA series, dated January 3, 1960. Havana was looking for partners beyond Moscow as its revolution took shape. The split between the Soviet Union and China gave small revolutionary states room to maneuver between the two giants. The short item records an early step in that courtship between Cuba and Beijing.
cia-0000132622: Support for Cuba from the whole Sino-Soviet bloc fills a CIA document dated June 5, 1960. Moscow and Beijing were rivals, yet both were backing Havana at once. Cuba played the two communist giants against each other to win aid from both. The short document surveys that support, from trade to arms, as analysts mapped it in the summer of 1960.
cia-0000135922: With a date of 6 January 1954, a CIA cable in the open files deals with a request that a case officer give a cover briefing to undisclosed people. The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.

cloud-dream-nine-gale-1922:
James S. Gale translated Kim Man-jung's Cloud Dream of the Nine in 1922, the first English rendering of the Korean classic. Kim wrote the Kuunmong in the seventeenth century, telling of a young monk who dreams a whole life of glory. In the dream he rises, loves nine women, and tastes every worldly honor.

Waking, he finds the splendor empty, and the Buddhist moral lands with gentle force. Gale, a missionary-scholar in Korea, carried the tale west as a jewel of Korean letters. The romance remains the most famous Korean novel of its age, dreamlike and wise in Gale's English.
constitution-belize-2022: Belize's Constitution, from 1981 with amendments, frames its Caribbean democracy. It guards rights. The Tower library holds the full text. It freed a colony. Crown left. constitution-tunisia-2022: Tunisia's 2022 Constitution, passed by referendum, recentered its presidency. It rewrote the Arab Spring pact. The Tower library holds the full text. It sparked a spring.
