coue-self-mastery-autosuggestion-1922:
Emile Coue teaches his famous formula in Self Mastery Through Conscious Autosuggestion, from 1922: every day, in every way, better and better. The French pharmacist tells patients to repeat the words morning and night. Imagination, he argues, beats willpower when the two come into open conflict within the mind.

His Nancy clinic drew crowds from many lands in the nineteen twenties. Coue insists his method is no miracle, only the mind healing itself by suggestion. Critics mocked, yet patients swore by the simple rite. The book marks the turning point of the autosuggestion movement, a seed of all later positive thinking.
crowley-diary-of-a-drug-fiend-1922:
Two young lovers slide into cocaine and heroin in Crowley's novel of 1922. The Diary of a Drug Fiend follows their fall, their craving, and their hard road back. The book's frank drug scenes made Crowley infamous in the British press of the day.

Crowley knew the drug world at close range and writes its highs and horrors with real bite. The cure in the tale rests on will, work, and the law of Thelema. Part confession, part warning, the novel shocked its first readers to the core. It stands as a landmark of drug fiction in English.
cummings-enormous-room-1922:
E. E. Cummings published The Enormous Room in 1922, his account of wrongful imprisonment in a French detention camp. The modernist classic of war and freedom tells what befell Cummings as a volunteer ambulance driver in 1917. French censors had read his friend's letters, and both men were jailed as suspects.

At La Ferté-Macé, Cummings shared one vast room with some thirty men of a dozen nations in filth and cold. Criminals, deserters, and madmen become, in his telling, individual souls of stubborn, comic, and tragic dignity. His prose, already bending syntax toward his later poetry, renders guards and prisoners with a painter's sharp eye for gesture. Released through his father's appeals, he ends with a hymn to the self no prison could uniform or break. The book stands with the finest memoirs of the First World War.
defoe-colonel-jack-1722:
Daniel Defoe published Colonel Jack in 1722, a criminal-to-gentleman arc of crime and reform. The novel is Defoe's great tale of social mobility and reformation in the Augustan age. Jack's rise mirrors Moll's, but with war, plantations, and duels in place of her marriages.

Jack, a London foundling raised among pickpockets, is kidnapped to Virginia and sold as a servant. He works his way to overseer and planter, learning mercy from his own hard years there. Back in Europe he fights in wars, weds four wives, and kills a man in a duel. Ever seeking to be a gentleman, he is haunted by the thefts of his boyhood in London. Defoe uses Jack to ask what birth, money, and manners truly make a gentleman.
defoe-journal-of-the-plague-year-1722:
Daniel Defoe published A Journal of the Plague Year in 1722, a pseudo-documentary of 1665 London. The book invented the documentary novel and disaster reportage in English prose for later writers everywhere. Defoe was five in the plague year and rebuilt it from bills, tales, and records.

A saddler, H. F., stays in London as plague kills tens of thousands around his parish. He records bills of mortality, shut houses with red crosses, pits, and fleeing crowds in Aldgate. Tales of nurses, quacks, and piper anecdotes break the grim tally of the dead each week. Fear of policy, such as shutting houses, runs beside fear of the disease itself in London. The calm, factual voice makes the horror feel close, modern, and hard to shake.
defoe-moll-flanders-1722:
Daniel Defoe published Moll Flanders in 1722, the great criminal autobiography of English fiction in prose. The book is a founding picaresque of the modern novel, told in Moll's own voice. Defoe knew Newgate and the London underworld, and his detail smells of both worlds in truth.

Moll, born in Newgate prison, is raised by a mayor's family and seduced young in Colchester. Five husbands, bigamy, incest by chance, and a career of theft fill her long, busy life. She grows rich as a thief, is caught, and is transported to Virginia with her Lancashire husband. There she prospers honestly at last and repents in comfort, if not quite in sorrow. The tale's energy and moral blur still spark argument three centuries on.
dekker-noble-spanish-soldier-1622:
Thomas Dekker's Noble Spanish Soldier, printed in 1622, is a late tragicomedy of the Spanish court. Dekker was by then an old hand of the London stage, famed for citizen comedy. Here he turns to kings, favorites, and a wronged lady.

The soldier of the title serves a king whose favor shifts like weather, and honor must survive court intrigue. Dekker mixes high passion with his usual vivid street and camp scenes. The play was once linked to a lost work on the same Spanish source. It shows the Jacobean stage's taste for foreign courts as mirrors of its own, full of ambition, love, and sudden falls.
der-sechs-tage-wercke-dieser-welt-geheim: Der sechs Tage-Wercke dieser Welt geheime Bedeutung, 1722. The six days' meaning. This book preserves that work. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
dewey-human-nature-conduct-1922:
Human Nature and Conduct, published in 1922, is Dewey's introduction to social psychology and the core of his moral thought. Morality, he argues, is not a set of rules stamped on human nature but a product of habits formed in society.

Dewey builds his account on three forces: habit, impulse, and intelligence. Habit steadies us but hardens; impulse breaks the pattern; intelligence, used well, rebuilds habit into chosen conduct. He attacks the split between means and ends that poisons moral theory. The book's dry title hides a humane, practical wisdom that shaped his later work on democracy and education.
die-geheimsymbole-der-alchymie-arzneikun: Die Geheimsymbole der Alchymie, Arzneikunde und Astrologie des Mittelalters, 1922. The secret symbols. This book preserves that study. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
dospassos-rosinante-1922:
Doran published Rosinante to the Road Again in 1922 and classed it among Dos Passos's essays. The title nods to Rosinante, the worn horse of Don Quixote. A contents list sets the essays beside his novels and his poems in A Pushcart at the Curb.

Sketches from travel in Spain fill the book: bullfights, peasants, poets, and old cities. A young American watches with wide-eyed wonder and a sharp pen. He finds in Spain a mirror for the clashes of his own country. Part travel book and part reflection, the volume shows the novelist as a keen-eyed wanderer between two worlds.
doyle-coming-of-the-fairies-1922:
Arthur Conan Doyle set out The Coming of the Fairies in 1922. The book deals with the Cottingley case in Yorkshire. Two young cousins said they had shot photos of fays in a glen. Doyle, a firm man of the spirit creed, took up their cause.

The book prints the photos and the tales of how they were made. Experts of the Kodak firm weigh in on the risk of fakes. Doyle holds the proof sound and the girls true in their claims. The book is the most famed case of trust in the fay tales of its age.
eliot-waste-land-1922:
T. S. Eliot published The Waste Land in 1922, a long poem in five parts about Europe after the First World War. Voices shift without warning: a fortune teller, a typist, a drowned sailor, crowds in London. Myths, Bible verses, and lines in several languages crowd the text. A dry, broken land stands for a broken culture.

Eliot seeks signs of rain, renewal, and meaning amid the ruins. Notes at the end point readers to his sources. Ezra Pound helped cut the draft to its final shape. The poem became the central work of literary modernism. It is dense and hard, yet its best lines are known worldwide.
eratosthenes-fragments-bernhardy-1822:
Eratosthenes ran the great library at Alexandria and measured the girth of the Earth with shadows and sums. His own books are lost, and only pieces quoted by later writers survive. Eratosthenica, in Gottlieb Bernhardy's 1822 collection, gathers those scattered fragments in one place.

His lost Geography founded the craft of mapping the world on a grid of lines. The fragments show his work on place, measure, myth, and the size of the inhabited earth. Scholars rebuild his thought piece by piece from these scraps. Bernhardy's file has been the base for that hard work since 1822.
europmc-pmc10763622:
Fischer led a phase 2a trial in 2022 of molnupiravir, an oral drug for early Covid-19. No easy oral drug yet blocked the virus from spreading or worsening. The trial enrolled 202 unvaccinated adults with proven infection and under seven days of symptoms. Doses of 200, 400, or 800 mg ran twice a day for five days.

The top dose cleared viral RNA a day faster than the dummy pill. Fischer reports a median of 14 days versus 15 days. By day 3, live virus showed in swabs from just 1.9% on the top dose, versus 16.7% on the dummy. By day 5, no live virus grew from the two higher dose arms. The drug was well tolerated at each dose.
europmc-pmc1174822:
Carroll revisits a 30-year-old thesis about how animal form evolves in this 2005 essay. King and Wilson proposed in 1975 that humans and chimps differ mainly in how genes are regulated, not in the proteins themselves. Their proteins were strikingly similar, too similar to explain the anatomical and behavioural gaps. Changes in the switches controlling gene expression, they argued, drive changes in anatomy and way of life.

Carroll assesses the thesis as comparative genomics and developmental biology pour forth new data, with the full chimp genome in hand. He distinguishes anatomy from physiology: coding changes clearly drive some physiological differences, such as vision and respiration. For form, though, theoretical and empirical evidence points to regulatory sequence changes as the major contributor, he argues. That conclusion challenges genomics, since regulatory DNA is hard to read.
europmc-pmc1241922:
Mahaffey, Clickner, and Bodurow analyzed blood mercury and fish intake in 2004. Data covered 1,709 women in a national survey from 1999 and 2000. The middle blood mercury value was 0.6 micrograms per liter. Values ranged from undetectable to 6.7 at the high end.

Blood mercury tracked fish and shellfish eating closely. Women aged 30 to 49 ran about 1.5 times the levels of younger women. Levels were lowest among Mexican Americans. Women who ate fish often had seven times the mercury of non-eaters. Mahaffey ties intake records to body burden with numbers. Levels ran highest in the other group, which included Asian and Pacific Islander women.
europmc-pmc1420322:
Burnham reviewed the Scopus database in 2006, a search tool for science, health, and tech journals. Scopus lets users search both older and newer work through the reference lists in each article. Libraries can use it for research and for choosing which journals to buy.

Burnham compares Scopus with its main rival, Web of Science. Neither tool covers all journals, and each fills gaps in the other. The review notes Scopus was built by Elsevier over two years, with input from 21 research sites. Burnham advises that a library which can afford just one should pick based on its own users' needs.
europmc-pmc1431722:
Malaria parasites ship proteins into the red blood cells they invade. Sargeant and co-authors hunted for those exported proteins in 2006, using new software to scan parasite genomes. They compared parasites that infect rodents with those that infect humans.

Some exported proteins were shared across both groups. Many others had grown in number in just one branch of the family. Sargeant calls this a lineage-specific expansion, growth limited to one line of descent. The pattern suggests each parasite line tailored its exported set to its own host. Such tailoring may help explain how the parasites dodge host defenses and cause disease.
europmc-pmc1513222:
Strong pain drugs carry a risk of misuse by the patients they help. Ives and co-authors followed 196 chronic pain patients on opioids for a year in 2006. Misuse meant acts like using unprescribed drugs, forging scripts, or selling pills. Urine tests helped detect it.

Sixty-two patients, 32 percent, misused opioids within the year. The most common sign was cocaine or stimulants in urine, in 40 percent of misusers. Past cocaine abuse raised the odds over four-fold. A past drug or DUI conviction and past alcohol abuse each raised odds about 2.6-fold. Younger age also tracked with misuse. Ives argues these markers can guide closer watch.
europmc-pmc1657022:
New neurons in the adult hippocampus grow dendrites, their input branches, on no fixed schedule. Plümpe and co-authors quantified that in 2006, following cells marked by the protein doublecortin. Most regulation of adult neurogenesis acts during this phase.

One fifth of marked cells were still dividing; over 70 percent were postmitotic, done dividing. The trip to full dendrite maturity took from three days to several weeks. Pushing precursor division up or down did not change dendrite timing. Plümpe concludes maturation starts at varying times after division ends, governed by its own micro-regulation.
europmc-pmc1968522:
Gately and Howell reviewed in 1993 how the anticancer drug cisplatin gets into cells, because tumors that keep it out resist treatment. Acquired resistance is a major problem in ovarian, testicular, and head and neck cancers. The most consistent change in resistant cells is that less drug accumulates inside them.

The classic view held that cisplatin simply diffuses across the cell membrane. Supporting facts: uptake scales with outside concentration, never saturates, and look-alike drugs do not compete. Newer work, though, shows specific drugs and signaling pathways can raise or lower uptake, which passive diffusion cannot explain. The authors develop the case that part of the traffic runs through a gated ion channel, a controllable pore in the membrane. That reframing points to ways of forcing more drug into resistant tumors.
europmc-pmc2002422:
Nielsen and co-workers examined breast tissue in 1987 from 110 medicolegal autopsies. The women were aged 20 to 54 and most had no known breast cancer. The team used detailed tissue examination plus X-rays of the removed tissue. Their aim was to find hidden cancers and early changes, called atypia, in young and middle-aged women.

Cancer was present in 22 women, which is 20 percent. Only one case had been known during life. Two women had invasive cancer, while the rest had in situ cancer, confined to ducts or lobes. Nearly half the cancers were in several sites or both breasts. X-ray found only 45 percent of confirmed lesions. Cancer was more common after age 40 and with alcohol abuse or liver disease.
europmc-pmc2077822: A medical research paper with further researches on the closure of the coronary arteries. The heart's vessels, studied. This article preserves that cardiac research. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2124622: A medical paper on true bone formation with red marrow in a sclerotic aorta. The vessel turned bone. This article preserves that pathology. Tomorrow's readers will find it. It retains its place in time. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2125022: General paralysis of the insane had a microbial cause, and this paper proved it by finding Treponema pallidum in patients' brains. The syphilis spirochete in the mind. The article preserves that landmark neurology. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2128222: A medical paper on the effects of intravenous dichloroethylsulfide injections in rabbits. The mustard gas. This article preserves that toxicology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2128322: A medical paper on the peptase, lipase, and invertase of hemolytic streptococcus. The strep enzymes. This article preserves that biochemistry. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2130922: A medical paper with studies on d'Herelle's bacteriophage, whether the lytic principle is volatile. The phage's nature. This article preserves that virology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2131122: A medical paper with experimental bone marrow reactions, anemia produced by collargol. The silver anemia. This article preserves that hematology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers.
europmc-pmc2131322: A medical paper on the structure of B. anthracis and reversal of the Gram reaction. The anthrax germ's structure. This article preserves that bacteriology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2131622: A medical paper on etiology of Oroya fever, effect of immune serum on bartonella. The serum cure. This article preserves that tropical medicine. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2276522:
Garton and co-workers examined tuberculosis bacteria in patients' sputum in 2008, hunting for dormant persister-like cells. A preliminary clue was that bacteria in sputum carry fat storage bodies, unlike lab-grown ones. The team stained microscopy-positive sputum samples from the United Kingdom and The Gambia, and compared gene activity in sputum bacteria with lab cultures in growing and non-replicating states.

Every sample contained fat-body-positive bacteria, ranging from 3 to 86 percent of the bacilli present. Lab bacteria forced into non-replicating persistence formed similar levels. Gene profiles from sputum matched slowly or non-replicating bacteria, not the actively growing cells traditionally assumed. Fat-body counts correlated strongly with how fast diagnostic cultures turned positive. Such dormant cells tolerate antibiotics, making them key targets for shortening treatment and understanding transmission.
europmc-pmc2323222:
Kaiser and a large team compared colon tumors with the developing colon in 2007. Their idea was that cancers may switch embryo genes back on. They measured gene activity in tumors from four mouse models and in 100 human colorectal cancers, then matched the patterns to stages of embryo colon growth.

All the tumors showed a striking replay of embryo colon gene activity from days 13.5 to 18.5 of development. Mouse tumors with a growth signal stuck on in the cell nucleus matched early, fast-growing stages. Tumors without that signal matched later, more mature stages. Human cancers also lost adult cell programs and tumor suppressor genes, genes that normally hold growth back. Some gained cancer genes not seen in normal development.
europmc-pmc2409622:
Garcea and colleagues measured turmeric's active compound in patients' livers in 2004. The compound, curcumin, prevented cancers in rodent studies and was hoped to protect humans too. Twelve patients with bowel cancer spread to the liver took curcumin pills for one week before surgery, at doses from 450 to 3,600 milligrams daily.

Tests of blood, bile, and liver found the body absorbs curcumin very poorly. Only low nanomolar levels of curcumin and its processed forms appeared in blood from the gut or the general circulation. No curcumin itself turned up in liver tissue, just traces of its breakdown products. A marker of oxidative DNA damage in liver, called M1G, did not fall after treatment. The authors concluded that doses able to load the liver enough to act are probably not feasible in humans.
europmc-pmc2535622:
Wong, Vichit-Vadakan, Kan, and Qian led a four-city Asian study in 2008 on whether short-term air pollution raises daily deaths. Most earlier evidence came from Western countries, and Asian cities differ in climate, exposure, and lifestyle. The PAPA project applied one shared method to Bangkok, Hong Kong, Shanghai, and Wuhan, testing four common pollutants against deaths from natural, heart, and lung causes.

In most cities, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide, fine particles, and ozone each tracked with higher daily mortality. The combined effects across cities matched or exceeded those reported in Western studies. The authors note that Asian residents may breathe more pollution because they spend longer outdoors and less time in air conditioning. They conclude Western risk estimates can reasonably be applied in Asia.
europmc-pmc2637922:
Feldman and co-authors tested two new drugs in 2009 that block mTOR, a protein hub that tells cells when to grow. The older drug rapamycin blocks only part of mTOR's work. Cells pair mTOR into two groups, called mTORC1 and mTORC2, and rapamycin barely touches the second group.

The new drugs, named PP242 and PP30, fit into mTOR's active site and block both groups. Treated cells stopped a key step in switching on Akt, a growth signal protein, and grew more slowly than cells given rapamycin. To the team's surprise, the stronger effect came mainly from fuller blocking of the first group, not the second. PP242 also halted protein building in settings where rapamycin had no effect at all.
europmc-pmc2732522:
Glynn, Whiteley, Bifani, Kremer, and van Soolingen reviewed in 2002 the worldwide occurrence of Beijing/W strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the tuberculosis bacterium. This strain family is genetically tight, has caused large outbreaks, sometimes with drug resistance, and dominates in some regions. They gathered published reports that used a DNA fingerprint method or other definitions to map its spread.

Across twenty-six studies, Beijing strains were most common in Asia but were found worldwide. Links to drug resistance varied sharply by place: strong in New York, Cuba, Estonia, and Vietnam, but weak or absent elsewhere. Few studies tracked change over time. Their ubiquity and frequent role in outbreaks make the family a priority for control.
europmc-pmc2736622:
Davidson and co-authors tested in 2009 chronic cyclodextrin treatment in mice with Niemann-Pick type C disease, a fatal brain disorder where cholesterol and fatty lipids pile up inside cells. Most cases stem from a faulty NPC1 protein, and treatments were limited. The clue came when the carrier liquid alone, cyclodextrin, seemed to extend life in an earlier drug trial.

Given every other day from early life, cyclodextrin delayed disease onset, cut cholesterol and lipid storage inside neurons, lowered markers of neuron damage, and extended survival beyond any prior regimen. Mice lacking the partner protein NPC2 benefited similarly. Mice with two other storage diseases showed no such clearing, which narrows the effect to this disease family.
europmc-pmc2765422:
Tadmouri and co-authors reviewed in 2009 consanguinity, marriage between close relatives, and reproductive health among Arabs. Arab populations hold some of the world's highest rates. First-cousin marriages reach a quarter to a third of all marriages in places. Rates are still rising in Qatar, Yemen, and the United Arab Emirates. The review weighs effects on fertility, pregnancy loss, infant death, and birth defects.

Evidence links such marriages to higher postnatal mortality and more congenital malformations, while effects on fertility and fetal wastage stay controversial. The clearest impact is more children born with two copies of recessive disorder genes. Data from the Catalogue of Transmission Genetics in Arabs show recessive disorders unusually common in the region, a pattern tied to the practice.
europmc-pmc2820522:
Yang and colleagues, with the Asian Lupus Genetics Consortium, ran a genome-wide scan in 2010 for lupus risk genes in Asian populations. Lupus is an autoimmune disease where the body attacks its own tissues, and most earlier gene hunts drew on European ancestry. The scan started with three hundred twenty patients and fifteen hundred controls. It then checked hits in a total of thirty-three hundred patients and forty-two hundred controls from Hong Kong, mainland China, and Thailand.

Two new risk regions emerged, in genes called ETS1 and WDFY4, each raising risk by roughly thirty percent. The risk version of ETS1 produced less of its protein product in blood cells. Seven known lupus regions also held up in Asians.
europmc-pmc2935122:
Kearney reviewed world food consumption trends and their drivers in 2010, with projections running to mid-century. Diets everywhere were shifting away from basic staples toward more varied foods.

Countries changing fastest face a nutrition transition, as richer and more processed diets spread alongside city living and food marketing. Trade opening over two decades also eased that shift. The health cost shows in rising obesity and long-term diseases such as heart disease and cancer. Kearney argues that farm policy and health policy must be planned together so future diets support people and the environment.
europmc-pmc2976722:
Bartram and Cairncross opened a four-part series on water and sanitation in 2010, calling clean water, toilets, and hygiene the forgotten foundations of health. Millions of deaths each year trace back to their absence, mostly among children in poorer countries.

Proven fixes are cheap and their total gains, from time saved to schooling kept, outweigh their costs. Even rich countries still face water-linked illness. International ambitions for drinking water and sanitation fall short of the need, the authors argue, and progress will stall unless health professionals push the topic up the policy agenda.
europmc-pmc3101722:
Almuhaideb, Papathanasiou, and Bomanji reviewed in 2011 the role of combined PET and CT scanning with a radioactive sugar tracer in cancer care. Cancer cells consume sugar greedily, so the tracer lights them up, while the paired CT scan pins each hot spot to exact anatomy in the same session. The review guides oncologists and surgeons on where this imaging earns its cost.

Its strongest uses are staging cancers before treatment, rechecking them after, and hunting recurrences when blood markers rise but ordinary scans show nothing. It can also reveal early whether a treatment is working, before tumors shrink, allowing failing regimens to change sooner. Across studies, scan results altered the planned management in roughly a quarter of patients. The authors sort the evidence cancer by cancer, noting where the method is proven and where it overpromises.
europmc-pmc3145422:
Enzo Palombo reviewed plant remedies against mouth bacteria in a 2011 paper in Evidence-based Complementary and Alternative Medicine. Tooth decay and gum disease rank among the most common infections worldwide, driven by a few of the hundreds of bacterial species living in the mouth. Standard antibacterial products can stain teeth, upset the stomach, and alter mouth flora, while resistance grows.

Plant extracts and pure plant chemicals, many from long traditional use, can slow the culprit bacteria, block the films and plaque they build, and reduce their grip on tooth surfaces. The review covers the best-studied candidates and the clinical trials testing their safety and effect. Palombo presents them as promising, low-cost options, especially where dental care budgets are thin.
europmc-pmc3213322:
Hai Huang and colleagues reported in this 2011 paper in Hepatology that histones, proteins that package DNA inside the nucleus, can act as danger signals after liver injury. When tissue is damaged without infection, released molecules called alarmins alert the innate immune system. The team tested whether histones escaping from injured liver cells play that role in mice.

After blood flow to the liver was cut and restored, circulating histone levels rose sharply. Blocking histones protected the mice, while injecting histones made the injury worse. The damage ran through the immune sensor TLR9 and its partner MyD88; mice lacking either did not respond to injected histones. In cell experiments, extracellular histones also boosted DNA-triggered TLR9 activation, linking them into the injury response.
europmc-pmc3228722:
Christopher Forsyth and colleagues tested whether the gut is leakier in early Parkinson's disease, in this 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Clumps of the protein alpha-synuclein, the disease's hallmark, appear in intestinal nerves, hinting the gut may be an early disease site. A leaky barrier could let bacterial products reach those nerves, but permeability had never been measured in patients.

Newly diagnosed patients showed significantly greater intestinal permeability than healthy controls. The leakiness tracked with stronger staining in gut biopsies for E. coli bacteria, for a marker of oxidative damage, and for alpha-synuclein itself, and with a blood marker of endotoxin exposure. The authors present this as the first demonstration of abnormal gut permeability in Parkinson's, with clues for earlier diagnosis and new treatment targets.
europmc-pmc3257222:
Kate Tchanturia and colleagues pooled a large dataset on mental flexibility in eating disorders, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. People with these illnesses often behave rigidly, especially around food, and small studies had blamed weak set-shifting, the ability to change strategy when rules change. The team tested over five hundred participants with a standard card-sorting measure of problem solving and flexibility.

The group included people with anorexia, people with bulimia, people recovered from anorexia, and healthy controls. Those currently ill performed poorly across most parts of the task. The recovered group did better than the ill groups but still made more stuck-in-a-rut errors than controls, suggesting flexibility problems partly linger after recovery. The authors say the results, from the largest such dataset yet, strengthen the case for treating inflexibility as part of these disorders.
europmc-pmc3257622:
David Vauzour and colleagues reviewed how plant polyphenols may protect against chronic disease, in this 2010 article in Nutrients. Polyphenols are everywhere in plant foods, and people who eat more of them show lower rates of cancer, cardiovascular disease, and brain degeneration. The review asks what these compounds actually do inside cells.

Rather than mopping up oxidants directly, polyphenols appear to work by interacting with signaling pathways that control cell function. The authors focus on two cascades, the MAP kinase family and the PI3 kinase/Akt pathway. In neurons, activating one branch promotes survival and may support cognition; in blood vessel linings it influences nitric oxide and blood pressure. They marshal population data, human intervention trials, and animal and cell studies for each disease area.
europmc-pmc3269422:
Brian Pasley and colleagues demonstrated that speech sounds can be reconstructed from activity in the human auditory cortex, in this 2012 paper in PLoS Biology. Neurosurgical patients, monitored with electrodes placed on the brain for clinical reasons, listened to spoken words while the team recorded from hearing areas of the cortex. The work asked how faithfully the brain's response encodes what was heard.

By decoding the recorded activity, the researchers rebuilt an approximation of the sound spectrogram of the speech the patients had heard. The result shows the auditory cortex keeps a detailed, readable representation of the acoustic features of speech, in the region that processes complex sounds beyond the first relay station. Beyond its basic science value, the demonstration matters for the long-term hope of devices that could read intended or heard speech directly from brain signals.
europmc-pmc3272222:
James Livingston and colleagues reviewed attempts to reduce the stigma attached to substance use disorders, in this 2012 paper in Addiction. Stigma discourages treatment and deepens harm, and many programs claim to fight it. The team searched the literature for interventions that had been properly evaluated, as opposed to merely described.

Thirteen studies qualified, of moderately strong quality. They targeted three audiences: the affected people themselves, the general public, and professionals such as medical students and police. Most paired teaching with face-to-face contact with people living with these disorders. Nearly all reported improvement on at least one stigma measure. Therapy in groups reduced self-stigma; motivational interviewing and positive personal stories shifted public attitudes; contact-based training worked on professionals. No intervention had been tested across different settings or groups, the authors caution.
europmc-pmc3322422:
Majounie led an international study measuring how often one gene defect lies behind two fatal brain diseases, reporting in 2012. The defect is a short DNA stretch repeated far too many times inside a gene called C9orf72. It had recently been tied to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, which paralyzes patients, and to frontotemporal dementia, which erodes personality and language.

Screening nearly six thousand patients from seventeen regions, the team found the defect in many inherited cases. It appeared in close to two fifths of inherited ALS cases and about a quarter of inherited dementia cases. It also appeared in a smaller share of cases with no family history. Every carrier shared an ancestral chromosome pattern, pointing to a single origin roughly fifteen hundred years ago. The defect almost always caused disease by old age, and the authors urge routine testing and counseling for patients.
europmc-pmc3349722:
Cheng and co-authors developed a computational method that predicts new drug targets by reasoning over networks. Their network-based inference approach exploits the web of known drug, target, and disease relationships, ranking candidate interactions that have not yet been tested in the laboratory.

The method performed well at recovering known drug–target pairs and, more strikingly, pointed to new uses for existing medicines. Five older drugs flagged by the algorithm were checked experimentally and confirmed in vitro to act on predicted targets. The authors propose the approach as a route to drug repositioning: finding fresh indications for approved compounds whose safety profiles are already understood.
europmc-pmc3446322:
Boetzer and Pirovano described GapFiller in 2012, a program that closes the holes left inside genome assemblies. Sequencing projects aim to puzzle millions of short reads into one complete genome, but drafts usually end as scaffolds riddled with gaps. Their automated strategy uses paired reads, sequenced from both ends of a DNA fragment, to bridge each gap.

Tested on bacterial and larger eukaryotic datasets, the method closed gaps reliably with only a few errors slipping through. Every gap shut in software is one less round of costly laboratory finishing work. The authors report the wet-lab burden needed to finish a genome drops drastically as a result. The free tool targets the least glamorous, most expensive step of genome projects.
europmc-pmc3556522: GLP-1 got an insulin mechanism. This 2013 paper maps how GLP-1 triggers insulin from pancreatic cells. The authors reveal the mechanism. Their work guides diabetes therapy. Meloni's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. The study shaped diabetes drugs.
europmc-pmc3572422: Sequencing reads got BLASR. This 2012 paper introduces BLASR for mapping single-molecule reads. The authors reveal the method. Their work spread through labs. Chaisson's team led the work. It is open source. The paper is widely cited. Labs use it worldwide.
europmc-pmc3615022: Pneumonia got a burden estimate. This 2013 review totals adult pneumonia cases. The authors weigh the test methods. Their review guides policy. Said's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped vaccine policy. The study shaped pneumonia policy.
europmc-pmc3633022: Allergens got AllerTOP. This 2013 paper introduces AllerTOP for allergen prediction. The authors reveal the server. Their work spread through labs. Dimitrov's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is open source. Labs use it worldwide. It is a classic.
europmc-pmc3673822: Sepsis got a brain-fog review. This 2013 paper reviews brain dysfunction in sepsis. The authors map the dysfunction. Their review guides intensive care. Sonneville's review is widely cited. It is a classic. ICUs rely on it. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3675122: HLA got a fill-in method. This 2013 paper fills in amino-acid variants in HLA genes. The authors reveal the method. Their work guides immunogenetics. Jia's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped transplant matching.
europmc-pmc3709422: Language got MUC and beyond. This 2013 paper extends the MUC language model. The author reveals the advances. Their work guides neurolinguistics. Hagoort's paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped language science. The paper is a landmark. The study shaped language models.

europmc-pmc9469622: Tian and co-authors published this research paper in 2022 on enhancing the treatment efficacy (how well something works) of nanoparticles (ultra-tiny specks) for cancer treatment using versatile aimed plans. fichte-addresses-german-nation-1922:
Fichte delivered his Addresses to the German Nation in Berlin in 1808, while French troops occupied the city after Prussia's collapse. The translation by R F Jones and G H Turnbull, from 1922, is the text here. Johann Gottlieb Fichte, a philosopher with a preacher's fire, spoke on Sundays to a crowd that risked much by listening.

His remedy for defeat was a new education, forming Germans who would be free in spirit before they were free in fact. Language, on his account, binds a people into a nation with a shared inner life. The Addresses made philosophy a political force in the Napoleonic age. Their fame, and their dangers, have grown ever since.
fitzgerald-beautiful-and-damned-1922:
F. Scott Fitzgerald published The Beautiful and Damned in 1922, his second novel and his darkest Jazz Age book. Fitzgerald had married Zelda and tasted the rich life he described. The novel asks what happens when beautiful young people simply wait for money to arrive.

Anthony Patch, heir to a reformer's fortune, marries the dazzling Gloria Gilbert. While a lawsuit over his grandfather's will drags on, the couple drink, drift, and decay in New York and Connecticut. Parties glitter and rot in the same paragraph. By the time the money comes, both are damaged past repair. It is Fitzgerald's bleakest portrait of wealth without purpose.
fitzgerald-tales-of-the-jazz-age-1922:
F. Scott Fitzgerald published Tales of the Jazz Age in 1922, gathering eleven stories and arranging them with joking notes about their origins. The book catches him at full volume between his second novel and The Great Gatsby. It mixes his glossy magazine tales with stranger, darker pieces.

May Day follows rich young men and war veterans through one violent New York night after the war. The Diamond as Big as the Ritz discovers a mountain of diamond and a family willing to kill to keep it secret. The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, born old and aging backward, also first appeared here in book form. Few collections map an era so completely.
fourier-theorie-chaleur-1822:
Joseph Fourier founds the math of heat in his Theorie analytique de la chaleur, in French from 1822. Heat flows through bars and rings by laws he writes as equations. Any curve, he shows, can be built from sums of simple sine waves, the seed of what we now call Fourier analysis.

The method outgrew its birthplace in heat to serve all physics. Signal work, quantum theory, and sound all descend from these pages in time. Fourier, who had marched to Egypt with Napoleon, wrote with rare clarity. His book stands among the great works of math, proof that one deep idea can refound whole sciences at a stroke.
frazer-golden-bough-abridged-1922:
James George Frazer first published The Golden Bough in 1890, and his 1922 one-volume cut made it a household book. Frazer, a Cambridge scholar, compared myths and rites from all over the world. He sought the roots of magic and religion in early human thought.

Inside are sacred kings killed for their people's good, tree spirits, and harvest rites. Frazer traces a path from magic to religion and then to science. His tales of dying gods shaped poets and novelists for years. The cut keeps the sweep of the twelve-volume work. Readers can dip in at any rite and find gold.
freud-beyond-pleasure-hubback-1922:
Sigmund Freud published Beyond the Pleasure Principle in German in 1920. The English text here is C. J. M. Hubback's translation of 1922. Freud notes that patients repeat painful memories, and soldiers relive war trauma in dreams. Such repetition compulsion, he argues, lies beyond the search for pleasure.

From this puzzle he proposes the death drive, a pull toward rest and the inorganic state. Life drives and death drives struggle through all living things. The idea marked the turning point of Freud's later theory. Clinicians have debated it ever since. The book is short, strange, and essential for any serious reader of Freud.
frus-1861-d122:
Writing to Paris on 4 May 1861, William H. Seward framed orders for William Dayton. The letter is document 122 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

By May, Dayton was settling into the Paris legation. Seward's orders framed his talks with the French foreign office. France would move only with Britain, but its emperor's lean toward the South made Paris a post of constant watch. France and Britain acted in step that spring, which doubled the weight of Paris news. Step in step action by the two great powers shaped every smaller court's choice.
frus-1861-d22:
Henry Sanford reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 May 1861. The dispatch is document 22 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

May 1861 was the month Britain set its neutral stance toward the American war. Small posts like Brussels felt the shift at once in trade and talk. Sanford's late May letter shows a minor capital reacting to choices made in the great ones. Small courts felt each shift of the great powers at once, and Sanford read those shifts well. He read the small signs of a small court with a big court's worth of care.
frus-1861-d222:
One more Washington letter went abroad on 15 May 1861, addressed to Mr. Fogg. It was printed as Document 222 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It belongs to the opening months of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d122:
In a report dated 7 August 1862, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 122 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d22:
One more Washington letter went abroad on 11 February 1862, addressed to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed as Document 22 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The letter comes from the winter of the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d222:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, addressed William Stuart on 5 July 1862 in a letter printed as Document 222 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart was then running the British legation in Washington for the absent Lord Lyons.

The Fourth of July had just passed in a capital anxious about the war in Virginia. Stuart reported home on that mood while answering Seward's stream of letters. Exchanges like this one kept the two governments talking through a summer when many in Europe expected the Union to fail. And some hoped to profit from it. Stuart had served at the legation for years before he took charge of it.
frus-1862-d322:
Document 322 is the second Dayton report dated 3 September 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, sent both reports to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Paired reports often split the formal from the personal: ministry business in one, court impressions in the other. Early September 1862 needed both kinds, since French policy was made in the emperor's circle. This letter's mate and the Seward letters around them let a reader rebuild the Paris legation's week in unusual fullness. Dayton's French was limited, and he leaned on his staff and on careful written notes.
frus-1862-d422:
Horace J. Perry opened July 1862 with a report from Madrid to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 1 July. It stands as Document 422 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's printed diplomatic record.

Perry wrote as McClellan's campaign before Richmond was collapsing, news that would test Union credit in every European capital. Spain's ministers had to judge whether the rebellion might yet win and what that would mean for Cuba. A Madrid report in such a week told Seward how much ground the Union was losing or holding abroad. The letter sits inside the long Spanish file that runs through the whole 1862 volume.
frus-1862-d522:
At The Hague, James Shepherd Pike received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 October 1862. It is Document 522 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress with the annual message.

October orders could at last use the autumn's facts: Antietam had stopped Lee, and emancipation was now the declared policy of the government. Seward's instructions spread both points to every post. At The Hague, where antislavery feeling ran strong, the emancipation order was welcome material for Pike's work. The dispatch belongs to the brighter October file, in which Washington's tone shifted from defense to quiet confidence for the first time since spring.
frus-1862-d622:
Jacob S. Haldeman wrote from Stockholm to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 24 April 1862. His report is Document 622 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Spring reports from Stockholm carried the season's improving American news into a friendly court and recorded its reception. Haldeman's post also touched the emigration then binding Sweden to the American Midwest. It bound them family by family. No other European file in the volume quite shares that human link. His April letter belongs to the quiet northern correspondence that balanced the volume's crisis files. It is proof of something easy to forget. Large stretches of the Union's foreign relations in 1862 were calm, correct, and even warm.
frus-1863p1-d122:
On 16 March 1863, William H. Seward closed a four-letter day with this note to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 122 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The last sheet of a batch often swept up what the rest had left: a late fact or a small order. Seward's fourth letter of the day sits in that place. The set it ends shows the London brief worked through in a single sitting, a habit Seward kept all spring. This letter is the tail of that work, plain and brief.
frus-1863p1-d22:
Charles Francis Adams opened the new year with this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 January 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 22 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, one of two he sent that day.

New Year's Day 1863 was the day the freedom edict took force at home. In London, Adams's work went on as before: watch the cabinet, weigh the press, guard the Union's cause. His pair of letters that day shows the post at full stretch. This one begins the 1863 run of the most read file in the volume.
frus-1863p1-d222:
Reporting on 26 June 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is document 222 in the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

For historians, this run is a prime source on Britain's choices. It shows how close London came to stepping into the war, and why it never did. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d322:
On 13 November 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward put the American position in writing to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. This note is document 322 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Washington believed Confederate agents used British ports, ships, and soil too freely. Seward pressed Lyons to have his government tighten its watch. It dates from the month of the Trent affair, when the seizure of two Confederate envoys from a British ship nearly caused a war. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d422: Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 23 March 1863. It is document 422 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, among the formal British papers in the Civil War correspondence. Through such notes London lodged protests and guarded its neutral rights against Union measures at sea.
frus-1863p1-d522:
Document 522 in the volume is a letter of 21 May 1863 from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington.
frus-1863p1-d622:
William Stuart, the British chargé d'affaires in Washington wrote this official letter to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 23 September 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d122: On November 12, 1943, Roosevelt wrote to Chiang Kai-shek, from the start of his voyage east. The letter is Document 122 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Chiang would reach Cairo by air from China, and the meeting of the three leaders there opened on November 22. The record gives the date and the names and no subject. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d22: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on August 11, 1943, as the two men prepared to meet at Quebec within days. His message is Document 22 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The Quebec Conference, where the allies would argue out the next year's strategy, opened on August 14. The record for this note names no subject. It stands in the Foreign Relations series among the papers that framed the autumn's larger meetings at Cairo and Tehran.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d222:
Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt sent a short most-secret telegram from Ankara on 16 November 1943, number 1880. It reports a small press item with a pointed meaning. Turkish censors had told foreign reporters that morning that no more dispatches about the battle for the island of Leros would be passed.

Steinhardt reads the ban as a wish to hide the growing help Turkey was quietly giving the British on the Aegean islands, where German reinforcements had landed and the defenders were outnumbered. As support, he notes that lighthouses on the Turkish coast near Leros had been put out the night before, so British boats could land Greek guerrillas on the island in darkness.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d322:
The secretaries of the Combined Chiefs of Staff issued a note, paper C.C.S. 407/1, at Cairo on 26 November 1943. It lists the subjects, left over from the Moscow Conference, that the American and British military missions in Moscow should now take up with the Soviet authorities.

Three heads are set out in detail. On shuttle bomber bases, the missions are to ask when the Soviets will name some ten bases for bombing runs from Britain and Italy, and when service crews may be sent in. On air transport, a weekly service is sought on three routes, by Alaska, by Britain, and by Tehran. On weather, the West asks for Soviet weather ciphers, offering its own in exchange, with named regions if the full swap is refused. The missions must report progress to the chiefs from time to time.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d422:
Louis Dreyfus, the American minister in Iran, telegraphed Secretary of State Hull from Tehran on 5 December 1943, number 1090, with news of another broken release date. The tightly held Declaration on Iran had appeared in print a day early.

The Persian-language newspaper Friend of Iran, published by the Soviet Embassy's press section, carried the full text of the declaration that morning. So far as Dreyfus knows, no other Tehran morning paper printed it in any form. On learning of the Soviet paper's publication, Prime Minister Soheily released the text to the Tehran press himself, and it will appear in all the afternoon papers. Hurley and Dreyfus had understood definitely that nothing was to be released by anyone until eight the next night, Moscow time, and the British and Americans will still hold to that hour.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d522:
Harry Hopkins wrote to Secretary of State Cordell Hull on December 20, 1943, back in Washington after the Tehran and Cairo journey. Hopkins, the President's special assistant, worked from the White House rather than from the State Department. The Department printed his message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Hopkins and Hull represented two different styles of Roosevelt's government: the personal envoy and the cabinet secretary. Business between them had to be joined up after a trip on which Hopkins had seen everything and Hull had seen the cables. A message in this channel shows that joining-up in progress. It also marks the summit season closing into ordinary, if urgent, administration.
frus-1944-quebec-d122:
State Department planners prepared this top-secret briefing paper, titled "Anglo-American-Russian Relations," for the Quebec Conference in September 1944. It was annexed to a memorandum Secretary Hull sent Roosevelt. The paper asks how the three great powers will relate once the war ends, and what role Britain will try to play between Washington and Moscow.

Its core is a long quotation from Admiral Leahy's letter of May 16, 1944. Leahy argued that keeping the three powers united was the cardinal aim of policy. Russia's strength was rising fast; America could defend Britain but could not defeat Russia in Europe. The paper urges blocking rival spheres of influence and drawing the Soviet Union into the planned world organization.
frus-1944-quebec-d22:
A further Churchill message to President Roosevelt is dated August 8, 1944, making a dense packet for a single day. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume alongside its companion.

Same-day companions in this file usually divide a military question from a political one, letting each be argued cleanly. August 1944 supplied plenty of both, from the race for Paris to the first arguments over Germany's future. For readers, this message rewards being read with its pair, as the two men themselves would have done, across one crowded day of a collapsing front.
frus-1944-quebec-d222:
Hull returned to the meat contract the next day, September 13, 1944, with additional observations of mounting anger. The embassy in Buenos Aires reported that Britain's Ministry of Food had told the Argentines it would sign a two-year contract at current prices. Britain would buy the entire exportable surplus for four years, prices re-examined at two. The word from London, Hull noted, came as a great relief to the Colonels.

To Hull, Britain treated the Argentine Fascist threat as minor policy; to America it was major. Failure, he warned, would give the Nazis a powerful center to renew their fight in this hemisphere. Given America's enormous aid, asking Britain to forego petty commercial advantages from a Fascist government was not asking too much.
frus-1945-50-intel-d122: A memorandum for the record, dated 8 August 1946, was written on the dispute's busiest day. That day, the National Intelligence Authority and Director Hoover both sent letters to the attorney general. Memoranda for the record fix a talk or an act in writing while it is fresh. The bare title names no author. So the paper's weight comes from its date, and from its place in the run of August papers that settled the hemisphere question.
frus-1945-50-intel-d22:
Morton Chiles of the FBI sent a memorandum to Director Hoover on 2 October 1945. It is one of the bureau's inside papers printed in the volume's opening run. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Field and headquarters men fed Hoover a stream of reports on the shifting intelligence scene. Chiles's memorandum adds a staff voice to the director's own letters, widening the picture of how the bureau watched its rivals. Readers building the FBI side of the story should gather these inside papers together. They show an agency that treated the bureaucratic fight of 1945 as seriously as any case, and staffed it accordingly.
frus-1945-50-intel-d222:
Dated 19 September 1947, this memorandum runs from the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter) to the National Security Council. Readers meet it as document 222 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. That season, the talk in Washington was of one big law to join up defense, foreign policy, and intelligence.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The points are stated once and left to stand; the file around it holds the answer they drew. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d322:
The title "National Intelligence Authority Directive No. 10" heads a text dated 30 July 1947. It survives in print as document 322 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The National Security Act was moving through Congress that year, and it would soon replace the wartime setup with the CIA.

A numbered directive joined a growing shelf of rules that told the new agencies how to run themselves. Later directives amend or kill earlier ones, so the number and date fix this one's place in the chain. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d422:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 4 was issued on 12 December 1947. It is document 422 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

These directives, called NSCIDs, were the standing rules of the new intelligence system. The Council used them to divide duties among the CIA and the older department and service shops. A directive from the first months of the CIA shows the rules being written while the work was already under way. The first directives leaned on the wartime OSS as a model, even as they broke new ground.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d122:
Slow down, the President told his Secretary of State on 20 October 1944. Roosevelt's top secret memorandum answers Hull's paper of 29 September on planning Germany's treatment. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

Preparations are all very well, Roosevelt writes, but speed is not essential now. He dislikes detailed plans for a country the allies do not yet occupy; a week, a month, or several months may pass first. One warning stands out. The European Advisory Commission is advisory, and he and the Secretary are not bound by its advice. Some points are clear already, demilitarization among them, and those can be approved at once.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d22: The same day he wrote Stalin, 18 November 1944, Roosevelt also sent Churchill a message, filed as document 22. It appears in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, published by the Department of State. Handling both allies on one day was the president's routine that fall, and the paired letters let readers compare what each partner was told.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d222:
Will Clayton warned against sweetening the lend-lease terms for Moscow in this 20 January 1945 paper. The assistant secretary's comments, addressed to Stettinius, are printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. They answer proposals lately made by Secretary Morgenthau on postwar trade with the Soviet Union.

The Treasury would now offer the 3(c) supplementary agreement without interest charges. Clayton objects that Washington told the Soviet negotiators, in full good faith and with Treasury agreement, that its last 3(c) offer was final. Better terms were said to be barred on legal and other grounds. To come back now with the same offer minus interest would tell Moscow that last summer's word was not true. It might kindle afresh the old Soviet suspicion of American good faith.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d322:
President Roosevelt's party reached the Crimea on February 3, 1945, and the official log of the trip tells the day hour by hour. His plane, guarded by five fighters, landed at Saki airfield after a 1,375-mile flight from Malta. Foreign Commissar Molotov, Secretary Stettinius, and Ambassador Harriman waited on the ground. Stalin had not yet arrived in the Crimea.

Roosevelt stayed aboard until Churchill's plane came in some twenty minutes later. The log names the Secret Service agents of the advance party and notes one escort fighter that turned back to Athens with engine trouble. Such logs anchor the conference story in times, miles, and weather.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d422:
Eleven American questions, eleven Soviet answers: this memorandum of February 9, 1945, sums up Antonov's replies for the United States Chiefs of Staff. On operations, there was no change but delay. Troops meant to move east at the New Year were engaged in the central sector of the Eastern Front.

On supply, Stalin said the Pacific sea route would be required. Foodstuffs and petroleum products topped the need. Some air transport would probably be wanted, though its capacity was small. The memo, written the same afternoon, turns a secret oral briefing into a planning document. Each short answer fed American timetables for the Pacific war.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d122:
President Truman told Stalin on July 5, 1945, that the press ban at Terminal would be announced that day. His secret message, number 309, is document 122 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Churchill had proposed the advance announcement so that newspapers would not send top reporters to Berlin for nothing.

Truman writes that, in line with their understanding, he is announcing that the press will not be allowed at Terminal. All that will be issued, he says, will be such official communiqués as the three governments decide on from time to time. He adds that a similar message has gone to Churchill. The three-power agreement kept the conference sealed, with news released only in joint statements.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d22:
Keep the trip quiet: Grew's memorandum of May 21, 1945, records a telephone call with Stettinius about the Hopkins mission. Grew told the Secretary that Hopkins was going to Moscow with Harriman, and that the fact should stay quiet until Hopkins arrived. The Secretary asked whether they were leaving together. Harriman was leaving that day; Hopkins would follow in a couple of days, with Bohlen.

Harriman had wanted to clear the trip with the Secretary, Grew added, but it had come to a head very quickly. Such a visit would be very helpful, he thought, since Hopkins seemed to have Stalin's confidence. The President had approved it. The memo shows the mission arranged in hours, by telephone.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d222:
A State Department briefing paper made the case for restoring France to great-power rank. Its extracts are printed as document 222 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. The paper, from Truman's briefing book, surveys France's return to world councils since her liberation in 1944.

 American policy treats France on the basis of her potential power rather than her present strength, the summary says. And that policy has been justified. Her usefulness will grow, the paper argues. So will her contribution to a peaceful world. This will happen if her wish for full partnership is met by anticipation rather than by tardy or grudging compliance. The extracts trace the steps so far. They include recognition of her government and a promised permanent Security Council seat. They also include a full share in the control machinery for Germany, including her own occupation zone.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d322:
Prepared for the President's briefing book, an undated paper sets out how the United States should handle Soviet economic moves in Eastern Europe. Its recommendations ask Truman to seek a Soviet pledge on several points. The first concerns property owned by Americans in the countries Moscow's armies occupied.

The paper asks that removals of such capital equipment stop, that gear already taken be returned, and that owners who cannot get it back be paid promptly and in full. It also asks free entry and travel for Americans, and no deals giving the Soviet Union a sole grip on trade or raw materials in those countries.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d422:
Ruhr coal figures fill Murphy's cable to Clayton of June 29, 1945, an informal summary of the situation. Stocks on hand, he reports, total between six and seven million tons on the surface. Production has jumped to 60,000 tons of marketable coal daily, beyond what the mines themselves burn.

That rate equals about a million and a half marketable tons a month. Murphy's sources estimate it will rise to four million tons monthly within two months. He also passes on a complaint: early delay owed much to a poor choice of British military personnel, when the 21st Army Group assigned some 4,000 officers and men to the task.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d522:
Polish economic hopes are reported in Harriman's cable from Moscow of June 26, 1945. At lunch on June 23 with Bierut, Osóbka-Morawski, and Mikołajczyk, he had recalled their earlier talk, in which the Poles emphasized their hope for economic assistance from the United States. He suggested an informal discussion of what they visualized, which he could report to his government.

Relief and rehabilitation, Harriman explained, would be dealt with by UNRRA, and in the medical field to some extent by the American Red Cross. Reconstruction, he said, must be dealt with on a business basis. Bierut readily recognized this principle, and said the new Polish government would wish to make a commercial treaty with the United States.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d622:
Edward Wolf, liaison man in Washington for the U.S. reparations team, wired Edwin Pauley in Moscow on June 30, 1945. The secret message is document 622 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It passes on oil figures from Ralph Davies of the Petroleum Administration for War.

Davies put the 1946 surplus oil of Russian-held Eastern Europe at some 60,000 barrels a day above local needs. Rumania alone accounts for 47,000 of that figure. Against it, Western and Mediterranean Europe would draw some 292,000 barrels a day from Anglo-U.S. sources in late 1945. Use of the eastern surplus, Davies argued, would ease a tight world supply. It would also save much tanker space if the oil moved west by land or from Constanta by ship.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1022:
Secretary of War Henry Stimson sent President Truman this top secret memorandum extract on July 16, 1945. The section shown treats the dismemberment of Germany. Stimson would grant Poland some western land to offset land she loses to Russia. But Russia, he insists, must show how the millions of Germans there will be cared for. They must not be dumped on American hands.

Beyond that, Stimson would not cut Germany further. The remaining land needs its full resources for any fair recovery, he argues. He asks for a study of international ownership of the Ruhr and Saar resources. He also attacks a plan to sever the Ruhr and Rhineland as a protectorate. It would tear out millions of pure Germans, he warns, and breed violent irredentism.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1122:
John Winant, the American ambassador in London, sent this dispatch to the Acting Secretary of State on 19 July 1945. Winant had held the London post through most of the war. From the embassy he reported British moods, press talk, and the thinking of the government he dealt with daily.

His cables gave Washington a view of its chief ally that the summit table could not supply. The team in Germany heard British claims in person. Winant heard what London said at home. This dispatch kept the home office reading the same signals. It is one piece of the embassy's close watch during the talks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1222:
Harriman wrote to the Secretary of State on 31 July 1945, from his post as ambassador to the Soviet Union. The cable went out two days before Potsdam closed. The Moscow embassy's word still mattered as the final terms were fixed.

Harriman had dealt with Stalin's government for two years. His judgments on Soviet aims carried a tested weight in Washington. A late dispatch from his hand belongs to the summit's endgame picture. It shows the Moscow post at work to the last, feeding the secretary the capital's mood while the deal was sealed in Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1322:
The Economic Subcommittee reported again on 24 July 1945. Its reports carried the staff-level work on Germany's economy up to the foreign ministers. This second report in the volume came a week into the summit, as the money terms hardened.

The group's charge covered the state of German industry, food, and trade, and the rules the peace would set for each. Its findings fed the protocol's money clauses. This report is the expert layer speaking a second time. Read with the first report, it shows the economic brief growing as the bargaining narrowed toward terms.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1422:
The Soviet delegation at Potsdam submitted a text on 14 July 1945, in the volume's closing run of conference papers. Three Soviet texts in the volume bear that date, the eve of the leaders' arrival at Potsdam.

Tabling several texts at once is a way of setting the agenda before others can. The Soviet side came to Germany with its program written out, and these papers are that program in pieces. For readers, the worth lies in sequence: Soviet asks first, then the talks, then the signed results. This text is one piece of the opening hand Moscow played at the last wartime summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-122:
Benjamin Cohen's notes for July 27, 1945 continue his running record of the Potsdam talks. Cohen advised the Secretary of State and watched legal wording closely. His notes were printed in the second Potsdam volume with the other American records of the sessions. Late July was the conference's crunch time, when drafts moved toward final form.

In Cohen's pages the reader follows remarks almost as spoken. He noted not just conclusions but the path to them. That path matters, since Potsdam's phrases were argued over for years. The notes show a careful lawyer guarding each commitment as it was made.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-22:
A United States delegation memorandum sums up the foreign ministers' meeting of July 19, 1945. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Its purpose was to fix the agenda for the heads of government that afternoon.

Five subjects were recommended in order. First came the Control Council's authority in German political questions, on an approved redraft. Poland came second, with a British paper sent to a subcommittee for drafting changes. If that group reported by four o'clock, Poland would be ready that day. Third came the disposition of the German fleet and merchant ships, on a Russian paper. Spain came fourth, again on a Russian paper proposing a joint policy toward Franco. Fifth came the carrying out of the Yalta declaration on liberated Europe and the satellite states.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d722:
Document 722 is a communication from the British Embassy in Washington to the Department of State, dated July 16, 1945. It arrived on the eve of the Potsdam Conference. Allied embassies fed their governments' views into Washington daily. This note entered the record printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Embassy notes are formal but pointed. A government uses them to place a view on the record in exact words. Readers see the alliance's plumbing: London speaking to Washington through set channels. The timing matters. Views lodged before a summit can shape its agenda. The document opens a window on the run-up, not just the talks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d822:
Barnes wrote from Bulgaria on July 27, 1945, in document 822. The representative in Sofia reported to the Acting Secretary of State. His letters in this volume span the whole conference. This one dates from the final week, when the Balkan files were closing. It joined the second Potsdam volume.

A final-week report from Sofia carries a valedictory edge. The summit's decisions would soon fix Bulgaria's frame. Barnes stated his facts for the record one more time. Readers see a mission aware that its reporting might outlast its influence. The document proves that awareness right: his words are still read.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d922: Drafters prepared this short report for the Economic Sub-Committee at Potsdam, left undated in the files. It admits failure in plain terms. The sub-committee had not reached agreement on certain basic principles of a reparations plan. It tells the Council of Ministers that no agreement on those basic issues now seems possible. The members offer to keep talking only if the ministers wish it. The draft sits in the Pauley Files, among the reparations papers of July 1945.
frus-1952-54Guat-d222: A FRUS telegram from the CIA station in Guatemala, 1952-1954. The agency plotted against Arbenz. This document preserves that cable. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
frus-1961-63v10-d22: Power changed hands in Washington in January 1961, and this FRUS editorial note captures the Cuba handover between presidents. Eisenhower briefed Kennedy on the island. The note provides that background. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
frus-1964-68v03-d22: A 1964-1968 FRUS telegram from the Vietnam volume. The field reported. This entry holds that cable. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
gao-gaoreports-b-298522: Ball Aerospace & Technologies took its August 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Aerospace giants get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-299022: Wackenhut's joint venture doubled its January 2007 protest — two case numbers, one security fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The venture challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299422: Information Ventures doubled its May 2007 protest — two case numbers, one information-services fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both claims at once. The firm challenged the awards as unfair; the call weighs each claim carefully. Paired filings get one thorough answer from the bid court.
gao-gaoreports-b-307122: The president's proposed rescissions got an impoundment ruling in this March 2006 GAO call, which tests whether the withheld funds were legal. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides if the impoundments stood. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-308822: A building mishap ate the Archives' books in this 2007 GAO ruling — damage to the revolving fund's records from a facility failure. The call sorts the fiscal fallout. Even the keepers of history, the ruling shows, can lose their own paperwork.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-22: Transfer students deserved fairer credit in 2005, and GAO's report says colleges could promote more consistent coursework consideration. The findings demand the fairness. The report warns that the switching students deserved their credits honored. The consideration had to be consistent. The switching students deserved their credits honored.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-722: Energy Department contracting was slow in 2006, and GAO's report says better performance measures and management were needed to address award delays. The findings demand the metrics. The report warns that the atomic agency's deals should not crawl. The contracting had to speed up.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-22: The pension cops were improving in 2007, and GAO's report says enforcement had gotten better, though more action could help. The findings credit the gains. The report warns that the retirement savings of millions needed sharper guarding. The watch had to stay sharp.
