gao-gaoreports-gao-07-522: The privacy office was learning to speak up in 2007 — GAO's report says notifying the public had improved, but hard challenges stayed. The findings grade the outreach effort honestly. The report's standard: the watched deserve to know that they are being watched.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-622: Underground miners needed a better safety net in 2007 — GAO's report says the mine agency and its partners could tighten watch and teamwork. The findings target the oversight gaps below ground. The report's demand: no miner should die for a paperwork failure.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-122: This 2007 GAO report tells the Pentagon to show its math on the new medical chain of command. Shuffling who runs care for troops and kin is no small move, GAO says — spell out the wins, the costs, and the risks first. The report is a demand for homework before the brass rearranges the military's doctors.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-22: GAO published its findings on catastrophic Disasters: Federal Efforts Help States Prepare for and Respond to Psychological Consequences, but FEMA's Crisis Counseling Program Needs Improvemen in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-422: GAO published its findings on native Hawaiian Education Act: Greater Oversight Would Increase Accountability and Enable Targeting of Funds to Areas with Greatest Need in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-622: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on combating Terrorism: The United States Lacks Comprehensive Plan to Destroy the Terrorist Threat and Close the Safe Haven in Pakistan's Federally Administered Tr. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
goldenweiser-early-civilization-1922:
Alexander Goldenweiser, a student of Boas, wrote this 1922 book to introduce students and general readers to anthropology. It presents the young science's main ideas about early civilization, race, and culture in clear, direct prose.

Goldenweiser attacks racial determinism, the claim that a people's worth is fixed by blood, and argues that culture explains what race cannot. He explains how inventions spread, how customs form patterns, and why no society stands still on a single ladder of progress. The book's calm, skeptical tone made it a classroom staple. It shows the Boasian view of culture reaching a wide audience.
hahnemann-organon-6th-edition-1922:
Samuel Hahnemann finished the sixth edition of his Organon of Medicine in 1842, but English readers waited until 1922 for it. William Boericke translated the manuscript Hahnemann had left behind. This last version holds the founder's mature doctrine, the form homeopathy's classic text finally took.

Its best known change is the LM potency scale, a gentler way of giving repeated doses. Hahnemann also reworked his teaching on long illnesses and on how a remedy acts. Because it appeared eighty years after he completed it, the sixth edition reads as a voice from the movement's first age speaking to a later one.
heindel-rosicrucian-philosophy-qa-1922:
Max Heindel set his Rosicrucian Philosophy in Questions and Answers in 1922. The form is plain: a short ask, then a full reply. The book serves as a mate to his Cosmo-Conception. It deals with the points new hands ask most.

Karma, birth anew, and the life past death fill much of the text. Heindel tells what the dead see, how the soul grows, and how to live well. Health, food, and prayer get plain, firm words too. The book shows the school at work on real doubts of real folk.
hesse-siddhartha-1922:
Hermann Hesse published Siddhartha in 1922, his lyrical novel of self-discovery on the roads and rivers of India. A Brahmin's son seeks enlightenment by the river in a tale Hesse built from his own spiritual searching. The book, quiet in Hesse's lifetime, became a scripture of the 1960s counterculture.

Siddhartha leaves home with Govinda, starves as a Samana, and hears the Buddha, yet declines to follow any teacher's doctrine. Wealth, love with Kamala, and despair by the river teach what sermons could not, in a cycle. Vasudeva, the ferryman, teaches him to listen to the river, where all voices join in the sacred Om of being. Govinda returns at the close and sees, in his friend's face, the smile of perfected unity in all things. Hesse's prose, spare as a parable, carries a lifetime's East-West seeking in miniature.
housman-last-poems-1922:
A. E. Housman was a Cambridge scholar of Latin who published only two slim books of poems in his lifetime. Last Poems, issued in 1922, was the second. It holds forty-one poems, many kept back for years after A Shropshire Lad.

The poems keep Housman's spare, hard music: short stanzas, plain words, and no wasted lines. Soldiers, hangings, lost youth, and the shortness of life return as themes. Housman refused to explain or soften his bleak outlook. Coming twenty-six years after his first book, this volume closed his lyric career with the same austere control that began it.
indagine-introductiones-apotelesmaticae-:
Johannes ab Indagine was a German priest and astrologer whose Introductiones Apotelesmaticae appeared in 1522. The elegant introductions of his title open three arts at once: chiromancy, physiognomy, and astrology. Palm, face, and stars each promise a reading of character and fate.

Indagine teaches the lines of the hand, the signs of the face and body, and the rules of the birth chart as one connected science. His book, often reprinted and translated, carried these arts to readers across Reformation Europe. It stands as the Renaissance divination encyclopedia, the one-volume guide to reading a person whole.
irish-free-state-constitution-1922:
The Irish Free State adopted its constitution in 1922, giving legal form to the Anglo-Irish Treaty of the year before. The settlement made the twenty-six counties a self-ruling dominion under the Crown. It also split the nationalist movement, and civil war was already raging as the charter passed.

The text creates a parliament in Dublin, a governor-general for the Crown, and an oath of allegiance that republicans hated. It promises free speech, fair trial, and religious liberty in strong terms, and it allowed easy amendment, which governments soon used to strip it down. Saorstát Éireann's founding statute bought partial freedom at the price of brother fighting brother. De Valera replaced it in 1937. The document stands as the treaty's law, paid for in civil war.
jersey-devil-evening-world-wombat-1909-0:
New York laughs at the scare in the Evening World piece of January 22, 1909. All week the papers had rung with tales of a winged devil in New Jersey. The World sends up the craze in fine style. Its wags sort the beast with mock care and place it, at last, as a wombat: a stout beast of the far south that no more flies than a pig.

The joke needs the panic to land, and that panic was real. The piece is a prime scrap of how press both fed and mocked the wave. It shows the craze at its peak.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-22:
Huronia in 1642 bleeds through the pages of Volume 22, from 1898. Jogues has escaped his captors, yet the mission still counts its wounds. Thwaites prints reports from a land cut off by hostile forces on the rivers.

Quebec watches from below, unable to send real aid north. The Iroquois blockade chokes trade, travel, and news for the Hurons. Priests tally losses, bury friends, and brace for worse to come. Still, not one report speaks of giving up the mission fields. Resolve holds firm even as the annual pages grow darker and more grim. Hope thins, but it never quite dies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mahamad-more-co:
Mahamad, the governing board of a Spanish-Portuguese congregation, is explained in a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia article. The board held four wardens and a treasurer. Its members were chosen from the full members of the synagogue. When a seat fell vacant, surviving members and eight former members formed an election committee. One member, picked by lot, named the new colleague.

The article describes a ruling circle that guarded itself. No man could sit on the board alongside his son, grandson, in-laws, brother, nephew, or cousin. A treasurer had to be twenty-five, and a warden forty, unless he had served as treasurer. The board's laws, the Ascamot, gave it sweeping control over members' lives. No marriage, divorce, lawsuit, or printed book went forward without its leave. In London it even banned members from joining parties against the government. The entry preserves the tight self-rule of the old Sephardic communities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-markens-isaac-1:
Isaac Markens, an American writer, receives an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in New York City on October 9, 1846, he was the son of Elias Markens, a linguist and Orientalist. He was educated in the city's public schools. He became a merchant first, then private secretary to Railway Commissioner Albert Fink.

The article centers on his turn to journalism and history. Markens wrote for the New York Commercial Advertiser and the Mail and Express. In 1888 he published The Hebrews in America. The entry values the book as the first work of its kind on American Jewish history. It is a series of historical and biographical sketches. Markens also served for years as secretary to the arbitration board of the joint railway committee. The notice preserves a journalist who gave American Jews their first collective portrait.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mazliah-judah-b:
Judah ben Abraham Mazliah of the Padova family, an Italian Talmudist, cabalist, and poet, was rabbi of Modena and died on August 10, 1728. Solomon Schechter and H. Brody entered him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The entry names two of his works, “Tokahat Megullah” and the cabalistic “Ozerot Sheleg.” It adds his poems: a prayer and an acrostic built on the seventy-two-letter name of God. It adds an epigram on human mortality that became an epitaph in the cemetery at Pinale.

The notice then turns into a family history, after noting that only a few of his legal answers were printed. His son Manasseh Joshua, brother-in-law of Isaiah Bassani, left responsa behind him. Another son, Menahem Azariah, became rabbi of Florence. He was a legal authority and tireless preacher who also wrote liturgical poems. The family line runs back to Abraham ben Samuel of Padua, married in 1530.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-ben-eli:
Menahem ben Eliakim, a German scholar of the fourteenth century from Bingen, is entered in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Richard Gottheil and M. Seligsohn as the maker of a working tool: the "'Aruk Goren," a dictionary of the Talmud giving German translations of all its difficult words, especially those borrowed from Arabic and Greek. He built it on the great "'Aruk" of Nathan ben Jehiel, extracting much and adding matter of his own.

The article's puzzle is the title, which seems to mean "a condensed 'Aruk"; Wolf read it as "Short 'Aruk," and a Latin rendering, "Aruch Breve," circulates in later literature. Wolf also argued, against appearances, that the book is not the anonymous "'Aruk ha-Kazer," despite their similar contents. The notice is short, resting on Steinschneider and Zunz, but it preserves the name of a lexicographer who made the Talmud readable for German Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moineshti-10922:
Moineshti, a small town in Moldavia's Bakau district, was an oil town built by Jews, as Richard Gottheil and E. Schwarzfeld write in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The census of 1820 counted forty-two Jewish taxpayers, already the larger part of the population. Their business was the petroleum wells that abound in the region.

In 1860 Wolf Lazarovici set up the first refinery, then a paraffin factory, and the Theiler brothers later developed the industry scientifically. Fires repeatedly burned the town, yet it prospered until 1880, when Jews expelled from nearby villages crowded in and thinned everyone's living. In 1882 the first Rumanian colonist group for Palestine was recruited here; by 1899, with 2,363 Jews, emigration to America was draining the town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morpurgo-11022:
Morpurgo is the name of an Austro-Italian family that came originally from Marburg in Styria. In the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, Isidore Singer and Vittore Castiglione give short lives of four of its members. The sketches run from an insurance founder of the seventeen hundreds to poets and economists of the eighteen hundreds.

Giuseppe Lazzaro Morpurgo founded the first Austrian life insurance company at Trieste, the seed of Assicurazioni Generali. Emilio Morpurgo served as a deputy and wrote on statistics, finance, and rural law. Rahel Morpurgo, a cousin of S. D. Luzzatto, wrote Hebrew poetry that was gathered after her death. Together the lives show one family's reach across Italian Jewish letters, business, and public life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ha-levi-h:
Moses ha-Levi ha-Nazir was a Palestinian rabbi of the seventeenth century. Gotthard Deutsch and Lazarus Grünhut wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He was the father of Joseph ha-Levi and son-in-law of Abraham ibn Hananiah of Hebron. His byname ha-Nazir marks him as a Nazirite, one under a special vow.

No book of his was printed under his own name. His responsa survive inside his son's Matteh Yosef and inside Hasdai ha-Kohen Perahyah's Torat Hesed. A manuscript collection of his responsa, Mayim Hayyim, was still in the family's hands when the entry was written. He also traveled as a messenger from the Holy Land, appearing in Constantinople and in Greece.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-munkacsy-bernha:
Bernhard Munkácsy was a Hungarian philologist and ethnologist born at Grosswardein on March 12, 1860. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He came of a famous rabbinical family, but his studies went to the Hungarian language. With Ignatz Kunos he traveled to the Csángó Magyar colonies in 1880.

The Hungarian Academy crowned his early works on the Csángó dialect and on Turkish loan-words. He then traveled the Kama and Volga country to study the Votyak language, and later the Urals for the Voguls. His Votyak lexicon and five volumes of Vogul poetry grew from those journeys. Budapest also made him inspector of religious instruction in all its schools.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-narboni-david-b: David ben Joseph Narboni was a rabbi of Narbonne in the first half of the twelfth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia gives him a short notice by its editorial committee and S. Kahn. He was probably a son of Joseph Gaon of Narbonne. In 1139 he sent Abraham ibn Ezra three questions on chronology, still studied with the great man's answers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nehemiah-11422:
Nehemiah rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem. Emil G. Hirsch, David Samuel Margoliouth, Wilhelm Bacher, and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the son of Hachaliah. The book bearing his name is the sole source on him. He was cupbearer to King Artaxerxes of Persia.

Bad news from Palestine moved Nehemiah to act. The king gave him letters and timber for the walls. As governor for twelve years, he rebuilt amid armed threats. Rich landowners led the camp against his work. He restored lands seized for debt to their owners. He gave up his own governor's allowance to help. Later he enforced the Sabbath and Temple dues. Plots, false prophets, and pedigree fights fill his memoir.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nun-11622:
Nun is the fourteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Crawford Howell Toy and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its name signifies a fish in Hebrew. The fish may echo its earliest shape. Two forms serve it in written words.

One form opens and fills a word's body. A longer form closes words at their end. The sound is a liquid made with the nose. In some settings it takes a French nasal ring. It swaps with its fellow liquids, lamed and resh. As a prefix it marks we in the imperfect. It also builds the nif'al stem of verbs. Often it drops or melts into the next sound. Its value in numbers is fifty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppeln-11722:
Oppeln is a city in Prussian Silesia, on the Oder. Gotthard Deutsch and Leo Bäck wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The first clear word of Jews there comes from the thirteen hundreds. They no doubt came at a much earlier date. Great roads from Hungary and Poland crossed there.

In 1557 the Jewish group was a small one still. It held just seventeen who paid tax there. A synagogue stood in the town by that time. No word of a burial ground comes down from then. In that same year the duke urged their casting out. The estates of the realm backed his plan at once. By 1565 all Jews were forced to leave Oppeln. None are named as living there till Prussian rule came.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oulif-charles-n:
Charles Narcisse Oulif was a French lawyer from Metz. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Metz in July of 1794. He died in Paris on March 3, 1867. He read at Metz and then at Strasburg in youth.

In 1815 Charles was the first Jew to take a law degree there. He was called to the bar at Metz that same year. From the start of his work, he fought for Jews. He fought to lift the checks laid on Jews in France. His chief fight was to end the harsh Jewish oath. He won that fight twice in the court of Metz. He had the word Jew struck from court texts there. In 1834 he took a chair of law at Brussels.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pereire-12022:
The Pereires were a French family of bankers and builders. Jacques Kahn, Meyer Kayserling, and Isidore Singer wrote the article. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its leading figure is Emile Pereire of Bordeaux. They rose from Bordeaux to the top of Paris finance.

Emile was born in 1800 and died in 1875. With his brother Isaac he reshaped French finance. In 1852 they founded the Crédit Mobilier and the Crédit Foncier. Emile also promoted railroad lines across France. His lines ran from Paris to the north and the south. The family spread into Spain, Austria, and Russia too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phinehas-b-samu:
Phinehas ben Samuel was the last high priest of Jerusalem. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Josephus counts him the eighty-third since Aaron. Nothing in his life had prepared him for the office.

Phinehas was a farmer in the village of Aphthia. In 67 the rebels chose their high priest by lot. The lot fell on this unfit and unwilling man. They dragged him to Jerusalem against his will. Priests dressed him and coached him at each rite. Worthy men wept at the mockery of it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-podolia-12222:
Podolia was a government in southwestern Russia, on the border with Austrian Galicia. Herman Rosenthal, S. Hurwitz, and Vasili Rosenthal wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It traces Jewish life in the region over many centuries. Polish and Russian records from 1550 name Jewish towns there. Old tombstones show that Jews lived there much earlier.

Centuries of persecution left the Jews of Podolia very poor. New movements found ready hearers there. Followers of Shabbethai Zebi spread their message in the region. So did the Frankists and the Hasidim. A table at the end gives the census of 1897 by district. It lists total population and Jewish population for each district.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ptolemy-iii-sur:
Ptolemy the Third, surnamed Euergetes, was king of Egypt. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He reigned from 247 to 222 B.C. The book of Daniel points to him in one passage. That passage tells of great wins in Syria. Outside proof backs the claim, the writers say.

The idols of the beaten lands were seized for Egypt. Gold and silver vessels went with them as spoil. A stone at Aduli backs this account in full. It says he brought back a vast weight of silver. It names two thousand five hundred statues of gods as well. Some were the very gods Cambyses once took from Egypt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-red-sea-12622:
The Red Sea is the water crossed in the Exodus from Egypt. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The name Red Sea does not appear before the Apocrypha. Older passages call the water Yam Suf in Hebrew.

The article argues Yam Suf means the Gulf of Suez. That gulf once reached farther north than it does now. The word suf may mean reed, the writers say. It may also be an Egyptian loan word. Some link the Red Sea name to red seaweed. Others point to red mountains or coastal peoples. The same Hebrew name covers another gulf too. The entry weighs names, maps, and old texts together.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rewbell-jean-fr:
Jean François Rewbell was an Alsatian deputy in France's National Assembly. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Colmar on October 8, 1747. He died there on November 23, 1807.

The article centers on the Jewish emancipation debate of 1789. Rewbell was an advanced republican, yet he opposed full rights. He joined Abbé Maury and two bishops against the motion. Clermont-Tonnerre proposed it, with Robespierre and Mirabeau supporting. Rewbell warned of deep hatred toward Jews in Alsace. He said citizenship for them would be dangerous there. He opposed the motion again in vain. In September 1791 the Assembly made Jews citizens. The entry shows a republican who drew a line at Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ronsburg-bezale:
Bezalel b. Joel Ronsburg was a Bohemian Talmudist and rabbi born in 1760. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Louis Ginzberg wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died at Prague on September 25, 1820. There he was judge and yeshivah head.

The article says Zacharias Frankel was one of his pupils. His Horah Gaber comments on the treatise Horayot. It appeared at Prague in 1802. His Ma'aseh Rab gives marginal notes on the Talmud. Those notes were reprinted in Prague and Wilna editions. Other works on ritual law stayed in manuscript. His surname comes from Ronsperg, a Bohemian city. At official naming he took the name Daniel Bezaleel Rosenbaum. Its initials stand for both his surnames, they note.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rubinstein-isaa: Isaac Rubinstein was an Austrian deputy born at Czernowitz in 1805. Isidore Singer and Emil Jelinek wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He sat on his town council and served as vice-president of the Czernowitz chamber of commerce and industry. That body sent him to the Austrian Reichsrath, where he sat from 1873 to 1878. He was active in charity work and held many honorary offices at home. He died at Ischl on September 1, 1878.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salem-peaceful-:
Salem is a place name first met when Abraham returns from battle in Genesis. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Melchizedek, king of Salem, comes out to meet the patriarch there.

Josephus, the Targums, later commentators, and Jerome identify Salem with Jerusalem. They take Salem as a shortened form of the city's full name. A Psalm line, in Salem is his tabernacle, supports that view strongly. Jerome elsewhere links Salem to Salim, in the Jordan valley near Scythopolis. The entry weighs both sites without forcing a single answer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ha-katon:
Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Samuel ha-Ḳaṭon. He was a tanna, a rabbi of the Mishnah age, of the second generation. He lived early in the second century of the common era. His name means Samuel the Younger. Some say it marked his great modesty.

No rulings of Samuel survive, but a few of his sayings do. Once, at a meeting on fixing a leap year, he stood up and left. He claimed he was the one who had come uninvited. He did that so a real outsider would not be shamed. Samuel is best known for the prayer against heretics, the birkat ha-minim. He composed it at the request of the patriarch Gamaliel II. It became part of the daily Shemoneh Esreh prayer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-satrap-a-v-prin:
Emil G. Hirsch and Louis H. Gray wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the satrap. A satrap ruled a province in ancient Persia. The Old Persian word means protector of the kingdom. Darius created the office. He chose satraps from Persians only, often men of royal blood. They first numbered twenty. Their main duty was to gather taxes and send the revenue to the king.

The article then tests the Bible's later mentions of satraps. Ezra, Esther, and Daniel speak of them loosely. Esther counts 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia. Daniel even gives Nebuchadnezzar a court of satraps. Josephus contradicts himself, giving 360 satrapies in one place and 127 in another. Such numbers show these late accounts carry little history. The article closes with older studies of the Persian system.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schulbaum-moses:
Isidore Singer and M. Margel wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Moses Schulbaum. He was an Austrian Hebraist. Schulbaum was born at Jezierzany, in Galicia, on April 25, 1835. His mother descended from Ḥakam Ẓebi. In 1870 he joined Michael Wolf's printing house at Lemberg as a proofreader.

When the Baron de Hirsch schools opened in Galicia, Schulbaum went to teach Hebrew. He taught at Kolomea from 1889. In 1897 he moved to the school at Mikulince, where he still teaches in 1905. He ranks among the foremost Neo-Hebraic writers. He turned Schiller's Robbers into Hebrew in 1871. He also revised Ben Zeeb's Hebrew dictionary in five volumes. Its last four parts were his own work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shushan-susa-pu:
Shushan Purim is the name for Purim as kept on the fifteenth of Adar. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the day. Esther's book sets that date for Purim at Shushan. In fact all large walled cities keep the fifteenth.

Esther's text hints both dates were feasts at Shushan itself. Rabbis sorted the practice into a clear rule instead. Open, unwalled towns celebrate on the fourteenth of Adar. Walled cities, like Shushan, celebrate on the fifteenth. The name stuck to Shushan because Esther names it directly. Other walled cities are only vaguely indicated there. Jews of Shushan do not keep the fourteenth, nor do open towns keep the fifteenth. The entry untangles a two-day festival puzzle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-b-yannai:
Simeon ben Yannai was a Palestinian amora of the third century of the common era. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He transmits a legal saying of his own father. He received it from his sister, who had heard it.

Some of Simeon's homiletic readings of Scripture still survive. On a psalm he links God's rising to Jerusalem's ashes. While Jerusalem lies in ashes, God's might will not arise. When she shakes off her dust, God will rise up. That day will reveal Him from His holy habitation. On another psalm he retells Israel's choice of bad leaders. The people picked Dathan and Abiram over Moses, he said. Earth then swallowed Dathan and covered Abiram's company. The entry joins family transmission with vivid preaching.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-socialism-13822:
Socialism is a theory that calls for public ownership of production. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac A Hourwich wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Jews were linked with the modern Socialist movement from its start. Two young Portuguese Jews joined Saint-Simon's first circle of disciples. They were the brothers Isaac and Emile Pereire.

Those brothers later built the first French railway. They became leading bankers under the second empire. A generation later, Karl Marx rose as a central figure. Marx was the son of a Jewish lawyer of Treves. Ferdinand Lassalle founded the German Socialist party in his turn. The article traces how legal limits pushed educated Jews toward democratic movements.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sonnenthal-adol:
Adolf Ritter von Sonnenthal was an Austrian actor born at Budapest in 1834. Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born there on December 21 of humble parents. He worked as a tailor's apprentice until age sixteen. A visit to the Hofburgtheater in Vienna changed his life.

That first play fired him to become an actor himself. Dawison placed him under Laube for training at the theater. He debuted in 1851 at Temesvar in a small role. In 1856 he joined the Hofburgtheater in Vienna for good. He later became its chief manager and then its director. The emperor ennobled the former tailor's apprentice for his art.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stephen-14022:
Stephen was a Hellenist Jewish convert to Christianity in the first century. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. Tradition says he was martyred at Jerusalem on December 26, 29 C.E. His Greek name matches the Hebrew name Kelil, meaning crown. Epiphanius counts him among the seventy disciples of Jesus.

Stephen served as one of seven deacons who handled the common fund. Accusers charged that he spoke against the Temple and Moses. His reply reviewed Jewish history from Abraham to Solomon's Temple. He then rebuked the people for their stubbornness. The crowd cast him out of the city and stoned him. Saul of Tarsus stood by and consented to the killing. The entry retells the account given in Acts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tamar-14222:
Tamar was the daughter-in-law of Judah in the book of Genesis. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. She married Judah's son Er, who died young. His brother Onan married her next and also died. Judah then sent her home to her father's house.

Judah feared to give her his third son, Shelah. When Shelah grew up unwed to her, Tamar acted. Disguised, she met Judah on his road to Timnath. He left his staff, seal, and belt as pledge. Facing death for unchastity, she produced those tokens. They proved Judah himself was the father. She bore him the twins Zarah and Pharez. Rabbinic lore makes her a daughter of Shem. The entry joins a bold Bible tale with later legend.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-te-omim-jonah-b:
Jonah ben Isaiah Te'omim was a Bohemian rabbi of Prague. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. He served at Nikolsburg and other Bohemian towns. In 1660 Metz called him to its rabbinate. He died at Metz on April 16, 1669.

In 1666 Posen appointed Te'omim as its rabbi. Metz persuaded him to stay instead of leaving. His book Nimukim notes a famed code commentary. It treats the Hoshen Mishpat section of law. Another work, Kikayon de-Yonah, holds his novellae. It covers three Talmudical treatises in depth. Amsterdam printed it in 1669 and 1670. The entry shows a rabbi two cities fought to keep.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tobit-book-of-1:
The Book of Tobit is a late Jewish tale found in the Apocrypha. Crawford Howell Toy wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Jews never received Tobit into their canon. The Council of Trent declared it canonical for Catholics in 1546. Its hero is Tobit, a pious man of Naphtali.

Exiled to Nineveh, Tobit gave alms and buried the slain. Royal favor let him store silver with a friend in Media. Under Sennacherib he fled and lost his property. Back home, an accident blinded him and left him poor. That same day Sarah prayed in despair in Media. Seven husbands had died on their wedding nights. Tobit sent his son Tobias to fetch the silver. The angel Raphael guided the boy in disguise.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tristram-henry-:
Henry Baker Tristram was an English clergyman who explored Palestine for science and Scripture. Joseph Jacobs and A. M. Friedenberg wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born in Northumberland in 1822, he took orders in 1845. Ill health forced him to live abroad. He crossed the northern Sahara before reaching Palestine in 1858.

He returned to Palestine in 1863 and again in 1872. His tours identified many Scripture localities. A Moab journey followed in 1873. He declined the Anglican bishopric of Jerusalem in 1879. His books include The Land of Israel, from 1865. The Natural History of the Bible came in 1867. Fauna and Flora of Palestine appeared in 1884. Few travelers knew the land's life so well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-uzziah-14622:
Uzziah, also called Azariah, was a king of Judah who reigned fifty-two years. Emil G. Hirsch and Ira Maurice Price wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He took the throne at sixteen, in Jeroboam II's twenty-seventh year. Kings counts his reign from 788 to 737 B.C. He was righteous, though he left the high places standing.

Chronicles shows him conquering Philistines and Arabians in war. Ammonites paid him tribute in his strong years. He refortified Judah and rebuilt its army anew. He farmed with his own hand as well. His realm was Judah's largest since the kingdom split. Pride ruined him when he burned Temple incense himself. Leprosy struck him during that act of usurpation. His son Jotham ruled while he lived apart.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vocalization-14:
Vocalization is the system for marking vowels in Semitic scripts. Crawford Howell Toy and Caspar Levias wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Most Semitic writing shows consonants only. Readers must supply the vowels themselves. That gap can make words unclear. Sacred texts made exact reading vital.

The entry traces three answers to the problem. The oldest used certain letters as vowel signs. Later systems added small marks to the consonants. Ethiopic built its vowel signs into each letter. Hebrew and Aramaic developed their own sign sets. The article explains how these systems grew over time. It is a guide to how ancient texts were read aloud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weil-adolf-1482:
Adolf Weil was a German doctor. He was born at Heidelberg on February 7, 1848. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He studied at Heidelberg, Berlin, and Vienna. He earned his degree in 1871. He settled in Heidelberg and taught there.

In 1886 Weil moved to Dorpat as professor. Illness forced him to resign a year later. From 1893 he practiced at Wiesbaden. His lasting fame comes from one 1886 essay. It describes a sudden infectious disease with jaundice and kidney harm. That illness still bears the name Weil's disease. His other books treat chest sounds, percussion, and typhoid fever.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wilda-wilhelm-e:
Wilhelm Eduard Wilda was a German jurist. Isidore Singer wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Altona on August 17, 1800. He died at Kiel on August 9, 1856. He studied at Hamburg, Göttingen, Heidelberg, and Copenhagen. The year 1826 took him to Berlin and on travels.

Wilda practiced law at Hamburg until 1830. He then taught at Halle for twelve years. Breslau called him as full professor in 1842. In 1854 he transferred to Kiel. He founded the field of comparative jurisprudence. His books treat medieval guilds and Germanic criminal law. In 1838 he founded a journal of German law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-worms-maurice-b:
Maurice Benedict de Worms (1805-1867) was an English money man and farmer in Ceylon. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Frankfort, he was a grandson of Meyer Anselm Rothschild. His father held high rank in the Frankfort Jewish group.

In 1841 he toured the Far East with his brother Gabriel. The two bought a large estate in Ceylon. That farm grew into the famed Rothschild Estate. Acre by acre they added land to the tract. By 1865 they held two thousand acres in crops. Six thousand more acres lay in woods yet to clear. The brothers were among the first settlers of the isle. In his will Maurice left large sums to Jewish good causes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-york-15122:
York is the chief town of Yorkshire in the north of England. Joseph Jacobs wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In Angevin days it was the second town of the realm. Jews came there in large counts in that age.

At the crown rite of Richard the First, two Jews went to London. They were Joce and Benedict, the great men of York. A riot broke out at the feast in that town. Benedict was forced to take baptism in that strife. The king let him turn back the next day by grace. He died soon after at Northampton on the road. Joce got free and went home to York in haste. His house was a mark of wealth in that town. A fire in the town then lit a fresh attack.
journal-of-discourses-vol-22:
Raids at their height fill Volume Twenty-Two, published in 1883. Federal marshals hunt polygamists across Utah Territory town by town. The underground years reach their darkest stretch in these reports.

Faith is practiced in secret, with lookouts posted and doors barred. Families divide as fathers vanish into hiding or prison cells. Sermons bless the hidden and curse the hunters in fierce terms. Devotion holds unyielding while the law strikes at hearth and home. The kingdom's hardest legal hour speaks here in its own defiant voice from the stand. Children of the raided grew up on stories from this volume.
joyce-ulysses-1922:
James Joyce published Ulysses in 1922, in Paris, his novel of a single Dublin day, June 16, 1904. Bloom, Stephen, and Molly traverse that day in the novel that redefined what fiction can do. Banned for years in Britain and America, it was published by Sylvia Beach's Shakespeare and Company bookshop.

Leopold Bloom, a Jewish ad salesman, buries a friend, dodges his wife's lover, and rescues Stephen in nighttown's brothel quarter. Stephen, hungover and broke, teaches, walks the strand, and argues Shakespeare in the library with Dublin's literati in the morning hours. Molly Bloom's unpunctuated monologue closes the book, a river of memory and desire ending in a great yes. Joyce maps each episode to the Odyssey and to an organ, art, and hour in a vast private scheme. Readers still divide on it, but no novel since has escaped its shadow.
julius-caesar-pg1522:
William Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, in this edition, opens with a full list of its people. Julius Caesar heads the cast, with Octavius, Mark Antony, and Lepidus as triumvirs after his death. Marcus Brutus and Cassius lead the conspirators named beside them. Senators Cicero, Publius, and Popilius Lena fill out the Roman state.

The contents map five acts from Rome's streets to the Capitol and the Forum. Later scenes move to Sardis and the plains of Philippi, where the civil war ends. Shakespeare builds the tragedy on the killing of Caesar and Antony's funeral speech turning the mob. Brutus's honor and Cassius's envy drive the plot. This edition lays out the whole cast and scene plan before the play begins.
kebra-nagast-budge-1922:
E. A. Wallis Budge translated the Kebra Nagast into English in 1922, complete, from the Ge'ez text. The Kebra Nagast, the Glory of Kings, is Ethiopia's national epic. It tells how the Queen of Sheba, called Makeda, visited Solomon in Jerusalem and bore his son Menyelek.

Menyelek, grown, brings the Ark of the Covenant from Jerusalem to Aksum, by the tale's design with heaven's favor. From him Ethiopia's kings claimed descent, and its church claimed the Ark itself. Budge, keeper of Egyptian and Assyrian antiquities at the British Museum, gave the epic its standard English form. The book still anchors Ethiopian identity and faith. No library of world epics is complete without it.
lancre-incredulite-sortilege-french-1622:
Pierre de Lancre, the Bordeaux judge who had presided over the Labourd witch trials, published his second great treatise in 1622. Its title announces its target: the incredulity and unbelief of the age about sorcery. De Lancre refutes the doubters with apparitions, pacts, and sabbaths set out at length.

The book is his demonological summa, the full-dress statement of his creed. He writes as a judge who saw the evidence and burned the condemned. Skeptics, in his view, shield the devil's servants. Few works defend the persecution with such learning and such confidence. De Lancre's summa shows the witch-judge answering his critics from the height of his own certainty.
las-casas-coleccion-obras-1822:
Juan Antonio Llorente edited the first collected works of Las Casas in Paris in 1822. The volume gathers the friar's key writings between two covers at last. Chief among them stands the Very Brief Account of the ruin of the Indies.

Shorter polemics and briefs on Native rights stand beside that famed tract. Readers can trace one man's lifelong case in a single portable book. Llorente's edition brought Las Casas back to wide notice in his age. The Apostle of the Indies speaks here in his own gathered voice. His brief for the peoples of the Americas still stings today.
lawrence-aarons-rod-1922:
Aaron's Rod, published in 1922, follows Aaron Sisson, a flautist in a Midlands colliery band who one Christmas Eve walks out on his wife, children, and job. His flute, his rod, becomes the sign of his lone male pilgrimage.

Aaron drifts through London bohemia and on to Italy, testing talk, love, and politics, and refusing every claim on him. The novel asks whether a man can be whole alone, or whether some submission to life is required. Lawrence revised it over years of illness and travel. It is the first of his leadership-era novels, restless and strange.
lawrence-england-my-england-1922:
Lawrence's 1922 story collection takes its name from the title piece, a story of Egbert, a gentle, useless man married into a family that despises his softness. When war comes, he enlists, and the story becomes an elegy for a sacrificed generation.

The volume also holds 'Tickets, Please', a comedy of a tram inspector hunted by the conductresses he courted, and 'The Blind Man', one of his finest tales. Several stories are set in the mining Midlands of his youth, now shadowed by war. Together they show Lawrence the storyteller at full range: tender, savage, and exact.
lawrence-fantasia-unconscious-1922:
Fantasia of the Unconscious, published in 1922, is Lawrence's sequel to Psychoanalysis and the Unconscious and his fullest statement of his private philosophy. It is part psychology, part cosmology, part parenting manual, and wholly Lawrence.

He sets out his scheme of chakras and polarities, the body's centers of feeling set against the mind's proud reason. Children, he argues, are ruined by ideals imposed from above and should grow from the body's wisdom instead. The science is fanciful and the tone certain. Behind the system stands a real plea: trust the living self over the mechanical mind.
les-secrets-les-plus-caches-de-la-philos: Francesco Maria Pompeo Colonna's book of 1722 promises the most hidden secrets of the ancients' philosophy. Its sample shows only scanner notices in this copy. The long French title states its aim plainly. Colonna claims to reveal what ancient sages kept concealed. Such books fed the market for hermetic secrets. It belongs to the late afterlife of Renaissance occult philosophy.
lewis-babbitt-1922:
Sinclair Lewis published Babbitt in 1922, a novel about George F. Babbitt, a real estate man in Zenith. Babbitt sells homes, boosts his city, and repeats the slogans of his class. At first he seems content with his house, car, and club. A creeping restlessness leads him to question it all.

For a time Babbitt rebels, takes a lover, and scorns his old friends. Fear and habit pull him back into line. Lewis writes with sharp satire and exact detail of speech and goods. The name Babbitt entered the language for a smug, conformist businessman. The novel remains a key portrait of American business life.
lilly-history-life-times-1822:
William Lilly, England's most famous astrologer, wrote his life story between 1668 and 1681, printed in the edition of 1822. Lilly cast charts for kings, generals, and worried Londoners through the Civil War. His History of His Life and Times tells how a Leicestershire servant's son rose to dine with the powerful.

Prophecies, feuds with rival star-men, and the politics of a kingdom at war fill the later chapters. Lilly speaks plainly about tricks of the trade and his own doubts, which makes the memoir shrewd as well as lively. No book opens the world of seventeenth-century London astrology from inside like this one.
luschan-volker-rassen-sprachen-1922:
Felix von Luschan, a German sage of the study of man, struck at the race scheme of his day in this book of 1922. Its title means peoples, races, and tongues, in German. Luschan had spent years in the field and in charge of a great store of skulls.

machen-secret-glory-1922:
A schoolboy touches a higher world in Machen's novel of 1922, The Secret Glory. Ambrose Meyrick endures a dull, harsh school while his soul feeds on Grail lore and the tales of saints. The holy hides in the schoolroom in Machen's telling.

malinowski-argonauts-1922:
Bronislaw Malinowski lived for long stretches in the Trobriand Islands during the First World War and learned the local speech. mansfield-garden-party-1922:

mckay-harlem-shadows-1922:
Claude McKay published Harlem Shadows in 1922, his sonnets of Harlem life and Jamaican memory in verse. Many call the book the spark that lit the Harlem Renaissance in the judgment of its historians since. McKay, born in Jamaica, wrote as a radical and a formalist at once in these pages of 1922.

modi-religious-ceremonies-parsees-1922:
Jivanji Jamshedji Modi was a Parsi scholar and priest who spent his life recording the customs of his community. His Religious Ceremonies and Customs of the Parsees, published in 1922, gives a full account of Parsi ritual life. Modi writes as an insider with a scholar's training.

moore-philosophical-studies-1922:

oneill-hairy-ape-1922:
Eugene O'Neill published The Hairy Ape in 1922, his expressionist play of Yank the stoker's brutal odyssey in industry. Yank searches for belonging in an industrial world, from ship's hold to Fifth Avenue,. O'Neill called it a comedy of ancient and modern life, though its end is a cage.

ouspensky-tertium-organum-1922:

pirandello-three-plays-1922:

plaw-117-101-2022: Public Law 117-101, approved on March 15, 2022 by the 117th Congress, raises federal funding for two health foundations. plos-pone-0000122:
Tariq Maqbool, Cedric Soler, Teresa Jagla, and colleagues published this developmental biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. Working with the fruit fly Drosophila, they study a gene called ladybird. The gene helps shape the muscles of the fly's legs as the insect develops.

Ladybird belongs to a family of genes that is conserved, meaning similar versions exist across many animals. The authors trace what the gene does as leg muscles form. The same gene family works in other species. So the fly results offer clues about how muscles are patterned in animals more broadly, including in limbs.
plos-pone-0000222:
Christine C. Boucard, Johannes M. Hoogduin, Jeroen van der Grond, and colleagues published this brain imaging paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Patients with retinal visual field defects have damage in the eye that leaves blind regions in their sight. Using proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy in the occipital lobe, the brain's vision area, the authors measured its chemistry.

The title reports their finding: metabolite concentrations were normal despite the visual defects. That means the brain tissue itself was chemically intact even where sight was lost at the eye. The result helps doctors separate eye damage from brain damage when reading scans of such patients.
plos-pone-0000322:
Joseph Schacherer, Douglas M. Ruderfer, David Gresham, and colleagues published this yeast genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Lab strains of the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae are used worldwide as if they were all the same. The authors analyze variation across the whole genome in commonly used strains and show how much they actually differ.

Small genetic differences between strains can change lab results. A variation catalogue lets researchers pick strains knowingly and interpret old results with care. The paper is a reference point for the yeast community and a warning for any field built on a model organism.
plos-pone-0000422:
Tae Won Kim, John H. Christy, and Jae C. Choe described a mating signal that doubles as a safety device, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. In the animal they studied, females prefer a particular sexual signal from males. The title states their further claim: that preference keeps females safe.

A preference can persist for more than one reason. It picks good mates, but it also protects the chooser. It may steer her toward signals that reveal a safe situation. Studies like this complicate the usual story of sexual selection, where showy signals are assumed to cost the female time or risk. Here, following her preference is the safer move.
plos-pone-0000522:
Johannes Bergsten and Kelly B. Miller reconstructed the family tree of diving beetles and found a battle of the sexes written in it, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Male diving beetles have gripping suckers; females of some species have rough backs that resist grip. The beetle phylogeny revealed a coevolutionary arms race between the sexes.

An arms race means each sex's adaptation provokes the other's counter-adaptation over generations. A phylogeny lets researchers order the changes in time and test whether the traits really escalated together. Diving beetles give an unusually clear example because the structures are physical and the tree is well resolved.
plos-pone-0000622:
Rudi Alberts, Peter Terpstra, Yang Li and colleagues sounded a warning for gene-mapping studies in PLOS ONE in 2007. Researchers map eQTLs, places in the genome linked to how strongly a gene is expressed. Local eQTLs, where the linked place is the gene itself, look like the most direct and promising leads.

The authors argue that many of those local hits are false. Ordinary sequence differences between individuals, called polymorphisms, can fool the measurement and fake a link. Their title states the finding bluntly: sequence polymorphisms cause many false cis eQTLs. Anyone trusting published eQTL maps needs to reckon with this source of error.
plos-pone-0000722:
Majid Eshaghi, R. Krishna M. Karuturi, Juntao Li and colleagues profiled when and how well DNA copies itself in fission yeast. In S. pombe, replication starts at many origins, sites rich in A-T sequences, firing at various times during S-phase. Genome-wide studies had focused on replication timing and where origins sit, less on how efficiently each origin fires.

Their global profiling adds efficiency to the map. The title reports a surprise: efficient replication and firing occur late during S-phase. Late was often read as sloppy or secondary. Showing late firing as efficient rewrites part of how the copying schedule is understood, with lessons for larger genomes too.
plos-pone-0000822:
Tang Chi Thuong and co-authors looked into a grave outbreak of staph infections in children who had just been vaccinated. The germ was community-acquired MRSA, a form of Staphylococcus aureus that resists a key drug. Such infections were on the rise around the world at the time. The team ran a field study after bad events were reported at an out-patient clinic.

The germs carried a toxin gene called Panton-Valentine leukocidin, which is linked to severe disease. An outbreak after shots demands care: was the vaccine at fault, the clinic's hygiene, or mere chance? The report, in PLOS ONE in 2007, works through that proof. Clear field work of this kind keeps vaccine programs both safe and trusted.
plos-pone-0000922:
Jeffrey Roizen, Christina Luedke, Erik Herzog and colleagues examined oxytocin's role in the daily timing of birth, in PLOS ONE in 2007. What sets the clock for labor is still only partly known. The answer matters for care of births that come too early, too late or stall.

Oxytocin is the hormone that drives contractions, so the team tested whether it also carries a time of day signal for birth. Many births cluster at certain hours, hinting at a body clock at work. Tying that rhythm to a known hormone would give doctors a clearer picture of normal labor. It could also flag when timing, not strength, is the problem.
plos-pone-0001022:
Claudia Acquisti, George Poste, David Curtiss and colleagues questioned a popular reading of missing DNA words, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Nullomers are short DNA sequences that never appear in a species' genome. Many had assumed their absence is the signature of natural selection removing harmful sequences.

If true, nullomers could point to drug targets and other useful sites. The authors ask whether selection is really the explanation, or whether chance and mutation patterns suffice. Their title frames the doubt plainly. The paper is a check on a tempting inference: an absent pattern is not, by itself, proof that selection banned it.
plos-pone-0001122:
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a cancer of the upper throat that is closely tied to Epstein-Barr virus and is especially common in southern China. Jiang Li and colleagues investigated the immune side of this cancer in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They asked whether the body's virus-specific defenses fail in people with the tumor.

The team assessed the look and function of T cells, immune cells meant to attack virus-infected cells, both in the blood and inside tumors. Their title reports functional inactivation of the Epstein-Barr virus-specific T cells. That failure could help explain how the tumor survives, and it shapes ideas for immune-based treatment.
plos-pone-0001222:
Autoimmune diseases arise when the gene networks controlling T-cell activation go wrong. Ricardo Palacios and colleagues modeled that network in humans, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Understanding complex diseases, they argue, benefits from recognizing the properties of the gene networks that control biological functions.

From their network analysis of human T-cell activation, the authors identify Jagged1 as a therapeutic target for autoimmune diseases. Jagged1 is a ligand in the Notch pathway, which helps govern immune cell behavior. A network approach can surface targets that single-gene studies miss, because it looks at control points rather than individual actors.
plos-pone-0001322:
Glucosinolates are the pungent defense chemicals of cabbage-family plants, deterring herbivores and pathogens while attracting specialist insects. Ida Elken Sønderby and colleagues used a systems biology approach to find the genes controlling one class of them, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Little was known about the genes that control these chemicals.

The authors identify three R2R3 MYB transcription factor genes with distinct and overlapping functions in regulation of aliphatic glucosinolates. Transcription factors are the switches of gene networks. Knowing the switches could let breeders tune these chemicals, which matter for pest resistance and human nutrition alike.
plos-pone-0001422:
William Freed and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on growing dopamine nerve cells from human embryo stem cells. Dopamine cells die in Parkinson's disease, so lab grown ones hold hope for repair. The team guided stem cells toward that fate, then sorted out the young nerve cells. They read the full gene pattern of the sorted cells.

The gene read out showed a strong signal from one stretch of chromosome 11. They also set the pattern side by side with that of real dopamine nerve cells. Close match would back the lab cells as a sound model. The data guide both graft work and drug screens for Parkinson's.
plos-pone-0001522:
Liya Wassie and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on TB patients in Ethiopia and their close contacts. A signal called IL-4 had been tied to TB, but its role stayed in dispute. The team had prior data from patients, contacts, and healthy controls in one cohort. Here they tracked signal gene levels over time in blood cells.

Signal levels moved in step with how patients' health changed. Contacts showed their own pattern as time passed. A blood mark that tracks disease state could help clinics judge who needs care most. It could also flag contacts who are sliding toward illness before signs show.
plos-pone-0001622:
Kosuke Fujishima and co-authors asked an old question about the origin of transfer RNA in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Transfer RNA, or tRNA, carries amino acids to the cell's protein-making machinery. In one archaeal parasite, Nanoarchaeum equitans, scientists had found tRNA genes split into separate 5-prime and 3-prime halves.

That find raised a clear question: did the first tRNA start as one gene or as two halves that later joined? The team ran a broad family-tree study of tRNAs across 45 archaeal genomes to test the idea. The full text gives the sequence evidence, the trees they built, and their case that modern tRNAs grew out of joined ancestral halves. The work speaks to how core parts of the cell first came together.
plos-pone-0001722:
Mariëlle I. Gallegos Ruiz and co-authors combined gene copy data with gene activity data in lung cancer, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Lung cancer kills about 1.2 million people a year worldwide, and the non-small cell form makes up 85 percent of cases. Better early diagnosis and treatment require knowing its molecular events.

By integrating gene dosage with expression, the team identified HSP90 as a potential drug target. Dosage is how many copies of each gene a tumor carries; expression is how active those genes are. The full text gives the tumor samples, the combined analysis, and the evidence for HSP90. Targets found by two data types at once are less likely to be noise, which is why this joining of methods matters.
plos-pone-0001822:
Paola Laiolo, Matthias Vögeli, David Serrano, and their co-authors tested whether bird song can forecast population survival in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Habitat fragmentation is growing worldwide, and those who protect wild birds need signs of whether populations will last. Learned behaviors, above all sound signals, might carry such signs.

The team explored whether song diversity predicts how long broken-up bird groups last. They report that it does, as the title states. The full text gives the groups tracked and the song measures. A mic survey is far cheaper than years of bird counts. A reliable song sign would be a practical tool for watching over wild populations.
plos-pone-0001922:
Xiaotu Ma, Aaron Tarone, and Wenyuan Li built a map of backup paths in yeast genes, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. A synthetic lethal pair is two gene faults that are harmless alone but kill the cell together, which hints the genes back each other up. Such pairs have long been used to guess what a gene does.

The team went past single pairs. They compared the whole pattern of lethal partners for each gene, since genes with like patterns tend to share a path. From those patterns they charted compensatory paths, the detours a cell can take. Maps like this help predict drug targets in germs and cancer.
plos-pone-0002022:
Thea Egelhofer and co-authors found a new early job for a family of yeast proteins, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The proteins, septins, group at the spot where a bud will emerge in budding yeast, during the G1 stage of the cell cycle. They were not thought to do much that matters at that early stage.

The team show that septins work in G1 pathways that shape the pattern of cell growth. When septins fail, growth goes awry before the bud even forms. An early role for septins rewrites a piece of the cell cycle map in a model organism used across biology.
plos-pone-0002122:
Slaven Erceg and co-authors described a lab method in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper for turning human embryonic stem cells into early nerve cells. Stem cells taken from embryos can copy the first steps of human growth in a dish. Cells made from them might one day help repair tissue, such as nerve tissue hurt by disease or injury.

The team grew the stem cells in a defined medium, a mix with known contents and no unknown animal products. Under those clean conditions the cells became neural precursors, early cells set to form parts of the nervous system. Work like this matters for both basic research and future cell-based treatments.
plos-pone-0002222:
Erbo Ying, Dan Li, Shaojun Guo, and co-authors described a simpler way to make glowing nanocrystals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. CdTe nanocrystals shine brightly and can tag cells for imaging under a microscope. Older recipes used tellurium sources that spoil on contact with air, which made the crystals hard to prepare well.

The team used stable sodium tellurite instead and made high-quality crystals in water in a single pot. A coating of mercaptosuccinic acid made the crystals bright and suited to bio-imaging. Easier recipes for bright probes help more labs light up cells and tissues for study.
plos-pone-0002322:
Erwin Boutsma, Sonja Noback, and Maarten van Lohuizen found a hidden start signal, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The signal sits inside the message of a chromatin protein. Ring1B belongs to the Polycomb group, proteins that orchestrate development, cell growth, and stem cell fate by reshaping local chromatin. Ring1B is the enzyme that tags histone H2A with a single ubiquitin mark, a key silencing step.

The authors show the protein's own messenger RNA carries an IRES. That is an internal entry point letting protein building start mid-message, in its highly conserved head region. Such a backup start could keep Ring1B flowing when normal protein synthesis is throttled, for instance under stress.
plos-pone-0002422:
A research team led by Navis reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Marjon Navis, Diana Edo Matas, Andrea Rachinger, and others. Its subject is molecular Evolution of Human Immunodeficiency Virus Type 1 upon Transmission between Human Leukocyte Antigen Disparate Donor-Recipient Pairs.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002522:
Work from Molokhia and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Mariam Molokhia, Paul McKeigue, Vasa Curcin, and others. Its subject is statin Induced Myopathy and Myalgia: Time Trend Analysis and Comparison of Risk Associated with Statin Class from 1991–2006. Statins are widely used as a cholesterol lowering medication, reduce cardiovascular death and morbidity in high risk patients.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002622:
Ralf Dressel led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was the tumorigenicity of mouse embryonic stem cells and in vitro differentiated neuronal cells is controlled by the recipients' immune response. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Ralf Dressel, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Embryonic stem (ES) cells have the potential to differentiate into all cell types and are considered as a valuable source of cells for transplantation. The summary also notes a further point. A critical issue, however, is the risk of teratoma formation after transplantation. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002722:
Published in PLOS ONE in 2008, research by Yen-Chun Liu and colleagues addresses global regulation of nucleotide biosynthetic genes by c-Myc. The catalog record names Yen-Chun Liu first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The c-Myc transcription factor is a master regulator and integrates cell proliferation, cell growth and metabolism through activating thousands of target genes. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002822:
Francesca R. Dani led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was exploring proteins in anopheles gambiae male and female antennae through MALDI mass spectrometry profiling. Authorship is credited in the record to Francesca R. Dani and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. MALDI profiling and imaging mass spectrometry (IMS) are novel techniques for direct analysis of peptides and small proteins in biological tissues. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002922:
Martin Hoffmann, Hannah Chang, Sui Huang and co-authors modeled noise in stem cell populations in 2008. A stem cell must either stay a stem cell or mature into a specialist cell, and its surroundings tip that balance. Switching between states was long pictured as a move between stable states of a gene network.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the authors focus on stochastic fluctuations, random noise in molecule counts, as a driver of that switching. Their model covers stem and progenitor populations together. The view helps explain why sister cells with the same genes can take different paths.
plos-pone-0003022:
Caroline Blais, Rachael Jack, Christoph Scheepers and co-authors showed in 2008 that culture shapes how people look at faces. Face processing was long thought uniform across humans. Since 1965, eye movement studies had consistently found a triangular scan over eyes and mouth, suggesting a universal pattern.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team reports that viewing pattern is not universal after all. Culture shapes the strategy used to read a face. That finding changes cross-cultural psychology and design alike, from interviews to face software trained on narrow samples. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003122:
Kobby Essien, Sridhar Hannenhalli and Christian J. Stoeckert offer this 2008 PLOS ONE computer-based study of malaria parasites. Species of Plasmodium differ in clear ways, such as which hosts they choose and which cell types they prefer to invade. The authors argue that part of the reason for these traits lies in limits placed on gene activity and on coding and noncoding parts of the genome.

Using computation, they compare those limits across parasites with unlike traits. The study gives readers a way to link DNA patterns to the varied behaviour of malaria parasites. It may help explain why species that cause the same disease still act so differently.
plos-pone-0003222: Hironobu Fukami and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 on the family history of stony corals. The title states its dual claim from mitochondrial and nuclear genes: stony corals stem from one common ancestor, but most named coral families do not. No abstract beyond the title was supplied, so no species or methods are added here.
plos-pone-0003322:
Norihiro Yumoto, Shuji Wakatsuki, Tomohiro Kurisaki and colleagues study proteins at the nerve-muscle junction in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Development of the neuromuscular junction starts with the forming of special postsynaptic zones in the central zones of muscles. Motor nerve terminals then arrive opposite the postsynaptic regions. The parts on both sides are then held firm.

The authors report Meltrin beta, or ADAM19, works with EphA4 in developing neural cells. It takes part in forming the neuromuscular junction. Readers learn of a new partnership in building the contact that lets nerves move muscle. Faults at this junction lie behind several muscle disorders present at birth.
plos-pone-0003422:
Jing Ai and co-authors studied a receptor that drives white blood cell growth in this 2008 paper. The receptor answers a signal that orders new granulocyte production. These cells are front-line fighters against infection. Faults in the receptor appear in a severe childhood blood disorder that can turn into leukemia.

The team focused on ubiquitination, a tag that marks proteins for removal. Tagging the receptor proved vital for cell survival and growth control. When tagging fails, the receptor's signal runs too long. The work explains part of how blood cell numbers are kept in balance.
plos-pone-0003522:
Jin Fan, Kevin G. Guise, and Xun Liu studied voluntary control of attention in this 2008 paper. People constantly choose which information deserves processing. That choice directs limited mental resources to what matters most. The rules, or algorithms, behind such control are often unclear.

Their work searched for the majority pattern in those control choices. Experiments probed how the mind picks winning signals. The results sketch the computing rules of willpower. Such rules may inform models of focus in brains and machines alike. Focus is a limited resource in work, school, and daily life alike.
plos-pone-0003622:
André Aleman and Marte Swart published this brain imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It compares how men and women respond in the brain to faces showing contempt or disgust. Contempt signals a sense of moral superiority over another person. Disgust is a close but distinct feeling.

The authors scanned volunteers while they viewed these facial expressions. Brain activity differed between the sexes for these social emotions. The pattern suggests men and women may process scorn and disgust through partly different brain routes. Such work helps explain how social judgments form in the brain.
plos-pone-0003722:
Andrea Ferrante, Matthew W. Anderson, Candice S. Klug, and colleagues published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Before the immune system can inspect a protein piece, the piece must win a place on a display molecule. A helper protein called HLA-DM runs that selection.

The team shows HLA-DM works by a compare-exchange routine when a pool of candidate peptides is available. It helps release weak pieces and lets stronger ones take their place. The mechanism reveals quality control in immune display, deciding which fragments T cells will get to see.
plos-pone-0003822:
Takuya Kobayashi, Nobuhiro Morone, Taku Kashiyama, and colleagues published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Protein research leans on tags: fluorescent tags for imaging live cells, affinity tags for isolation, and epitope tags for detection. Using several tags at once creates problems of its own.

The team engineered a novel multifunctional green fluorescent protein tag. One tag serves a wide variety of protein research tasks in a single package. The versatile label gives labs a single tool for jobs that once needed separate constructs and extra cloning. One tag also means fewer mix-ups between samples in the lab.
plos-pone-0003922:
Eduardo K. Moioli, Paul A. Clark, Mo Chen, and co-authors joined two stem cell types to grow blood vessels in 2008. Weak vessel growth is a major block in tissue repair. Nutrients and oxygen can diffuse only a few hundred micrometers into new tissue. Lab-grown tissues therefore starve without their own vessel networks.

The team proposed pairing blood-forming stem cells with mesenchymal stem cells. Together the two types acted in synergy to vascularize engineered tissues. A working vessel supply raises the size of tissues labs can grow. The approach moves tissue engineering closer to real organ repair.
plos-pone-0004022:
Rhys E. Green, W. Grainger Hunt, Christopher N. Parish, and co-authors tested actions protecting condors from lead in 2008. Released California condors range widely across Arizona and Utah. Many birds pick up lead from spent ammunition in carcasses. Blood lead levels in the flock rise as a result.

Their PLOS ONE article judges how well reduction actions worked. Programs urged hunters to use non-lead ammunition in condor range. Birds were also recaptured and treated when lead ran high. Measuring success tells managers whether voluntary action can save condors. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004122:
Sanda Sturlan and colleagues published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject is a weakened influenza A vaccine virus called delNS1, which cannot copy itself properly. The virus is known to stir up the innate immune system, the body's fast first line of defence.

Because that same system can also attack cancer cells, the team asked what delNS1 does to blood immune cells. They report that the virus triggers immediate killing activity in all major groups of peripheral blood mononuclear cells. The result helps explain why this vaccine strain packs such a strong immune punch.
plos-pone-0004222:
Christine Johnston and colleagues published this study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Kaposi sarcoma is the leading cause of cancer in Uganda and occurs in people with and without HIV. Its cause, human herpesvirus-8, must copy itself and spread for both transmission and tumour growth.

The team characterised where and how often HHV-8 could be detected on mucosal surfaces in Ugandan patients. They weighed how HIV infection and Kaposi sarcoma change the virus's replication and shedding. Knowing where the virus hides and spreads helps explain its grip on the region. Kaposi sarcoma's place as Uganda's leading cancer makes the question urgent.
plos-pone-0004322:
José Pedro Nunes and João Carlos Silva published this cardiology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Coronary angiography allows doctors to evaluate the anatomy of the coronary arteries directly, by imaging the vessels that feed the heart. The team searched for correlations between the magnitude of coronary artery disease seen on angiography and a number of systemic parameters, body-wide measures.

Their group comprised 116 patients, 80 of them men. If blood or body measures track the state of the arteries, they could flag disease without a catheter. The study tests how much the body's general state mirrors its heart vessels.
plos-pone-0004422:
Salty soil blights about a fifth of the world's farm land. Jie Pan, Jin Wang, Zhengfu Zhou, and co-authors looked to a famously tough bacterium for help in PLOS ONE in 2009. Deinococcus bacteria are known for shrugging off extreme radiation. Their gene IrrE acts as a master switch for that hardiness.

Past tries to breed salt-hardy crops had only modest success. The team moved IrrE into two very different hosts: the gut bacterium E. coli and oilseed rape, a crop plant. In both, the borrowed switch raised tolerance to salt, as the title reports. The work hints that one strong stress gene might help crops grow where salty ground now stops them.
plos-pone-0004522:
Birds warming their eggs also keep egg bacteria in check, show Matthew Shawkey, Mary Firestone, Eoin Brodie, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Microbe infection is a major killer of early life stages in animals that lay eggs. Parents defend their young in many ways, but the defenses of birds had been little studied.

It had been proposed that incubation, the parent's sitting on the eggs, limits the growth of microbes that might cross the shell. The team tested that idea and found incubation does inhibit the growth and diversification of bacterial communities on eggs. Warmth and dryness, in other words, double as sanitation. The finding adds a hidden benefit to a familiar behavior, and may help explain egg care across egg-laying species.
plos-pone-0004622:
Cells can divide more times than expected while the chromosome-end enzyme telomerase is active, models Krastan Blagoev in PLOS ONE in 2009. Telomerase is active early in development and later in stem and germline cells. It is also active in the majority of human cancers. One known function of telomerase is to extend the ends of linear chromosomes.

Each cell division shortens those ends a little, which normally limits how many times a cell can divide. Telomerase counteracts that shortening. Blagoev studies cell proliferation in its presence, asking how growth behaves when the usual countdown is paused. The question sits at the crossing of aging and cancer: the same enzyme that keeps stem cells young may also license tumors to grow without limit.
plos-pone-0004722:
Alex Yuan and colleagues showed that stem cells pass tiny RNAs to other cells in small sacs, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cells shed tiny sacs from their surface into the fluid around them. Such sacs are a normal part of human blood and help keep blood balance, among other roles.

The team asked if sacs from embryonic stem cells carry microRNAs and hand them on. They found that transfer does occur. That means stem cells can tune gene use in nearby cells without direct touch. The finding adds a new route to how cells talk and heal.
plos-pone-0004822:
Heidi Noels and colleagues showed that auto ubiquitination induced degradation of MALT1-API2 prevents BCL10 destabilization in MALT lymphoma, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The translocation t(11;18) is the most frequent chromosomal aberration in MALT lymphoma and results in constitutive NF-kB activity via an API2-MALT1 fusion protein. Properties of the reciprocal MALT1-API2 product were never investigated, as it was assumed absent or rapidly lost in tumor cells.

The reciprocal product degrades itself, protecting BCL10. That balance shapes signaling strength in lymphoma. Fusion biology is more two sided than thought. Details may suggest therapeutic leverage. The work also raises clear questions that targeted studies can now address.
plos-pone-0004922:
Gene-chip studies scan thousands of genes at once. They hunt for molecular signatures of disease. But a signature found by luck helps no one. Constantin Aliferis and co-authors examined this problem in PLOS ONE in 2009. They asked what gives complex microarray analysis enough statistical power. Powered studies produce signatures that hold up.

The team tested how design choices change reliability. Sample size and analysis method both mattered. So did the checks used to confirm significance. Their work maps the trade-offs researchers face when planning a study. It offers practical guidance for building gene-based tests that other labs can reproduce.
plos-pone-0005022:
Type A influenza infects many animals. Its hosts include humans, pigs, horses, marine mammals and birds. Shuo Liu and colleagues mapped the whole family's diversity. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The viruses sort into sixteen hemagglutinin subtypes. They also sort into nine neuraminidase subtypes. Combinations of these define the strains.
