The study charted the phylogeny and distribution of all these viruses. It shows how flu diversity spreads across hosts and regions. The panorama is a baseline for surveillance. Tracking the next pandemic strain starts from such maps. The work also reveals how freely flu genes move between species. That movement is what makes this virus so hard to corner.
plos-pone-0005122:
Gene therapy needs viruses that home to the right tissues. Peptide libraries displayed on viral capsids can select such homing. Stefan Michelfelder and colleagues tried the selection inside living animals. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The virus was adeno-associated virus. Random peptide libraries decorated its surface. Biopanning in vivo did the selecting.

The screen successfully expanded the virus's tropism. It did not achieve complete restriction to one tissue. The virus reached new targets but kept old ones too. The study maps both promise and limits of steering viruses. Future work must add restriction to expansion. Knowing the gap is progress. It tells engineers what problem to solve next.
plos-pone-0005222:
A popular lab recipe claims that chemicals can turn rat bone marrow stem cells into neuron-like cells. Many labs have used that recipe and reported success. Barnabé and colleagues put the claim to a stricter test in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Treated mesenchymal stem cells did take on molecular traits of neurons, as the title states. But they lacked the basic functional properties that real neurons must have, such as proper electrical behavior. The gap between looking like a neuron and acting like one is a warning for stem cell claims.
plos-pone-0005322:
Reproduction in mammals is governed by neurons that release GnRH, a hormone that starts the whole fertility chain. Those neurons take in signals about time of day and energy balance. Ward and colleagues mapped the peptidergic neurons that wire into GnRH neurons in mice in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Peptide-releasing neurons conveying circadian and energy information connect directly to the GnRH cells. That wiring explains how clocks and hunger can gate fertility. The map is basic anatomy with broad reach, from farm breeding to human fertility disorders. Hunger and the clock both speak to the cells that start puberty and keep adult health on track. And this wiring map shows the lines those talks travel on, day and night, in the mouse brain.
plos-pone-0005422:
Paul Vigne, Michel Tauc, and Christian Frelin studied fruit flies and low oxygen in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. When blood flow returns to tissue that has lacked oxygen, the fresh oxygen can itself cause harm. That problem shapes how bad heart and blood vessel disease becomes.

The team used newly hatched adult male fruit flies, which cope well without oxygen. Flies kept on a very strict diet were better protected from harm when oxygen returned. The result points to diet and body chemistry as factors that can change how tissue survives a lack of oxygen.
plos-pone-0005522:
Evelyn Teran, Aron Branscomb, and Joni Seeling studied a protein that can both block and boost a growth pathway, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The Wnt pathway guides development and can drive tumours when it runs unchecked. A protein called Dpr helps set its strength.

The team showed that Dpr works as a switch with two states. In one state it holds Wnt signals back; after a chemical tag is added by another enzyme, it pushes the signals forward. A two-way switch like this lets cells fine-tune a powerful pathway.
plos-pone-0005622:
Hanane Agherbi and co-authors studied a tumour suppressor region in aging cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. One DNA region, INK4a/ARF, holds three genes that block tumours. It is shut down in many human cancers, and the ways it is controlled were not fully known.

The team showed that a protein complex called Polycomb silences the region as cells age into senescence. They also linked that silencing to when the region's DNA is copied. The timing detail may explain why the region's loss is so common in cancer. Senescence is a guard against cancer, so the silencing that comes with it has a double edge worth study.
plos-pone-0005722:
Roy Blum and co-authors compared gene activity in young and adult prostate stem cells in 2009. Stem cells from the prostate may hold clues to how prostate cancer starts. The team read the full set of active genes in both fetal and adult stem cells.

They found a shared core set of control genes in both stages. Some of those same controls go wrong in cancer. That overlap makes the stem cell program a map for spotting cancer's first steps. The study also names new signal paths tied to these cells, giving labs fresh targets to test in prostate disease.
plos-pone-0005822:
Ethan Mann and co-authors showed in 2009 how the release and breakdown of DNA shapes the films Staphylococcus aureus builds. These biofilms coat surfaces and implants, shielding bacteria from drugs and immunity. DNA spilled from dead cells acts as a glue in the film.

Genes that control cell lysis, including cidA, govern how much DNA is freed. Other factors chew that DNA up, loosening the film as it matures. Tuning either side changes how the film holds together. That suggests anti-biofilm strategies aimed at the DNA glue, a growing idea in implant infection care.
plos-pone-0005922:
Young brain cells must know when to stop dividing and start their real work. In 2009, Shigeru Tanaka, Imran Shaikh, Antonio Chiocca and colleagues studied that switch in the cerebellum of young rodents. Their PLOS ONE paper centers on GPR3, a receptor linked to the Gs protein, in granule cell precursors.

The title states the core result: GPR3 holds back the growth of these young cells as they move and mature after birth. Without such a brake, the cerebellum could not build its layers on schedule. The work names one of the stop signals that shape the growing brain and may guide later studies of brain growth gone wrong.
plos-pone-0006022:
Citation counts have long been the coin of scientific worth, yet science now lives online. Johan Bollen, Herbert Van de Sompel, Aric Hagberg and colleagues gathered thirty-nine rival measures of impact in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper runs a principal component analysis, a method that finds the few big patterns hiding in many measures at once.

If most measures collapse into a few shared dimensions, then impact is simpler than the crowd of metrics suggests. The study helps universities and funders judge work with their eyes open. It also marks a moment when the field began, in earnest, to grade itself with more than the citation count alone.
plos-pone-0006122:
A trusted lab drug turned out to carry a stowaway. Carlos Lafourcade, Longhua Zhang and Bradley Alger report in 2009 that a contaminant of DHPG, a standard agonist for group I metabotropic glutamate receptors, suppresses GABA release on its own. Their PLOS ONE paper shows the suppression runs through neither the mGluR nor the CB1 receptor routes it was credited to.

Group I receptors, types 1 and 5, are central to neuronal communication, so work built on DHPG is widespread. A contaminant doing the real work puts past results at risk of misreading. The paper is a standing warning on reagent purity, and it gives labs a reason to check a shelf staple before building on it.
plos-pone-0006222:
An enzyme called prolyl oligopeptidase, or POP, has been linked to schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Gemma Comellas and colleagues designed test substrates for it in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They used the one-bead one-compound method, where each tiny bead carries a different candidate molecule.

The study reports the first solid-phase substrates made for POP. Good substrates let scientists measure the enzyme's activity quickly and screen blockers against it. Those screens are early steps toward drugs for brain disorders tied to POP. The bead method itself shows how to build test molecules for other enzymes.
plos-pone-0006322:
When T cells switch on to fight infection, hundreds of their proteins change level. Wei-Yun Sheng and Tzu-Chien Wang profiled those changes in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper using proteomics, a survey of the full protein set. Very little was known about what the differentially expressed proteins actually do in activated T cells.

The survey found the energy enzyme GAPDH inside the nucleus of activated T lymphocytes. A familiar metabolic workhorse appearing in the nucleus suggests a second job. Proteomic maps generate such surprises systematically. Following them up can reveal new layers of immune control.
plos-pone-0006422:
Maria Garcia and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Rb, a protein best known for holding back tumors. Rb helps control the cell cycle, cell growth into mature forms, and the start of cancer. The team asked whether Rb also plays a part when a virus infects a cell and the NF-kB pathway switches on.

Their title states the finding plainly: turning on that pathway after virus infection requires Rb to be present. A tumor guard thus doubles as part of the immune alarm. The work widens what Rb is thought to do inside cells. It also links cancer biology with the study of virus defense.
plos-pone-0006522:
Jason Locasale and Alejandro Wolf-Yadlin rebuilt cell signal networks from protein data in PLOS ONE in 2009. New tools can now weigh many proteins at once with care. They can track tags added to proteins as signals move through a cell. The authors used a method called maximum entropy to infer the network from such data, adding as few guesses as they could.

Their method rebuilds live signal networks from large sets of protein measures. A clear map shows where signals branch and where a drug might act. The approach suits the big, noisy data sets that new tools produce. It is a tool for systems biology, the study of the cell as a whole.
plos-pone-0006622:
Adam Pluskota and co-authors used see-through worms to watch tiny particles at work in PLOS ONE in 2009. Uses of nanotechnology are growing fast. Yet little is known about how built nanoparticles act inside animals with many cells. The team used the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans, a tiny worm whose body is clear. That clarity lets one watch where particles go in a living animal.

Their title says these particle-body interactions become clear to see, and that silica nanoparticles harm the worms' reproduction. Early proof of harm in a model worm guides safer design of nanomaterials. The study helps build the safety science that the nano age needs.
plos-pone-0006722:
Tamaki Wada and colleagues reported an efficient way to make spinal motor neurons from stem cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Severe motor neuron diseases have no cures or strong treatments. Getting real spinal motor neurons from human tissue is extremely hard. Technical and ethical barriers both stand in the way. Embryonic stem cells offer an alternative source.

The method works with human and monkey embryonic stem cells. It differentiates them into spinal motor neurons with high efficiency. It also enriches the neurons so cultures are purer. Reliable supplies of these neurons support disease research in the dish. They also support testing of possible drugs before animal or human trials.
plos-pone-0006822:
Peter Lapan, Jing Zhang, and Andrew Hill used imaging to watch cancer cells change through direct contact in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cell-to-cell contact controls many key processes. Metastatic tumor cells colonize new sites through such interactions. Stem cells also take cues from their niche neighbors. Laboratory methods often miss contact effects by growing cells apart.

Their image-based assessment captured growth and signaling changes in contacting cells. Pictures over time reveal behavior that single snapshots hide. Contact-driven changes could explain steps in metastasis. They could also guide how stem cells are cultured. The method gives cell biologists a window on interaction itself.
plos-pone-0006922:
Li Zhou, Yoshiharu Takayama, Philippe Boucher, and colleagues reported a cell biology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. They examined a protein called LRP1 in the walls of blood vessels. LRP1 helps guard against atherosclerosis, the clogging of arteries. It does so by controlling a growth signal receptor in vascular smooth muscle cells.

The team traced how LRP1 limits activation of that receptor, known as PDGFRβ. They followed the signal into a downstream pathway involving phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase. Their results explain how vessel wall structure stays orderly. The findings matter for understanding how arteries harden and narrow in disease.
plos-pone-0007022:
Ole Søgaard, Nicolai Lohse, Jan Gerstoft, and colleagues studied pneumonia outcomes in HIV in PLOS ONE in 2009. People with HIV face a raised risk of pneumonia. That risk persists even on modern antiretroviral treatment. The team used a nationwide Danish cohort covering 1995 to 2008.

They measured death rates after a hospital stay for pneumonia. They also searched for factors that predicted who would die. Such prognostic knowledge guides care for a still-vulnerable group. It shows where extra monitoring or earlier treatment might save lives in the treatment era. The nationwide cohort gives those patterns a population-wide base.
plos-pone-0007122:
Marta Bull, Gerald Learn, Indira Genowati, and colleagues examined HIV in the female genital tract in PLOS ONE in 2009. Earlier studies suggested the virus there forms compartments separate from blood. Those studies covered fifty-seven women in total and mostly used free virus. The team looked again, comparing cell-free and cell-associated virus in women with chronic infection.

They found the genital tract virus was not a distinct population. It consisted of uniform, low-diversity variants instead. That distinction matters for transmission and prevention research. What leaves the body may be a narrow sample of the virus, not a separate strain.
plos-pone-0007222:
Nicholas J. Gibson, Leslie P. Tolbert, and Lynne A. Oland studied the developing sense of smell in PLOS ONE in 2009. Olfactory receptor neurons send axons into the brain. With help from glial cells, those axons sort into bundles aimed at specific glomeruli, the smell-processing units.

The authors examine special membrane lipid domains in this system. They ask how those domains affect EGF receptor activation and the stability of cell adhesion molecules. Their work explains part of how a developing olfactory system wires itself into stable, working smell circuits in insects.
plos-pone-0007322:
Kentaro Q. Sakamoto, Akinori Takahashi, Takashi Iwata, and colleagues attached cameras to albatrosses in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Albatrosses fly hundreds of kilometers across open ocean to find prey. Despite growing work on their foraging behavior, little was known about how the birds actually locate food at sea.

The team used a bird-borne camera to see the ocean from the albatross's view. They report an association between albatrosses and a killer whale in the Southern Ocean. Following large predators may help the birds find prey. The footage gives rare direct evidence of that strategy.
plos-pone-0007422:
Olivier Masson and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on LRP1, a receptor protein that sits on the surface of cells. LRP1 was already known for its role in how the body handles fats. The team asked a different question: what does LRP1 do while new fat cells are being made?

They found LRP1 present at high levels in mouse precursor cells on their way to becoming fat cells. Levels were also raised in the fatty tissue of obese mice and obese people. That pattern marks LRP1 as an active driver of fat cell formation rather than a bystander. The results name a possible target for future obesity research.
plos-pone-0007522:
Kyle McQuisten and Andrew Peek published a comparison study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on designing small interfering RNAs. These short RNA pieces can silence a chosen gene inside cells. Not every design works equally well, though. Machine learning tools promise to predict which ones will succeed. The authors pitted three approaches against each other: artificial neural networks, general linear models, and support vector machines.

Each method was tested on how well it predicted effective siRNAs. The head-to-head comparison also weighed the feature sets fed into the models. For researchers, the value is practical guidance. Choosing the right predictor means fewer wasted experiments on designs that fail. The study turns a crowded field of algorithms into clearer advice for anyone building gene-silencing tools.
plos-pone-0007622:
Hiromasa Tanaka and Tau-Mu Yi published a methods study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on mapping the wiring of cell signaling networks. A core goal of systems biology is to redraw those arrow diagrams completely. Genetic epistasis, comparing mutants, is a classic tool for ordering a pathway's parts. The authors present a strategy they call Alternative Inputs. It probes one network through several different entry signals.

Feeding a circuit different starting signals reveals the order of its components from new angles. Each input lights the network in a different pattern. Combined, the patterns pin down who acts upstream of whom. A systematic reverse-engineering method serves anyone facing an unmapped pathway. The study is a piece of strategy: how to interrogate a black box until it confesses its wiring.
plos-pone-0007722:
Maria Miragaia and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It surveys a mobile piece of DNA in a common skin bacterium. The bacterium is Staphylococcus epidermidis, usually harmless on human skin. The DNA element, called ACME, carries genes for using arginine.

Mobile elements can hop between bacteria and spread new traits. The authors mapped how varied ACME is across many strains of this species. That diversity hints at how often the element moves and spreads. Tracking such elements matters because they can also carry traits that help bacteria resist treatment.
plos-pone-0007822:
Didier Delignieres and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It models how people tap along with a beat. Tapping in sync with a metronome is a basic timing skill. Tapping in syncopation, landing between beats, is harder.

In syncopation, the timing errors show stronger long-range patterns over time. The authors extend a classic linear phase correction model to explain that rise. Their model ties the patterns to how people fix small timing errors. The work helps scientists understand the brain's clock. It also speaks to music performance and rhythm disorders.
plos-pone-0007922:
Anna Ghelli and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It shows how a person's mitochondrial background can raise the stakes of a toxin. Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy is an inherited blinding disease. It comes from point mutations in mitochondrial genes for complex I.

Many mutation carriers never lose vision, a puzzle called incomplete penetrance. The authors studied cells carrying haplogroup J, a common mitochondrial background. Those cells were more sensitive to a toxic compound, 2,5-hexanedione. The result shows how background DNA and environment jointly decide risk. It may help counsel carriers about exposures to avoid.
plos-pone-0008022:
Natacha Protopopoff and colleagues ranked what drives malaria in Africa's highlands for PLOS ONE in 2009. Malaria is returning to high ground where people have little built-in defense, so outbreaks there can kill many. Control budgets are thin, so each measure must count.

The team scored the risk factors, from climate and land use to housing and care access, by their true weight. A ranked list lets programs spend first where the gain is largest. Blanket efforts waste scarce funds; aimed efforts, the authors argue, can blunt deadly highland outbreaks.
plos-pone-0008122:
Yongsoo Kim and colleagues watched the adult mouse brain's stem cell nursery in PLOS ONE in 2009. One brain zone keeps making new nerve cells for life. Its stem and progenitor cells were thought to roam, since their offspring, young neurons, plainly travel far.

The parents, it turns out, stay put. The team also found that a growth receptor holds back the young neurons' travel when it acts. A nursery with still parents and roaming young is a tidy design, and knowing it helps efforts to coax the brain to repair itself.
plos-pone-0008222:
Igor V. Bondar and colleagues studied visual neurons in monkeys in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Many neurons in the temporal lobe respond only to certain complex patterns. Faces and objects are classic examples of such stimuli. This selectivity is thought to arise through experience. Whether it stays stable over long periods was an open question.

The team recorded pattern-selective responses in monkey temporal lobe neurons over time. Long-term stability would mean visual memories can rely on fixed cell responses. Instability would imply the visual system keeps reshaping itself. Their measurements speak to how the brain stores what things look like.
plos-pone-0008322:
Işin Çakir and colleagues studied appetite control in the brain in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Sirt1 is a conserved enzyme involved in many processes in cells. It affects differentiation, cell death, metabolism, and aging. It depends on NAD+, a molecule tied to energy state. The team investigated Sirt1's role in the hypothalamus, the brain's energy balance center.

Using a rodent model, they showed hypothalamic Sirt1 regulates food intake. A brain enzyme linking energy signals to eating is a notable finding. It could point to new approaches for obesity. It also deepens understanding of how the brain senses fuel.
plos-pone-0008422:
Lance B. Price and colleagues studied circumcision and microbes in a PLOS ONE paper from 2010. Circumcision is associated with large reductions in HIV and other infections among men. Female partners also show reduced bacterial vaginosis. The mechanisms behind these benefits were partly unclear. The team assessed the penis microbiome before and after circumcision.

They sampled the coronal sulcus of twelve HIV-negative Ugandan men. Circumcision changed the mix of bacteria living on the penis. Altered microbiota could explain part of the protection observed. The study adds biology to a major public health intervention.
plos-pone-0008522:
Sanjai Sinha and co-authors study prescribing for heart failure in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Beta-blockers reduce deaths in patients with systolic heart failure. Yet primary care doctors prescribe them at low rates. The team compare what doctors say they prescribe with what they actually prescribe. They also look for physician traits that predict prescribing. Data cover heart failure patients in primary care practice.

Self-reported and actual prescribing do not always match. Certain physician characteristics predict higher actual prescription rates. Closing the gap could save lives, since the benefit is well proven. The study points to which doctors may need support or prompts to prescribe.
plos-pone-0008622:
Marcel Adam Just and co-authors propose a theory of noun meaning in the brain in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Their article describes a set of biologically driven semantic dimensions. Those dimensions underlie the neural representation of concrete nouns. In other words, brain codes for objects rest on basic sensory and motor features. The team demonstrate how the resulting theory can identify simple thoughts. They do so through fMRI patterns recorded while people think of nouns.

A model built on those dimensions predicts brain activation for new nouns. It can even identify which noun a person is thinking of. Such a neurosemantic theory links word meaning to brain biology. It advances efforts to read semantic content from brain scans.
plos-pone-0008722:
Ivan Tancevski, Egon Demetz, Philipp Eller, and colleagues tested a thyroid-like drug aimed only at the liver. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The compound, T-0681, mimics thyroid hormone in liver tissue. Such drugs can raise receptors that pull cholesterol from the blood. A liver-only action might spare the heart from thyroid side effects.

The team measured reverse cholesterol transport, the path that carries cholesterol out for disposal. They also watched artery plaque build-up in treated mice. Better transport paired with slower plaque growth would support the approach. The study weighs promise against the risks of thyroid mimicry.
plos-pone-0008822:
David Simpson, Edward Kabyemela, Atis Muehlenbachs, and colleagues tied a blood protein to severe anemia in pregnancy malaria. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Placental malaria kills about ten thousand mothers yearly in Africa. First-time mothers face the greatest risk. Inflammatory signals like TNF-alpha were already linked to the anemia. The team measured apolipoprotein A1, a fat-carrying protein, in exposed women.

Higher A1 levels tracked with severe anemia in first pregnancies. The protein may mark the inflammatory state driving red cell loss. A blood marker could flag mothers needing urgent care. Protecting first pregnancies remains a malaria priority.
plos-pone-0008922:
Zhuoshun Yang, Biao Zhang, Dapeng Li, and colleagues showed mast cells recruiting immune suppressors inside liver tumors. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tumors often grow amid chronic inflammation that should attack them. Instead, inflammation and immune suppression become braided together. Mast cells pile up in this liver cancer model and worsen matters. How they tilt the tumor's immune balance was the question.

Mast cells mobilized two suppressor groups: myeloid-derived suppressor cells and regulatory T cells. The IL-17 pathway carried the mobilizing signal. Suppressors then shielded the tumor from attack. Breaking the mast cell signal could unshield liver tumors for therapy.
plos-pone-0009022:
Francisco Ortega and co-authors listed the tiny RNA regulators in human belly fat, in PLOS ONE in 2010. MicroRNAs are short RNA pieces that fine-tune gene activity. Some are tied to body fat and differ between fat depots. No profile yet existed for fat cells as they mature, the team noted.

They profiled microRNAs in human under-skin fat tissue. They also followed the profile as precursor cells became fat cells. Certain microRNAs rose or fell in step with that change. The catalogue points to which tiny RNAs may steer weight gain or loss.
plos-pone-0009122:
Michèl Schummer and co-authors compared breast tumours with healthy breast tissue to find new warning proteins, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Early detection saves lives in breast cancer, above all for poor-outcome cases. Good markers for predicting a patient's course are still scarce. The study drew on two carefully characterised sets of tissue.

One set contrasted patients whose outcomes were good with those whose were poor. The other set came from healthy women and served as the control. Proteins that differed across the sets became candidate markers for follow-up. Markers that flag aggressive cancer early could change screening and care.
plos-pone-0009222:
Vibha Gupta and colleagues published this structural biology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It examines an enzyme from the tuberculosis bacterium, a germ wrapped in a fatty coat. The enzyme, biotin protein ligase, has flexible loops near the spot where it grabs its target. In water those loops are disordered, waving around without a fixed shape.

The team studied what happens when the water is removed. Drying locked the loose loops into ordered, active shapes. That switch shows how the enzyme may fold only when conditions are right. Understanding such shape changes in a tuberculosis enzyme can guide the design of new drugs against the disease.
plos-pone-0009322:
Laura Gosoniu, Andre Mia Veta, and Penelope Vounatsou published this malaria mapping study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Angola runs national surveys that sample malaria indicators across the country. Survey points are sparse, but health planners need estimates everywhere. The space between sample points must be filled in with care.

The authors applied Bayesian geostatistical modeling to the Angolan survey data. Their model blends the survey results with geography to predict risk in unsampled places. It also states how uncertain each prediction is. Such maps help target bed nets, spraying, and clinics where malaria is truly worst, not just where it was measured.
plos-pone-0009422:
Jung Nyeo Chun and co-authors published this cancer cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hsp60 is a helper protein usually found inside mitochondria. Some of it, though, sits free in the cell's main body, the cytosol. There it seems to help cancer cells survive.

The team traced how cytosolic Hsp60 keeps cancer cells alive. It works by regulating IKK, a controller of the survival pathway NF-kappaB. With that pathway on, cancer cells resist signals telling them to die. A helper protein moonlighting outside its usual home thus becomes a possible drug target.
plos-pone-0009522:
Zhike Zi, Wolfram Liebermeister, and Edda Klipp measured a yeast stress pathway with care in PLOS ONE in 2010. Yeast cells face fast swings in the saltiness of their surroundings. A pathway led by the protein Hog1 helps them adapt. The team changed osmotic stress up and down over time. They tracked how the pathway answered each swing.

Quantitative measures like these let modelers test their math against real cell behavior. The pathway did not just switch on and off. It graded its response to the pattern of stress. The study shows how a single cell computes a fitting reply to a shifting world.
plos-pone-0009622:
Robert Thacker and co-authors surveyed sponges on a giant Caribbean atoll in PLOS ONE in 2010. Saba Bank, in the Netherlands Antilles, is one of the largest atolls on Earth. Its reefs were little studied despite their size. A multi disciplinary team sampled the bank for its living diversity. Sponges were a focus, since they are diverse and ecologically key on reefs.

The survey gave a first full account of the bank's sponge fauna. Many species were recorded there for the first time. Such an inventory is the base for any plan to protect the area. It also shows how much life a single remote reef system can hold.
plos-pone-0009722:
Transcription factors are proteins that grip DNA at set spots and switch genes on or off. Rahul Siddharthan set out to predict those grip spots more accurately. His method appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Finding the spots by experiment alone is slow and costly.

The classic tool, the position weight matrix, scores each DNA letter on its own. The new dinucleotide version scores pairs of neighboring letters instead. Pairs carry information that single letters miss. Better scores mean better guesses at where regulators bind, which guides gene studies. The method builds directly on the classic matrix rather than replacing it.
plos-pone-0009822:
Growing nerves must cross the midline of the nervous system in the right pattern. Joy Dorsten and colleagues studied what goes wrong when a guidance gene is missing in embryos. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The missing gene is frazzled, which normally helps axons decide where to grow. Without it, extra Abelson tyrosine kinase disrupted commissure formation, the bridges axons build across the midline. Some axons even left the embryonic central nervous system entirely. The result shows how two signals balance each other during wiring. Embryos build the nervous system step by step.
plos-pone-0009922:
Leaf-cutter ants farm fungus for food, and their gardens host whole microbial worlds. Jarrod Scott and colleagues mapped the microbial community in those gardens and in the ants' refuse dumps. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Microbial community structure means which microbes live there and in what shares. The fungus gardens are tended chambers where ants grow their crop. Refuse dumps hold the spent material the ants throw out. Comparing the two shows how ants manage microbes, friend and foe alike. The ants cut leaves not to eat, but to feed their fungus.
plos-pone-0010022:
Fotios Drenos and Thomas Kirkwood took on a common claim about aging genes in PLOS ONE in 2010. The claim says genes that harm health late in life escape natural selection, because their effects come after breeding age. Apolipoprotein E is a prime case, since its variants affect heart disease and Alzheimer's disease risk.

Using a simulation built on known genetic and lifestyle risk factors, the authors tested that claim directly. Factors in the model included sex, diet, smoking, and alcohol use. Their work shows late-life effects may not sit safely beyond selection after all, which changes how aging genetics can be read.
plos-pone-0010122:
Bilal A Azakir leads a 2010 PLOS ONE study of dysferlin, a muscle membrane protein whose faults cause several muscular dystrophies, inherited muscle-wasting diseases. Dysferlin helps patch torn muscle surface membrane, but few of its protein partners were known.

Fishing dysferlin out of mouse muscle cells, the team found it bound to alpha-tubulin, a building block of microtubules, the cell's internal rail tracks. The binding was confirmed in several tests and did not depend on calcium. Under the microscope, the two sat together along track-like lines in mature muscle cells. The authors suggest microtubules help haul dysferlin to the surface where repair happens.
plos-pone-0010222:
The authors were Jeremy Driskell, Yu Zhu, Carl Kirkwood, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study built a fast test for rotavirus, a common gut virus. Gut viruses range from mild stomach illness to life-threatening disease. Rotavirus kills many children in developing countries, so quick, sensitive detection matters where lab resources are thin and illness spreads fast.

Their method uses surface enhanced Raman spectroscopy, a light-based fingerprint technique. It reads molecular signatures of the virus rapidly and with high sensitivity. A field-ready version could speed diagnosis during outbreaks and guide care for sick children.
plos-pone-0010322:
Paul Cross, Dennis Heisey, Brandon Scurlock and others tackled brucellosis in elk for PLOS ONE in 2010. Brucellosis is a bacterial disease that can pass from wild animals to livestock. Managers often assume that more host animals means faster spread. Yet hard numbers for that link in big wild mammals were scarce. The authors set out to estimate it from field data.

They used layered Bayesian models, a method that blends past knowledge with new counts. The models mapped where the disease was rising against how dense elk herds were. That kind of map helps officials choose where to focus control work. It also tests a core idea behind many wildlife disease plans. Crowding, in short, is treated here as a measurable risk, not a guess.
plos-pone-0010422:
Philippa Mitchell and colleagues used a tiny worm to separate fresh from lasting responses to alcohol in PLOS ONE in 2010. Long drinking followed by stopping brings withdrawal: anxiety, agitation, sometimes seizures. A small drink relieves it, which traps people in dependence. The worm C. elegans shows its own versions of these responses. The team applied behavior tests and genetics to tell acute reactions from chronic adaptation.

Small signaling molecules called neuropeptides played different roles in the two phases. That split matters because treatments for binge effects may not touch dependence. A worm that separates the phases gives drug research a sorting tool. Its simple genetics let single molecules be blamed or cleared fast. Alcohol's grip, the study suggests, is at least two grips.
plos-pone-0010522:
Jessica Lou and co-workers found that DNA-damaging agents can block production of a low-oxygen response protein in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells sense low oxygen through a factor called HIF. It pairs an oxygen-sensitive part, HIF-1alpha, with a steady partner. HIF lets cells and tissues adapt when oxygen runs low. Tumors exploit it to grow blood vessels. The team asked how DNA-damaging treatments, common in cancer care, affect it.

Those agents cut the making of new HIF-1alpha protein. That side effect could help explain why some treatments starve tumors. It might also harm normal tissue healing after therapy. Either way, a hidden link between DNA damage and oxygen sensing is exposed. The study connects two major fields of cancer biology.
plos-pone-0010622:
Kai Wang and colleagues studied the first cell split in mouse embryos, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A fertilized egg cluster soon divides into inner cells, which form the baby, and outer cells, which form the placenta. Two gene switches, Oct4 and Cdx2, push cells toward opposite fates.

Cdx2 must silence Oct4 in the outer cells. The team found that a helper protein, Brg1, is required for that silencing to work. Without Brg1, Oct4 stayed on in cells meant to become placenta. The result shows how early embryos lock in their first major decision.
plos-pone-0010722:
Matthew Johns and colleagues studied flu shots in US military personnel during the 2009 pandemic, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A new H1N1 virus spread worldwide that year. The vaccine against it arrived late, so many people relied on whatever protection the earlier seasonal shot might give.

The team tracked illness among service members with known shot records. Earlier seasonal vaccination gave, at best, limited protection against the pandemic strain. Some groups showed a small benefit; others showed none. Honest numbers like these help planners avoid false comfort and push for faster pandemic vaccine production.
plos-pone-0010822:
Zhichao Jin and colleagues audited research methods in Chinese medical journals across a decade, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Clinical research output from China grew enormously between 1998 and 2008. Growth in count says nothing about quality. Sound design and correct statistics are what make a study's answer believable.

The audit sampled journals from both years and graded design and analysis. Standards had improved, yet common flaws persisted in both rounds. Misused tests and unclear designs still weakened many papers. An honest baseline tells editors and trainers exactly which skills to teach next, instead of assuming progress.
plos-pone-0010922:
Harish Nagarajan, Jessica Butler, Anna Klimes and co-authors published this genome sequencing study in PLOS ONE in 2010. New sequencing machines read DNA fast but only in short scraps, and no one had yet assembled a complete genome from those scraps alone, without help from older methods. The team aimed to prove it could be done.

Their four-phase strategy combined two short-read technologies to build the full genome of a Geobacter variant prized for producing unusually strong electric current at electrodes. The finished assembly covered the bacterium's whole chromosome, about three point seven million letters. Nagarajan and colleagues deliver a proof of principle that complete genomes can come from short reads only. That lowers the cost of sequencing microbes that turn waste or fuel into electricity.
plos-pone-0011022:
Yun Lu, Christopher Futtner, Jason Rock and co-authors published this lung cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. SOX2 is a stem cell factor found at high levels in some lung tumors. The authors asked whether too much SOX2 is merely a passenger in those tumors or a driver capable of causing them.

They confirmed SOX2 overexpression in human squamous lung tumors and some adenocarcinomas, then built mice that switch on extra Sox2 in lung lining cells during development or in adulthood. Both settings produced extensive overgrowth, and the smallest airways remodeled into a trachea-like layered lining. Over the following months about half the highest-expressing mice developed carcinoma. Lu and colleagues prove SOX2 overexpression is oncogenic in lung, a stem cell program turned cancer driver.
plos-pone-0011122:
Chatterjee, Adak, Singh and colleagues sampled high mountain air in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their station sat in the northeast Himalayas in India, far above most towns. They analyzed the fine particles floating there, called aerosols, and what those particles are made of.

The chemistry tells which particles arise locally and which drift in from far away. Even remote peaks receive pollution carried on winds from lower land. That reach matters for climate, since particles affect clouds and sunlight. The data give a rare baseline for a region where long term air records are scarce.
plos-pone-0011222:
Vala, Martins, Imaizumi and colleagues gave low radiation doses in cancer tests for PLOS ONE in 2010. Radiation usually aims to kill tumors, but the team tested whether small doses could have the opposite effect. In their experiments, low doses were checked for effects on tumor growth, spread and blood vessel formation.

Low doses promoted tumor growth and spread by boosting new vessel formation. That paradox urges caution when planning radiotherapy near tumors. Scatter doses to nearby tissue might aid vessels that feed remaining cancer. The finding could reshape how treatment doses and fields are planned to avoid that risk.
plos-pone-0011322:
Cohen, Lawrence and Margulies modeled septic lungs in dishes for PLOS ONE in 2010. Lung air sac cells taken from septic rats were grown in culture. In sepsis, these cells' tight seals loosen and the lung barrier leaks. The team asked whether cultured cells keep that septic behavior outside the body.

The cultured cells did mimic the living septic lung, with altered junctions and barrier function. A faithful dish model lets researchers test sepsis treatments without whole animal experiments at every step. It speeds the search for drugs that restore the lung barrier. The model also confirms that sepsis leaves a lasting mark on the cells themselves.
plos-pone-0011422:
Kristen Taylor and co-authors reported in 2010 that high blood sugar and a chronic inflammation signal together disable a class of guard cells. Gamma-delta T cells patrol body surfaces and respond fast to germs, and people with obesity and metabolic disease suffer more infections. The team used mouse models to test what dulls these guards.

Mice with high blood sugar and lasting exposure to the inflammation signal TNF-alpha had fewer gamma-delta T cells, and the remaining cells responded weakly. Neither insult alone told the full story; the double hit did the damage. The result helps explain the infection risk that travels with diabetes and obesity. It also suggests that controlling sugar and inflammation together, not either one alone, may be needed to restore this first line of defense.
plos-pone-0011522:
Stephanie Topp and co-authors tested in 2010 whether HIV treatment can be folded into ordinary clinics in Lusaka, Zambia. Antiretroviral therapy was often delivered in separate, donor-funded programs, apart from the primary care that the same patients use for everything else. Separation strains both systems and stigmatizes patients, so the team studied the feasibility of integration at facility level.

Their work asked a practical question of staff, space, and patient flow: can the same nurses and rooms handle routine care and HIV treatment together? Feasibility evidence of this kind is what ministries need before changing national policy. If integration works, overstretched systems gain efficiency and patients gain one door instead of two. The study treats organization itself as a medical intervention, which in a strained health system it truly is.
plos-pone-0011622:
Ashley Sherrid and co-authors studied how tuberculosis bacteria handle low oxygen, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The TB bacillus can stop growing and lie dormant when oxygen runs low, as happens inside lung granulomas during infection. How the bacteria enter, hold and leave that dormant state is a major research focus.

The team characterised a gene regulator tied to the Clp protease, a protein-shredding system, and tracked the response when oxygen returns. Their findings expose controls the bacteria use to wake from dormancy. Those wake-up controls are attractive drug targets, since dormant TB is notoriously hard to kill.
plos-pone-0011722:
Christine Ward-Paige, Joanna Mills Flemming and Heike Lotze warned about a bias in reef fish surveys, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Divers increasingly count fish visually underwater to assess populations and to judge whether protected areas work. Such censuses underpin many claims about natural reef communities.

The authors show that counts taken slowly, rather than as instant snapshots, systematically overestimate fish numbers. Fish wander into the survey area during a long count and get tallied extra. Protection plans built on inflated counts may therefore miss their mark, so survey methods need correcting.
plos-pone-0011822:
Jing Yan Tang and co-authors tested a plant compound that spurs new blood vessels, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Vessel growth, called angiogenesis, plays a part in a wide range of body processes, and many diseases trace to its poor control. Radix Astragali is a Chinese herb used for heart and vessel ills, and it had been shown to hold vessel-linked gains.

Its compound calycosin spurred vessel growth in zebrafish and in human vessel cells, acting through estrogen receptors and the MAPK signal path. A natural agent that grows vessels could help wounds heal and injured tissue recover, where new blood supply lines are needed.
plos-pone-0011922:
John Schneider and colleagues surveyed in 2010 Indian truck drivers about two HIV prevention options still new at the time. Long-haul drivers face elevated HIV risk, and prevention plans often fail at the first step: whether people will accept them. The options were daily preventive medicine, called pre-exposure prophylaxis, and circumcision.

Using a staged behavior model, the team measured the drivers' initial commitment to each option, working with ninety drivers. Knowing whether the barrier is awareness, interest, or firm intent tells health workers where outreach will pay off. For a mobile population that clinics rarely keep in touch with, that first commitment is the foothold everything else depends on.
plos-pone-0012022:
Timothy Dickson and Charles Mitchell tested in 2010 how insects and fungi, alone and together, cut seed production in grassland plants. Herbivores and fungal pathogens each reduce plant fitness, and their joint effects may add up, cancel, or multiply. Few studies had measured those joint effects on seeds in wild, non-crop populations.

Excluding each enemy in turn across four common grassland species let the team separate the costs. Seeds are the currency of plant futures, so even modest cuts change which species dominate a meadow. The results help ecologists predict grassland change as insect and fungal communities shift with climate and land use.
plos-pone-0012122:
Alison McCormack, Sally Mak, Jaimie Henderson, and co-authors tested a gene-silencing treatment in monkeys for PLOS ONE in 2010. A brain protein called alpha-synuclein sits at the center of Parkinson's disease, and too much of it seems to add to its harm. Lowering the protein in the brain region that dies in Parkinson's could, in theory, slow the disease.

The team delivered small silencing RNA into that region of the primate brain and checked the effect on the protein. Showing that levels can be turned down safely in a large animal brain is a needed step before any human trial. It supports a treatment strategy aimed at the root protein rather than at symptoms alone.
plos-pone-0012222:
Ying-Wooi Wan, Ebrahim Sabbagh, Rebecca Raese, and co-authors searched for a gene signature that forecasts lung cancer's course, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lung cancer kills more people than any other cancer, and even early-stage tumors return in a large share of patients after surgery. Doctors had no fully validated gene test to say whose cancer will return or whose will answer chemotherapy.

Blending several modeling methods, the team settled on a signature of twelve genes tied to both outlook and drug response. A test like this could steer strong treatment to those who need it and spare others its harms. It is a step toward cancer care chosen per patient rather than per stage alone.
plos-pone-0012322:
Emanuela Santini, Veronique Sgambato-Faure, Qin Li, and co-authors traced the abnormal movements caused by Parkinson's treatment in rodents, in PLOS ONE in 2010. L-DOPA remains the best Parkinson's drug, but years of use often bring involuntary movements called dyskinesia. In the dopamine-starved striatum, those movements grow from overactive signaling down two chemical pathways driven by one receptor type.

The team separated the changes in the two pathways as dyskinesia develops, rather than treating them as one surge. Distinct changes mean distinct drug opportunities: calm the branch that drives movements while keeping the branch that restores motion. That separation is the central puzzle of Parkinson's therapy, and finer maps bring an answer closer.
plos-pone-0012422:
Koichi Suzuki, Wataru Takigawa, Kazunari Tanigawa and colleagues searched ancient Japanese skeletons for leprosy DNA, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Proving that a disease existed in the past takes more than bone damage, since several illnesses scar bones alike. DNA from the leprosy bacterium would be direct proof, but old bone holds only traces, making detection very hard.

By first copying all DNA in the sample to boost the signal, then running targeted tests, the team recovered leprosy bacterium DNA from archaeological remains. The success gives historians and doctors a firmer timeline for leprosy in Japan and a method other ancient-disease hunters can borrow.
plos-pone-0012522:
Sungmin Lee, Verónica Ramenzoni and Petter Holme modeled how shared memories form in groups, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. People understand the world by linking events that influence each other, and groups aggregate many such links into collective memory — the shared story of what happened and what matters. How that shared version emerges from private ones was the question.

The authors built a model in which linked event pairs spread and merge through social contact. Collective memory arose as a natural outcome of many small exchanges, not from any central editor. The model offers testable ideas about how communities come to remember the same past.
plos-pone-0012622:
Pena Dias, Talbot, Senecal and co-authors used rats to study a receptor that worsens diabetes-related harm. The kinin B1 receptor switches on under chemical stress in diabetes models. Their 2010 study fed young rats glucose water to trigger insulin resistance, then tested what this receptor does.

Turning the receptor on seemed to keep the stress going, feeding high blood pressure, pain sensitivity and other problems. Blocking it could therefore break a harmful loop rather than treat one symptom at a time. The work names a target worth testing for the many complications of diabetes.
plos-pone-0012822:
Duarte, Foti, Nakatani and co-authors presented a new way to name hepatitis C virus types using a liquid microarray. Treatment for hepatitis C depends heavily on which genotype a patient carries. Wrong typing can mean the wrong drug plan and a failed cure.

Their 2010 method reads genotype markers on tiny beads suspended in liquid, rather than on a fixed chip. Liquid arrays can be adjusted more easily as new variants appear. A reliable, flexible typing test helps clinics match each patient to the right course.  The assay was checked against samples of known genotype.
plos-pone-0312222:
Abrham Shumbulo, Mihret Jemal, and Abraham Bosha ran a field trial at Wachemo University in southern Ethiopia to find the fertiliser mix that grows the most garlic. Ethiopian garlic yields are held back by tired soils and the lack of advice tuned to each area. Their plots combined five rates of a blended mineral fertiliser with four rates of chicken manure, repeated across blocks through one growing season.

The heaviest manure paired with a high-but-not-highest mineral dose won clearly, producing marketable bulbs more than ten times the unfertilised yield. It also brought the best dry matter and sweetness readings and the highest profit per hectare. Manure alone also lifted bulb quality. The authors recommend the winning combination to local growers, while noting the mix was tuned on one demonstration field and season.
plos-pone-0331722:
Candicia M Kotra and Lisa L Gezon looked at trade in khat, a leaf people chew for its lift, in northern Madagascar. Around Diego-Suarez they spoke with city managers and growers, watched sales points, and asked twenty sellers to keep daily diaries of earnings and costs. They set khat earnings beside earnings from selling vegetables.

Khat selling paid more than vegetable selling, even though prices swung with the seasons. Sellers with family ties to khat farms earned the most by far. Khat also brings jobs and town taxes that pay for local services and building work. Vegetables still draw sellers who lack farm family links. The study shows a drug crop quietly holding up much of the local economy.
plos-pone-0335322:
Mehakpreet Thind and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Working with mice, they test how a low-protein diet affects gut injury. Two challenges are involved: infection with Citrobacter rodentium, a mouse gut pathogen, and colitis induced by dextran sulfate sodium, a chemical that injures the bowel.

As the title states, feeding too little protein worsens the mice's susceptibility to both kinds of intestinal injury. Nutrition and gut defense are tightly linked, and this experiment shows the cost of protein shortage under attack. The work speaks to researchers studying malnutrition and bowel disease, where underfed patients often fare worst.
plos-pone-0341522:
Yency Forero and colleagues asked whether repeat blood tests beat a single reading for judging lung spots. The marker they tracked is a protein fragment shed by lung tumors. Doctors usually read it once. The team instead followed it over time in over a hundred people with lung nodules. The patients came from a Vanderbilt tissue bank. The logic borrows from repeat prostate testing, where trends guide care.

At the first reading, cancer patients already ran higher than benign cases. Over time, the average paths did not split cleanly. But cancer cases swung more from visit to visit. The size of that swing separated the groups with very few false alarms. A jumpy trend may tell doctors more than any single value can.
plos-pone-0342122:
TongZhu Yu and colleagues improved the route-planning brain of tracked transport robots that haul materials through coal mine tunnels. These roadways are rough, narrow, and cluttered, so a robot must plan an efficient overall route yet dodge obstacles in real time. Their 2026 algorithm upgrades the classic A-star search with a two-way adaptive strategy and builds terrain risk into the cost of each path, then hands local steering to a reactive avoidance method.

In simulated mine roadways the planner steered around obstacles cleanly while producing shorter routes and finding them faster than the standard approach. Risk weighting kept paths out of dangerous ground. The authors offer the method for intelligent underground transport in mining.
plos-pone-0345722:
Zhicheng Tan, Shanlin Sun, and Guo Li present in 2026 a neural network for spotting tiny hot targets in infrared images, such as distant ships or vehicles. Such targets give weak signals and little texture, so they are easy to miss or confuse with background noise. Their network uses a retention style attention that links far apart parts of an image without blurring fine detail.

An added module joins space and frequency views to pass clear target features through the system. Tests on several public datasets beat leading methods and cut training time by nearly a third. Faster, sharper spotting helps watching traffic and coasts from a distance.
plos-pone-0345922:
Alexandra Ferguson and colleagues use control theory to steer a living neuron with electric current, in this 2026 PLOS ONE neuroscience paper. Their test bed is a pressure-sensing cell in the medicinal leech, and the goal is to make it fire a target signal while spending as little stimulation energy as possible.

Optimal pulses were computed in advance from a simplified model that was deliberately not fitted to the real cell. Remarkably, the living neurons lost tracking accuracy at exactly the same points as the simulated ones as energy was cut. The match suggests the model's dynamics capture something real about the cell, a step toward gentler neural stimulation for medicine.
plos-pone-0347122:
Erik E. Osnas re-estimated the numbers of Steller's eiders, a threatened sea duck breeding on Alaska's Arctic Coastal Plain, using flexible statistical models instead of traditional survey arithmetic. Rare and patchy birds make crude counts jumpy. His models combined survey datasets, accounted for missed birds, and mapped density across the region year by year.

The population, it turns out, breathes on a roughly six-and-a-half-year cycle, swinging between a few hundred and more than two thousand birds. Long-term growth hovers near zero. Birds concentrate in the northern survey triangle and may be shifting further north. Osnas warns that trends should compare the same phase of the cycle, or the rhythm will masquerade as decline or recovery.
plos-pone-0347422:
Stuart Flint and colleagues study how views of aging link to character traits. Their survey paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. It covered more than two thousand adults aged sixty-five and up. Half lived in Britain and half in Canada. Each filled a short form on aging attitudes. Each also wrote open answers about growing older.

An AI tool read the language of those written answers. It grouped people into two character clusters. Each cluster held its own outlook on later life. The written themes tied outlooks to habits such as staying active. How people feel about aging shapes health and daily choices. Programs for older adults, the authors argue, should fit each outlook.
plos-pone-0347922:
Xiaoxue Sherry Gao and Rong Rong studied a snag in survey science. How can you pay people to state their health beliefs with care? Pay schemes need a truth that can be checked. Health outcomes are private, and they unfold slowly. Worse, people could bet against their own health to win either way. The pair found a way around both traps.

They asked people about close peers, not about themselves. A first survey got real health facts from peers much like the group. Those facts set the pay in the main task. Beliefs about peers then lined up well with each person's own past health. The pair say peer beliefs can stand in for self-beliefs. Health researchers can use the trick.
plos-pone-0348022:
Tharwat A. Selim and colleagues surveyed the flies of Egypt's Sharkia Governorate across the seasons of 2022 and 2023, cataloguing species that carry disease and checking which bacteria ride on the common house fly. Twelve species from five families were identified. The 2026 study combined trapping counts with diversity statistics and laboratory culture of microbes from fly bodies.

The house fly dominated all year, and overall diversity dipped slightly in winter, when several blow fly species vanished. Some species held steady while others swung sharply with temperature. Four of five bacterial isolates from house fly surfaces were species capable of causing illness. The authors warn that these insects are active mechanical carriers of pathogens in the region.
plos-pone-0348122:
Zhonghai Bai and a large team combined two views of a moving hand to recognise gestures from video more reliably. One view captures the hand's shape through statistical descriptors treated with special geometry that respects their curved mathematical home. The other tracks motion, summarising how brightness flows across a grid from frame to frame. Either view alone misses part of the story.

Fused together, the combined description beat both single views on two public benchmark sets, scoring above ninety-nine percent on one and above ninety-seven on the other. The representation stays compact and its parts remain interpretable, which helps developers debug mistakes. The authors aim the framework at touchless controls, sign language tools, and other systems where a camera has to read hands in real time.
plos-pone-0348522:
Daniel Merenstein and co-workers lay out a large trial plan to settle how acute sinus infections should be treated. Sinus trouble sends millions to clinics yearly and drives a fifth of antibiotic prescriptions, yet most cases are viral. Their 2026 protocol describes a practical trial in primary and urgent care across six United States regions, recruiting several thousand adults.

Patients who have not improved after nine days are assigned by chance to antibiotics, a steroid nose spray, both, or dummy pills, with salt-water rinsing kits for all. Symptom scores days later form the main measure. As a protocol, the paper reports no results yet. Its size should finally show which patients gain from antibiotics and which can skip them.
plos-pone-0348622:
CORRECTION: Satsuki Fukushima and co-authors correct their rat study of cell therapy for a weak heart. The study weighed ways to place muscle cells into hearts hurt by a heart attack. The note fixes a group size in the methods. It also fixes a death rate in the results and a note in a key table. A fresh, correct table comes with it.

The team also clears up a shared image. One chart panel matches a chart in linked work. The control tissue came from a joint run of two projects, a step meant to spare rats. The note adds more detail on how the rats were watched and put down.
plos-pone-0349022:
Prakash Babu Kodali and Maya Vijayaraghavan used two rounds of India's big national family health survey to ask how often doctors and other health workers tell men who smoke to quit. They focused on men who smoked cigarettes or bidis and had seen a health worker in the past year. They compared survey rounds from the middle of the last decade with the most recent one.

Advice to quit rose slightly between the rounds, reaching a little over half of these men. Older men, heavier smokers, and men already diagnosed with a long-term illness were more likely to be advised. Men from Scheduled Tribe communities were notably less likely to hear the advice. The authors say a huge chance to help men quit is still being missed at routine visits.
plos-pone-0349122:
A bulging aorta can be repaired from inside the vessel. The fix avoids open surgery. Late leaks still threaten some patients, though. Hong-Jae Choi and colleagues built a model to forecast long-term survival. They studied more than twelve thousand repair patients. Treatment years ran from 2002 to 2019.

Five learning methods fed into one stacked model. Thirty-four patient variables went into the forecasts. The stack ranked risk better than any single method. It won at both one month and one year. Importance charts show which traits drive each forecast. Surgeons can use the output in counseling. Patients hear a personal outlook, not a generic average.
plos-pone-0349622:
Andrea Levy and Ursula Rothlisberger tested two fast computer tools that predict where metal based drugs will bind on proteins. Such drugs show promise against cancer, yet finding their grip points is hard. Both tools were trained only on zinc sites, a narrow start. The test asked whether they could still spot true binding sites for other metal drugs on known protein shapes.

For every protein tried, at least one true site was found by the tools. Results wobbled when protein side chains sat in odd poses, a known weakness. The authors propose a pipeline: cheap predictors flag likely hot spots first, then costlier physics methods refine the shortlist. Drug hunters could save large computing bills that way.
plos-pone-0350122:
Carlotta Gualco, Maria Grazia Grasso, Giorgia Presicce, and co-authors mapped the world's research on helping people with multiple sclerosis get into work, stay in work, or return after absence. The disease often strikes in prime working years, and job support services exist but are little studied. Their 2026 scoping review searched seven databases and included twenty-eight studies describing distinct programs, appearing from the mid-nineteen-nineties through 2025, largely in Western nations.

Most programs combined several elements: rehabilitation, education, and workplace adjustments. Patients valued personal, empathetic support, help managing symptoms, and legal advice, while logistics and health problems blocked participation. Studies have grown more experimental lately, with feasibility trials multiplying. The authors judge the programs broadly feasible and call for stronger outcome evidence.
plos-pone-0350222:
Muhammad Tafazzal Hossain and colleagues tested shop bought cheese in Sylhet, Bangladesh, for a germ that resists common drugs. Over six months they gathered one hundred and twenty cheeses from twelve brands. In the lab they counted the germ, checked which drugs still worked, and searched for genes that make toxins.

About two thirds of samples carried the germ, often above safe limits, and about three in ten carried the drug resistant form. All resistant samples beat several widely used drugs. Many also carried toxin genes that can cause food poisoning and skin harm. The authors warn that everyday cheese can carry a real health risk when hygiene and cold storage fail.
plos-pone-0350622:
Mahim Hassan Chowdhury and a team in Bangladesh test whether two variants in a gene that controls the cell's main tumor guard raise breast cancer risk. The guard protein and its controller keep each other in balance, and inherited tweaks can tilt that balance. The case-control study genotyped women with breast cancer and healthy women, and also measured blood levels of both proteins to see whether gene type and protein level move together.

One variant's mixed form raised risk clearly across several genetic models, while its double form looked protective in one model; the second variant showed no clear link. Patients carried more of the controller protein and less of the guard, with levels tracking gene type. Chowdhury and colleagues say the variant deserves study as a risk marker in South Asian women.
plos-pone-0350822:
Adam P Burch, M Kristen Hall, and Ruth A Schwalbe studied a sugar tagging enzyme in neuroblastoma, a childhood nerve cancer. The enzyme adds a branch that can block further sugar chain growth, and it has a reputation for slowing tumours. Human cancer cells with the enzyme gene removed were compared with normal cells, and rat cancer cells with extra enzyme were also tested.

Removing the enzyme sped cell growth, movement, clumping, and invasion into surroundings. Tagged sugars of the blocked type nearly vanished, while other sugar types rose. Restoring the gene reversed the changes, and extra enzyme in rat cells calmed movement and invasion. Low enzyme activity marks more aggressive disease in this cancer model.
plos-pone-0350922:
Patricia Quintero-Rincon, Karina Caballero-Gallardo, and Oscar Florez-Acosta built dissolving microneedle patches from chitosan, a shell derived material, loaded with tequila agave root extract. Tiny needles that melt into skin promise painless delivery. Chemical profiling, shape and heat tests, enzyme assays, and skin and melanoma cell tests compared two extract loadings.

Rosmarinic acid led the extracts rich chemistry. The lower loading kept needle tips sharp, while the higher loading roughened surfaces and bent tips. Patches kept most antioxidant and skin enzyme effects of the extract, stayed gentle on normal skin cells, and killed melanoma cells in a dose linked way. Loading balance decides whether beauty or drug patches from agave can work.
plos-pone-0351122:
Gabriele Bertotti and colleagues tested whether eating more polyphenols, plant compounds in fruit, vegetables, tea, and cocoa, links with lower pain sensitivity in migraine patients. Seventy two adults with confirmed migraine kept three day food records and took pressure pain tests on head and other sites, plus disability and stress surveys.

Higher intake went with higher pressure pain thresholds at two head muscles and lower disability scores. Adjusted models kept those links. People with longer migraine history also ate more polyphenols, perhaps learning by trial what helps. A snapshot cannot prove diet eases migraine, but the pattern supports trials of polyphenol rich diets for pain control.
plos-pone-0351222:
Ebrahim Zarepour Nasirabadi and colleagues surveyed about seven hundred fifty parents of toddlers in Tabriz, Iran, about child car seats: what they know, own, and actually use. Road injuries kill children worldwide, and Iran's seat use lags its car ownership. Questionnaires at nineteen public health centers probed awareness, trust, cultural attitudes, and practical barriers.

The knowledge-behavior gap is stark. Nearly all families owned a car and most knew the age and weight rules, yet under half owned a seat, and over half of those rarely or never used it. Knowing how to install one correctly was the weakest knowledge point. Cultural and cost barriers filled out the picture. Campaigns that only teach rules will miss, the authors imply: the binding constraints are price, habit, and the hands-on skill of fitting the seat.
plos-pone-0351322:
Correction notice: Christina M Ferreira and colleagues correct their study that used tiny worms to judge how harmful closely related Salmonella Newport strains from the environment can be. One author name was misspelled, two main figures were swapped, and species names needed italic styling in places. Corrected figures are supplied with this notice.

Readers should use the corrected author spelling, Arjumand Ghazi, and match each figure image to its caption in the new order. Figure captions themselves were already in the right order. The worm survival results and strain comparisons stand as captioned once the images are placed correctly. Anyone citing or reusing the figures should take them from the corrected version.
plos-pone-0351422:
Hitomi Hagawa and four colleagues test a corn-derived ingredient that may help skin defend itself. Their 2026 study works with human skin cells called keratinocytes. Pollution and ultraviolet light bombard skin with oxidative stress. That stress speeds ageing and disorders. The ingredient is hydrolysed corn starch containing a sugar chain named maltotetraose. The team asked whether it switches on the cells' own antioxidant machinery, governed by a protein called NRF2.

Gene screening gave the first answer. Treated cells turned up several antioxidant genes, including three classic NRF2 targets. Protein tests confirmed more NRF2, and showed it moving into the cell nucleus where it works. Under deliberate oxidative attack, treated cells carried lower levels of harmful reactive oxygen. The effect runs through the skin's built-in defence pathway, not through a surface coating. Cosmetic formulators gain a food-derived candidate for protective skin products.
plos-pone-0351622:
Lung adenocarcinoma, the most common lung cancer type, builds a neighborhood of immune cells that can help or hinder it. Jie Yao, Changshuai Zhou, and Liren Ding focused on an enzyme called KYNU inside macrophages, the immune system's cleanup cells, in this 2026 PLOS One data study.

Blending single-cell and bulk gene data from public atlases, they found the enzyme concentrated in macrophages and monocytes. Macrophages carrying it switched on genes for showing tumor pieces to other immune cells, and signaled more with B and T cells. Tumors rich in such macrophages behaved differently on immune measures. The authors call the analysis exploratory, a map for experiments rather than settled biology.
plos-pone-0351722:
Xiaolong Zhang and three colleagues study how elite sprinters and power athletes should schedule their competitions in an Olympic or World Championship year, in this 2026 PLOS ONE analysis. Their dataset holds nearly fifteen thousand athlete records from global championships between 1993 and 2019. Statistical clustering sorted athletes into three seasonal styles: those who focused almost entirely on the big event, those who raced often, and those who treated races as training.

The frequent racers performed best at the main event. Athletes using races as training gained by moving toward the frequent-racing style, while big-event specialists gained nothing by switching. The authors' message to coaches is that the fashionable peak-for-one-day calendar suits only some athletes.
plos-pone-0351822:
Hannah Potter and four colleagues refine a low-tech trick for restoring seagrass meadows in this 2026 experiment. Seagrass is vanishing worldwide, and seeds sown bare are often eaten or churned up before they can grow. Wrapping seeds of a common eelgrass in clay balls protects them, but the recipe matters. The team tested clay mixes and drying methods in tanks, placing balls on the sediment surface or burying them, then tracked how well balls held together and how seedlings emerged.

A clear trade-off appeared. Bare seeds and buried balls of one clay type produced the most seedlings and longest shoots, while dense balls rich in certain clays survived deployment best but suppressed emergence. A mix lacking loam performed worst on every measure. Even so, surface balls beat typical field germination, and the authors see a scalable tool pending open-water trials.
plos-pone-0351922:
Linh Nguyen and Tham Vo redesign how neural networks learn from social graphs. Their 2026 paper builds a framework called DAGRL. Standard graph networks pass messages between neighbours. That captures local closeness well. It smears together signals that live at different scales, though. Friend-of-friend patterns, community structure, and whole-network shape all blur into one average. The authors argue that local and global information deserve separate handling before they meet.

Dual attention mechanisms do the separating. One attends to fine-grained local interactions. The other reads the graph's global organisation. Their outputs combine into richer node representations. The framework is aimed at the usual proving grounds: classifying nodes, clustering communities, and inferring relationships. For analysts of online networks, cleaner separation of scales could mean spotting both tight cliques and the slow tides moving an entire platform.
plos-pone-0352022:
Nuhad Dumit and colleagues surveyed hospital nurses caring for Syrian refugees in Lebanon and Jordan, asking how the work was wearing on their own bodies and minds. About a thousand nurses answered in Lebanon and two thousand in Jordan. The survey covered back pain, general weakness, and emotional exhaustion alongside hours, workload, and workplace strain.

Strong back pain troubled more than six in ten nurses in both countries. General weakness was reported by nearly six in ten in Lebanon and more than seven in ten in Jordan. Emotional exhaustion also ran high, and higher in Jordan. Age, gender, and working hours were among the factors tied to the outcomes. Nurses holding up refugee care are themselves a strained workforce, and the numbers argue their health belongs on the response agenda.
plos-pone-0352122:
Abdi Negasa and colleagues modeled the value of a cheap breathing device for young children in Ethiopia. The device is called bubble CPAP. It pushes air gently to keep small lungs open. It can be built locally, unlike costly imported machines. The team compared it with standard low-flow oxygen in general hospitals. Their model counted deaths and healthy years gained.

For every ten thousand children with severe pneumonia and low blood oxygen, the device saved about thirty-one more lives. The cost per healthy year gained sat far below the usual limits for Ethiopia. Every check on the model gave the same answer. The authors urge wider use of the locally built device.
plos-pone-0352322:
Yu Weng tracks the keystrokes of translators racing the clock. The 2026 study recruited sixty-five Chinese-to-English translators: thirty-five novices and thirty seasoned professionals. Each translated comparable texts under three deadlines: short, standard, and unlimited. Software logged every pause, burst, and revision. Analysis worked at two levels, from micro-pauses up to how whole sessions were organised. The question was how experience changes the rhythm of work under pressure.

Looser deadlines helped everyone. Text came in longer, steadier segments, with more immediate self-correction. Beyond that, the groups split. Experienced translators kept stable rhythms in every condition. They separated drafting from revision and spent time orienting first and polishing last. Novices blended everything reactively. Curiously, a moderate deadline made novices work most like experts. Unlimited time, which should have freed them, went unexploited. Training programmes can teach the expert cadence deliberately, rather than hoping years supply it.
plos-pone-0352422:
Jing Wang and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One cell study on kidney damage caused by the iodine contrast dye used in medical imaging. The work centers on a mitochondrial housekeeping protein called ClpP. Human kidney cells exposed to the dye in culture lost viability, their mitochondria fragmented, and programmed cell death rose; gene sequencing showed the dye switched on ClpP and related machinery.

When the team knocked ClpP down, the cells fared better: mitochondrial shape and energy held up more, a key fusion protein recovered, and fewer cells died. The authors suggest that restraining this protein softens contrast injury, at least in a dish, and nominate it as a target worth testing in animal models of contrast-related kidney damage.
plos-pone-0352922:
Romaric Jac led a team of eight authors studying capelin in Canada's Gulf of St. Lawrence, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Capelin are small forage fish that feed many larger species, so their movements matter to the whole food web. The team asked whether capelin stay faithful to home regions or disperse widely.

Jac's group read chemical traces in otoliths, the ear stones that record a fish's history in its layers. Those fingerprints reveal which fish are locals and which traveled in. The answer shapes how fisheries should be managed: local stocks need local protection, while wide-ranging fish need broader plans. For an ecosystem under climate pressure, knowing stock structure is basic care.
plos-pone-0353122:
Confessor and colleagues surveyed Japanese gamers at risk of social withdrawal in a 2026 study. Nearly six hundred players reported their withdrawal risk and gaming tastes. People who withdraw from society might also avoid social play, or might find online contact safer than face-to-face life.

Higher withdrawal risk tied to weaker interest in achievement and challenge-driven play. Other social tastes varied by gamer personality type. Games meant as bridges back to social life must match those tastes, or they may push players further away. The findings caution designers that one social game formula will not fit all withdrawn players.
plos-pone-0353622:
Calahorro and colleagues built a free computer tool in 2026 to screen chemicals that may disturb hormones in fish. Testing every chemical on every kind of fish in the lab would take far too long.
