Their tool predicts how strongly a chemical will grip the hormone sensor proteins that start many toxic effects.

The tool screened the sensors of more than one hundred kinds of fish against natural and man-made steroid drugs. One fish group showed sensors that grip the drugs tightly, marking them as more at risk. Follow-up cell tests confirmed two chemicals from a health research set could switch the sensor on, flagging them for closer safety checks.
plos-pone-0354022:
Han-Trong and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, build a noise filter that adjusts itself while it runs, for sensors whose noise keeps changing. Steady filters fail when interference drifts, and heavy filters are too slow for small devices. Their design stacks stages of a classic adaptive filter and decides on the fly how many stages to run and how fast each should learn.

A statistical test watches whether the cleaned signal still echoes the noise reference, and stops the chain when the echo is gone. Corrections handle signals that resemble themselves and changing loudness of noise. On simulated and real measured data, the method cut errors sharply against the classic single filter and ran several times faster than a fixed-threshold rival. The authors aim it at low-delay monitoring on cheap hardware, from factory floors to body sensors.
plos-pone-0354122:
Araya Tipsungnoen and six colleagues review more than a decade of catheter procedures that close a heart duct in children, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study from a Thai hospital. The duct, which should seal after birth, sometimes stays open and is now usually plugged through a vein rather than by open surgery. Three hundred and forty-one patients treated between 2010 and 2023 were checked for difficult procedures and major problems.

Trouble arose in about one case in seven, though nobody died from the procedure. A wider duct, a longer duct, and a duct shape other than the usual cone each roughly tripled the odds of difficulty. Three devices slipped free and needed surgery. Anatomy, the authors argue, should guide how carefully each case is planned.
plos-pone-0354522:
Chen and colleagues, in a 2026 review, work out how much balance training is enough for older adults. Falls are a leading danger in old age, and training that sharpens the senses and muscles can rebuild balance. But trials vary wildly in dose, and more may not always mean better. The team pooled twenty-four trials with over a thousand participants and modeled dose as a curve.

Training clearly improved both moving balance, such as standing up and walking, and still balance, such as standing steady. For moving balance the dose curve bent: gains grew, then softened around a total of roughly a thousand minutes of training. Still balance showed no such dose pattern. Age also mattered: older participants gained less in moving balance, while their still balance gains held up. The authors urge prescribers to dose balance training like medicine, enough to work, not endlessly more.
plos-pone-0354822:
Sylvia Aponte-Hao and seven colleagues use province-wide health records to ask who still ends up severely ill with COVID-19 after vaccination, in this 2026 Alberta study. They followed more than two and a half million adults who completed at least a primary vaccination schedule, tracking hospitalizations and deaths tied to the virus. Only a small fraction, about two in a thousand, suffered a severe outcome.

Risk concentrated sharply. Older age carried much higher hazard. A heavy burden of other illnesses multiplied risk many times over, and conditions such as cardiovascular disease and dementia stood out individually. Men fared slightly worse than women. The patterns held among people who took additional booster doses. The authors say the findings can guide booster policy and early treatment toward the vaccinated groups who remain genuinely vulnerable.
plos-pone-0355722:
Kristina Åhlund, Anette Johnsson, and Maria Rönnerhag review in 2026 what helps or blocks nurses and physiotherapists learning together in hospital wards. Their scoping review searched three databases and kept a small set of studies that covered both professions in adult hospital care. Learning together matters because each group must grasp the other's role to care well.

Friendly team habits, chances to get to know each other, and supportive organisation helped learning. Tight structures, strained contact between professions, and a closed ward culture held it back. The authors argue that lasting learning needs regular contact built into normal work, plus leaders who welcome joint work even as staff change.
plos-pone-0356722:
Wenjing Li and colleagues worked out how to collect and store urine so the free-floating DNA it carries survives for later testing. Their 2026 methods study used urine from healthy volunteers. It then confirmed the recipe with patient samples. The team varied preservative dose, spinning steps, storage temperature and time, and thawing method. DNA yield and purity were scored throughout.

Untreated urine degraded within a day at room temperature. The winning protocol spins the urine first. It adds a modest dose of preservative to the liquid portion, and freezes deep for long storage. Gentler freezing failed after about two months. Quick thawing proved safe, while extra spinning after thawing cost DNA. Such groundwork matters because urine DNA tests promise painless cancer and transplant monitoring.
plos-pone-0356822:
Uxía Yáñez and colleagues analyzed more than three and a half thousand uterine samples from mares. They wanted to settle a practical question in horse breeding. When bacteria grow in a mare's uterus culture, does it signal real inflammation or harmless contamination? Their 2026 study paired culture results from two sampling methods, swabs and low-volume washes. Microscopic inflammation scores came from the same samples.

Any bacterial growth raised the odds of inflammation with both methods. Counterintuitively, wash samples growing a single species were more often inflamed than those growing three or more. The busier growth looked more like contamination. One streptococcus species was the standout culprit across methods. Pairing culture with cytology, the authors argue, keeps antibiotics for mares who actually need them.
plos-pone-0357022:
Samson Tashome Abashu leads a team of four auditing the paperwork behind HIV care in Jimma, Ethiopia, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Treatment programs run on records; bad data means invisible failures. The team reviewed two hundred thirty-four patient files across five public facilities in mid 2022. They scored the resources available and the quality of the data itself. They also checked whether anyone actually used the information for decisions.

The three scores landed in the seventies, a middling verdict. Completeness was good, above ninety percent, and consistency acceptable. Timeliness was the wound, under half of reports arriving when due. Some facilities lacked the electronic record system, internet, or even printers. No staff in the testing service had been trained on data quality, and performance review meetings were not happening as scheduled. The authors say Jimma's HIV data are usable but fragile, held up by habit more than by systems.
plos-pone-0357622:
Ying Shi, Yi Bao, and Chuanxiong Li published a 2026 systematic review in PLOS ONE on using musculoskeletal ultrasound to steer rehabilitation after rotator cuff repair. Shoulder rehab after tendon surgery usually advances by calendar, yet patients heal at different speeds and pushing early risks re-tear. Ultrasound watches the tendon and muscle directly. The reviewers searched three databases for studies linking ultrasound measures to rehab decisions, finding eleven.

Three measures dominated: shear wave velocity, a stiffness index, plus the muscle's cross-sectional area and echo brightness. Stiffness climbed steadily across the first year after surgery, giving a rough baseline trajectory for normal healing. An unusually high stiffness reading soon after surgery flagged higher re-tear risk and argued for slowing the program down. The evidence is early and thin, but it sketches how imaging could replace fixed timetables with healing-based progression, a shift trials should now test.
plos-pone-0357922:
Pierre Charlier and colleagues record five ways of sensing the heartbeat at the same time, to give engineers a shared reference. The signals include the heart's electric trace, its sounds, its chest vibrations, and two pulse measures taken at the skin. Each method is well studied alone, yet side-by-side comparisons under one setup are rare, which makes combining them into one monitor hard.

Electric and pulse signals proved steady in shape and timing, while sound and vibration signals varied more with sensor placement and body differences. Each signal also carried its energy in a distinct pitch band, and delays against the electric trace matched known body timing. Charlier and colleagues publish the benchmarks to guide filter choices and multi-signal heart monitors.
plos-pone-0358122:
Max Y. Lu and colleagues published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on how interest in anesthesiology changes during medical school, using national data on American medical students who entered between 2014 and 2017. Women and sexual minority students are underrepresented in the specialty, and little was known about low-income trainees. The authors sorted students into four paths: never interested, gained interest, lost interest, or kept interest from entry to graduation.

Nearly all students, over nine in ten, were never interested, and only a small fraction kept the interest throughout. Women started out less interested than men, and women and sexual minority students were less likely to develop interest during school, even though those who began interested kept it at similar rates. Low-income students showed no clear differences. The specialty, they argue, loses trainees mainly by failing to spark interest early, especially among women, not by losing those already keen.
plos-pone-0358222: Maghembe, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE study comparing the evolution of two related human genes. The genes make enzymes in the prostaglandin pathway, which drives pain and inflammation. Maghembe found coding differences that sort by population, and flagged spots in the protein that may change drug response. Such maps can explain why pain drugs work unevenly across groups.
plos-pone-0358422:
Phuoc Giau Dang and four colleagues published a large cohort study in PLOS ONE in 2026. They asked how type 2 diabetes affects recovery after a specific kind of low-back surgery, done through a scope from the back to join one level of the spine. Their data came from a global pool of matched patients.

By pairing patients with care so that diabetes was the main contrast, Dang's group could weigh the added risk that comes with the disease. Results like these help surgeons counsel patients before an operation. They also help hospitals plan care for a group that often heals more slowly and faces more problems after surgery.
plos-pone-0359522:
Han Zhang and six colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It concerns the renovation of architectural heritage, old buildings valued for their history. The authors study ornamental motifs, the decorative patterns on such buildings, and the visual concerns people bring to them.

Two outcomes are examined together: the enjoyment people take from the designs, and their wish to protect the buildings. If beauty moves people to protect a building, work that respects its ornament protects too. Heritage planners and architects restoring historic districts are the readers for this link between looking and saving.
pmc-12848322:
Preechanukul and colleagues compare virus-specific T cells in hepatitis B alone against combined hepatitis B and HIV infection. People with both infections are often left out of cure studies. The team profiled CD8 T cells in three groups of patients, all on suppressive antiviral therapy, using gene and protein readouts.

Co-infection samples scored high for stem-like, precursor-exhausted cells that keep the power to multiply. Hepatitis B alone leaned toward terminally worn-out cells instead. The co-infected group also showed stronger, broader responses to viral proteins and better response to checkpoint blockade in tests. Well-controlled dual infection, the authors argue, need not mean weaker immunity.
pmc-13198522:
Kalter Hali and colleagues reviewed sleep quality after shoulder joint replacement in a 2026 survey. Shoulder arthroplasty swaps a worn joint for an artificial one, easing pain and restoring motion. Whether sleep improves too was poorly mapped, so the team gathered all studies reporting sleep outcomes.

Eighteen studies with more than twenty-five hundred patients qualified. Poor sleep before surgery was near universal. Gains in the first six weeks were small, then sleep improved markedly by six months and held after that. Still, about one in seven patients kept struggling to sleep comfortably. Nearly all studies used self-report scales, and only two used wearable trackers. Better objective sleep data are needed.
pmc-13200022:
Ankita Mondal and colleagues evaluated India's child meal program and modeled fixes in a 2026 study. The Supplementary Nutrition Programme gives a morning snack and hot lunch to children aged three to six at day-care centers. The team checked meals against national standards across twenty-seven states and territories.

Energy standards were met in just over half of states, and protein in about three quarters before digestibility adjustments. Only about one fifth of states met fat needs. Calcium and three vitamins fell short in most states. Meals leaned on cereals with few nutrient-rich foods. A math planning tool found foods that close gaps, though many fixes cost more than the per-child budget allows.
pmc-13200422:
Julia Levin and colleagues asked whether a little-known tick germ can infect people in a 2026 cohort study. Borrelia valaisiana is a spiral germ carried by ticks in Sweden, kin to the Lyme disease germ. Its power to sicken humans was unproven, so the team revisited a large tick-bite study from 2007 to 2015.

They compared thirty-three people bitten by germ-positive ticks with sixty-seven matched controls bitten by germ-free ticks. Blood tests showed antibody conversion, a sign of immune response, far more often in the exposed group. Symptoms such as neck pain, muscle aches, and headache appeared in the exposed group, but at rates like controls. None sought medical care. Infection seems possible yet mild.
pmc-13203322:
Fluoride protects teeth but may roughen orthodontic wires, and a 2026 laboratory study led by Karen Lisette Vega Bravo measures that wear. The in vitro study brushes nickel-titanium archwires with fluoride or fluoride-free toothpaste and tracks surface roughness as a sign of corrosion-driven damage.

Thirty wires were split into three groups covering fluoride paste with brushing, fluoride paste alone, and fluoride-free paste with brushing. Simulated brushing ran twice daily for twenty-eight days before final measurements were taken. Roughness climbed significantly in both fluoride groups and barely moved without fluoride, leading the authors to suggest fluoride-free paste for patients wearing these wires long term.
pmc-13217222:
Allwsh and Kucher test a blood protein as a possible marker for autism in children in Kurdistan, Iraq. Finding biological indicators to detect and track autism remains a major unmet need. The protein, soluble alpha-klotho, has been tied to several brain disorders, which makes it a plausible candidate worth checking in this setting.

The study measures klotho levels in children with autism and judges how well those levels characterise the group. A marker that separates cases cleanly could support earlier referral in places with few specialists. The authors frame the work as an early step: candidate markers must survive larger, careful tests before any clinic can lean on them.
pmc-13242122:
Liu and colleagues at Sichuan Agricultural University fed brewery waste to pigs and sequenced gut and muscle to explain better pork. Sixty pigs ate diets replacing soybean meal with fermented extruded brewers' grain up to twenty percent. The trial ran ten weeks across five rations. Growth, carcass, and meat traits were recorded.

The highest replacement grew pigs faster on less feed per gain. Meat grew more tender and marbled, with richer flavor chemistry. Gut microbes shifted toward short-chain fatty acid producers. Muscle proteins pointed to an energy-sensing pathway linking microbes to mitochondrial growth.
pmc-13242422:
Cintia Hiromi Okino and colleagues compared how three sheep breeds handle Haemonchus contortus, a gut worm that drains blood and weakens flocks. Their study appeared in Veterinary Research Communications in 2026. They followed Santa Inês, White Dorper, and Texel lambs raised under low to high levels of parasite exposure. Blood tests and tissue samples from the stomach lining showed how each breed coped.

Santa Inês lambs, a breed known for natural resistance, stayed much the same across all challenge levels. White Dorper and Texel lambs fared worse as exposure rose, and Texel lambs showed signs of a form of anemia. Santa Inês sheep also carried more infection-fighting white blood cells and higher activity of a protective gene in the stomach. The results point to breed choice as a practical tool against this parasite.
pmc-13243322:
Tobias Brodkorb and co-authors followed women for roughly eight years to compare sexual function after two kinds of laparoscopic hysterectomy. Their study appeared in the Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics in 2026. Seventy-four women who had joined an earlier prospective study answered the Female Sexual Function Index again, forty-five after total hysterectomy and twenty-nine after the supracervical operation that leaves the cervix. Both groups had surgery for benign disease.

Overall scores ended up statistically indistinguishable between the two operations. The total-removal group held steady against its own earlier results. The cervix-sparing group, however, declined significantly over time, with lubrication the clearest loss. That slide still did not leave the group worse overall than the other. The authors conclude both methods protect sexual function comparably in the long run. The lubrication finding gives surgeons one specific change to warn cervix-sparing patients about.
pmc-13245022:
Farman Ullah and co-authors read an Alice Munro novella as a case study in what Alzheimer's does to the self. Their essay appeared in Philosophy, Ethics, and Humanities in Medicine in 2026. “The Bear Came Over the Mountain” follows Fiona, whose memory collapses, and her husband Grant, who becomes her caregiver. Using narrative gerontology, the authors examine how identity survives when one partner's story can no longer be told by its owner.

Their analysis centers on the we-narrative: the shared identity a couple builds over decades, which dementia strains but does not simply erase. Fiona's fading recall shrinks her freedom and unravels her story, while Grant's move from spouse to carer rewrites his role. The novella's disjointed form mirrors the cognitive disorder it depicts. Selfhood in dementia, they conclude, is relational, held partly in other people's keeping. The reading offers families a language for care that honors the bond.
pmc-13247522:
Parisien-La Salle and co-authors untangled two adrenal disorders in one patient, in this 2026 JCEM Case Reports article. A twenty-nine-year-old woman was referred for excess hair growth, with high blood pressure since eighteen and early puberty signs in childhood. Scans found tumors on both adrenal glands. Hormone tests confirmed pheochromocytomas, rare tumors that flood the body with adrenaline-like chemicals, alongside a mild inherited enzyme deficiency called nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

Both glands were removed, confirming the paired tumors. Genetic testing found two separate inherited explanations: a harmful germline change in the MAX gene, which had vanished entirely from her tumor tissue, driving the pheochromocytomas. A homozygous CYP21A2 change behind the enzyme deficiency. The authors note how rare the combination is.
pmc-13249222:
Sun and co-authors tuned driving behavior models for snowy roads, in a 2026 PLOS One study. Simulators predict how closely cars follow each other, but their built-in models assume normal grip and visibility. Snow changes both, so the team calibrated five classic car-following models using an encoder that reads long time series plus a neural network constrained by physics.

Checks against a public highway dataset and real snowy driving tests showed the new calibration beat the standard genetic algorithm approach, improving accuracy by about an eighth. It also transferred across all five models rather than fitting just one. The authors offer the method to sharpen winter traffic simulation and safety testing.
pmc-13249422: Riddle wrote this short eLife commentary in 2026 on boosting memory with brain stimulation. It discusses a pooled analysis by Badillo Goicoechea and colleagues of studies that used magnetic pulses on brain areas linked to the hippocampus, the region that helps form lasting memories. The pooled results suggest that stimulating this linked network, rather than the hippocampus itself, can improve recall of past events. Riddle explains why that targeting choice matters for future memory research.
pmc-13249822: Wooten and colleagues published this correction in Scientific Reports in 2026. It amends their paper on a returning bacterium clone tied to a multi-year die-off of muskoxen in the high Arctic. One author, Beverly Morrison, was left off the author list in the original version. The notice restores her name and prints the corrected author contributions section, which spells out who did the design, methods, analysis, and field work. The paper's data and conclusions are unchanged.
pmc-13249922:
Qiu and colleagues tested a water-free stannous fluoride toothpaste for sensitive teeth, in two 2026 randomized trials. One hundred four and one hundred thirteen adults with dentin hypersensitivity brushed twice daily with either the new paste or a standard fluoride paste for eight weeks. Dentists probed sensitivity with air blasts and touch instruments, and participants rated their own pain and quality of life.

By four weeks, and more strongly by eight, the new paste beat the standard on every measure: lower air sensitivity scores, higher touch thresholds, and better self-ratings. Gains grew progressively rather than plateauing early. The authors present the anhydrous formula as a patient-centered option for daily relief.
pmc-13250222:
Rafei and colleagues review abdominal wounds treated at a teaching hospital during Sudan's armed conflict. Their 2026 Trauma Surgery and Acute Care Open study covers patients operated on at Wad Madani Teaching Hospital in the months after fighting began in April 2023. The abdomen holds vital organs with little bony protection, making it highly vulnerable in war.

Thirty-three patients had complete records, most of them young civilian men. Stabbings caused just over half the wounds and gunshots about a third, with the small and large intestines hurt most often. Combat cases arrived later, stayed longer in hospital, and died more often, while overall deaths came to about one in sixteen patients. The authors call for faster referral, conflict-ready surgery, and stronger infection control.
pmc-13250322:
Widad Abd Ali led this 2026 case report of a rare chest wall growth in a baby boy. At four months old, he was found to have a firm lump on his left back ribs. The growth type, called a hamartoma, is harmless but can look like cancer on scans.

Scans showed a large mass centred on the sixth rib, damaging bone, plus two smaller lumps on the same side. Needle samples confirmed the diagnosis. A team of specialists chose staged surgery to remove all three lumps and rebuild the chest wall with mesh, and tests confirmed full removal. The child stays under regular scan follow-up, and the authors stress team review before operating.
pmc-13250722:
Mathias Mosfeldt and colleagues put hip fracture death-prediction models to an outside test in this 2026 study. Many such models exist, but few have been checked on patients from other hospitals, the step that shows whether their numbers can be trusted.

The team ran three earlier models on 5,055 hip fracture patients treated in Stockholm between 2010 and 2020. All models performed acceptably at predicting death at one, three, six, and twelve months. The gradient boosting model did best. Because death rates were lower in Sweden, the models were re-tuned, and two corrected versions were posted online for doctors to use with their own patients.
pmc-13252822:
Fatma Savur, Serkan Güler, and Gülistan Oyur probe smoking's hidden toll in thyroid eye disease in this 2026 study. The disease, an immune attack linked to thyroid problems, was quiet in all patients studied, yet smoking may still have been doing damage underneath.

The team compared 24 smokers and 20 non-smokers with the inactive disease plus 32 healthy controls. Smokers showed higher disease activity scores and higher levels of a thyroid-stimulating antibody, alongside lower blood selenium, a protective mineral. Detailed eye scans found thinner tiny blood vessels at the centre of vision in smokers than in controls. The authors suggest vessel loss on scans can betray ongoing harm even when the eye looks calm.
pmc-13253922:
Haritha Mullagura and co-authors build a baseline model of diseased lung arteries in a 2026 study. Pulmonary arterial hypertension means lasting high pressure in lung arteries, driven by wall reshaping and energy shifts. Their framework combines vessel shape, wall makeup, and blood flow in model artery trees.

Compared with healthy vessels, model PAH arteries were far stiffer, rising from about 7 to 10 kilopascals to 300 to 800. Walls grew thick while outer width stayed fixed, narrowing the open channel. Energy cost per length more than doubled, so the authors suggest vessels adapt by shifting where energy is spent.
pmc-13256222: A short 2026 retraction notice in Open Forum Infectious Diseases withdraws an IDWeek conference abstract by Monirujjaman Biswas on hepatitis A linked severe acute liver injury in adults in Delhi, India. The journal says the abstract overlapped significantly with a previously published abstract, without giving credit to it. It also says the authorship of the publication cannot be verified. The notice gives no study findings, so the retracted work is described here only at the level of its subject and the reasons for withdrawal.
pmc-13257122:
Jo and co-authors report outcomes for twenty-one patients with relapsed or refractory B-cell lymphoma treated with epcoritamab, a bispecific antibody engaging T cells against CD20. Seventeen had large B-cell lymphoma and four follicular lymphoma, treated at one institution from late 2023. In some cases the team tracked killer T cell subsets and receptor repertoires over time.

Among patients who could be judged, nine of fourteen with large B-cell disease and all four with follicular lymphoma responded. One patient with feared brain relapse reached complete remission on the drug. In three patients who stopped treatment after complete remission, memory killer T cells topped effector cells and repertoires looked skewed. The authors frame these immune patterns as exploratory hints needing larger studies.
pmc-13257522:
Athina Shkembi and co-authors present a light-driven way to build pyrrolidines, ring-shaped molecules prized as chemical building blocks. Their 2026 method revisits the Hofmann-Loffler-Freytag reaction, an early route to altering distant carbon-hydrogen bonds. The classic chemistry is here recast as a cleaner photochemical process.

Ultraviolet A light starts the reaction, so no catalyst is needed to get it moving. A base-driven ring closure then finishes the pyrrolidine products. Working without a catalyst and under mild conditions makes the route simpler and more sustainable. The paper offers synthetic chemists a greener option for making a widely used class of compounds.
pmc-13259622:
Dandan Wang and colleagues rebuilt an enzyme that stitches carbon chains, guided by quantum-level detective work. Fructose-6-phosphate aldolase already helps turn methanol into sugars in test-tube cascades. Its inner mechanism was murky, blocking smart redesign until this 2026 study.

Calculations pinpointed one step, forming a Schiff-base link, as the bottleneck of the whole reaction. Mutations aimed at that step delivered variants working thirty-four times more efficiently than the natural enzyme. Dropped into a designed cascade, the improved enzyme converted methanol into mannitol at high yield. The work sharpens tools for carbon-neutral chemical manufacturing from one-carbon feedstocks.
pmc-13259922:
Miriam Vignando leads a 2026 brain study of hallucinations in Parkinson's disease psychosis. The team used electroencephalography, which records the brain's electric signals, during a visual task that presents unexpected images. They modeled effective connectivity, meaning the directed influence brain regions exert on each other. The study covered twenty people with Parkinson's disease and visual hallucinations, and eighteen with Parkinson's disease but no hallucinations.

Patients with hallucinations showed reduced top-down links and stronger bottom-up links in visual and frontal brain regions. That pattern suggests faulty updating of sensory predictions and over-reliance on raw visual input. Patterns differed by hallucination type: complex hallucinations involved one-sided changes, while hallucinations across several senses showed wider two-sided disruption. Task activity also tracked the spread of a serotonin receptor type, pointing to possible drug targets.
pmc-13260022:
Jordan Curry leads a 2026 mixed methods study of ExerciseGuideUK, a personalized web-based exercise platform for people living with and beyond lung cancer. People joined from Hull University Teaching Hospital and used the platform for eight weeks. The team measured usability, ran structured surveys, and interviewed users about whether it suited them. A method called the Pillar Integration Process was used to merge the number-based and interview findings into one picture.

Eighteen participants enrolled, with a mean age of sixty-five years. Of those approached, recruitment reached 30.5 percent, and retention was seventy-seven percent. Notably, a full 25.4 percent of screened people were excluded over digital access problems, even though some owned smartphones. Users rated it highly for ease of use and engagement, valuing goal-setting tools, breathlessness strategies, and personal exercise plans. Barriers included treatment side effects and low confidence with technology.
pmc-13263222:
Caian L Vinhaes and colleagues report a late lung infection in a transplant patient in Brazil in a 2026 case report. The patient, a 45-year-old woman with cystic fibrosis, had received two transplanted lungs eight years earlier. She developed worsening breathing symptoms, and scans showed nodular lesions with cavities, hollow areas, in the lungs.

Cultures from lung washings and sputum grew Nocardia cyriacigeorgica, a soil bacterium that preys on weakened immune systems. The infection broke through despite preventive treatment. Doctors treated her with two antibiotics, meropenem and a sulfa combination, without the usual drug sensitivity testing. Her symptoms and scans improved. The authors urge vigilance for this germ in transplant patients with stubborn lung infections.
pmc-13263322:
Xunlian Quan reports a 2026 journal article on using large language models, AI text systems, in collaborative English translation classes at Chinese universities. A total of 372 students worked in groups. Some groups paired students only with each other, while others added an AI partner.

Final translation quality did not differ significantly between the two setups. Students using AI nevertheless felt more efficient and more satisfied with the work. Observation showed their process changed shape. Instead of drafting text themselves, they spent more time judging and negotiating over AI output. pmc-13271422:

pmc-13272222:

pmc-13272522:

pmc-13272622:

pmc-13273022:

pmc-13276122:

pmc-13276222:

pmc-13278022:

pmc-13289922:

pmc-13290522:

pmc-13290722:

pmc-13290822:
Variants in the gene for the cell glue E-cadherin track how bladder cancer behaves, Laís Capelasso Lucas Pinheiro and colleagues report in a prognostic study from 2026. Urothelial bladder cancer recurs often, and losing E-cadherin marks tumors turning invasive, so the team asked whether inherited CDH1 variation shapes that course.

Genotyping 334 patients found the heterozygous form of one variant tied to lower one-year recurrence risk, and a two-variant haplotype protected against recurrence within two years. Tissue imaging fit the story: muscle-invasive samples had lost E-cadherin and epithelial order compared with non-invasive tumors. A bioinformatic scan also mapped a dense repeat landscape in the gene, including new Alu insertions in exon 16 that may act as regulatory hubs. Pinheiro and colleagues propose CDH1 profiling for recurrence risk stratification.
pmc-13290922:
A billion people live with allergies but not with allergy care, Sheng-Guang Li and colleagues argue in a narrative review from 2026. The 'forgotten billion', mostly in low- and middle-income countries and marginalized groups elsewhere, face gaps in diagnosis, essential medicines, immunotherapy, trained staff, and policy attention.

Asthma shows the chasm starkly: in 2019 it caused about 21.6 million lost healthy years and roughly 461,000 deaths, some 90% of the burden in poorer countries, while basic inhaled steroids are often unavailable or unaffordable there. The review gathers fixes that worked at scale. Task-shifted care in Malawi, primary care training in South Africa, community health worker visits in Boston, public access programs in Brazil, and Finland's national strategy all feature. The authors urge systems-first equity over specialist-centered innovation.
pmc-13291122:
A fish extract added to a stomach drug is tested by Hery Djagat Purnomo and colleagues in 2026. Rats with aspirin-harmed stomachs formed the test model. Aspirin cuts protective chemicals and raises stress in tissue. The drug omeprazole lowers acid but does not rebuild lining.

Thirty male rats split into six groups. One group got omeprazole alone. Three groups got it plus rising striatin doses. Vessel growth and repair markers were measured. Ulcer size and tissue form were checked at the end. Vessel signals showed no clear group gap. Repair marker results form the core comparison. Striatin comes from the fish Channa striata.
pmc-13291322:
Football joy and sorrow were tracked live across five lands. Hannes M Petrowsky leads a 2026 data paper on the 2024 European championship. Fans answered short surveys tied to match days. Mood, kindness aims, and trust in leaders were all probed.

The set holds 1,012 fans from five countries. England, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, and Poland took part. Each fan answered four to eight survey waves. Waves stopped when their team fell out. Thirty measures track swings after wins, draws, and losses. Traits, beliefs, drinking, and betting were also logged. Match facts like shots and cards complete the file. Future teams can mine it for sport and society links.
pmc-13291522: A correction notice from 2026 fixes figure legends in a rice study by Sheng Huang and colleagues on a magnesium transporter. Only the correction note is present here. Three legends in the supplement were placed in the wrong order. Each legend now moves to its correct figure. The supplement has been fixed online. No data or findings are changed in this note alone.
pmc-13291722:
Calista Sha and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a perivascular epithelioid cell tumor, or PEComa, arising in the lung. Their patient was a 71-year-old man who had two earlier lung cancers treated with lobectomies four years before. Follow-up imaging then revealed a new cystic lesion in his left upper lobe.

Surgeons removed the lesion with a wedge resection, and tissue testing classified it as a localized PEComa. The tumor stained positive for Melan-A and Cathepsin-K but negative for HMB-45, an unusual pattern. Because lung PEComas are very rare, the authors add this case to the growing picture of how these tumors appear under the microscope.
pmc-13292322:
Bruce Rosen and Sami Miaari ask a 2026 workforce question with census data: how do Arab physicians' incomes compare with Jewish physicians' incomes in Israel? Arabs made up 25 percent of working-age employed physicians in 2023, up from 8 percent in 2010. The analysis used the 2022 census, covering 7,089 physicians; 1,333 of them were Arab.

Average gross income for Arab physicians, NIS 358 thousand, sat 26 percent below the NIS 483 thousand average for Jewish physicians. Arab doctors were far younger, more often male, concentrated in the North, and less often supervisors or specialists. Adjusting for age and sex alone shrank the gap to 1 percent in regression results. The authors say the gap is mostly an age-structure story that could narrow as Arab physicians reach peak-earning years, depending on access to prized posts.
pmc-13292522:
Lesley Uttley's team reviews a 2026 methods gap: how researchers gather and use expert opinion when hard data run out. Using health technology assessment as the test case, they reviewed studies of how experts get consulted in decision-making research. Twenty-three studies qualified, and the ways experts were tapped sorted into six broad families.

Methods ranged from casual one-off chats to formal elicitation protocols with structured estimates. Rigor and reporting transparency swung wildly across studies, leaving room for hidden conflicts and quiet researcher choice. The authors answer with a proposed framework named INTEGRITY, bundling social, methodological, and reporting safeguards. Their rule of thumb: informal input suits low-stakes exploration, while high-stakes policy and spending calls demand structured, transparent elicitation.
pmc-13293422:
Xin Chen and co-authors study, in a 2026 paper, how public attention to parcel delivery services shifted in China just after COVID-19 controls eased. Social media posts offer a live window on what users praise or fault in daily services.

Posts on Weibo from December 10, 2022 to January 10, 2023 were scored for reach, sorted into topics over time, and read for mood by a trained model. Mood leaned negative and swung with shopping peaks, infection waves, and holidays. Six topics stood out, with goods safety and after-sales care as old staples and courier rights as a new concern. Official and personal accounts viewed the issues differently.
pmc-13294222:
Amalie Thorsti Møller Rønnstad and coauthors profile eczema among adults with asthma in a 2026 Danish registry study. Hospital patients aged 18 to 45 diagnosed between 2000 and 2019 were surveyed on eczema severity with a patient scoring tool and on asthma severity with current GINA steps. Responses totaled 4,126 people, a 15% response rate.

Eczema appeared in 5.2% of respondents, mostly women, with childhood start for both skin and lung disease in most cases. Mean eczema score was 25.4 in the reported units, in the mild-to-moderate range. Skin severity did not track asthma severity. Head, neck, and hand involvement was common and scored worse, and a third flared during asthma attacks.
pmc-13294322:
Anna Maria Iatrou and coauthors describe a Streptococcus canis outbreak on a Greek mink farm in a 2026 report. In late February 2024, about 300 of 5,100 mink in West Macedonia, or 5.9%, developed pus-filled abscesses, mostly on the head, and some showed depression, weakness, and lethargy. Similar illness had struck the year before.

Autopsy found local abscesses and, in two animals, pus-driven brain and membrane inflammation. Culture plus nanopore sequencing confirmed the same bacterium in every checked sample. Ampicillin and erythromycin looked effective in lab testing, and animals responded to ampicillin. Seasonal return points to housing stress and injury as triggers to fix.
pmc-13294922:
Guanghui He and co-authors compare two ways to recover heat from burnt ventilation air methane in a 2026 modelling study. Mine ventilation air carries very dilute methane that is hard to use but harmful to release. A flow reversal reactor can burn it, yet the best way to reclaim the heat is disputed.

A one-dimensional model of the reactor compared central cooling with drawing off hot gas. Central cooling accepted wider flows and weaker methane levels and gave steadier centre temperatures with less thermal shock. Hot gas withdrawal reached higher peak recovery in some settings but swung far more in temperature, favouring central cooling overall in the cases studied.
pmc-13295122:
Can Zheng and colleagues publish the full chloroplast genome of a grape-family vine in a 2026 article. Causonis japonica is the type species of its genus and holds medicinal and classification value. Its shifting looks have long caused confusion with close relatives across East Asia.

The circular genome spans 158,414 bases in the usual four-part layout, with two matching repeat sections. Annotation found 139 genes, covering protein coding, transfer RNA, and ribosomal RNA types, with a modest overall GC share. Comparing full chloroplast genomes across the family placed the species on its own branch, clearly separate from Cissus and Tetrastigma relatives.
pmc-13295522:
Medha Suman and colleagues model hidden links between gene marks and proteins in pituitary tumours in a 2026 study. Non-functioning pituitary adenomas often regrow after surgery, and no reliable test sorts patients by that risk. DNA methylation and protein data were joined through hypernetwork modelling to find the drivers.

Samples covered 25 tumours that progressed and 15 that stayed quiet after surgery. Progressing tumours showed a tight, busy hub network centred on copying, reading, and packaging DNA plus cell scaffolding proteins. Quiet tumours spread their hubs across protein handling tasks instead. The contrast offers candidate markers and mechanisms for predicting regrowth.
pmc-13295622:
Guoxin Mei and colleagues hunt the cause of many embryos in one seed in a prized Chinese tree in a 2026 study. Phoebe bournei, a protected timber tree, often packs several embryos into a single seed for unknown reasons. Seed chemistry, growing conditions, and gene activity were compared side by side.

Neither seed makeup nor environment tracked meaningfully with the multi-embryo trait in their checks. Gene activity differed clearly instead, pointing to internal control as the main driver. Two genes ran higher in multi-embryo seeds, making them prime suspects for steering the process and useful leads for growing and conserving the tree.
pmc-13295822:
Beatrice Kudzaishe Shava and colleagues plan a pilot of one-session therapy in Zimbabwe in a 2026 protocol. Common mental disorders are widespread, yet multi-session talking cures create long waits where providers are few. The Friendship Bench programme, delivered by lay counsellors, will offer a single-session version to new clients.

The study will follow 350 first-time clients in Harare and nearby areas for six weeks. Uptake, fit, and acceptability lead the aims, with symptom change, hope, connection, and daily function also tracked. Interviews will add client voices on the experience. Results will judge whether a larger trial of the brief format is worth running.
pmc-13297522:
Infections may push the immune system toward attacking its own myelin in multiple sclerosis, while other infections seem to calm it. Dafni F T Frohman and Stella E Tsirka survey that contrast in a 2026 review covering viral triggers, antibody-driven autoimmunity, and parasite effects.

Epstein-Barr virus stands out among the viral suspects, with evidence tying it to mistaken-identity antibodies and disordered B cells that may start or worsen the disease. Worms and certain protozoa point the other way, steering immune responses toward regulation and tolerance and apparently shielding the nervous system. The authors close by considering what these opposing influences could mean for diagnosis and for designing future treatments.
pmc-13298722:
Hotels and motels are an overlooked setting for fatal overdoses, report Andrea Stewart and colleagues in a 2026 CDC field analysis. Drawing on the SUDORS surveillance system across 47 jurisdictions, they examined drug overdose deaths in these lodgings from 2022 through 2024.

At least 9,651 such deaths occurred over the three years, including 2,327 in 2024 alone, and 56.2% of victims died in their home county. A potential bystander was nearby in 34.7% of deaths, yet help came late or never in 63.5% of those cases, sometimes because the bystander was also using substances. The authors suggest stocking reversal medication and treatment information in lodging settings.
pmc-13299522:
Cells keep their chromatin-bending HMGB proteins on a tight leash, and Elena V Chikhirzhina with co-authors review the enzymes holding it in a 2026 article. HMGB proteins assist replication, transcription, and DNA repair, but their levels must be controlled to avoid trouble in cancer and heart disease.

One control route is the ubiquitin tag: E3 ligases mark HMGB proteins for destruction, while deubiquitinases strip the tags off and rescue them. The review catalogues the enzymes identified so far and their proposed roles, whether they grip HMGB proteins directly or work through intermediaries. The authors frame the ligase-eraser balance as a dial on HMGB activity inside the cell.
pmc-13299722:
Heart patients keep having events even when cholesterol and sugar are controlled, and Zijin Sun with co-authors blame immune cells reprogrammed by metabolism in a 2026 review. Sugar and fat overload, they argue, rewires immune cell energy circuits toward permanent inflammatory settings.

Metabolic leftovers double as epigenetic cofactors, stamping a trained-immunity memory into circulating cells and even the bone marrow stem cells that birth them, which explains why inflammation outlasts good numbers. The signal spreads between organs along heart-fat, gut-heart, and heart-blood axes, forming an amplification loop. The authors survey therapies aimed at erasing that maladaptive training.
pmc-13299922:
Metabolites from a probiotic bacterium tightened leaky dog gut cells and cooled their immune neighbors, show Andreea Cornelia Udrea and colleagues in a 2026 cell study. Working with canine epithelial and macrophage-like cell lines, they applied cell-free fluid from Limosilactobacillus reuteri cultures during bacterial toxin challenge.

Epithelial leakage of a tracer dye fell to 94.9% of the challenged control value, a significant improvement that came without switching junction genes on or off, and a stress marker eased instead. Immune cells raised the protective BCL2 signal, lifted their survival ratio, and cut inflammatory messengers IL-6 and CCL2. Protein profiling agreed. The authors see promise for gut support products designed for dogs.
pmc-13301422:
An ancient gout drug keeps auditioning for heart duty, and Hui Zhen Lo with colleagues weigh the latest evidence on colchicine for coronary artery disease in a 2026 review. They walk through the major trials, from LoDoCo2 and COLCOT to CONVINCE and CLEAR-SYNERGY, plus recent meta-analyses, asking whether damping inflammation prevents repeat events.

Early trials flattered the drug, and guidelines warmed to it as a cheap partner to cholesterol lowering. Newer results cooled that enthusiasm, suggesting the benefit is smaller or narrower than first hoped. The authors keep the door open, calling for sharper trials that pin down which patients gain enough to outweigh side effects and drug clashes.
pmc-13302722:
A rising temperature on day one, not the reading at the door, forecasts stroke recovery, Crhistian-Mario Oblitas and colleagues show in a 2026 registry study. Records of 5,883 patients, most with ischemic stroke and the rest hemorrhagic, supplied admission temperature, the first-day peak, and the climb between them. Outcomes were judged at three months, with paracetamol given above 36.5 degrees.

Admission temperature said nothing about later function. A climb during the first twenty-four hours multiplied the risk of a poor outcome roughly tenfold after ischemic stroke and sevenfold after hemorrhage. That first-day rise also best predicted who would respond to fever treatment, making it the marker the authors recommend watching.
pmc-13305222:
Shuang Xue and co-authors review how flavonoids, common plant compounds, steer the cell recycling system called autophagy in a 2026 narrative synthesis. That recycling keeps cells balanced, yet too much or too little feeds many diseases.

Five years of experiments were gathered across artery disease, heart and liver illness, lung problems, Parkinson's disease, blood cancer, and solid tumors. Flavonoids adjusted recycling and selective recycling paths with good safety in early work. Poor absorption in the body remains the main block to clinic use. Better formulas and solid human trials are needed next.
pmc-13305322:
F. E. M. in 't Hout and colleagues report a 2026 case where leukemia after kidney transplant shared one origin in both donor and recipient. Transplant patients face raised cancer risk, but cancers almost always start in the patient's own cells.

A 55-year-old man developed acute myeloid leukemia five years after receiving a kidney from an unrelated living donor. The cancer cells carried a female chromosome pattern matching the donor, plus a hallmark gene swap. The donor had developed the same leukemia four years before him. Shared markers prove that leukemia-starting cells passed with the donated organ.
pmc-13306322:
Khadija Manhou checked a crop simulator against salty watering of winter wheat in Morocco's Tadla Plain in a 2026 study. The AquaCrop model was tuned on the 2023 season for the Achtar variety, then tested against 2022 field records.

Tracks covered leaf canopy, water use, soil moisture, plant mass and grain yield under salt stress. Tuning matched canopy closely, with error below 1% on average in reported figures, and mass and yield errors stayed low as well. Separate-year checks also followed water patterns well, supporting use of the model for irrigation choices where fresh water runs short.
pmc-13306522: A 2026 retraction notice withdraws a 2013 study of a Polyalthia longifolia leaf extract and its safety and DNA protection claims. Publisher John Wiley & Sons agreed the move after figure problems went beyond an earlier correction. Overlapping panels appear under differing conditions, and other panels resemble figures in a separate paper. The notice is brief and gives no new scientific results, so the withdrawn findings should no longer be relied upon.
pmc-13307822:
Faten A AlRadini and co-authors survey in 2026 why Saudi women do or do not take the HPV vaccine and cervical smear tests, using a health belief frame. Their online survey drew 1334 women from all regions of the country, aged 16 to 65 years.

Only 6 percent had taken at least one vaccine dose, and only 21 percent had ever had a smear test in this group. Lack of trust and fear of side effects led the reasons for refusal among those who said no. Women who felt at risk, saw clear benefit, or had a smear test were more prone to accept the shot. Doubt and felt barriers pulled the other way.
pmc-13308622:
Achilles Bergne and co-authors find in 2026 a giant strain response in thin films of hafnium zirconium oxide, a chip friendly material used in memory devices. Past a field of 24 kilovolts per centimetre, the film flips between plain and polar forms and stretches far past its normal range.

Strain passed 10,000 picometres per volt when a steady bias held the film near the flip point in their tests. Big squeeze effects, soft crystal frames, and shape shifts team up to drive the outsized move, not simple charge flips alone. Light, probe, and model checks all backed that view. Tunable strain could serve tiny motors, sensors, and shape shifting surfaces built on silicon.
pmc-13308922:
Monika Bapna and Sarah B Corley report in 2026 a case of inflammatory linear verrucous epidermal nevus of the vulva. The growth forms a rare itchy line, starts in youth, and is often misread by clinics. Their patient, a woman in her mid fifties, had decades of itch, burn, and pain on the right outer lip since her teens.

Creams for psoriasis and rubbed skin gave only brief relief, and biopsies over the years pointed each way in turn. A long, one sided, drug proof plaque should raise this call, the authors urge clinics to recall. Fractional carbon dioxide laser care brought real gain where creams had failed for years on end.
pmc-13309022:
Waira Mona and co-authors present in 2026 HoloBio, a free Python tool with a point and click face for holographic microscopy of living samples. Such imaging gives label free measures of cell shape, mass, and motion, yet shared, easy software has lagged the optics for years.

Two modes split live work at video pace from later work on saved holograms in the tool as built. It fits lens and lens free rigs in many layouts, and it packs cell tracking, phase maps, thickness gauges, and counts. No coding skill is needed to run the full flow in the lab. Shared rules should help labs match results across sites and studies.
pmc-13310222:
Chad Yanyatan and co-authors test two multi-ingredient supplements against aging slowdown in worms in a 2026 study. Slowing age decline means guarding healthy years, not only adding years. Human trials of such products take years and huge cohorts, so the tiny worm C. elegans offers a fast first screen.

Two commercial blends of vitamins, minerals, plant extracts, and related compounds were fed to worms, and movement was filmed over life with an imaging tool. Worms on the first blend kept moving faster with age than worms on the second blend or plain solvent in the reported runs. Gene activity shifts accompanied the movement gap. The authors treat mobility as a healthspan signal worth following into deeper study.
pmc-13310722:
Kieran Smith tested strong salt water injections in sleeping horses in a 2026 safety study. Doctors use chest scans that track air and blood flow, and salt water can sharpen the blood signal. Whether the method is safe in horses was unknown, so the team tried repeated doses under anesthesia.

Six adult horses were put to sleep twice and got salt doses every 15 minutes for an hour. Chest readings fell as hoped, but blood pressure dropped and heart rate rose in many checks. Blood salt levels also climbed, and breathing patterns changed at times. Caution is needed before routine use in horses.
pmc-13310922:
Sandhya Subash and co-editors open a 2026 collection on predicting and managing drug drug interactions. When drugs are taken together, one can change how the body handles another, which risks failure or harm. Risk grows with many drugs, new targets, and care in high risk units such as intensive care and cancer wards.

Twelve pieces span body based models, marker guided methods, drug level checks, transporter biology, gene effects, and smart computing. One study used level checks to pair two strong drugs safely despite a known clash. Real world proof and human guided smart tools mark the new path for safer combined care.
pmc-13311022:
Chongyang Zhao and co-authors set out a plan to audit how evidence networks mix study types in a 2026 protocol paper. Network meta analysis joins direct and indirect proof across many treatments. Mixing randomized trials with non randomized studies without care for design gaps can skew effects and rankings.

The planned study will hunt published networks from 2020 to 2025 that mixed both types. Each main analysis will be sorted into four classes, from hidden naive pooling to clean design aware work. Rates will be tracked over time and by field traits. Paired results will show how often effects flip or rankings shift when design is handled well.
pmc-13311122:
Hanan Awad Hassan Ali and colleagues classify motor states from implanted brain recorders in Parkinson disease in a 2026 study. Adaptive brain stimulation needs exact reads of ON, OFF, and sleep states. New implants record brain waves at home for weeks, yet home value was unproven, so sensor, diary, and brain data were fused.

A first test used three patients over about 30 days of records, then a wider set used thirteen patients. A neural network on time and frequency traits scored best, with strong marks on diary based labels in both sets. Wearable sensor labels scored lower but still well. Home brain records can support state aware care.
pmc-13311622:
Mei Xue, Yu Wan, and Fei Wang present a 2026 survey of parents in Changzhou, China, on what they know and do about brain development in children born a few weeks early. These children face higher risk of learning problems.

The survey covered 499 parents whose children, born at 32 to under 37 weeks, were now of preschool age. Average knowledge scores reached only 7.22 out of 18, while attitude and practice scores sat mid-range in this group. Knowledge tracked with both attitude and practice, and modeling showed knowledge feeding practice directly and through attitude. The gaps point to where parent teaching could help most.
pmc-13311822:
Emily Beckerman and colleagues, in 2026, present a feeding trial on spirulina algae in broiler chicken diets and its effect on growth and meat quality. The algae is rich in protein and pigments.

A total of 270 Ross 708 chicks were raised in 18 pens on diets with no spirulina or with 2.5 or 5 percent, across starter, grower, and finisher phases. Growth, feed intake, and feed efficiency did not differ clearly among diets. Gut microbe balance shifted toward fiber-fermenting and probiotic-linked kinds. Meat measures mostly held steady, though skin and meat yellowness rose. Spirulina looks safe as a partial feed swap.
pmc-13311922:
Zhizheng Li and colleagues present their 2026 study on how far cone-beam CT placement of impacted lower wisdom teeth drifts from the true position found at surgery. Errors of a few millimeters matter near nerves.

For ten deep cases, printed surgical guides marked the crown edges predicted by scans, and gaps to the real crown were measured in surgery. Sixty more cases gave a horizontal measure only. Real crowns sat forward and lower than scans showed, with mean shifts near five millimeters. Deeper impactions drifted more. Surgeons should leave extra margin when planning cuts in the back jaw.
pmc-13312022:
Chenyao Li and fellow students present a 2026 interview with Pengxin Liu, a ShanghaiTech professor who is also a science influencer with more than 1.6 million followers on Weibo. The piece began as a student project to introduce Liu's second identity to undergraduates at their residential college.

Liu describes starting his account in 2019 while a postdoc at ETH Zurich, first explaining skincare ingredients and later hand and surface hygiene during the pandemic. He argues that basics matter more to the public than advanced topics, and that fighting misinformation means joining public debate and even policy work. The conversation also covers the skills and payoffs of public science education and its cross-disciplinary nature.
pmc-13312522:
Shamsul Qumar and co-authors present a 2026 global genomic analysis of Campylobacter jejuni, a leading cause of bacterial food poisoning for which poultry is a major reservoir. Heavy antibiotic use in livestock has bred multidrug-resistant strains, so the team compared genomes from human and chicken hosts in a One Health frame linking animal and human risk.

The analysis covered 1,125 high-quality genomes, including five newly sequenced chicken isolates, and sorted their genes into 4,489 clusters with a conserved core of 1,360. Family trees split into three big clades with little regard for geography; human strains appeared everywhere, while chicken strains concentrated in one clade, hinting at host adaptation. All five new isolates resisted several drugs. Across the set, 31 known resistance genes turned up, underlining the scale of the resistance problem.
pmc-13313022:
Julian Link and colleagues probe, in a 2026 study, how the length of a small carbon spacer steers the self-assembly of short peptides into ordered materials. Such peptides are prized building blocks because they are easy to make and program. How a tether between the peptide and a sticky aromatic cap trades flexibility against directional bonding had not been isolated as a variable.

The team attached a naphthalene block to isoleucine-cysteine-alanine tripeptides through spacers of six, three, or zero methylene units and watched assembly with spectroscopy and microscopy. The longest spacer consistently aggregated most strongly, the middle one less so, and the rigid zero-length version never formed ordered nanostructures at all. The authors conclude that spacer length is a powerful dial for tuning peptide assembly, balancing how freely molecules can move against how precisely they can lock together.
pmc-13314422:
Jianping Zhang and co-workers report a 2026 case of a rare lymphoma paired with kidney amyloid disease. Waldenström macroglobulinemia is a slow B-cell lymphoma marked by marrow spread and a lone IgM protein in blood, and kidney AL amyloidosis is an uncommon partner that is hard to treat.

Their patient was a 71-year-old woman with 10 months of leg swelling and growing fatigue. Tests showed the lone IgM protein with lambda light chain, nephrotic syndrome, mild anemia, and swollen groin lymph nodes. Marrow and node samples proved the lymphoma, blood tests found the MYD88 L265P mutation, and a kidney biopsy showed Congo red-positive amyloid deposits with lambda limits in the filters and walls. The report pairs the case with a review of past cases to guide doctors facing this rare blend.
pmc-13315722:
Cheng Wang and Rongze Fan present FedSynHAR in 2026, a light federated learning system for recognizing human activity from wearable data without sharing raw records. Private data stay on each device, yet uneven data across users, differing local models, and tight computing and bandwidth limits on edge hardware make joint training hard.

Their design prunes networks by gradient importance on both server and client sides, cutting cost, and uses channel-guided mutual teaching between local and proxy models to repair pruning losses. Tests on the UCI-HAR and PAMAP2 datasets showed faster convergence and solid accuracy under uneven data splits.
pmc-13316222:
Yan Chen and a large team used duckweed in 2026 to recover phosphorus from wastewater while growing useful biomass. The plant Spirodela polyrhiza was grown in simulated wastewater at varied phosphorus levels under mixed feeding conditions, tracking removal, growth responses, and what the harvest could become.

Top total phosphorus removal reached 93.78 percent at a level of 17 milligrams per liter in the reported tests. Under low phosphorus the plants stored starch up to 214 milligrams per gram of dry weight, while richer levels pushed protein and lipid making. Mineral-rich biomass could serve as feed, fuel stock, or fertilizer.
pmc-13316622:
Shokooh Karimi and fellow researchers review, in a 2026 article, pyroptosis as a fresh drug target in glioblastoma, the most aggressive common brain tumor in adults. Standard care leans on triggering apoptosis, a quiet cell death that many of these tumors resist.

Pyroptosis is a loud, inflammatory death driven by gasdermin proteins, and evidence links forcing it with slower tumor growth. The review maps the pathways that switch it on, lists drugs and compounds that tune it, and covers the role of small regulatory RNAs. Much remains unclear about exact wiring, the authors note. Still, aiming therapy at this death route could give patients options when older treatments fail.
pmc-13317222:
Kulapat Chulsomlee and colleagues ran a 2026 randomized trial comparing two steroid routes for pain after total knee replacement: a shot around the joint with triamcinolone versus hydrocortisone into a vein. Good pain control speeds thigh strength recovery, the engine of walking again.

Fifty-nine patients split between the two routes and were tracked for six months. By day three, the joint-shot group had lost far less thigh strength and bent the knee further. Their stand and walk tests also slowed less, while blood inflammation markers ran lower on days one and three and at week two. Benefits faded later, but the early edge matters most for rehab momentum. Local delivery, they conclude, wins the first crucial days.
pmc-13318722:
Ting Luo and co-authors give a 2026 narrative review of digital health tools for muscle loss in dialysis patients. People on maintenance haemodialysis often develop sarcopenia, with weak muscles and poor function. Wearables, phone apps, and remote platforms might help monitor and treat it. Evidence, though, is uneven across tools.

Activity monitors, apps, and remote follow-up look ready for supportive use. Continuous biosensors and some AI prediction systems remain at proof-of-concept stage. The review weighs potential effects, limits, and future directions for each type. It highlights dialysis-specific data, such as weight gain between sessions and activity on dialysis days. The authors call for multicentre studies and head-to-head comparisons before wide adoption.
pmc-13319022:
Ali Deniz Erkmen and Sedat Akgöl present a 2026 retrospective observational study of surgery choices in endometrial cancer. Surgery is the cornerstone of treatment, usually removing the uterus and ovaries. Approaches range from open surgery to laparoscopy and a vaginal endoscopic route called V-NOTES. The study compares who receives each approach and their tumour features.

In routine practice, allocation is far from random. Open surgery tends to go to patients with advanced, high-grade, or node-suspected disease. Minimally invasive routes suit earlier, lower-risk cases. Sentinel node staging increasingly pairs with the newer approaches. The authors set out the perioperative and pathological characteristics behind these choices. Their aim is fairer interpretation of outcome comparisons in a field where selection shapes results.
pmc-13321022:
Ariany T.A.S. Denofre and colleagues write a 2026 letter and case series on hidradenitis suppurativa affecting the breast. The skin disease can scar and deform breast tissue and harm women's quality of life. A 2021 scheme named four breast patterns, but it misses some sites, such as armpit to breast and nipple area disease, and surgery is not standardised.

The team reviewed 108 patients, 68 women and 40 men, followed at a university hospital clinic from 2018 to 2022. They set out to count and describe breast involvement, widen the pattern scheme, and separate look-alike conditions such as granulomatous mastitis with the help of ultrasound. Clearer sorting should guide kinder, better planned surgery.
pmc-13321222:
Jordan G. Okie and a large team study three centuries of invention in a 2026 article. Covering breakthroughs from 1690 to 1990, the team asks what traits of inventors, teams, and settings fostered major innovation. Their broad, evidence based approach sorts inventions by maker, place, category, and era.

Most breakthroughs came from one or a few creative people in supportive settings, though teams and institutions grew more central over time. Innovation hubs differed by field, with rural areas strong in home and farm tools, cities in transport and communication, and institutions in weapons and medicine. Chance and opportunity, more than lone genius, emerge as the mother of invention in their telling.

pmc-13323122:
Ricardo Jorquera-Gutierrez, Pedro R Gil-Monte and Pedro Gil-LaOrden model burnout among Chilean education workers in a 2026 survey study. Hongjuan Wang and co-authors compare fungi in root-zone soil and bulk soil of Masson pine plantations, in a 2026 field study from a subtropical conifer setting. pmc-13323922:
Xiaoge An, Tingting Wu, Rong Gou and Yudong Fang review CAR-T cell therapy for age-related disease, in a 2026 article. Cell senescence sits at the core of ageing, driving many late-life diseases and feeding chronic inflammation through the secretions of senescent cells.

pmc-13325122:
Winyoo Sangthong and Jakkapan Sirijaraensre compute how zeolite swaps change a carbon dioxide conversion reaction in a 2026 chemistry study. The reaction joins CO2 with small epoxides over gold-bearing zeolites, and catalyst acidity is the lever.

pmc-13325422:
Zongliang Xu and co-authors review PRDM1, a gene switch that shuts other genes down, in a 2026 article. The protein guides B and T cell growth, steadies immune balance, and can hold back tumors.

pmc-13329222:
Jiayi Yu writes a 2026 letter to the editor about a trial of pain control for spine fusion surgery. The trial compared plain ropivacaine with ropivacaine plus dexmedetomidine or morphine, placed into back muscles. Yu praises the clinical question but raises two method points for readers to weigh.

Yu asks how many patients started the infusion and how long it ran. pmc-13329522:
Mustafa Ansari and colleagues review how menopause affects overuse injury and stress fracture risk in a 2026 article. Falling oestrogen harms bone, tendon repair, and muscle, but the review argues that load, joint stability, and social factors matter too. Bone loss can reach 2 percent to 5 percent per year in early menopause, as summarised in the review.

Strength training, diet support, and bone scans remain little used, most of all in marginalised groups. pmc-13329822:
Jiayi Chen and colleagues track nutrition decline during radiotherapy for oesophageal cancer in a 2026 prospective study. Sleep was probed by interview, a standard index, and wearable devices.

Baseline sleep trouble and advanced nodal stage each linked to higher odds of decline in the main model. The team built a phone prototype, the Esophageal Care Companion, with risk-aware prompts for each treatment phase.
pmc-13333522:
Xue Li and collaborators ask in a systematic review and meta-analysis from 2026 whether lupus raises a patient's odds of glaucoma. About a third of people with systemic lupus erythematosus develop eye involvement. pmc-13334122:
Jun Mo Kim and co-authors reported a 2026 case of a toddler whose cheekbone was reshaped by a small cyst near the eye. Epidermoid cysts are common congenital lumps around children's eyes, but their effect on growing bone is less familiar.

The patient was a 26-month-old girl with a periorbital epidermoid cyst pressing on the frontal process of the zygoma. Imaging showed a tidy cystic lesion with smooth indentation of the bone surface and no signs of aggressive disease. Surgeons removed the cyst completely through a lateral brow incision while preserving the periosteum, and pathology confirmed the diagnosis. At follow-up the cheek contour restored itself without grafts, thanks to the bone-forming power of young periosteum. The report also reviews how to tell pressure remodeling from true bone lesions.
pmc-13337822:
Kathrin A. Gurke Brücksken leads a 2026 lab study of largazole in triple-negative breast cancer. Largazole blocks histone deacetylases and may also curb Musashi proteins that support tumor stem traits. The team asked whether it weakens cancer cells and makes radiation work better.

DNA break markers and colony tests measured response after radiation, pointing to a possible pairing for resistant disease.
pmc-13339022:
Pauline B. M. Hendrickx, Anne des Rieux, and Maartje M. C. Bastings coat DNA origami with lipids to deliver gene-silencing RNA in a 2026 study. Folded DNA carriers are precise but degrade fast, enter cells poorly, and escape poorly once inside. A fat coating adds cell-like behavior.

Tunable coating keeps DNA design freedom while adding delivery strength, a useful blend for RNA medicine.
pmc-13339122: Lijing Wang issued a 2026 correction. It covers only Table 2 of a study on vitamin D and long cycles in polycystic ovary syndrome. The model fit values were wrong as printed. pmc-13339622:
Henry Cardwell and a large team study aziridine, a small nitrogen ring, with intense light and heat in a 2026 experiment. Ionization energy and breakdown paths matter for chemistry in harsh settings. Measurements used coincidence spectroscopy at the Swiss Light Source.

pmc-13339822:
Sheng Li and colleagues report a changed operation for stubborn repeat brain surface bleeding in a 2026 case series. Organized chronic subdural hematoma returns often after simple drainage, mostly in older patients. Their method combined open removal, artery blocking, and muscle grafting.

Function scores improved across four scales after surgery as reported. Problems hit five patients, at 29.41 percent in the reported share, including fluid pockets. Early results support the combined approach for organized repeat cases.
pmc-13340422:
Flexible supercapacitors built from MXene nanosheets are paired with rat safety testing in a 2026 study led by Tanveer Ali. The device, pairing Ti3C2Tx MXene with activated carbon, reached an areal capacitance of 66.43 mF cm–2 and kept 95% of it after 5000 charge and discharge cycles.

pmc-13341422:
A transcription factor driving corneal aging under high sugar is identified by Sujun Zhou and Hong Zhang in a 2026 study of diabetic eye disease. Diabetic keratopathy brings slow corneal healing and repeated surface defects, with few good treatments available.

pmc-13341622:
Operating the virtual warehouse may matter more than its content load, in a 2026 study by Yen-Ting Chiang's team. Their immersive VR game trains Taiwanese technical high school students to spot warehouse hazards safely, and 167 learners supplied data for structural modeling.

pmc-13345822:
Moteeb Alhamidani interviews first-year medical students about how their way of learning science is changing in a 2026 qualitative study. Several tried to map links across lectures, work they found rewarding but heavy. Most also changed study habits, self-testing more after old methods fell short. Students, Alhamidani concludes, can describe their own learning change with surprising nuance. Its staying power stays unknown.
pmc-13347222:
Aogan and colleagues project how climate change will shift habitat for four Stipa grasses across Central Asia, in a modelling study from 2026. These grasses dominate steppe lands and feed livestock. pmc-13347922:
Tameshnie Deane traces a long path for people with albinism. Her review study came out in 2026. It runs from exclusion toward global rights advocacy. pmc-13348022:

pmc-13348422:

pmc-13350022:

pmc-13351922:

pmc-13352522:

pmc-13360222:

pmc-13361522:

pmc-13362322:

pmc-13363822:

pmc-13364322:

pmc-13365422:

pmc-13374822:

pmc-13379722:
Magdalena Skrodzka and co-authors study the social side of recovery after the September 2024 flood in Poland, testing a model of how shared trauma changes identity. pmc-13380522:

pmc-13382022:

pmc-13383422:

pmc-13383922:
