pmc-13385522:
Siyu Ji, Nan Zhang, and Xin Hu review how heart disease may feed back to worsen cancer in a 2026 article. The concept, called reverse cardio-oncology, reverses the familiar harm that cancer drugs do to the heart. Evidence from population, animal, and cell studies suggests heart conditions reshape the tumor's surroundings.

Candidate routes include stress hormone activation, poor oxygen delivery, inactivity, and factors shed by diseased heart tissue. Signals like VEGF, vesicles, and inflammatory messengers may jointly aid vessel growth, immune suppression, and spread. The authors urge human tissue studies and heart-cancer chip models to test these still-provisional links.
pmc-13386822:
Elliot J. Lefkowitz and co-authors report a 2024 workshop on classifying viruses below the species level in a 2026 article. Four United States bodies, spanning bioinformatics, public health, and allergy research, co-hosted the April meeting at NIAID. Experts in virology, computing, and public health debated clades, genotypes, and lineages.

Talks covered real-time tracking of virus change, fair naming systems, and systems like Pango lineages for respiratory viruses. Timely lineage data can speed vaccine updates, speakers stressed, but names must avoid stigma. The report urges shared tools that join genetic data with traits like severity and immune escape.
pmc-13387122:
Arvin Bozorg Chenani, Ramadan Ahmed, and Sarath Vayolipoyil present a severe leg clot emergency in a 2026 case report. A 55-year-old man arrived with four hours of sudden swelling, pain, and numbness in his left leg. The limb was tense, blue, and hugely swollen, with pulses fading during examination.

Blood tests showed inflammation and a markedly raised clot marker, and ultrasound found extensive vein blockage. Wider imaging traced clot from the leg veins into the vena cava, plus clots in the lungs. The condition, phlegmasia cerulea dolens, threatens the limb itself, so fast recognition drives the report's message.
pmc-13387622:
Patricia Valiente-Rodriguez and colleagues report cytomegalovirus disease hiding behind prematurity problems in a newborn in a 2026 case report. The girl was born at 26 weeks weighing 800 grams, with lung and brain findings each blamed on early birth. The window to confirm congenital infection closed at 21 days without testing.

At 70 days she developed severe pneumonia needing high-frequency ventilation, with no bacterial cause found. Lung washings carried very high virus levels while blood levels ran far lower, a split the authors stress. Testing also revealed a combined immune deficiency, and antiviral therapy steadily lowered the viral load.
pmc-13390522:
Ye Tan and co-authors re-analyse, in 2026, public data on whether gene-silencing chemical marks suppress brain-related long RNAs in glioblastoma. Glioblastoma, an aggressive brain tumour, varies greatly in its epigenetic pattern, and earlier studies of these long noncoding RNAs started from broad tumour-wide screens.

Starting instead from RNAs enriched in brain, the team matched tumour gene activity with promoter methylation in the main discovery set, where 52 patients had both data types. Candidates had to show a strong negative link between methylation and expression, then faced checks in three outside datasets. Neuro-oncology readers gain a focused shortlist of silenced brain RNAs that may merit laboratory follow-up.
pmc-13391122:
Abdulrahman M Alharbi and co-authors review, in 2026, the pattern and triggers of diabetic ketoacidosis at a specialist hospital in Buraidah, Saudi Arabia. This acute diabetes complication drives admissions and heavy resource use, and local trigger patterns differ between health systems.

Records of 193 patients admitted from 2023 to 2025 were examined for demographic, clinical, and biochemical features, the event that precipitated each episode, and links between triggers, severity, and time to resolution. Diabetes teams in the region gain a local evidence base for prevention, such as sick-day education or infection pathways, rather than relying on trigger rankings imported from other countries.
pmc-13391222:
Lifang Hu and colleagues examine, in 2026, why bone-forming cells stop multiplying when mechanical loading is removed, as in bed rest or spaceflight. Loss of load is a main cause of a form of osteoporosis, yet the molecular brake on osteoblast growth was unclear.

The team focused on CDK12, a kinase that helps switch on gene transcription through RNA polymerase II. By silencing and overproducing CDK12 in osteoblasts, they test whether it carries the unloading signal that slows cell division. Bone biologists gain a candidate pathway linking a physical cue, loss of load, to the transcription machinery, which could eventually suggest drug targets for disuse bone loss.
pmc-13391722:
Katelyn McKindles leads a 2026 genomic portrait of a fungal parasite that infects bloom-forming algae in Lake Erie. Chytrid fungi are key parasites of aquatic microbes, yet algal-infecting forms are understudied and genomic resources for them remain scarce.

Many strains of the fungus were picked from Sandusky Bay across two bloom years. Each strain lives only on one host alga. Gene reads from single cells built a genome for each strain, plus one shared pool for all. This is the first such set for its group. Lake scientists gain gene-level insight into a fungus that may help shape toxic blooms in fresh water.
pmc-13393422:
Hisae Mogi and six colleagues found that the amino acid methionine doubles as a signal telling the bacterium Shewanella oneidensis whether to invest in breathing without oxygen. This microbe is famous for pushing electrons onto metals outside its cells, a trick useful in fuel cells. A transcription factor called MetR, long known for running methionine production, turned out to hold the switch.

When methionine runs scarce, the cell ramps up its own methionine factories while MetR represses the electron transfer and anaerobic respiration machinery. When methionine is plentiful, at even modest levels, the repression lifts and electron transfer surges. The same control appeared in a second species, Aeromonas hydrophila. The authors read the logic as budgeting: costly amino acid building outranks respiration gear until supply allows both, a strategy with targets for optimising microbial fuel cells.
pmc-13394422:
Lyu and co-authors test, in 2026, whether the drug GS-9620 can calm psoriasis-like inflammation, working through autophagy, the cell's internal recycling system. Psoriasis affects about 2 percent of people and involves skin cells multiplying too fast under immune attack. The team treated mice with imiquimod-induced psoriatic skin using GS-9620 or the standard drug methotrexate, and applied it to inflamed human skin cells in culture.

GS-9620 reduced redness, scaling, and epidermal thickening in the mice, and lowered inflammatory cytokines including IL-1-beta, IL-6, and TNF-alpha in skin and blood. Spleen levels of IL-17A-producing T cells, a key psoriasis driver, fell after treatment. The drug restored the autophagy proteins ATG5, ATG12, and ATG16L1 while suppressing the NLRP3 inflammasome, a molecular alarm that releases IL-1-beta. Because blocking autophagy undid the benefit in cell experiments, the authors credit enhanced recycling for the anti-inflammatory effect.
pmc-13394722:
Shiyong Li and co-authors map, in 2026, how fluids carry waste out of the mouse brain along arteries. Spaces around brain arteries feed tissue and clear waste, but the driving force was unclear. Live imaging showed solutes moving both ways in these spaces, paced by the pulse of the artery wall. Fluid bulk flow did not explain the motion.

Waste from brain tissue drained into the network and rode pulses toward small vessels and veins. Tying off a neck artery slowed pulses and left more amyloid stuck in the spaces. The authors call the pulse a pump for brain cleaning. Failure of that pump may add to disease.
pmc-13395322:
Simone Toffoli and co-authors use, in 2026, a smart pen to read how Italian schoolchildren write by hand. More than 700 pupils, from first grade to early middle school, wrote two standard tasks on paper with a sensor pen. The pen logged time, force, smoothness, tilt, and rhythm as they wrote. Those signals were set against standard clinical scores.

Pen signals tracked the clinical scores well, above all for time measures. Growth curves from the pen matched known handwriting learning paths, with many skills levelling off by third grade. Computer models split strugglers from fluent writers with success. The authors say the pen could flag trouble early in class. Quick flags mean faster referral for help.
pmc-13396322:
Amir Sharafkhaneh and colleagues reply to a letter questioning their finding of higher death rates in people with narcolepsy that is not type 1, in a 2026 exchange. The critics asked whether mixed diagnoses or hidden factors, rather than the sleep disorder itself, explain the gap.

The authors explain that their comparison group, labelled other narcolepsy, was meant to be broad, covering type 2, unspecified cases, and possibly some look-alike sleepiness conditions, as real clinic records allow. To limit miscoding they required at least two diagnosis codes spaced 30 to 390 days apart. They accept the limits of record-based grouping while defending the approach.
pmc-13396722:
Yiru Huang and co-authors scanned the resting brains of teenagers and adults whose eyes do not align, to separate the brain effects of the misalignment itself from those of a lazy eye. Their 2026 cross-sectional study compares 17 people with comitant strabismus and 19 with strabismic amblyopia, where one eye's vision has faded from disuse.

A measure called fALFF reads the strength of slow, spontaneous brain fluctuations while a person lies still, with a correction that strips out bodily noise. Group averages differed in age by only a few years around the mid-twenties. The comparison isolates what amblyopia adds on top of the shared eye alignment problem, which guides how each condition is treated.
pmc-13397522:
Sumun Khetpal and fellow authors test whether small drains placed after nose-reshaping bone cuts cut down bruising and swelling. Their 2026 study covers patients of one senior surgeon who had primary rhinoplasty with osteotomies, the controlled bone breaks that narrow the nose. Those cuts tear small vessels and stir inflammation, leaving many patients black-eyed for days.

The senior author added drains right after the bone work to draw off fluid before it could settle in the tissues. Charts of patients with and without drains were compared for how much bruising and puffiness followed. The idea sits alongside older tricks such as steroids and blood-pressure care, and the results help surgeons judge whether the extra step earns its place.
pmc-13398522:
Dafa Zhou and colleagues uncover who keeps a fruit fly's guardian protein alive. Their 2026 study centres on Diap1, which blocks the caspase enzymes that execute programmed cell death. Three death proteins (Rpr, Hid and Grim) attack Diap1 under stress, yet what steadies the guardian in calm times was unknown.

Removing the enzyme Hdac3 switched cell death on, and restoring Diap1 blocked it completely, tying the pair together. Only the copy of Hdac3 sitting in the cytoplasm did the protective work, even against radiation-triggered death. Hdac3 steadies Diap1 by stripping acetyl tags from it, a housekeeping trick whose failure in human cells may feed both degeneration and cancer.
pmc-13399022:
Yang Ding and colleagues check what half-knee replacement does to the kneecap joint it leaves behind. Their 2026 study follows 32 patients (35 knees) after medial fixed-bearing unicompartmental replacement, with an average follow-up of 4.5 years. Whether kneecap joint wear should bar this smaller operation stays controversial, and its effect on stresses across that joint was unmapped.

Knee scores, pain scales and a battery of X-ray angles were compared from before to after surgery. A finite element model then computed how stress spreads across the patellofemoral joint once the medial compartment is replaced. Pairing lived outcomes with virtual mechanics should tell surgeons which worn kneecaps tolerate the partial fix.
pmc-13399122:
Fang and co-authors unravel, in 2026, how the protective protein CREBRF gets destroyed in diabetic kidney disease, worsening stress inside kidney tubule cells. CREBRF normally restrains endoplasmic reticulum stress, the protein-folding overload that injures tubules under high glucose. Working in HK-2 tubule cells exposed to high glucose and in streptozotocin-diabetic mice, injected at 50 milligrams per kilogram, they traced CREBRF's regulation upward.

CREBRF was downregulated in the disease models, and restoring it calmed endoplasmic reticulum stress and reduced tubule injury. The acetylation enzyme NAA10 tags CREBRF with an acetyl group, and that tag invites the ubiquitin ligase BTRC to mark CREBRF for degradation, a disposal signal. Blocking the chain preserved CREBRF and its protection. Diabetic status in the mice was confirmed at blood glucose of 250 milligrams per deciliter or higher. The authors name the NAA10-BTRC-CREBRF axis as a candidate intervention point in diabetic kidney disease.
pmc-13399522:
Devadharshini B and colleagues randomized recreational sprinters with kneecap pain to compare two rehabilitation styles, reporting in 2026. Patellofemoral pain, aching around or behind the kneecap, sidelines many runners. One group received dynamic proprioceptive training, exercises that challenge balance and joint position sense. The other followed a conventional strengthening program.

Sixty sprinters with pain in one knee took part, thirty per group, training under supervision three times a week for twelve weeks, with assessors blinded to group assignment. Both groups improved significantly on pain, balance, and hopping measures by the trial's end. The proprioceptive group, though, gained more where it counted. At twelve weeks its pain scores beat the strengthening group by about one point on the numeric rating scale, its Y-balance reach by 5.73 centimeters, and its single-hop distance by roughly 36 millimeters, as the between-group differences show. The authors suggest adding sensorimotor work to standard rehabilitation.
pmc-13400222:
Nivedita Mitta and colleagues describe rescuing aneurysm repairs gone subtly wrong at the groin, in a 2026 series on closure-device failure after percutaneous EVAR. Among 751 consecutive percutaneous repairs at one tertiary center from 2018 to 2023, closure malfunction occurred in 66 cases. Ten patients, twelve limbs, had this flow-limiting luminal pattern with controllable bleeding and were fixed from inside.

Device choice followed the lesion: bare stents for dissection flaps without bleeding, covered stents where the wall was injured or leaking contrast. Technical success was universal. At a median follow-up of 2.5 years, imaging showed 100 percent primary patency, with no clinically significant restenosis or occlusion in any treated limb. Where the lesion is focal and the artery otherwise intact, though, an immediate catheter-based bailout through existing access restores flow and spares a tired patient a groin exploration.
pmc-13400322:
Nadine Ben Romdhane and colleagues survey, in 2026, skin cancer awareness and sun habits among surfers in California. Surfing means long hours of strong sun on skin, a known risk for skin cancer. Earlier work came mostly from Australia, so the team asked United States surfers directly.

Five hundred complete replies, from surfers with a mean age near 30 years, were analyzed. Nineteen percent said a biopsy had confirmed skin cancer, most often on the head and neck. Rates rose sharply with age and were higher in fair skin types. No cases appeared in the darkest skin group. The letter urges better sun protection and skin checks for regular surfers.
pmc-13400422:
Ali Houmani and a large group review, in 2026, cholesterol crystals in the brain and their possible part in Alzheimer disease. The brain is rich in cholesterol, most of it made locally. When cholesterol forms sharp crystals, it can spark inflammation in nearby tissue.

The authors cite crystal examples in brains of people with Alzheimer disease. They also trace crystals freed when artery plaques rupture: carried to the brain, these can block flow, inflame vessel walls and trigger strokes or brief attacks. Statins and aspirin can dissolve crystals and have helped prevent such events. Preventing crystal formation, or clearing crystals early, may therefore lower brain injury, though human proof remains thin.
pmc-13400622:
Kahona Zushi and a large team report, in 2026, that a sulfur compound can upgrade a muscle stem cell activator called HGF. With aging, a reactive nitrogen chemical marks HGF on fast muscle fibers, weakening its grip on its receptor and slowing muscle repair. Protecting that grip could help preserve muscle.

Treating HGF with lipoic acid trisulfide more than doubled its receptor binding, even beyond the unmarked protein. The same treatment shielded the protein from the aging mark, especially at one vulnerable site. Two related antioxidant controls gave no such benefit, pointing to a distinct mechanism. Given to mice before a muscle disuse model, the compound prevented the harmful marking seen in untreated animals.
pmc-13400922:
Makarim Elfadil M Osman and co-authors trace, in 2026, the evolution of terpene synthase genes in coffee, the family that builds aroma-related terpene compounds. Coffea arabica is a hybrid species formed from two diploid parents, so its gene family carries a double inheritance. How that family expanded and diversified was the question.

Genome searches found 69 family genes in arabica, against 40 and 55 in its two parent species. Tandem duplication, where copies arise side by side, drove most expansion, and arabica mostly kept parental copies under strong purifying selection. Gene activity data across tissues showed many copies active with specific patterns, some shared between duplicates and some diverging, linking evolution to regulation.
pmc-13402322:
Juan Tang and co-authors describe a light-powered route that converts furans into pyridazines by editing the ring skeleton itself, with no outside photocatalyst added. Skeletal editing, swapping atoms inside a molecule frame, lets chemists scan new structures fast during drug lead work. Here a hydrogen-bonded complex between the furan and hexafluoroisopropanol absorbs the light and does the activating.

Once excited, the complex wakes oxygen from the air, and the reactive oxygen species formed crack the furan ring open into a two-ended dicarbonyl chain. Hydrazine then closes that chain into the pyridazine, a ring prized in medicines. The method covered a broad range of starting furans, tolerated complex and drug-derived pieces, and moved into continuous flow with better speed and scale. Mechanistic and computing studies back the picture of how the editing proceeds.
pmc-13402422:
Naghizadeh and co-authors sort, in 2026, the population of Iran's Azar cohort into lifestyle subgroups and relate them to hypertension, using latent class analysis on 15,006 eligible participants followed across five periods. Seven behavioral indicators defined the classes: smoking, substance abuse, alcohol use, secondhand smoke exposure, sleep quality, physical activity, and obesity. Model selection supported three classes for women and seven for men.

Among women, 65.3 percent fell into a class defined by secondhand smoke exposure and poor sleep quality, 25.7 percent were low risk, and 9 percent high risk in the classification. Among men, 13.3 percent landed in a smoker class and 3.6 percent in the high-risk class across the seven groups. After adjusting for age and socioeconomic status, hypertension prevalence and incidence climbed steadily from healthier to riskier classes in both sexes. The authors recommend aiming interventions at clustered risks, especially inactivity, poor sleep, and obesity, in the highest-risk subgroups.
pmc-13402722:
Dan Han and colleagues turn three years of messy hospital infection records from a Chinese district hospital into a clean, public dataset built for artificial intelligence research. Raw surveillance files from the 1100-bed hospital drifted in format month to month, mixed Chinese free text, and buried risk factors inside long strings. Their Python pipeline standardizes schemas, translates terms with a checked bilingual dictionary, splits risk strings into 19 flags, and strips identities under k-anonymity rules.

The result holds 1240 infection episodes and 57 variables, openly deposited under a CC-BY license with a full codebook. Completeness topped 95 percent for 54 variables, and risk splitting matched human experts closely. Three starter classifiers predicted drug resistance patterns with accuracy scores from 0.74 to 0.82, proving the data carry learnable signal. Code is shared so other hospitals can copy the cleaning act.
pmc-13403022:
Sindhura Kasturi and colleagues report a 14-year-old girl diagnosed with primary biliary cholangitis. It is an autoimmune liver disease that destroys the small bile ducts inside the liver and almost never appears in children. The disease creeps toward fibrosis and cirrhosis and is a staple of adult hepatology. Pediatric cases are so few that each one recalibrates what clinicians consider possible.

She presented with raised liver enzymes, a quiet opening that in a teenager could point at many passing causes. Workup instead landed on this rare cholestatic disease, marked by bile stasis and the threat of liver failure over time. The authors publish the case to raise awareness. Persistent enzyme elevation in an adolescent deserves the full adult differential, including primary biliary cholangitis, before years of silent duct loss accumulate.
pmc-13403722:
Chang Yuan and a large team fed a snail sugar chain to farmed crayfish in 2026 to see if it could lift growth and immune strength. The blue crayfish is prized in Chinese farming for fast growth and good size. Groups got five feed levels of the snail compound over 60 days.

Fed crayfish ended longer and heavier than the plain-feed group. Their main digestive gland showed less damage, and germ-fighting plus calming functions rose. Gene reads found 957 changed genes, with 14 named as key candidates. Pathways for fat handling and cell cleanup stood out. The compound looks fit for use as a health feed add-in.
pmc-13405022:
Minju Lee and Mi Yu survey nurses in a South Korean tertiary hospital about violence from patients and families, in 2026 work. Such violence interrupts care and strains staff, yet its links to care quality are seldom modelled together. Two hundred nurses giving direct care answered the survey in autumn 2024.

Verbal abuse was the most common form, averaging 2.58 on a five-point scale in the reported results. More violence tracked with more work interruptions and higher burnout, and with lower rated quality of nursing care. Path analysis tested whether interruptions and burnout carry part of the harm to care quality. The authors argue that protecting nurses is also a patient safety measure.
pmc-13405122:
Rehab Mahmoud Abd El-Baky and co-authors package the antibiotic metronidazole inside sugar rings to fight a urinary bacterium, in 2026 work. Proteus mirabilis causes catheter-linked urine infections and infection stones, and often resists drugs. Improving an old drug's solubility is one route around resistance.

Three cyclodextrin hosts were mixed or kneaded with the drug, and the products were checked with heat and infrared methods. Two hosts improved how fast the drug dissolved, and one cut the amount needed to stop bacterial growth four-fold in the reported tests. At lower doses the packages also curbed bacterial swimming, urease activity and biofilm growth. The approach targets virulence as well as growth.
pmc-13405922:
Gyu Bin Lee and co-authors measure thigh muscle activity during a balance test in runners with unstable ankles, in a 2026 preliminary study. Thirty-two novice recreational runners took part, half with chronic ankle instability and half healthy. Reach distance alone may miss how muscles organise the task.

Electrodes on four thigh muscles recorded activity during the modified Star Excursion Balance Test, with the forward reach as the main task. Groups did not differ significantly on performance or muscle activation in the reported analysis. Within the unstable group, the affected leg reached less far before correction for multiple testing, but that gap faded after adjustment. Knee bend reach and composite scores complete the picture.
pmc-13406822:
You Zhang and co-authors, in 2026, tackle a testing problem from aircraft engineering: how to press on an engine pylon from many directions at once, accurately, without adding unwanted twisting forces. Fixed test rigs cannot reproduce real flight loads well enough.

The team designed a six-leg parallel loading mechanism and improved the search for its best geometry with an optimisation method borrowed from biology. Variables that matter most get searched harder, guided by sensitivity estimates, while weaker ones keep wider freedom. Simulations cut computing time from about 30 hours to 3 hours while improving workspace, stiffness, and load capacity. A built prototype held force errors under 0.64 percent across 240 loaded positions.
pmc-13407322:
Yanfei Huang and co-authors, in 2026, compared a small river fish at four stretches of China's Xiangjiang River that differ in how heavily chain dams regulate flow. Using ear-stone microstructure to read age and growth in 920 fish, they charted body size, reproduction, and egg traits from above the dams to the river's lower reaches.

Fish grew slowest in the heavily regulated Hengyang stretch, at 0.099 per year against 0.23 above the dams, and produced far fewer eggs there, though eggs were larger. The lowest stretch paired poorer growth with many small eggs, while a tributary-fed middle stretch partly recovered growth. The authors advise spacing and siting future dams with such life-history trade-offs in mind, since tributaries and estuary habitat softened the damage.
pmc-13408922:
Mohamed Aboelatta and a multisite Mayo Clinic team report in 2026 how tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy performs once it leaves clinical trials and enters routine care for metastatic melanoma. The treatment grows a patient's own tumour-hunting T cells in bulk and returns them with high-dose interleukin-2, a combination with real cardiac risks. Records covered delivery, responses, immune recovery, and heart monitoring.

Responses were meaningful, including some complete clearances, though patients whose melanoma had reached the brain fared worse. Recovery of CD4 T cells lagged for months after treatment, a practical warning for infection vigilance. Heart monitoring with a sensitive troponin blood test during interleukin-2 infusion may flag patients at low risk of serious cardiac events, which may simplify who needs the closest watching. The study supplies the delivery and safety detail that trial papers rarely include.
pmc-13409322:
Stefano Masi and co-authors re-pool the gold-standard trials in 2026 of two venerable blood pressure drug families in patients at high cardiovascular risk who do not have heart failure. Seventeen double-blind, placebo-controlled trials covering nearly eighty-eight thousand people were combined, nine testing ACE inhibitors and eight testing angiotensin receptor blockers. Whether the two families truly share one effect was itself put to the test.

Against placebo, ACE inhibitors cut cardiovascular death, overall death, and heart attack rates by meaningful margins. The receptor blockers, in the portion reported, did not show the same pattern of benefit. Event rates in the placebo groups of the two trial sets were comparable. The contrast is not an artefact of sicker controls. The authors' analysis challenges the comfortable assumption that the families are interchangeable in this population.
pmc-13410922:
Thomas Graves and co-authors study in 2026 why immigrants in the United States skip medicines they need. Skipping doses over cost wastes treatment and raises later health bills. National survey data from 2019 to 2022 covered adults born abroad, weighted to stand for over 53 million people.

Just over half had taken some medicine in the past year. Immigrants on medicines were far more likely to hold United States citizenship than those taking none. Newcomers in the country under five years delayed care over cost much more often than longer-settled peers. The five-year mark matters in law too, since permanent residents often wait that long for Medicaid, which may explain part of the gap.
pmc-13412122:
Sevil Okan, Fatih Okan, and Murat Beyhan look back in 2026 at what hospital records can foretell about breathing after COVID-19. Their retrospective study covered 101 patients who had been hospitalized with the infection and returned at least two months after discharge. Lung function tests, a six-minute walk, chest scans, and admission blood work were compared across severity groups.

Patients who had severe or critical illness arrived with higher inflammation markers and stayed longer in hospital. Intensive care patients walked shorter distances and more often showed restrictive lung patterns at follow-up. Disease severity scores and scan grades alone, however, did not predict later function. The authors point to inflammatory burden and critical illness as the stronger warning signs.
pmc-13416122:
Kyong T. Fam leads a large team showing that blocking a bacterial wall remodeling enzyme restores vancomycin's power against resistant Enterococcus faecium, in 2026. The enzyme, SagA, snips peptidoglycan, the mesh forming the bacterial wall. Cutting its gene stunted wall repair and growth in the drug proof germ.

New bond forming blockers, the first for this enzyme family, gave the same softening effect in dishes. Vancomycin worked better across distinct patient strains once SagA was shut down, and the effect held in live infection models too. Wall hydrolases join the list of druggable helpers that could rescue old antibiotics.
pmc-13416622:
George D. Dimitriadis and Vaia Lambadiari argue for GLP-1 receptor drugs as add-ons to insulin in type 1 diabetes, in a 2026 commentary. Most people with type 1 diabetes miss glucose targets despite better insulins and devices, facing low blood sugar, weight gain, and heart plus kidney risk. Excess glucagon and growing insulin resistance feed the problem.

GLP-1 drugs cut glucagon, slow stomach emptying, aid weight loss, and improve insulin sensitivity. A two year Danish registry study of off label semaglutide in 879 users found hemoglobin A1c down by about half a percentage point in six months. Insulin prescriptions fell by about eight percent.
pmc-13417222:
Cristian-Olimpiu Martonos and colleagues describe the tiny ear bones of dog fetuses late in pregnancy, in a 2026 anatomy study. At 55 to 56 days, the middle ear already holds the hammer, anvil, and stirrup bones found in adult mammals. Specimens were examined by dissection, tissue slices, and careful measurement.

The hammer bone was largest, the stirrup smallest and triangular. All three were still partly cartilage and actively turning to bone, with hollow spaces and remodelling cells visible. Bone hardening had begun in the stirrup legs and base plate. The basic pattern is set before birth, the authors conclude, while maturation continues afterward.
pmc-13417722:
Shukla and colleagues report a 2026 review of harm reports tied to tracheobronchial stents, tubes that hold windpipes open. They gathered United States device reports from 2014 through 2023. They sorted 525 reports by the reason for the stent and the kind of problem that followed.

Airway narrowing was the most common reason for placement, followed by cancer pressing on the airway. The most common problem was failure of the stent to open as intended, about three in ten of the 768 events logged. Patient injuries were far fewer: 94 were recorded, led by airway blockage or collapse, with six deaths in total. Stents placed for floppy, weak airways drew more blockage, lung infection, and intensive care events than other stents. The pattern helps doctors weigh device risk by condition, not just by device.
pmc-13418922:
M. Ryleigh Davis and colleagues use the James Webb Space Telescope to read the makeup of Neptune's small inner moons and dusty rings. Neptune's giant moon Triton was likely captured long ago, an event that may have smashed or rebuilt the small moons near the planet. The team observed the rings plus three moons named Larissa, Galatea, and Proteus.

Their light spectra showed a deep band near 3 micrometers tied to water ice on the moons, weaker in the rings. Frozen carbon dioxide appeared on Proteus alone among the moons studied. Missing ice overtone bands hint that the surfaces are not plain ice but the exposed insides of icy bodies. That reading favors moons rebuilt from wreckage after the capture, carrying their inner material on the outside.
pmc-13420122:
Lei Peng and colleagues pool trial and study data on enhanced recovery programs for neck spine surgery, the bundle of care steps that speed healing after operation. Such programs are spreading in spine work, yet firm proof for this one operation, front-of-neck disc removal with fusion, stayed sparse. The search covered four databases from their start to December 2025 under standard review guidelines.

Across 2330 patients in the pooled set, the programs cut hospital stay and reduced nausea and vomiting after surgery. Safety held steady, and patient satisfaction leaned positive without reaching firm proof. The certainty behind the pooled claims rated moderate to high. Spine units weighing the bundle's setup cost get a grounded case for adoption in this operation.
pmc-13420222:
Pauline Hessenauer and colleagues test whether wood DNA can reveal where a tree grew, a tool for fighting illegal logging and false labels in the timber trade. Their study covers five North American tree species in commerce, with lodgepole pine as the test case. Gene markers drawn from across the genome carry a faint record of place, since local adaptation and drift shape them over generations.

Three marker sets were compared: random picks, markers tied to adaptation, and a set chosen by machine learning. Models then guessed latitude and longitude for each sample, landing between 15 and 383 kilometers from the true origin in mean error across species, by the reported range. Retail products told a rougher story, with most holding at least one false claim. Forest agencies gain a check that works after wood leaves the stump.
pmc-13420322:
Yunyun Huang and colleagues follow older adults in China across a decade to test whether better sleep tracks with better psychological well-being. Their data come from a national longevity survey with four waves in 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018. The study held 2,371 adults aged 65 years and above who took part in every wave.

A growth curve model that bends once over time fit the data best in the authors' comparison. Within that model, improved sleep quality linked strongly to improved well-being across the years. Mental health in old age is a rising public concern in China, and sleep is one of the few drivers families can act on directly. The long follow-up gives the link more weight than a single snapshot could.
pmc-13423322:
Fangran Liu and Paul David Blakeley investigate SF3A3, a splicing protein, as a driver and warning sign in liver hepatocellular carcinoma, the commonest form of liver cancer. The protein helps assemble the machinery that edits RNA messages, yet its role in this cancer had barely been characterised.

Mining cancer genome and tissue atlases, the team found SF3A3 levels higher in tumours than in matched healthy liver, while the gene's promoter carried fewer silencing marks. High levels tracked with advanced stage, higher grade, and TP53 mutation, and patients with high levels survived significantly less long. Levels also rose alongside infiltration by tumour-associated fibroblasts. Pathway analysis linked high expression to receptor signalling sets, supporting SF3A3 as a prognostic marker.
pmc-13424422:
Naohisa Yoshida leads a twelve-author project building an artificial intelligence whose job is to police other AI systems used in colonoscopy, catching their false alarms. Such detection aids flag many harmless spots, and the team trained a vision model on 436,637 images from seventy-eight recorded procedures run on two commercial platforms.

Their model judged whether each platform's flag was real with accuracy above 99% on both systems. It then scored thirteen fresh clinical videos, finding false positives in 8.08% of one platform's flags and 2.47% of the other's. Active learning, where the model requests labels for its hardest cases, sharpened training. The authors offer the checker as a quality manager for clinical AI.
pmc-13424622:
Tohamy reports in 2026 a material made from hibiscus waste that both senses acidity and destroys a common dye pollutant. Synthetic azo dyes such as methyl orange spread through wastewater and resist breakdown.

Removal reached just under four fifths of the dye under acid conditions. Computer modeling traced the speed to a collapse in the energy gap that electrons must cross, which lets charge move almost instantly through the structure.
pmc-13425122:
Rui Qiang Li and colleagues analyzed diet and lung function in adults aged 50 and older in a 2026 study drawing on two large cohorts. Participants numbered 8,640 in the Guangzhou Biobank Cohort Study and 4,029 in the United States NHANES survey, with a mean age near 62 years in the combined description. The exposure was the Composite Dietary Antioxidant Index, a summary of antioxidant intake from food.

Higher index scores were linked with better forced expiratory volume in one second after adjustment in the Guangzhou data. Its percent predicted value rose as well, and NHANES showed a similar pattern for that measure. pmc-13426422:
Wilde and colleagues published a 2026 study on what pushes a fat tumor toward its nastier form. Liposarcoma grows from fat tissue and comes in calm and aggressive forms. Switching PPARG on in aggressive cells made them store fat and slow down. Tumors in mice also grew less when the switch was flipped on. Forcing tumors to mature may become a new treatment angle. Calm and aggressive zones thus look like stages of one disease.
pmc-13427722:
Mohan Julien and colleagues publish, in a 2026 data paper, detailed dive records for young sea turtles in the southwestern Indian Ocean. Juvenile turtles are hard to follow, yet their early years shape whether populations recover. Small open-source loggers tracked green and hawksbill juveniles at four sites, including Réunion Island, Mayotte, and Aldabra Atoll. Between 2021 and 2022 the devices gathered more than 100,000 records from 37 turtles.

Readers can study dive depth, timing, and daily rhythms across sites with different human pressure. The dataset also shows that cheap, open hardware can sustain serious wildlife monitoring. Conservation planners gain rare evidence on a life stage that is often guessed at.
pmc-13428122:
Chavalala, Makhado, and Lebese published a 2026 study on men's health habits in rural Limpopo. Men in the area often delay care until illness grows severe. The project mixed a literature review, field studies, and a planning analysis. Its goal was practical strategies that health services could actually run.

The team built 14 strategies from the merged findings and planning step. Ideas include hiring more male nurses and male community health workers. Male-only sections in clinics and outreach campaigns also made the list. Cutting waiting times and regular staff training appear among the steps. The authors say the plan tackles stigma and wrong beliefs about clinic use. Better uptake, they argue, starts with services shaped around men's daily lives.
pmc-13429022:
Maryam Ghelichli, Gholamreza Roshandel, and Sina Sohrabi map, in a 2026 study, oral cancer cases across Golestan Province in northeastern Iran. Oral cancer ranks among the world's ten most common cancers and kills when caught late. Registry data covered the years 2014 through 2021 for the whole province. Mapping software placed cases by city, and yearly rates were computed per hundred thousand residents.

In total, 390 patients were registered, split almost evenly between men and women, with an average age near 56 years. Yearly standardized rates ranged from about 4 to about 7 cases per hundred thousand. One northern city, Maraveh Tappeh, averaged over 12 per hundred thousand, the province's highest. Rates wobbled over time rather than trending steadily. Health planners can aim screening and prevention at the northern cluster the maps reveal.
pmc-13429122:
Shan Wang and co-authors test, in a 2026 mouse study, a fat-wrapped drug delivery aimed at the energy crisis that follows a stroke. When blood flow returns to starved brain tissue, a second wave of injury strikes. Astrocytes, the brain's support cells, can burn sugar without oxygen and pass the fuel to neurons, if their calcium stays controlled. Treated mice showed less calcium overload in the cortex, stronger sugar-burning activity, more lactate fuel, and less damage in the memory center. Blocking that sugar-burning route erased the protection, proving the mechanism mattered. Dish tests with a calcium blocker drug mirrored the pattern in astrocytes. The study offers a delivery method and a mechanism that future stroke treatments could build on.
pmc-13429222:
Nagihan Aka and colleagues ask, in a 2026 Turkish study, whether wider preventive antibiotics protect earthquake survivors' wounds. After the February 2023 earthquake in southeastern Türkiye, injured survivors were transferred to a major hospital away from the disaster zone. The study covered 83 patients whose wounds were clean on arrival. Wound infections that developed later, and the preventive antibiotic choices behind them, were pulled from records.

Thirteen patients, about 16 percent, developed infections after admission. Infected patients had more often received the broadest preventive antibiotics, the opposite of protection. Needing intensive care was the strongest independent risk factor by far. Antibiotics given before transfer, in contrast, linked to lower infection risk. Three quarters of the germs grown were heavily drug-resistant, led by two notorious hospital species. The authors argue that infection control discipline, not ever-wider drugs, is the weak link in disaster wards.
pmc-13431022:
Xinyu Wu and colleagues show how tiny cell parcels called exosomes can push macrophages, immune eating cells, toward their inflammatory M1 state. The parcels carry an enzyme, METTL3, that tags RNA messages with a chemical mark called m6A, which can change how the message is used.

Macrophages loaded with extra METTL3 showed higher m6A levels and turned on M1 markers and inflammatory signals. Blocking METTL3 flipped the pattern, calming the same markers and signals. The enzyme worked by maturing a small RNA, miR-155-5p, which then drove the inflammatory switch and its alarm pathways. Mouse tests matched the dish results, so Wu names this chain as a target for inflammation and tumour therapy.
pmc-13431322:
Buket Celik and co-authors built a heart patch in 2026 from fine spun fibers. Two added parts lace the fibers: cleaned heart tissue from newborn pigs and helpful compounds left behind by gut germs. Heart attacks leave lasting harm because adult heart tissue regrows poorly. A patch that gives both support and healing signals could help fill that gap.

The germ-derived part fought a hardy drug-proof skin germ, blunted cell harm from harsh chemicals, and calmed swelling signals in lab tests. It also shielded young rat heart cells from such harm and backed tissue reshaping. The finished patch showed even fibers, strength in a useful range, and slow breakdown over a week. Cells stayed alive well on the patch, and the added part kept its active traits after the build.
pmc-13431422:
Yao, Tu, and Cao present a cautionary case in this 2026 report. A young man with psoriasis and refractory Crohn's disease developed hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. In that rare syndrome the immune system spirals into destructive overactivation. His bowel disease had resisted multiple therapies before he started the immune-suppressing drug upadacitinib in 2023.

Even on treatment, his colonoscopies showed suboptimal control, and in November 2024 he arrived at hospital with fever and elevated liver enzymes. Testing revealed herpes simplex virus type 1 as the trigger for the immune storm, on top of years of accumulated immunosuppression. Antiviral drugs and hormone therapy stabilized him, and he was discharged in stable condition. The authors stress that no single drug caused the crisis; the convergence of active Crohn's disease, layered immune suppression, and an acute viral infection did.
pmc-13431522:
Florencia Martino and co-authors measured read-level errors in 2026 for a portable gene reading method used on small round viral genomes. The method first copies round DNA with a rolling method that can add its own noise. Pinning down that noise matters when many kin viruses mix in one sample at uneven depth.

The team spiked a known round phage genome into plasma DNA that held target viruses, at set doses. Custom tools counted swaps, extra bases, and lost bases in each read. Error rates sat near two per hundred bases across four test sets. Full rebuild of the known genome worked once the dose passed a floor level, and joint reads matched the true genome in full at modest depth. Below the floor, recovery turned patchy.
pmc-13432822:
Giuliana Ciappina and co-authors reported in 2026 on giving a built shingles vaccine to cancer patients in the thick of drug care at one Italian hospital. Shingles can stall cancer care, and immune-weak adults earn a firm push to take the shot, yet real-world reads during live care stayed thin. The clinic offered the two-dose course to all solid-tumor patients on body-wide drugs from mid 2022 on.

Forty-two patients took at least one dose, and near nine in ten finished both. Shot-site pain led the side list, while fever and head pain stayed mild and brief. No grave shot-linked harm and no care delays showed. Across near a year of watch, no shingles cases turned up, though the small set caps firm claims. Folding the shot into clinic flow proved workable.
pmc-13433322:
Simone D'Ambrogio and co-authors mined a trained net in 2026 with a formula hunt to pull out a plain rule for how people judge whether a fact is worth fetching. People chase facts about their world, yet the worth math stayed murky. Volunteers weighed options while the team fit nets to their picks.

The plain rule that won leans on the gap in proof between options, not on doubt about each one alone. People seek even proof across picks, the rule says, over shaving doubt one pick at a time. The rule beat stock doubt-based rivals and held on a fresh data set. Deep scans at high field caught five small hubs plus two rim zones. One hub coded worth and pick pull in opposed ways, fit to judge fetch versus choose.
pmc-13434122:
Xiaoyu Hu and co-authors charted the sugar coats of proteins in 2026 across eighteen human organs, the widest such map yet for this common tag kind. The tags steer protein fold, cell greet, and signal roads, yet organ maps stayed patchy. Mass reads on samples from seventy-four people fed the atlas.

The map counts near fifty-eight thousand full sugar builds and a twin count of plain mixes, set on more than seven thousand sites across five thousand proteins. Organs stamp their own tag styles, with cross-talk between two cap kinds in view. Learning models trained on the map can call a sample's organ from its tags. The atlas stands as a base read for sound tag traits per organ.
pmc-13434422:
Scapini, Lattanzi, Brandau, and Cassatella take stock of human neutrophils that calm T cell responses. The review centers on the PMN-MDSC group, studied most in cancer and inflammation. Progress was long held back by two things. There were no exact sorting markers, and very few of these cells float in patients' blood.

The authors set out tests for telling suppressor neutrophils from normal ones. They also note evidence that their roles extend beyond calming.
pmc-13434822:
Yusuf Bayraktar and Zühal Aksakallı Bayraktar test what drives tourist street food joy in Türkiye in 2026. Surveys from 310 tourists feed a model that links urge, involvement, and final experience. Planned behavior ideas were merged into that chain for a fuller test.

Attitudes and the views of others swayed intent to eat street food. Felt control over the choice did not sway intent. That intent then drove both involvement and experience. Involvement carried part of intent into experience, as the chain predicts. Sellers should sell taste and social proof, the data suggest. Ease claims matter less than expected.
pmc-13435222:
Quentin Damiens and coauthors review slow stomach emptying in Parkinson disease in 2026. The gut nerves carry the same clumps seen in the brain, and gut hormones and flora shift as well. A slow stomach makes the main drug, levodopa, absorb in fits and starts.

Erratic uptake feeds the on off swings that plague daily life. Spotting the gut flaw is hard, since signs mimic other gut ills and no scale fits this pairing. A scan of stomach emptying stays the gold test despite flaws. The review weighs domperidone as the lead drug option. Gut marks plus long term data may one day tailor doses.
pmc-13435622:
Michaela Tinggaard and coauthors swab older adults in Denmark for silent pneumococcus carriage from 2019 to 2022 in 2026. Nose and throat swabs plus surveys came from 1,764 adults aged 65 and up. Older adults may act as a hidden store of the germ, the team reasoned.

Carriage showed in 9.8 percent of adults, most often at the throat. Types found spanned sixteen kinds, largely kinds not in the child vaccine. Most types matched kinds that cause invasive disease in this age group. Grandparents of young children carried the germ more often. Wider vaccines for older adults may be needed, the authors argue.
pmc-13437022:
Salcedo-Porras and colleagues test a DNA imaging method on blood cancers where a gene called MECOM is rearranged, a change that marks high risk disease. Standard chromosome banding often misses or muddles these swaps. Their 2026 study runs optical genome mapping, which reads very long DNA strands directly, on 252 samples. The samples are high grade myeloid neoplasms, growths of the marrow's white cell line. Results are compared with banding and probe tests over two years.

Mapping found MECOM swaps in 12 cases. Standard methods caught only six; the rest hid behind normal looking chromosomes, tangled patterns, or failed cell cultures. Mapping also untangled complex swaps and named many partner genes. In five cases the detail changed the diagnosis or risk class, and so could change treatment. Rearrangements of this gene, the authors conclude, are missed often enough that high resolution testing belongs in hard cases.
pmc-13437322:
Longlian Deng and co-authors asked whether removing the main tumor helps patients whose gut or pancreas neuroendocrine cancer has already spread. Their 2026 study used a United States cancer registry covering 2004 to 2023 and found 4,033 patients with distant spread. Of these, 786 had their primary tumor removed, and the team matched 353 pairs of similar patients to compare fairly.

In the matched groups, patients who had surgery lived far longer. Median overall survival reached twenty-six months against eight, and cancer-specific survival showed the same wide gap. Adjusted models put the risk of death at roughly half for the surgery group. Extra checks supported the pattern, and the link looked stronger in patients who never received chemotherapy and in those with smaller tumors. The authors are careful to call this an association from registry records, since doctors choose surgery for patients they judge fit enough.
pmc-13439022:
Fatemeh Haririzadeh Jouriani and colleagues tested whether a cocktail of local probiotic bacteria can switch on the cell-cleaning program that calms gut inflammation. Autophagy, the process by which cells digest damaged parts, is entangled with inflammatory bowel disease. That ordering matters: prevention outperformed rescue. The authors conclude their native strains can influence the autophagy pathway and could serve a preventive role, at least in this dish-based model. pmc-13439722:
Cutts and co-authors argue that Australia needs one national early warning chart for maternity care in this 2026 position paper. They propose a change in the upcoming third edition of the health service standards. The national safety and quality commission should revise its standard on recognizing deteriorating patients. That revision should create one national chart for the whole country: a single Maternity Early Warning System chart. A shared chart would let hospitals compare outcomes, standardize responses to warning signs, and train midwives and doctors on one system wherever they work in the country.
pmc-13440122: Uryu and colleagues, with the Japanese Journal of Clinical Oncology, correct a funding line in their lung cancer study. The study compared survival for patients on public aid and others with EGFR mutant lung cancer. The grant named in print was wrong and has been replaced. The new line names a JSPS KAKENHI grant as the funder. No results, methods, or claims in the study change.
pmc-13440622:
Kim and colleagues ask whether the brain separately stores where objects belong in this 2026 neuroscience study. The models came from similarity judgments about 190 everyday objects. Brain-wave recordings from two datasets then tracked which type the neural signal reflected, moment by moment.

Contextual associations, such as where an object is found, were present in the neural patterns too, but their explanatory power largely overlapped with the conceptual models. pmc-13441722:

pmc-13444322:

The kit may speed hunts for enzymes that turn waste into goods.
pmc-13446222:
Lam and co-authors ask whether getting ahead in money also means getting ahead in health in this 2026 study. Cumulative advantage means early advantages compound over a lifetime. pmc-13446322:

pmc-13446722:

Two tissue-image panels in Figure 2A share an overlapping section, the notice says. Those panels were meant to show different conditions at different hours. Reused source data under mismatched labels would undercut the results shown. The editors have asked the authors to explain and await their reply. Readers are warned to treat the findings with care meanwhile. The journal says its office will keep probing the matter further.
pmc-13447122:

pmc-13447222:

pmc-13448122:
Damm and colleagues report a 2026 study of back surgery outcomes across old age, using Sweden's national spine register. pmc-13450522:
Shujuan Zhou and colleagues ask in 2026 whether some rectal cancer patients can keep the rectum after strong pre-surgery treatment. pmc-13451922:

pmc-13452222:

pmc-13452322:
Dimitris Challoumas and co-authors work out in 2026 how big a gain must be for an elbow swap patient to truly feel it. For pain, the bar came to one point on a ten-point scale, and for a top function score it came to eleven points by one rule and sixteen by the other. Bend arcs had bars in degrees as well. No past study had set the bar for this surgery. The values aim to guide shared choices and trial reads.
pmc-13452822:
Valeriia Ladyhina and five co-authors follow drug resistance genes on ten Swedish pig farms over time, in a country where farm antibiotic use is low. pmc-13453722:
Tian Gui Zhang and nine co-authors report a rare hormone type tumor of the common bile duct that blocked bile flow and yellowed the skin. Surgeons removed the duct and nearby nodes and rebuilt the bile path; she stayed disease free for 24 months. The team also gathered 25 past cases, finding jaundice in 65 percent and pain in 46 percent. Full removal with node clearing was the most common fix.
pmc-13453822:

pmc-13454222:
Waleed Salih Rasheed and six co-authors screen high school students in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq for sexually transmitted infections. The students averaged 16.31 years old, with slightly more girls than boys, and grade ten the largest group.

pmc-13454322:
Hikaru Tamura and five colleagues describe a 2026 physics experiment on coherence, the shared wave behavior of many atoms acting as one. Instead of the soliton trains seen in older work, the team saw phase-coherent density waves shaped by noise growth and shock-like spreading. Over time the order broke down into short patches. Flipping the force back restored broad coherence on its own, which the authors link to defects forming and vanishing. The findings inform theory for unstable quantum systems.
pmc-13455222:

Asian Marsdenia species split into two subclades in their tree.
pmc-13456922:
Kristel G. Soto-Flores and six colleagues report, in a 2026 study, drug-resistant gut bacteria from urine samples at a private laboratory in Lima, Peru. The strains already defeated carbapenems, last-line antibiotics, by making destroying enzymes. The team analyzed 84 such strains of Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli, hunting one gene that disarms the backup drug amikacin.

Thirteen strains carried that gene, and all thirteen proved resistant to amikacin and its cousins. Every carrier also held three more resistance genes, riding together on a plasmid type known for easy sharing. Lab mating tests confirmed the plasmids jump between bacteria, and genome checks showed resistance genes packed beside mobile elements. The authors warn that one shared plasmid can spread a whole resistance bundle through a hospital, and they call for tighter surveillance in clinical settings.
pmc-13457322:
Yasuhiro Ishiyama and colleagues present the design of a randomized trial comparing two surgical robots for colon cancer operations. Their 2026 protocol paper contrasts the da Vinci SP system, which works through a single port, with the established multi-port da Vinci Xi system. Earlier comparisons were retrospective, meaning researchers looked backward at past cases, so this prospective trial at one Japanese center aims for cleaner evidence about whether the single-port approach gentles surgery.

The trial will enroll 200 patients with stage 0 to III colon or rectosigmoid cancer and assign them evenly by chance to one robot or the other. The main measure is patient-reported pain on days one and three after surgery, scored on a standard numeric scale. Secondary measures cover operating variables, complications, inflammation markers, pathology results, and patient satisfaction, giving a broad picture of recovery.
pmc-13458822: 3D-printed titanium cages — their results in surgery reconstruction for infectious spondylodiscitis, in full surveyed. Wentian Li, Akina Li, Gayani Petersingham, and others review the results. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is spinal surgery. It cages infected spines in titanium. Spondylodiscitis, infectious.
pmc-13459022:
Joseph Lee and co-authors audited in 2026 whether large language models can sort emergency department patients by urgency without introducing bias. Triage decides who is seen first, so errors in either direction carry real costs. The team compared several language-model approaches with conventional machine learning, testing how each coped with shifted data and with missing information.

Language models proved hardier than the older methods when conditions changed, and picking similar past cases as examples helped far more than model reasoning did. Careful counterfactual testing then exposed a problem: model choices differed by sex, and those gaps widened within certain racial groups. Finding biases at these intersections, the authors argue, should happen before any hospital deploys such tools.
pmc-13459322:
Tuba Gül and co-authors tested a simple blood ratio as a warning sign for death in hospital after acute stroke. The ratio divides C-reactive protein, an inflammation marker, by albumin, a blood protein that falls during illness. Their 2026 study analyzed 483 adults hospitalized for stroke over one year at their center. It excluded patients whose cancer, autoimmune disease, or liver failure would distort the markers, and asked which admission values predicted dying before discharge on their own.

Patients who died had higher glucose, white cell counts, CRP, and the ratio itself, plus lower hemoglobin, than survivors. In the adjusted model, only the ratio and glucose remained independent predictors of in hospital death. A cutoff ratio of 1.06 identified later deaths with 74 percent sensitivity and 65 percent specificity. The overall discrimination score was 0.774 on the usual curve measure. The authors offer the ratio as a cheap early triage aid.
pmc-13459422:
Su Xinjin and co-authors engineered a two layer glass particle that releases healing metal ions in the right order after spinal cord injury. Recovery unfolds in phases: early inflammation and scarring block repair, while later stages need nerve growth and re-insulation of fibers. Their 2026 study built particles about 125 nanometers wide with a magnesium bearing outer shell over a zinc bearing core. Magnesium releases first and zinc later in that design, and the system was tested in mice with injured spinal cords.

The early magnesium release calmed inflammation by pushing immune macrophages toward their healing M2 state, which also limited scar formation around the injury. Later zinc release then promoted nerve cell growth, axon regrowth, and remyelination, the rebuilding of insulating sheaths. Treated mice showed significant behavioral recovery compared with the injury course described. The authors frame staged ion delivery as a bridge between the inflammatory and regenerative phases.
pmc-13459622:
Jifan Tan and co-authors asked whether preimplantation genetic testing, screening embryos before transfer, raises the chance of a risky twin type when a single embryo splits. The type of concern is monochorionic diamniotic, where identical twins share one placenta. Their 2026 retrospective study reviewed 30,121 single-embryo transfer cycles over ten years, focusing on 251 identical-twin pregnancies after frozen blastocyst transfer, and compared testing cycles against standard IVF and sperm-injection cycles.

Identical twinning occurred in 1.97 percent of transfers overall, with no significant difference between day-three and later embryos. The placenta-sharing type, however, clustered in the genetic-testing group: standard IVF carried an adjusted odds ratio of 0.40 and sperm injection 0.38 for that twin type relative to tested embryos, both significant. Tested cycles were roughly two and a half times as likely to produce the shared-placenta outcome. Complications and newborn outcomes were also compared.
pmc-13460222:
Linjia Zhu, Xiaoqiang Chen, Dong Chun, Qiuyan Lin, and Shaofei Yuan designed in 2026 a layered nanoparticle that first loosens the lung tumor's surroundings and then attacks the cancer cells. Solid tumors grow abnormal vessels and dense collagen, raising internal pressure and blocking drug carriers. Their two-layer particle responds to acidity: the outer layer releases ligustrazine, while the inner core carries triptolide inside a folic acid tagged shell that tumor cells take up readily.

In the acidic tumor setting, the outer agent released first and lowered internal pressure, letting particles penetrate deeper. The inner particles then entered lung cancer cells efficiently and delivered their payload. Cell experiments and characterization supported the staged design. Animal evaluation in thoracic tumor models is the stated next step for this barrier-breaking strategy.
pmc-13460922:
Huzafa Ali and co-authors review in 2026 the growing place of interventional radiology in eye care, where image-guided, minimally invasive procedures are changing how ocular disease is found and treated. Imaging strands include MRI, CT, ultrasound, dye-based vessel studies, and OCT angiography, a noninvasive scan of the eye's tiny vessels that the authors favor over older dye methods for viewing the microcirculation.

Treatment applications range from chemotherapy delivered straight to a tumor's artery, to blocking abnormal vessels, to needle biopsies steered by CT. Precision is extreme in the eye, and the field is limited by equipment access, scarce specialists, and high costs. Artificial intelligence, nanotechnology, simulation training, and virtual reality tools are presented as the next wave for safer, more exact care.
pmc-13461322:
Bandar Salah Almailabi surveyed in 2026 young people held in Saudi social observation centers to test how psychopathic traits, moral disengagement, and cognitive empathy combine in delinquent behavior. His structural model drew on surveys from 171 young people across nine centers. It measured callous traits, the mental excuses that switch off moral brakes, understanding of others' viewpoints, and self-reported offending, all checked with resampling methods.

Stronger such traits meant more moral disengagement and more delinquency, and that switching-off carried a small part of the link between traits and behavior. Empathy pushed the other way: it predicted less delinquency directly and weakened the trait-to-behavior link in teenagers who had more of it. The model explained a little over a third of the spread in offending.
pmc-13461622:
Jun Zhang and colleagues weigh the feed value of four woody plants that dominate desert steppe in Inner Mongolia, in a 2026 field and laboratory study. Grassland there faces winter grazing pressure, so knowing which shrubs truly nourish animals matters for restoring worn pasture. The team sampled plots in Siziwang Banner in late summer. Leaves and stems were tested apart for protein, fat, ash, and fiber.

Leaves beat stems across all four plants, with more protein and less fiber, so testing whole plants hides large gaps. One plant, Krascheninnikovia ceratoides, stood out: its leaves held protein near the level of good legume forage, and it ranked first for leaves and whole plants. A second plant led for stem quality. The weakest plant overall was judged better kept as a living barrier against erosion than as feed. The authors advise favoring the top two plants when reseeding degraded pasture.
pmc-13461822:
Pineda-Sandoval and colleagues surveyed a 2026 study of infidelity among university students in Honduras, linking it to remembered parenting and narcissistic traits. Cheating, meaning seeing someone else without a partner's consent, is common and harmful yet its causes stay unclear. The sample was 399 students at the National Autonomous University of Honduras.

Forty-five percent of men said they had cheated, against twenty-six percent of women in the survey. Among women, no parenting or trait variable predicted infidelity in Pineda-Sandoval's models. Among men, remembered parental warmth linked to less cheating head-on yet to more of it through higher narcissistic traits. Parental rejection also linked to more cheating in men, hinting at paths that differ by sex and need long-term study.
pmc-13462322:
Zilong Wei and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether Raman spectroscopy, a light-based method, can diagnose glioma, the most common brain tumor. Surgeons do better when they remove the tumor, yet its edge blends into healthy brain. Raman readings capture a chemical fingerprint from how laser light scatters off bonds. The team read three glioblastoma cell lines and one brain support cell line.

A sorting method separated all four cell lines cleanly. A machine learning model found spectral bands differing between cancer and normal cells. The same band differences showed up in patient material: tumor samples from three glioblastoma patients against one bruised brain sample from a trauma patient. The authors conclude the approach can tell glioma cells from normal glial cells in lab lines and clinical samples. They frame it as a feasibility step toward tumor checks during surgery, not yet a proven tool.
pmc-13462422:
Lee and Lee develop new statistical estimators for treatment effects in this 2026 methods paper. Estimating an average treatment effect from observational data becomes unstable when some patients were almost certain, or almost certain not, to receive the treatment. Usual fixes trim those patients away, which changes the question being answered. The authors instead propose smooth overlap weights that focus on patients whose treatment status was genuinely uncertain.

They build overlap-weight versions of two standard efficient estimators, including a targeted maximum likelihood estimator, and add machine-learned components. In simulations and real-data studies, the overlap versions showed lower bias and lower error than trimmed versions when all methods targeted the same effect. A cross-fitting step, similar to cross-validation, also improved how the uncertainty of the estimates was calculated.
pmc-13462522:
Huang and co-authors reviewed a 2026 account of the gut after severe trauma, arguing the intestine drives later organ failure rather than merely suffering it. Heavy bleeding and shock starve the gut lining of energy and oxygen. Their interactome concept treats outcome as a dialogue among host immunity, gut microbes, and pathogen strength together.

The review traces how the gut ecosystem slides from balance toward a pathobiome, a disease promoting microbial state, after injury. Huang lists drivers including overactive pattern sensors, loss of protective chemical signals, disturbed bile acids, and treatments that destroy colonisation resistance. Proposed countermeasures range from feeding helpful gut chemicals and prebiotics to acupuncture and multi-target herbal compounds. The authors urge shifting care from killing pathogens toward restoring host and microbe balance.
pmc-13463622:
Jael Miranda and six co-authors study CD45, a protein that tunes how neutrophils cross the gut wall. Neutrophils are first-response white cells that kill germs and start repair. Too much crossing, though, feeds long-term gut diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease.

Blocking CD45 in lab and mouse tests cut neutrophil crossing into the colon sharply. Mice bred to lack CD45 only in neutrophils also healed more slowly after colitis and after small colon wounds. Without CD45, the cells shed less of a key grip protein and lost activity in a partner enzyme. The pathway marks a drug target for calming gut inflammation while aiding repair.
pmc-13463722:
Shi and co-authors reviewed in 2026 what is known about the gut microbiota in polycystic ovary syndrome. The microbiota are the trillions of microbes living in the digestive tract. The syndrome is a hormone disorder affecting roughly one in nine women of reproductive age. The review gathers studies of microbial differences in patients. It also covers the diet and probiotic strategies now being tested against them.

Patients consistently show an imbalanced gut community. Diversity runs lower, and bacteria such as Lachnospira are scarcer. Production of short-chain fatty acids also falls. Those are the helpful chemicals gut bacteria make from fiber. The authors describe a three-way loop linking microbes, insulin resistance, inflammation, and excess male-type hormones. Each problem worsens the others. Mediterranean and ketogenic diets, probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotic products all show early promise. Studies vary widely, though, and large long-term trials are missing.
pmc-13463922:
Johannes Oldenburg and colleagues re-analysed two real-world studies of a long-acting clotting factor used to prevent bleeds in haemophilia A. The treatment, efmoroctocog alfa, replaces the missing factor VIII that people with the disease cannot make.

The analysis covered 333 patients split by age, body mass, disease severity, and past inhibitor history, meaning past immune reactions to treatment. Yearly bleed rates stayed low across nearly all subgroups, with medians between 0.0 and 0.6 bleeds per year. Patients injected about two to 2.3 times per week in every subgroup, with similar weekly factor use overall. Children used slightly more factor per kilogram, and heavier patients slightly less, Oldenburg reports, supporting use across the board.
pmc-13464122:
Michał Chmielewski and six co-authors test self-guided exercise for blood cancer patients in stem cell transplant units. Long stays in protective isolation drain strength and mobility, and supervised rehab is often out of reach. Their program used a simple bedside cycle that patients pedaled on their own.

Patients who cycled kept more of their walking ease and daily function than patients on standard care alone. Losses in strength and stamina ran smaller in the exercise group across the hospital stay. The setup costs little and needs no extra staff time at the bedside. The authors present self-rehab as a practical add-on to transplant care that units can adopt widely.
pmc-13464422:
Abuetabh and colleagues asked in 2026 whether a ketone supplement can protect muscle during semaglutide-driven weight loss. Semaglutide is the blockbuster obesity drug. As much as 45 percent of the weight shed on such drugs can be lean tissue rather than fat. Obese, glucose-intolerant mice were treated for three weeks. One group got the drug alone. Another got the drug plus an oral ketone ester that raises blood ketone levels.

Semaglutide alone shrank lean mass. It weakened strength and endurance. It silenced energy-production genes in muscle and switched on muscle-wasting genes. Adding the ketone ester preserved muscle mass and performance. Fat loss continued undiminished. The supplement also blocked the drug's harmful gene-expression shifts. Muscle loss may partly reflect broken energy machinery and poor ketone use inside muscle fibers. The authors present ketone therapy as a candidate companion for this drug class, pending human trials.
pmc-13465122:
Enas S. Al-Absi and three co-authors benchmark an AI embryo sorter against hand sorting in a zebrafish facility. Labs rear thousands of embryos daily for drug and development studies, and hand counting strains staff and slows work. The machine counted and sorted in one pass across nearly 118,000 embryos.

Hand counting alone still beat the machine on raw speed per minute. The sorter, though, freed staff from the bench and cut strain risk. It undercounted by about thirteen percent and missed roughly half of the glowing embryos used in gene studies. The authors advise the machine for bulk routine work and hands for delicate jobs. Learning from each run should close the gaps over time.
pmc-13466422:
Abdullah Al-Obaidi, Farah Samawi, and Mehmet Halıcı report a laboratory study, published in 2026. It looks for a common yeast in the blood of people with rheumatoid arthritis. This is the autoimmune joint disease. Fifty patients were tested. Fifty healthy controls were tested too. The test sought Candida albicans DNA. A gene amplification method was used. Levels of IL-17A were also measured. IL-17A is an inflammatory messenger.

The yeast's DNA appeared in thirty-eight percent of patients. Only ten percent of controls showed it. IL-17A levels were highest in the DNA-positive patients. A strong statistical link joined the two measures. The authors read this as an association. Fungal presence goes with stronger IL-17 driven inflammation. They stop short of claiming the yeast causes the disease.
pmc-13466522:
Zhu and colleagues reported in 2026 a rare pregnancy emergency: a womb twisted by a giant fibroid late in pregnancy. Uterine torsion, a rotation past 45 degrees, can strangle blood flow to mother and baby alike. The patient carried a large benign muscle tumor, and the fetus lay sideways. Surgeons found the womb rotated over 90 degrees clockwise.

Untwisting by hand failed repeatedly. The fibroid filled the working space and the womb's muscle stayed tightly contracted. The team adapted, partly rotating the womb and cutting into the back wall of its lower segment. A healthy baby was delivered head-first through that incision. The newborn scored a perfect 10 on the Apgar health check at both one and five minutes. The mother recovered without complications and went home on schedule. The authors urge early suspicion when big fibroids meet an abnormal fetal lie, and flexible plans when standard moves fail.
pmc-13467222:
Matthew Turner, Ahmad Fattouh, and Iain Whitaker review how lab growing conditions shape cartilage cells destined for reimplantation into damaged knees, in a 2026 narrative review. Cell therapy takes a patient's own cartilage cells, grows them up, and plants them back into a defect. A core frustration is drift: flat-grown cells stretch out and switch from the round, type-two-collagen-making form to a stringy type-one form.

Physical, chemical, and electrical features of the culture dish all push that drift one way or the other. Osteoarthritis, the end state these therapies fight, is also a leading cause of disability in older adults and in younger people after joint injury. The authors call for standard preparation rules so results can be compared across clinics.
pmc-13467422:
Clemente Maria Iodice and fourteen colleagues published this 2026 review on using a slow-release dexamethasone implant, a steroid pellet in the eye, during surgery for epiretinal membrane. That film wrinkles the retina's centre. Surgery to peel the membrane is standard, but postoperative swelling at the macula, driven by inflammation, often blunts recovery. Following review guidelines, the authors weighed studies of implants given during surgery or later for swelling, covering vision, biomarkers and safety.

Implants sped settling of inflammation and swelling, with retinal thickness improving. Vision benefits were less certain: some trials showed earlier recovery, others no long-term advantage over surgery alone. Side effects were the steroid ones, raised eye pressure manageable with drops and cataract progression. Implanting during the operation looked more useful than implanting later, though delayed treatment helped eyes with swelling. The authors recommend the adjunct for patients at higher risk of inflammation, pending stronger trials.
pmc-13467822:
Biton and colleagues test how the form of feedback from a collaborative robot, or cobot, shapes the human working beside it, in 2026 human-robot interaction research. Workers received auditory signals, visual signals, both together, or none, across two tasks: a turn-taking task with loose teamwork and a shared-control task demanding tight teamwork. The team measured completion time, workers' ratings of comfort and interaction quality, and heart rate variability as a marker of bodily stress.

In the turn-taking task, no feedback gave the shortest completion times but the poorest perceived interaction quality and somewhat higher autonomic activation. Combined sound-and-vision feedback slowed completion yet improved comfort and task understanding. In the high-collaboration task, an extra projected display was layered onto the feedback options.
