Biton concludes the best form depends on teamwork demands: speed, comfort, and bodily calm trade against one another in each task.
pmc-13468322:
Lena Bal and colleagues subject dental filling resins in 2026 to a rough simulated life: stomach acid, then coffee, then cleaning. Ninety-six disks from four flowable resin composites were first measured for surface roughness and color. The samples then soaked in dilute hydrochloric acid for 48 hours to mimic gastric acid, followed by 24 hours in coffee to mimic staining, before being split among three cleaning procedures.

Color change was tracked at each stage with standard difference formulas, separating the damage done by acid and coffee from the recovery cleaning achieved. The four materials differ in filler and resin makeup, which is exactly what the protocol probes: which formulations roughen, stain, and clean up best. Patients with reflux or heavy coffee habits wear their fillings through something like this sequence daily, so the comparison speaks directly to material choice for them.
pmc-13468522:
Jing Lei and co-authors report an imaging study, published in 2026. It predicts recovery after clot-removal treatment in minor stroke. The stroke was caused by a blocked brain artery. Fatty deposits had narrowed the artery. The team examined the small lenticulostriate arteries. These tiny branches may signal good backup blood supply. High-resolution scans were taken before treatment.

The patients were treated between 2020 and 2022. Greater total length of these small arteries predicted a favourable outcome. This held independently of other factors. Mediation analysis indicated the link ran through blood flow. Cerebral blood flow was measured in the same territory. These vessel features could help clinicians judge who benefits most from the procedure.
pmc-13468822:
Haoran You and colleagues built AS-UNet, a lightweight neural network that outlines landslides in ordinary colour satellite and drone photos. Landslides are small, irregular, and easily confused with bare soil, so fast automatic mapping aids disaster response.

Three additions drive the design: strip-shaped attention that follows long thin shapes, a gate filtering which details pass forward, and a custom loss. The loss blends pixel, region, edge, and confidence terms to handle rare landslide pixels and fuzzy borders. On held-out images the model scored 77.82 percent overlap accuracy, running at about 381 frames per second. With only 8.634 million parameters, You presents it as an accurate yet efficient tool for rapid hazard mapping.
pmc-13469422:
Francesco Rundo and co-authors report a small pilot study from 2026 on how people with mild memory problems react to extended reality devices. Twenty one patients with mild cognitive impairment and ten healthy volunteers tried three setups under supervision. One used a touch television, one a room sized projection space, and one a fully enclosing headset, each paired with everyday task content.

Both groups rated all three setups favorably overall. The room projection setup was picked most often for future use, above all by the patient group. The authors stress that device, task, and immersion were bundled together, so no setup can be declared best. They call for balanced follow up studies with proper comfort and sickness measures before clinical use.
pmc-13469722:
Abdulmajeed Alghamdi, Mnassar Alyami, Inad Alqurashi, and Cliff C Zou propose in 2026 a game based defense that hides smart home gadgets from Wi-Fi eavesdroppers. Even encrypted traffic leaks packet sizes and timing, letting an observer fingerprint which device is active. Padding and fake traffic often fail because machine learning spots their artificial timing.

Their defense copies real traffic from a paired device and injects the copy into another device stream. Across nearly two hundred test scenarios, this mimicry cut the best attacker accuracy to about a third, while synthetic cover traffic at the same cost left accuracy above ninety percent. A worked out game strategy held a practical defense near random guessing for four device classes. The authors note that an attacker who learns the pairing can undo the trick.
pmc-13469822:
Yngve Mikkelsen and co-authors run an experimental study in 2026 on why some language models produce weak embeddings for searching clinical documents. A companion study had found that encoders not trained for retrieval performed poorly and their internal geometry nearly collapsed. That work did not show where inside the models the damage starts or whether training domain or training goal is to blame.

The team extracted layer by layer embeddings from thirteen model setups across three clinical text collections, using two query styles. They tracked search quality and geometric measures at every layer, then refit the panel with a per query statistical model. A whitening correction built only from the document collection was tested as a fix that needs no retraining. The study aims to guide model choice for clinical search systems.
pmc-13470622:
Luis J. Herrera and co-authors report in 2026 a phase two trial of a glow guided imaging drug used during lung cancer surgery. Surgeons removing lung tumors can struggle to find small lesions and judge whether cut edges are clear. Patients at six sites received abenacianine, a dye that lights up under near infrared light after homing to enzymes active in tumors, a day or so before their operations.

Of eighty nine treated patients, forty had at least one event the team counted as clinically significant. Imaging found lesions that standard surgical methods missed in thirty three patients. It also uncovered extra hidden cancers in three patients and flagged margins lying close to the tumor in eight. One cancerous lymph node was caught as well. No serious drug related side effects appeared, and the authors call the agent safe and well tolerated.
pmc-13470822:
Ana Beatriz Rosa da Silva and colleagues simulate in 2026 atom thin ribbon devices wired to carbon chain electrodes, asking which design choices govern current flow. Eight junction layouts combined graphene or phagraphene ribbons, the latter mixing five, six, and seven membered rings, with zigzag or armchair edges and two electrode attachment points.

Quantum transport calculations showed the attachment point decided the character of each device. One site gave weak, one way conduction ruled by sharp resonances. The other opened broad, high transmission paths. Ring layout then tuned the strength: a zigzag phagraphene device at the good site carried several times the current of its graphene twin and conducted nearly symmetrically. Edge shape mattered mainly through these combined effects.
pmc-13471322:
Sage E. Hawn and colleagues set out best practices for collecting and handling biological samples in mental health research. Big team studies now measure markers in blood, saliva, and urine across many sites, which raises the stakes for consistency.

Choices made early, such as blood versus saliva or plasma versus serum, shape cost, quality, and what results can mean. The guide urges standard steps for collecting, storing, shipping, and checking samples across all sites and time points. Analyses must also account for technical confounders, the hidden quirks of machines and batches that can fake effects. Hawn frames shared standards as the way team science keeps its larger samples trustworthy and comparable.
pmc-13471522:
Nguyen and co-authors describe a 3-month-old Vietnamese boy whose worsening wheeze turned out to be miliary tuberculosis, a disseminated form of TB that seeds the lungs with tiny nodules. Their 2026 case report follows a baby who failed standard bronchiolitis treatment and had no BCG vaccination scar despite being vaccinated at birth.

Chest CT showed diffuse miliary nodules and swollen, dead-centered lymph nodes squeezing the airway. Standard samples failed: stomach fluid tested negative by both smear and the Xpert molecular assay, and diagnosis came only when a nasopharyngeal swab tested positive for rifampicin-sensitive tuberculosis on the same assay. On a six-month anti-tuberculosis regimen the infant improved rapidly, a lesson the authors aim at clinicians in high-burden settings.
pmc-13471622:
Dare and co-authors evaluated a bottom-up project that let oncology staff in four Québec institutions design fixes for their own working conditions. Their 2026 qualitative evaluation drew on documentary records and one-on-one interviews with 17 workers conducted in early 2023, covering the workshops and the changes that followed.

Fourteen areas of vulnerability surfaced across the units, and six were chosen as targets for intervention. Participation in the diagnostic surveys ran from 53 to 80% of workers in three units but only 31% in the fourth, foreshadowing uneven momentum. Improvements were modest in the short term, the authors concede, yet they argue that genuine frontline involvement during a staffing crisis is itself the lever for durable change.
pmc-13473422:
Cai and colleagues applied a risk analysis method called FMEA in 2026 to cut infection risk in a hospital operating room. A ten-member team listed possible failure points across staff, equipment, materials, methods, environment, and monitoring, then scored each risk and tracked a combined risk priority number monthly.

The team found 49 risk points, ten of them high-risk. After targeted fixes, the risk scores for high-risk items fell by roughly 43 to 79 percent. Cleaning and disinfection of rooms rose from about half of cases done correctly to 85 percent. Correct hand disinfection, hand hygiene, and skin preparation rates all climbed by twenty points or more. One measure, instrument pre-treatment, improved but not significantly. The authors say the scoring system keeps attention on the riskiest steps.
pmc-13473822: Chen and colleagues published a correction in 2026 to their systematic review and meta-analysis of oral microbiota in stroke patients. An affiliation, the School of Nursing at Guizhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine in Guiyang was left out of the published article. The correction adds it as affiliation three for five of the authors and republishes the full corrected author and affiliation list. The original article has been updated; no findings or conclusions change.
pmc-13474122:
Yuqing Zhang and co-authors craft a new material in 2026 for replacement heart valves made from pig tissue. Standard valves are hardened with a chemical that stiffens and calcifies within ten to fifteen years. The team instead linked the tissue with a custom chain-like agent plus glutathione, a natural cell guard. The treated tissue was checked for strength, blood fit, and cell growth.

Implants placed under rat skin drew in healing-type immune cells rather than attack cells. Calcium buildup stayed low, and fresh lining cells grew over the surface more readily. The material also resisted harmful oxygen radicals in lab tests. Longer-lasting valves could spare patients repeat open-heart surgery.
pmc-13474722:
Adetunji and co-authors compared blood magnesium in 83 Nigerian adults with type 2 diabetes against 83 matched non-diabetic controls at a teaching hospital. Their 2026 cross-sectional study also modeled beta-cell function and insulin resistance and screened for kidney damage and peripheral artery disease.

The gap was stark: median magnesium in diabetic patients was 0.40 millimoles per liter versus 0.88 in controls, a difference significant below p 0.001 in the analysis, and every single diabetic participant counted as magnesium-deficient. Levels tracked with beta-cell function at a rho of 0.47 and with fasting insulin at 0.42 across the cohort, yet showed no relationship with blood sugar control itself or with kidney and artery complications. The team reads magnesium as a marker of metabolic dysfunction and argues for routine measurement in diabetes care.
pmc-13474822:
Liang and colleagues tested yeasts taken from cow stomachs in 2026 to see whether native strains can steer rumen fermentation, the microbial breakdown of feed that powers cattle. They grew two Pichia yeast strains from rumen fluid and added each at three doses to lab vessels of rumen contents, alongside untreated controls. The team tracked gas chemistry, protein measures, and which bacteria gained or lost ground during fermentation.

Neither strain changed acidity, yet both cut ammonium nitrogen, a waste product of protein breakdown, by up to 13.3 percent at 24 hours and 22.0 percent by 48 hours in the vessels. One strain, Pichia membranifaciens, raised total volatile fatty acids, the energy products of fermentation, by 15.4 percent and favored fiber-digesting bacteria such as Ruminococcus. Surveys of real herds found both yeasts present but scarce, so the authors propose animal feeding trials next.
pmc-13474922:
De Sciscio and colleagues in Italy charted in 2026, step by step, how one protein building block sours with age in water. The block, asparagine, sheds its side arm in a slow chain of shifts. The souring dulls drug proteins on the shelf, so drug firms must forecast its pace. The team took a two block stand in and paired two watch tools, magnet and light reads, with deep math sims. Each shift in the chain got its own timed count.

Lab counts and sims agreed on all four steps of the chain. A ring shaped half way form sits at the heart of the path, and it forms in two steps, not one. That two step path is the slow gate of the whole souring. The counts also showed why sour or sweet water speeds or slows the chain. The team pitches the map for shelf life tools.
pmc-13478022:
Arshiya Firdaus and coauthors report a 2026 prospective study of follicular output rate as a predictor for in vitro fertilization. The rate compares follicles ready at trigger day with the starting follicle count, capturing how well ovaries responded in that specific cycle. The study enrolled 166 patients treated between October 2023 and January 2025, analyzed separately by polycystic ovary status.

Among 136 patients without polycystic ovary syndrome, higher output rate groups produced more eggs, more mature eggs, and more good-quality embryos. Pregnancy rates rose across the low, medium, and high groups, from about 15 percent to about 37 percent, and live birth rates differed as well. The rate stayed linked to pregnancy after adjustment, though its standalone discrimination was modest. The authors suggest using it alongside hormone and follicle counts for counseling.
pmc-13479422:
Li and colleagues mined single-cell data in 2026 from human carotid artery plaques to find how vessel-lining cells and immune macrophages talk to each other as atherosclerosis builds. They compared calcified plaque cores with matched nearby healthier tissue from the same patients, clustering the cells and mapping which signal pairs switched on or off. Candidate signals were then checked in dish experiments pairing vessel cells with resting or inflammatory macrophages for 24 hours.

The analysis found 15 cell clusters, with six subpopulations closely tied to the disease state in the plaque tissue compared. Three signaling pathways changed most, named MK, GALECTIN, and SPP1, with the MK pathway standing out as the most prominent shift. Its signal pair, MDK binding NCL, rose in the plaque-linked cells, and dish tests confirmed higher levels when vessel cells met inflammatory M1 macrophages than with resting controls.
pmc-13479622:
Kristian Taekker Madsen and coauthors published a 2025 prospective study on whether completing artery-opening treatment, judged by a CT-based blood flow measure, predicts long-term outcomes in stable chest pain. Nine hundred patients with new stable angina and at least one narrowing of thirty percent or more on CT scanning were followed for a median of seven years.

Flow reserve values were computed for every vessel from the CT images. Patients counted as completely revascularized had every flow-limiting vessel treated. The long follow-up lets the authors test whether the early outcome advantage of complete treatment persists, and whether a non-invasive definition can substitute for invasive pressure wires. The multicenter design spans several European heart centers, strengthening the generalizability of any prognostic signal.
pmc-13480122:
Resha Reya Ganthan and colleagues describe a 2026 case of dangerous heart rhythm traced to high-dose methadone. A 56-year-old man on the drug carried a small implanted recorder that logs heart rhythm over months. The device caught three bouts of a fast, twisting rhythm, with one fainting episode lasting over ninety seconds.

Traces showed the classic pause-linked start pattern, with a stretched QT interval on the heart tracing before each bout. Dose cuts proved hard to sustain, so the team fitted a wearable shock vest as a bridge. He later accepted an implanted defibrillator for lasting protection, and the vest period passed with no shocks needed. The case shows the worth of long-term rhythm logging when the trigger drug cannot be safely stopped.
pmc-13481122:
Jolly and a team in Finland scanned in 2026 the brains of 120 five year olds to link build with fluency. Most past work split kids into folk who stutter and folk who speak smooth. This team instead scored each child's speech slips on a scale, from taped chats. They split slips into stutter like ones and plain ones, then set the scores beside grey matter maps from MRI scans.

More stutter like slips went with more grey matter in the front of the brain. Two spots stood out across all their checks: one on the left mid front, one on the right upper front. These zones help plan and watch one's own acts. Plain slips showed no such link, and skin thinness gauges showed none either. Boys slipped more than girls, but the brain link was the same for both. The team urges long term tracking of these kids.
pmc-13481822:
Jeremy Dai and co-authors report a 2026 effort to give meaning to a bladder symptom score used after nerve injury. The score serves people with spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, or spina bifida, yet raw numbers meant little without bands for mild, moderate, and severe. The team mapped the score against three established scales using past datasets, one with 230 patients and a larger one with 1,479 people with cord injury.

Total scores now split into mild, moderate, and severe bands that held up across four study groups in nearly all checks. Patient ratings of their overall bladder problem matched the bands well. For the short form, a gain of about two points marks the smallest change patients are likely to feel. Clinics can now read trial results and daily scores with shared yardsticks.
pmc-13482622:
Soula and colleagues forecast vegetation health in 2026 with a hybrid deep learning model that reads satellite greenness forward in time and across whole landscapes. Their target is NDVI, the satellite index of how green and vigorous plant cover is, an early warning of crop stress. The model chains a bidirectional memory network, reading sequences both ways, with a convolutional network for spatial patterns, fed by weather and soil moisture data.

The pairing is built to catch changes that are sudden or slow, local or widespread, which single-direction models tend to miss in vegetation records like these. In head-to-head tests the authors report their forecaster stayed competitive with the strongest existing NDVI prediction models, matching the state of the art rather than trailing it. They offer it for climate tracking, where foreseeing a greenness fall lets farmers act before stress becomes damage.
pmc-13483422:
Klaassen and colleagues asked whether fluid from the front of the eye can stand in for fluid from the back when tracking advanced diabetic eye disease. Removing back fluid, the vitreous, requires major surgery, while front fluid, the aqueous, is far easier to sample. Their 2026 study measured 92 proteins in paired samples from 41 patients having vitreous surgery for proliferative diabetic retinopathy, where rogue blood vessels scar the retina.

Thirty-two proteins moved together between the two fluids, and a stricter selection narrowed the reliable set to 21 proteins. Three stood out for links to scarring, and two others tracked the spread of the abnormal vessels. Many proteins showed no front-to-back link at all, so substitution works only for the chosen panel. Klaassen offers the shortlist as a basis for safer disease monitoring.
pmc-13483622:
Ellie Jones and co-workers map which quit-smoking methods from past trials might help pregnant women who also have mental illness. In this 2026 review, six databases were searched for trials that had worked in people with mental illness. Each method was coded with a shared list, then checked against the standard quit plan used in pregnancy care in the United Kingdom.

Sixteen trials passed the screen from more than twelve thousand records. Most paired talk support with drug help. Talk that draws out a person's own reasons to quit was the most used style. Of 39 methods found, 26 looked strong. Nearly all strong methods already sit in standard pregnancy care. The gap may lie in how care is given, not in what is on offer.
pmc-13486322:
Watad and Sperling survey how nurses' compassion relates to their ability to bear patient deaths. Their 2026 cross-sectional study covers 256 nurses in internal medicine wards at two Israeli hospitals, where end-of-life encounters are frequent. Validated questionnaires measured compassionate care, self-compassion, compassion fatigue and satisfaction, and how they cope when a patient dies.

Compassionate care correlated positively and substantially with coping with death, explaining about a third of its variation, and also with self-compassion and compassion satisfaction. Its correlation with compassion fatigue ran strongly negative. Self-compassion and satisfaction each predicted better coping, while fatigue predicted worse. Nurses who had taken advanced professional training scored better on nearly every measure, and older, more experienced nurses coped better with less fatigue. The authors suggest training and self-compassion support as levers for sustaining end-of-life care quality.
pmc-13486422:
Takafumi Soejima and Mari Kitao model how family and workplace support carry the effects of cancer symptoms into daily quality of life for young survivors. Published in 2026, the cross-sectional survey gathers 192 Japanese young adults with self-reported cancer diagnoses through an online questionnaire from January 2022. Fatigue, mood, thinking complaints, two kinds of support, and quality of life are measured with standard scales.

Social quality of life scores sat notably below national norms for Japanese adults aged 20 to 39. Most participants were women, about three fifths had undergone surgery, and two thirds held permanent jobs. Equation modeling traces indirect paths from symptoms through support levels into separate quality-of-life domains, with workplace support effects detailed in the full report. Employers and families hold different levers, and young survivors need both pulled deliberately.
pmc-13486722:
Sahebi-Kuzehkanan and team optimized the spinning impeller of a rotary blood pump, the device that keeps blood moving for failing hearts. Designers must raise pressure without shredding blood cells, two goals that pull against each other. Their 2026 study varied fifteen blade and flow-path parameters across 290 simulated designs, checked the simulator against a national benchmark pump, then trained three shortcut models to predict performance without new simulations.

A neural network shortcut proved most trustworthy on unseen designs, while two rivals overfit their training data. The best design raised outlet pressure by about 23 percent over the baseline pump in simulation. It simultaneously cut the average shear stress, the scraping force that damages blood, by about 26 percent. The team also cast a prototype motor stator, the stationary part, from iron oxide material. Sahebi-Kuzehkanan presents the pipeline as a complete route from computer search to hardware.
pmc-13486822:
Hiraoka Masakazu and colleagues tracked the retinas of patients with an inherited blinding disease for two years using an unusually sharp imaging method. The disease, retinitis pigmentosa linked to the EYS gene, kills light-sensing cells slowly, and standard tests notice change late. Their 2026 study at Kobe Eye Center enrolled 50 patients, with 27 eyes suitable for adaptive optics imaging, a technique that corrects optical blur to count individual cone cells.

Cone density fell significantly in every region measured as early as six months into follow-up. A standard scan measure, the ellipsoid zone length, only showed significant shrinkage at the full 24 months. Visual field scores did not change significantly at any point in the two years. Hiraoka argues cone counting could serve trials as an early warning gauge of progression, long before patients notice further vision loss.
pmc-13487222:
Singh and team paired nature-inspired search algorithms in hybrid teams to tune a neural network that diagnoses tomato leaf diseases from photos. Network settings like learning rate strongly sway accuracy, and hand tuning wastes time. Their 2026 study fixed the network's shape and let four hybrid optimizer pairs search the settings, training on more than twenty-one thousand leaf images across ten disease and health classes.

The ant-lion and dragonfly pairing won, reaching about 98 percent accuracy on the held-out test images reported. Two other hybrids finished within a whisker, while the ant-lion and particle-swarm pairing lagged near 95 percent in the same evaluation. Hybrids beat single optimizers on stability and convergence reliability at modest computing cost, according to the authors. Singh argues automated hybrid tuning suits farm advisory tools that must retrain on local disease photos.
pmc-13488222:
Masaki Orihara and colleagues report a 2026 case of septic shock in the operating room that looked like drug allergy. A 72-year-old woman had elective liver surgery under combined general and epidural anesthesia, after earlier bile duct infection had settled with treatment. Right after a reversal drug was given during waking, her blood pressure crashed and her skin flushed red all over, a picture that strongly suggests anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction.

Later tests pointed elsewhere, with a high infection marker, blood cultures growing Klebsiella pneumoniae, normal allergy markers, and negative skin tests for the suspect drugs. She recovered with sepsis treatment and later tolerated the same anesthetic drugs in another operation. The authors remind teams to keep sepsis in mind at extubation.
pmc-13488322:
Ngone Diaw and colleagues run a three-year wastewater surveillance study of norovirus in Senegal in a 2026 analysis covering 2020 to 2023. Norovirus is a highly contagious cause of stomach illness with no vaccine or specific treatment, and Senegal had no routine community monitoring. The team paired wastewater viral loads from multiple collection sites with clinical case data, using statistical and machine learning models to compare timing and spread between two virus groups.

Group GII dominated throughout the period and circulated more persistently than group GI in model estimates. Viral loads differed sharply by site, and wastewater peaks often arrived before rises in reported cases. Reproduction number estimates from wastewater also turned upward earlier. The authors present sewage monitoring as an early warning tool.
pmc-13490022:
Tuna Apuhan and colleagues describe mixed tumor behavior in Lynch syndrome carriers sharing one gene variant in a 2026 case series. Lynch syndrome is inherited faulty DNA repair, usually flagged when tumors show unstable repeat DNA and lost repair proteins on staining. Four patients from three unrelated families carried the same early stop variant in the MSH2 repair gene and developed breast or colorectal cancers, and available tumor tissue was tested both ways.

Only one case showed the classic pattern of lost protein and unstable DNA. Three cases kept normal protein staining, and two were stable on the DNA test in the reported results. The authors suggest partial protein function from a backup start site, plus differing second hits in each tumor. Germline results, tumor traits, and family history must be read together.
pmc-13490622:
Trapala and a team in Mexico tackled in 2026 a drug design puzzle around PTP1B, an enzyme that damps insulin signals and is a target in type 2 diabetes. Four known blockers of the enzyme work in unlike ways, and no one had tested how their mix behaves. The group paired lab enzyme tests with computer docking and motion models of the drugs and the enzyme.

Suramin proved the strongest blocker of the four, and chlorogenic acid by far the weakest. Some pairs worked as a simple sum of their parts, while one pair, suramin plus the drug FC122, fought each other and did worse than hoped. The pattern matched how each drug binds and slows the enzyme, a match the authors call kinetic compatibility. They argue that this match predicts pair results better than binding site maps alone.
pmc-13491522:
Veronica B Maphanga and six colleagues report a 2026 laboratory study of frankincense oil as a possible calming agent. Boswellia carterii resin is used traditionally in East Africa for disorders of the nervous system. The team tested the tree's essential oil, its main compound alpha-pinene, and the compound's two mirror-image forms in zebrafish larvae.

Chemical analysis confirmed alpha-pinene in the oil as a mix of both mirror forms. In behavior tests, the oil calmed larvae at the two higher doses, and alpha-pinene worked at every dose tried. Computer docking suggested the compounds bind the CB2 receptor about as strongly as a known activator of that receptor. The authors note that laboratory confirmation of the receptor link is still needed.
pmc-13491822:
Enoch Aninagyei and five colleagues follow in 2026 people in Ghana's Fanteakwa South District who carry malaria parasites without feeling sick, asking who falls ill next. Silent infections keep transmission alive, yet progression varies mysteriously between neighbors. The team screened 353 residents with rapid tests and sensitive DNA methods, recorded blood group and hemoglobin type, then checked carriers weekly for twenty-eight days.

DNA testing found infection in about half the participants, well above rapid test results, with children and adolescents carrying the most. Over follow-up, thirty-seven percent became test-positive with symptoms brewing, and over two fifths of those converted in the first week alone. Blood groups A and AB converted earliest, group O lagged, and carriers of the sickle trait hemoglobin did not progress at all. The authors back risk targeting based on these traits.
pmc-13493722:
Wang and colleagues present a 2026 review asking whether IL-23 blocking drugs, a class of biologics used for psoriasis and joint disease, can wake up dormant tuberculosis or cause new infections. The concern matters most in Asia-Pacific countries where tuberculosis is common. The team searched eight databases plus grey sources and gathered 58 publications covering 41 separate studies of three such drugs.

Across 33 of 34 psoriasis studies, no dormant infection woke up and no new tuberculosis appeared, even in some patients who had not finished preventive treatment. A single case was reported in one survey, in a patient taking one of the drugs. None of the eight joint-disease studies recorded a case either. The authors conclude the tuberculosis risk with this drug class looks very low, while noting that screening practices varied between studies.
pmc-13493822:
Bhaskar Prince, Prabhat Kumar, and Sunil Kumar Singh tackle in 2026 the energy hole problem that kills wireless sensor networks from the inside out. Sensors near the base station relay everyone else's data, burn out early, and leave a dead zone that severs the network. Their remedy clusters sensors into uneven groups sized by distance, elects cluster heads by leftover energy and position, and sends a mobile collector touring the cluster borders.

Cluster sizes follow the radio's own energy math, so traffic loads balance instead of piling onto the center. Head duties rotate on an energy-aware schedule rather than a fixed clock. Simulations in a standard network tool showed the design using roughly twenty-one percent less energy than comparable published schemes. Extending network life matters anywhere sensors must run unattended for months.
pmc-13495222:
Jiayi Huang and colleagues map, in a 2026 scoping review, automated tools that judge the quality of research evidence for public health choices. Rating evidence by hand is slow and uneven between raters, so software help has been proposed. The team searched ten databases in English and Chinese through early 2025 for studies that built, used, or tested such tools.

Twenty studies qualified, mostly from the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia, and most used observational designs. The reviewers counted twelve distinct tools. About two thirds were open to the public, and over half were built for randomized trials. Half still sat at the trial stage and needed a human watching over them. Reported gains covered speed and consistency, yet proof that results travel to new settings was thin. The authors call for wider testing before health agencies lean on these tools.
pmc-13495322:
Mei Jiang, Tao Huang, Daoyuan Jia, and Ling Huang pool, in a 2026 review and meta-analysis, studies asking whether obesity lowers two ovarian reserve markers in polycystic ovary syndrome. The markers, anti-Müllerian hormone and inhibin B, help judge egg supply and carry weight in diagnosing the syndrome. Whether body weight bends their levels was unclear.

Thirty-eight studies with about fifteen thousand women qualified, all of sound quality. Women with obesity and the syndrome had lower levels of both markers than leaner women with the syndrome, the inhibin gap being the wider one. The hormone gap stood firm under rechecks, while the inhibin result rested on a single study and needs care. The authors urge weight-aware reading of these markers in clinic and call for work on how fat tissue drags them down.
pmc-13495422:
Mutiara Septiani and colleagues report, in a 2026 study, a simpler route to polymethylhydrosiloxane, a silicone oil eyed as a filler for the eye after retinal surgery. The eye's natural gel can fail and let the retina detach, and stand-in oils are needed. Making this oil the usual way takes extra steps, so the team merged two stages into one hydrolysis-condensation of a chlorinated starter.

By tuning time and heat they dialed the oil's thickness from thin to medium, and the best yield beat the earlier reported mark. Light-bending values and added lens power landed inside the range clinics require for such fillers. Chemical fingerprints confirmed the oil kept its key silicon-hydrogen groups and backbone through the shortcut. The authors offer the recipe as a faster path to a candidate eye filler, with medical testing still ahead.
pmc-13495522:
Latif Ullah Khan and colleagues test, in a 2026 plant study, whether melatonin shields oilseed rape from vanadium, a metal that poisons farm soils. The metal stunts growth, dims leaf green, and floods cells with damaging oxygen radicals. Seedlings grew under four setups: plain, melatonin alone, vanadium alone, and both together. The team tracked growth, leaf health, and gene activity.

Vanadium alone shrank the seedlings and raised oxidative damage. Melatonin softened every blow: growth and leaf pigment recovered, defense enzymes worked harder, radicals were cleared faster, and the plants took up less vanadium overall. Gene data pointed to shared control switches for stress defense, leaf protection, and chemical pathways that build protective compounds. The authors propose melatonin sprays as a practical aid for crops on vanadium-tainted land, pending field proof.
pmc-13499122:
Slawomir Wantuch and sixteen colleagues published this 2026 preclinical study of stem cell gene therapy for Pompe disease, an inherited disorder where missing enzyme GAA lets glycogen clog muscle, heart and brain. Enzyme replacement helps but reaches tissues poorly. The team engineered GAA with a peptide tag that targets a strong cell-uptake doorway, then loaded the gene into blood stem cells and transplanted them into mice lacking the enzyme.

The transplanted cells seeded the mice with a lasting supply of the upgraded enzyme. Compared with the natural enzyme version, the tagged enzyme cut glycogen accumulation further in muscle and in brain, tissue the therapy barely reaches. A urinary glycogen marker fell, and the skeletal and cardiac disease features were corrected in the mice. The authors argue the uptake tag gives gene therapy an edge over enzyme replacement and untagged constructs, and they support moving the approach toward clinical testing.
pmc-13499222:
Bin Mu and colleagues report in 2026 a new way to build polymers inside ordered molecular assemblies without needing perfect starting alignment. In classic topochemical polymerisation, building blocks must sit in a crystal at exactly the right distance and angle before linking, a fragile requirement that limits the method. Their design uses fluid columnar liquid crystals with a core-shell layout, where rapid molecular motion lets reactive sites meet briefly and react.

Despite imperfect starting order, conversion of building blocks into polymer ran nearly to completion, and the column shape steered growth into tidy helical chains. Warming could undo the chains and regenerate the starting material completely, a reversible trait they demonstrated in a skin-worn film that hid and revealed fluorescent information near body temperature. The work widens design options for recyclable polymers and wearable devices.
pmc-13501722:
Benhao Ye leads a ten-author team presenting a 2026 review of neutrophilic asthma, a severe form of the disease that shrugs off steroid treatment. Rather than blaming one broken molecule, the review frames steroid resistance as the product of a self-reinforcing conversation among airway cells. Neutrophils, epithelial cells, T helper cells, macrophages, and B cells all feed the problem. Their signals converge on the glucocorticoid receptor, the steroid's target, and progressively disable it.

Therapies that attack single nodes of this network have disappointed, so the authors highlight a shift toward rational combinations that cut several strands at once. They also propose a biomarker-anchored endotyping framework, a way to sort patients by measurable biology so network-targeted treatments reach the right people. Knowledge gaps in how the web forms and persists are mapped as priorities. The piece aims to give clinicians an integrated map of a stubborn asthma subtype.
pmc-13501822:
Tianshen Quan leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 randomized trial comparing two kinds of exercise for children who have both ADHD and developmental dyslexia. Open-skill exercise, here table tennis, demands adaptation to a changing game. Closed-skill exercise, here track and field drills, repeats set movements. Thirty children aged seven to eight and a half were split between the two programmes for twelve weeks of thrice-weekly sessions. Fifteen developing children did the closed-skill programme as a comparison.

Affected children started behind their peers on inhibition, working memory, flexibility, and visual perception tests. After training, both exercise groups improved. Yet the table tennis group improved more across executive measures, including Stroop interference and memory tasks, and across every visual perception outcome after adjustment. The authors present open-skill sport as a drug-free support for this group, while the small sample marks it as early work.
pmc-13502622:
Yang Li, Congcong Jin, and Kang Min Ok report a 2026 crystal result in which hydrogen peroxide, built into a crystal, multiplies its light splitting fourteen-fold. Materials that split polarized light steer it, and the field wants crystals combining a short UV cutoff with splitting power, two traits that usually trade off. Growing 4-hydroxypyridine from peroxide solution yielded a solvate crystal holding one peroxide per molecule. Its cutoff sits at 278 nanometres, in the solar-blind region, and its splitting power reached 0.609 at 546 nanometres.

Structure shows why. In the pure crystal the molecules sit at right angles to one another, cancelling their optical bias. Peroxide hydrogen bonding rearranges the packing into near-parallel rows, so the biases add instead. The peroxide contributes little light bending itself; it acts as a structural director, and the ordered lattice's local field boosts the effect. The team names the approach peroxide-assisted solvate engineering.
pmc-13502922:
Hanan Ibrahim and Zack Hudson write a 2026 ethics analysis of a collision between black-box medical AI and British doctors' legal duty to be candid after harm. AI tools now support NHS triage, diagnosis, and risk scoring, and the best performers are neural networks no clinician can interrogate at the bedside. The authors build their argument on a vignette: a sepsis case misclassified with AI assistance, after which the care team must explain what happened.

Their distinction is between clinical uncertainty, which candour duties already handle, and structural opacity, which destroys traceability of why a recommendation appeared. A clinician who cannot reconstruct the reasoning cannot discharge the statutory Duty of Candour or their professional accountability. The authors argue interpretability should count as a safety requirement in high-risk settings, not an optional extra traded against predictive scores. Deploying opaque systems there carries a presumption of ethical impermissibility.
pmc-13503422:
Nebe, Moll, and Krischel traced in 2026, in a German-language history, the forgotten women pioneers of urology and the long fight for their place in the field. A working group for women urologists, founded at the national society's 2021 congress, revived public debate on visibility. The authors argue the issue is not new: it is bound up with how the specialty formed and who was allowed to join it.

The account reaches back to the 1870s campaigns for women's higher education, when writers claimed schooling as a human right, not a privilege. German universities admitted women only gradually between 1900 and 1909, and hurdles in training and practice lasted far longer. Early women doctors did real scientific work that later accounts overlooked.
pmc-13503722:
Chaoqun Xu and seven co-authors unveil a new converter for moving vast amounts of clean power over long lines, in a 2026 paper. Direct current lines suit this task, yet the first type can fail during switching, and the second type wastes more power and costs more to run.

Their hybrid design mixes both lines of work and adds modes that force or aid switching, which removes the failure risk. A test unit rated at 120 kilovolts and 360 megawatts ran as hoped. The design now serves in two large projects in China, one in Henan and one in Inner Mongolia. The team lays out the switching logic and the full system build in the paper.
pmc-13505022:
Mavis Pearl Kwabla leads a team auditing how well follow-up lab tests are recorded during tuberculosis treatment in Ghana, in a 2026 study. World guidance asks for sputum checks at set points in treatment to confirm the drugs are working. Paper registers at labs, treatment centers, and district offices should agree.

The team linked 773 confirmed cases across three registers in five districts of the Eastern Region. At each check point, from half to nearly all cases lacked a recorded result in at least one register, with the final check the worst kept. Records agreed across registers in more than half of cases. Adults had poorer documentation than children. One district did far better than another, which hints at local practice gaps the authors say managers should close.
pmc-13505122:
Nawar Malhis and Jörg Gsponer present MoRFchibi 2.0, a tool that predicts binding segments inside disordered protein regions, in a 2026 paper. Some protein stretches lack a fixed shape until they grip a partner, folding only on contact. Those segments, called molecular recognition features, are hard to find by experiment.

The new version beat all rival predictors in head-to-head tests, including top entries from three rounds of a public assessment contest. It even topped tools fed with predicted protein structures and large protein language models. Its scores come from an ensemble of small neural models adjusted for how common such segments are in training data. That design keeps each score easy to read and to mix with like tools. The authors aim it at mapping interaction sites across whole proteomes.
pmc-13505622:
Prakash wrote this 2026 commentary on how rice divides labor between two similar enzymes that activate its defense hormone. Jasmonic acid becomes active only when attached to an amino acid, forming JA-Ile, and enzymes called JAR synthetases perform that attachment. The commentary discusses work by Li and colleagues, who used gene editing to knock out rice's three JAR genes one by one and in combination.

One enzyme, JAR1, was switched on when brown planthoppers attacked. It drove defense. JAR2 chiefly controlled spikelet development, the formation of the rice flower structures. Plants lacking both main enzymes had no detectable active hormone at rest and died at the tillering stage, showing the pair also sustain basic growth together. A third enzyme proved weak and contributed little to either growth or defense.
pmc-13507122:
Yingke Wu and colleagues search, in 2026 work, for the best promoter to control Cas9 in homing gene drives tested in fruit flies. Gene drives copy themselves into offspring at high rates and could suppress pest or disease-carrying populations. Too much or badly timed Cas9 activity creates resistant copies and harms body tissues, so promoter choice matters greatly.

The team built thirty-five drive versions with distinct promoters and linked results to single-cell gene activity maps. Strong activity in reproductive cells raised conversion, while excess activity in female germ cells raised embryo resistance. Early germline activity worked best in males. A design placed in the target gene cut harmful body activity. Tight control in time, place, and amount is the goal.
pmc-13507222:
Hong Zhou, Yiyang Qin, Jiahuan Ren, Yan Zhang, and Shangbing Gao present 2026 work on a vision network that spots road damage in messy street photos. Damage ranges from hairline cracks to wide potholes, and thin cracks curve in irregular ways, which defeats single-scale detectors. Their network builds on a fast YOLO detector with new fusion blocks in its backbone and neck.

One block mixes grouped convolutions across scales to catch damage of every size. A second branch set uses snake-shaped convolutions that follow curving cracks, plus a light attention step for merging. Tests on three public road datasets showed a strong balance of accuracy and speed. Cities could survey pavement more cheaply from street imagery.
pmc-13507322:
Heyder and a large team probe a family of orphan receptors, proteins whose natural trigger is unknown, in the ovaries of three fish species. The SREB family has three members in most backboned animals, and fish vary: zebrafish mirror mammals, mummichogs swapped one member, and pufferfish carry all four. In their 2026 study, the team exposes ovary tissue to three compounds that switch these receptors on and reads which genes respond.

Zebrafish ovaries answered most strongly, with gene shifts in energy making pathways and in cell adhesion, how cells stick together. Mummichog ovaries answered weakly, pufferfish lay between, and no species changed its ovary hormone levels after short exposure. The gene networks touched growth, metabolism, nerve, and vessel themes beyond reproduction alone. The authors see both shared and species specific roles for these receptors, a base for work on fertility and fish breeding.
pmc-13507822:
Amit Nampalliwar and five co-authors review attempts to link Ayurvedic body types with modern gene science, in work published in 2026. Ayurveda sorts people by three patterns called Vata, Pitta, and Kapha, known together as Prakriti. A newer field, Ayurgenomics, tries to match those patterns to measurable biology. The review searched work across genetics, gene regulation, proteins, metabolism, and drug response for signs tied to each type.

Studies hint that the three types differ in metabolism, inflammation, immune activity, and how they handle stress and drugs. Diet, lifestyle, aging, and stress may also switch genes on or off in ways that fit each type. The authors caution that cohorts are small, tools vary, and markers are not yet proven. They call for standard measures, long-term studies, and trials before clinics rely on these links.
pmc-13508322:
Zhongmao Fu and seven co-authors build prediction charts for bowel cancer patients whose standard tumor marker test reads normal, in 2026 work. That marker, CEA, misses many cases, leaving a blind spot where cancer can hide among benign bowel disease. The team reviewed 553 marker-negative cancer patients and 200 patients with benign disease. Blood markers, inflammation ratios, and tissue features fed two chart tools. One chart aimed to spot cancer, and the other to forecast survival after diagnosis.

Among screened cancer patients, over three fifths were marker-negative, confirming the blind spot is large. The eight-factor diagnostic chart sorted cancer from benign disease with strong accuracy in both test groups. The survival chart beat the standard staging system at ranking risk in validation data. The authors offer them as aids for spotting missed cancers and tailoring follow-up in this overlooked group.
pmc-13508422:
Yaxi Li and six co-authors compare thin and thick chest drains for treating a collapsed lung, in work published in 2026. A collapsed lung, or pneumothorax, needs the trapped air drained so the lung can expand again. Records split 95 patients by their first tube, 55 thick and 40 thin. The team compared success, drainage time, lung re-expansion, hospital stay, complications, and pain medicine use.

Overall success, drainage time, re-expansion, and stay length were statistically alike between sizes. The thick tube group did need stronger total doses of pain medicine. In the subgroup whose collapse followed lung disease, thin tubes drained faster and re-expanded lungs sooner. The authors treat that edge as promising but in need of proof from a forward-looking trial, and they note pain was judged from drug doses rather than patient scores.
pmc-13508622:
Hope Wilson leads a fifteen-author team asking whether social background shapes how provoked vein clots present and end in American children, in 2026 work. Clots in children can recur and can leave vein damage in a limb, called post-thrombotic syndrome. Adult studies tie lower income and some racial and ethnic groups to worse clot outcomes, yet child trial data were scarce. The team re-analyzed a randomized trial of clot treatment length, keeping the 409 United States participants. Clot features and two-year outcomes were compared by age band and social proxies.

Clot location split clearly by age. Leg clots led in babies and children, while arm clots led in teenagers. Lasting vein damage at two years hit teenagers, at sixty-two percent, against about a third in babies and younger children. The findings point to age-tailored follow-up after childhood clots, with teenagers watched for vein harm.
pmc-13509722:
Kanwarjot Singh and eight co-authors argue that the timing of oxygen given during a sickle cell pain crisis matters more than the amount, in a 2026 review. Sickle cell disease changes hemoglobin so red cells stiffen and block small vessels once they release oxygen. The review pulls together lab work on how stiffening starts, clinical studies of oxygen treatments, and reports on home-based care in lower-resource settings.

Lab evidence shows a short delay before hemoglobin hardens, and that delay shrinks fast as oxygen falls. A small early rise in oxygen can stretch that delay many times over, opening a window of roughly half an hour when a crisis might still be stopped. Care today often waits until low oxygen is measured. The authors urge systems, including community care before hospital arrival, to give oxygen at first symptoms instead.
pmc-13510322:
Vasileios Papadopoulos and five co-authors study a rare hole through the collarbone where a branch of a neck nerve passes, in 2026 work. The group examined 115 dry collarbones of Greek origin, noting how often the hole appeared, its size, and its position, with four observers measuring separately to check agreement. They then pooled past studies in a meta-analysis that kept single-bone rates apart from true body-level counts.

Past reports differ widely in material and counting habits, and many treat left and right sides as if pairing did not matter. The pooled work separates rates per bone, side leanings from paired bones, and directly counted cases where both sides carry the hole. Quality of each source study was graded with a tool made for anatomy research. The authors say cleaners counting will help surgeons and image readers judge how often this variant should be expected.
pmc-13512022:
Mamand and co-authors review the risks and remedies of polypharmacy, taking five or more medicines at once, in older adults. Their 2026 narrative review searches three databases for studies from 2016 to 2026 in people aged 65 and over, synthesising forty primary studies spanning trials and observational work. The focus is practical: deprescribing, team-based care, patient education, and digital prescribing support.

Across settings, polypharmacy was consistently and independently tied to drug interactions, preventable hospital admissions, and functional decline. Pharmacist-led medication reviews and interdisciplinary team interventions produced the strongest improvements among the management strategies examined. The authors also weigh structured tools such as the STOPP and START criteria for flagging inappropriate prescriptions. Their synthesis frames polypharmacy as a system problem, driven by multimorbidity and fragmented prescribing, that responds best to regular structured review rather than one-off clean-outs.
pmc-13512122:
Mengjia Feng, Chaoyue Zhao, Wenbo Li, Zichen Cui, and Jianzeng Guo add a pinch of an organic semiconductor called anthrone to silicone gel, in 2026 work. The aim is stronger insulation for high-voltage modules. The gel seals power devices, yet weak insulation under strong fields and heat limits its use. One blend, with the lowest tested loading, performed best overall.

That blend raised breakdown strength by about a fifth at room temperature and kept most of it at high heat. The voltage where partial discharge starts climbed sharply, while discharge count and size fell. Heat resistance also improved, with the five-percent weight-loss point pushed higher, plus slightly better heat flow and less thermal swelling. The authors credit electron trapping by the additive, which slows the avalanche process behind breakdown. The recipe is pitched as a molecular-level fix for gel dielectrics.
pmc-13514622:
Sun and Luo validated a questionnaire measuring digital maturity, meaning how thoughtfully children handle digital life rather than mere access or familiarity, among Chinese primary school students. Their 2026 study responds to a gap: the concept had barely been tested in children or outside Western settings. A first sample of 434 students, averaging about ten and a half years old, was used to check the inventory's measurement quality.

Sun found the inventory performed satisfactorily in the Chinese context, and digital maturity predicted artificial intelligence literacy uniquely, beyond simply being a digital native raised with technology. A larger combined sample of 1,026 students then sorted into three distinct profiles through latent profile analysis. The profiles were an unbalanced low group, an inconsistent medium group, and a relatively high group. The authors argue schools should track maturity profiles, not just device access, when building children's artificial intelligence readiness.
pmc-13515222:
Ramanathan Kasimanickam, Priunka Bhowmik, and Zhihua Jiang review, in a 2026 article, uterine disease in dairy cows after calving. The weeks after birth bring sweeping hormone, metabolic, and immune shifts while the uterus shrinks back and clears birth debris. Bacteria almost always enter, and healthy cows restore balance through immune defence and tissue repair. When those defences fail, infections such as metritis and endometritis take hold, fertility falls, and losses mount.

Named culprits include Escherichia coli, Trueperella pyogenes, and Fusobacterium necrophorum, which often act together to deepen inflammation and tissue damage. Modern DNA-based tools, from gene sequencing to reading the genes microbes switch on, have reshaped views of this hidden community. The authors stress how microbial succession, hormone recovery, metabolic stress, and immune strength interact across the transition period. Their closing case favours precise tests, microbe-informed treatments, careful antibiotic use, and herd routines that protect reproduction and welfare together.
pmc-13516322:
Jinjin Zhang and four colleagues study liver harm from GenX, a replacement chemical in the PFAS family found in drinking water, in a 2026 mouse study. Adult male mice received GenX by mouth for twelve weeks, some with chlorogenic acid, a plant polyphenol, alongside. Liver cells in dishes were also exposed to graded doses. The team weighed livers, inspected tissue, measured blood fats and enzymes, and profiled gene activity.

GenX enlarged livers, seeded them with tiny fat droplets, drew in inflammatory cells, and drained their sugar stores. A protective antioxidant fell while a damage marker rose, and blood liver enzymes, cholesterol, and triglycerides all climbed. Gene signals centred on the PPAR pathway, which steers fat making, uptake, storage, and burning. Cell-cleaning proteins shifted as well. Chlorogenic acid partly softened several of these changes. Zhang's team links the harm to disturbed fat control, oxidative stress, and inflammation.
pmc-13516522:
Ilyas M Kabdesh, Albert A Rizvanov, and Yana O Mukhamedshina review gene therapy design for Rett syndrome in a 2026 article. The disorder stems from faults in MECP2, a gene whose protein must sit in a narrow dose window: too little or too much both wreck the brain. That sensitivity makes plain gene replacement by virus risky. The review surveys control systems that could keep a replacement gene on a leash.

Options include promoters borrowed from the gene itself, cell-specific switches, and microRNA elements that trim output in the wrong cells. Self-regulating designs let the transgene sense and correct its own level. A bolder route wakes the healthy copy silenced on the second X chromosome, using XIST-based control or direct epigenome editing. CRISPR-based tuning and combined platforms layer these brakes together. The authors judge that safe Rett therapy will need several such layers at once.
pmc-13518822:
Maren Wehrheim and colleagues report a brain study, published in 2026. It covers how the brain reads facial expressions. Rhesus macaque monkeys served as a model of human seeing. The monkeys judged six expressions much as humans do. The team compared their behaviour with artificial neural network models. Recordings from the face-processing area of the brain were also compared.

Broadly trained networks matched monkey behaviour better than face-dedicated ones. The best-matching networks mirrored the geometry of the monkeys' brain patterns. Early responses in the recorded brain area best predicted the expression judgements. The coding overlapped partly with the coding for face identity. It did not overlap fully.
pmc-13518922:
Renáta Kovács-Berta and four colleagues survey pregnant women in Hungary across two COVID-19 waves in 2026, tracking depression, hopelessness, and confidence. Pregnancy already strains mental health, and a public health crisis can deepen the load. Wave 1 drew 692 women and Wave 2 drew 459, each completing standard scales plus a pandemic questionnaire.

Major depressive symptoms appeared in 11.8 percent in Wave 1 and 10.5 percent in Wave 2, a nonsignificant difference. Mild hopelessness touched roughly three in ten women in both waves. Confinement strain and daily disruption ran higher in Wave 1. Emotional distress and poor coping predicted worse scores most strongly, while self-efficacy consistently protected. Screening tuned to pregnancy, the authors urge, belongs in crisis care.
pmc-13520322:
David Machaku and colleagues analyse in 2026 what research ethics committees in Tanzania actually comment on when reviewing trial plans. Comments on 67 protocols from 2021 to 2023 were sorted against an eight-principle framework for ethical research.

Structure of the protocol and scientific quality drew the most comments by far. Fair partnership, social value and independent review drew far fewer. One committee commented more on partnership, although it handled only two protocols, so its figures are unstable. The authors propose balanced checklists and reviewer training, warning that a sound design alone does not guarantee a fair study for participants and communities.
pmc-13520422:
Nobuo Nishijima and colleagues build in 2026 software that reads chest CT reports and assigns lung cancer tumour stage automatically, following the ninth edition staging rules. Stage labels often sit buried in free text, which makes large real-world studies slow and costly.

The system mixes deep learning with rule checks, first judging whether a report holds enough detail, then assigning the substage. Most reports in training and test sets held enough detail. Accuracy scores stayed above 0.93 across sets, rising slightly when only fully detailed reports were staged. Automating this chore could unlock registry-scale research without manual chart review.
pmc-13520522:
Chenyu Jia and colleagues review in 2026 how faulty mitochondria, the energy hubs of ovarian cells, drive early loss of ovarian function before age forty. Reserve eggs deplete irreversibly in this syndrome, while mitochondria sit at the crossroads of energy supply and cell death decisions.

Pathways covered include several death programmes and signalling cascades triggered by mitochondrial damage. The authors propose a combined model linking damage to follicle fate, while flagging conflicting evidence and model limits. Therapies under discussion range from mitochondrial nutrients and stem cells to gene editing and replacement, each weighed for safety, ethics and readiness for patients.
pmc-13521022:
Haisch and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on whether pathology AI needs the sharpest, full-color slides. Digital slides are huge, and models routinely train on max detail by default. That default eats computing power, yet its benefit was never firmly proven. The team searched pathology and wider imaging work for direct evidence.

Direct proof for max detail turns out to be scarce in the literature. Several studies kept high accuracy after cutting resolution down substantially. Careful grayscale conversions also kept most diagnostic features intact for models. Crude cuts did hurt fine distinctions, so balance matters in the findings. The authors call for proper benchmarks before defaults harden further. Less data per slide could cut storage and training costs sharply.
pmc-13521222:
Chanthirasekaran Raju reports in 2026 a targeted survey of intestinal spirochete infection in Indian laying hens, a gut disease likely missed on farms despite India ranking among top egg producers. Samples came from recently dead hens in flocks already suspected of illness.

Intestinal scrapings from 59 hens across 12 farms were tested for Brachyspira bacteria with gene-based methods. Positive results appeared on most farms and in about two thirds of samples, with higher detection in older birds. Affected flocks showed loose droppings, wet litter and stained dirty eggs, with modest laying drops in one third. Sequencing named four Brachyspira species as preliminary identifications.
pmc-13521322:
Tarun Maheshwari and Keerthy Ajay Kumar present an anatomy case report, published in 2026. It describes unusual extra openings in a single dried human skull. On one side, the foramen spinosum was doubled. This small hole carries a meningeal artery and a nerve branch. The hypoglossal canals were also multiplied. One side was doubled. The other side was tripled.

Such combined variation in one skull is rare. It can reroute the nerves and vessels passing through these channels. Skull base surgeons and radiologists should recognise these variants, the authors stress. Imaging review and surgical planning are the moments that matter. An unexpected extra canal raises the risk of accidental injury. Operations near the skull base are the concern.
pmc-13521522:
Gregory Bormes and colleagues pilot in 2026 a fully home-based protocol for measuring dim-light melatonin onset, a marker of body clock timing, without clinic visits or staff contact. Saliva sampling under controlled dim light normally demands a laboratory evening.

Ten volunteers, half with circadian sleep disorders and half controls, followed a four to six week remote plan with mailed kits, trackers, diaries and two sampling evenings. Valid timing values emerged for most assessments, with six people valid twice. Failures stemmed from bright light slips or hormone levels outside thresholds. Confidence grew after the first attempt, supporting wider remote circadian research.
pmc-13521922:
Alexey Koshkin and colleagues profile in 2026 immune cells inside human pancreas tissue from obese and non-obese organ donors, linking obesity with pancreatic inflammation that may seed diabetes and cancer. Spatial, gene and functional methods mapped cell neighbourhoods in fine detail.

Obese pancreas held denser resident memory T cells with strong killing features, clustered around macrophages. Two macrophage families emerged, one repair-oriented and foetal-derived, the other lipid-linked and inflammatory. Obesity shifted balance toward the inflammatory family, which interacted closely with memory T cells and irritated duct tissue. Those circuits nominate targets for interrupting chronic pancreatic inflammation.
pmc-13522322:
Junjie Li and colleagues chart in 2026 the growth of artificial intelligence research in breast cancer pathology through a bibliometric map of 1,089 publications from 2011 to 2025. Output climbed sharply after 2017 and peaked in 2025 within the dataset.

Most items were original articles. Leading contributors were the United States, China, India and the European Union, with the University of Toronto the most productive institution. Topic modelling found fourteen themes, dominated by deep learning for slide image analysis at over half the corpus. Landmark citation and keyword patterns show where new entrants can find crowded ground versus open niches.
pmc-13522422:
Cynthia M Kroeger and colleagues report 2026 estimates of post-traumatic stress disorder in Australia from a large national mental health survey carried out between 2020 and 2022. Trained interviewers assessed the disorder alongside fourteen other conditions in nearly sixteen thousand people. Results were also compared with an earlier national survey from 2007 to see whether rates had shifted.

Lifetime prevalence was just over seven percent, with women showing more than twice the odds seen in men. Projected lifetime risk and time to remission also differed by sex, with remission taking far longer on average for women. People with the disorder more often had anxiety, mood problems, suicidal thoughts, asthma, and diabetes, while overall rates had not changed since 2007.
pmc-13522522:
Alexander Paredes and colleagues reveal how a hospital pathogen controls its uptake of iron in a 2026 structural biology study. The bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa forms biofilms and causes hard-to-treat infections. Its two-part sensing system responds to ferrous iron outside the cell, yet the details were poorly understood. Crystal and solution structures were determined for the response regulator protein, and its binding to DNA was tested directly.

The regulator bound the control region of the genes that encode the main ferrous iron transport system. Gene activity studies showed it controls many genes across the strain, not just iron uptake. Unusually, the protein appears to sense iron itself through a histidine-rich stretch, without needing its partner sensor. The authors suggest this control point could become a target against hospital infections.
pmc-13522622:
Yu-Kun Wang and collaborators quantify how staple crops move mercury through the environment in China in a 2026 field study. Wheat, rice, and maize were sampled at three hundred one sites nationwide. Chemical signatures were used to tell whether the mercury in plants came mainly from the air or from the soil, since mercury is a toxic element of global concern.

The three crops together took up a substantial annual amount of mercury, split almost evenly between air and soil sources. Three farming regions were predicted as accumulation hotspots. After harvest, roughly a third of the mercury returned to soil in residues, while a larger share entered the food chain through grain eaten by people and straw fed to livestock. Crops thus act as a central hub in mercury cycling.
pmc-13522822:
Seaman Jones and colleagues track a decade of vaping in the United States using the Tobacco Use Supplement to the Current Population Survey, comparing 2014-2015 with two later waves. Their 2026 repeated cross-sectional analysis adjusts for demographics to obtain nationally representative estimates of current e-cigarette use across sex, age, race, region, and education groups.

Adult vaping held steady across the first two waves, then rose significantly by 2022-2023, reaching a little over three percent of adults in the adjusted estimate. Growth was broad: Black and Hispanic adults each saw increases of well over half relative to their starting rates, though their absolute levels stayed below those of White adults. The user profile changed character too, since the share of vapers who had never smoked cigarettes climbed steeply. By the last wave they were roughly a third of adult vapers and two thirds of young adult vapers.
pmc-13523222:
Miao Yu leads a team describing an unusual variant of a hepatitis B virus protein in a liver cancer patient in a 2026 study. The viral X protein helps the virus replicate and interacts with host cells, and changes in it may shape cancer development. The gene region from one infected patient with liver cancer was analyzed by melting analysis and direct sequencing against a standard genotype reference.

Several amino acid changes clustered in the protein's activation region, alongside loss of its tail end spanning the final stretch of the chain. Melting behavior shifted in line with the altered sequence. Computer-based structural reading suggested the combined changes could alter the protein's shape and interactions, although no functional proof was obtained. The authors present the complex pattern as an addition to knowledge of viral variation in this genotype.
pmc-13523322:
Zimei Tang and colleagues build a machine learning model to predict repeat surgery outcomes in thyroid cancer in a 2026 retrospective study. Six hundred seventy patients with recurrent or persistent papillary thyroid carcinoma who had reoperation at one hospital between 2012 and 2024 were included. Twelve algorithms were trained and compared, and an explanation method was used to show which factors drove each prediction.

A random forest model performed best, with strong discrimination in both training and validation groups. Thirteen variables entered the final model, spanning age, body mass, tumor size and spread, blood markers, inflammation, and timing of reoperation. The authors argue that an interpretable model of this kind can flag high-risk patients early and help clinicians tailor treatment plans after recurrence.
pmc-13525522:
Kayral and Kavak compared diabetes burden and health spending in Türkiye against other OECD countries from 2010 to 2021. They viewed the numbers through value-based health care, the idea that spending should be judged by outcomes achieved. Their 2026 analysis drew on global disease burden estimates, OECD health statistics, and World Health Organization accounts, using trend and regression methods.

Kayral found Türkiye's diabetes-related disability burden stayed consistently above the OECD average, and the gap widened from about eighteen percent higher to about thirty-four percent higher across the period. Preventable hospital admissions for diabetes were also far more common in Türkiye. Across OECD countries, higher per-person spending was linked to lower burden, but in Türkiye spending rose alongside burden instead, signaling efficiency problems. The authors prescribe stronger primary care, prevention, outcome measurement, and financial protection to convert spending into health.
pmc-13525622:
Athukorala maps a sprawling literature in this 2026 scoping review of remote patient monitoring. The focus is hypertension and type 2 diabetes. These are managed between clinic visits by home devices and data pipelines. Following scoping review standards across three databases, the review charted 400 full-text publications into 701 distinct technical and operational evaluation entries.

Hardware was dominated by automated upper-arm blood pressure cuffs, at 32.8 percent of entries, and data mostly flowed through passive cloud uploads, 43.2 percent, rather than active Bluetooth pairing. The biggest obstacle was not the gadgets: workflow friction and daily routine disruption topped the barrier list at 27.1 percent of entries, ahead of patients' digital literacy gaps at 15 percent and clinician inertia at 8.4 percent in the charting. Barriers compounded each other in the co-occurrence analysis. The author recommends building on shared FHIR data standards and designing around clinic workflows from the start.
pmc-13526122:
Se Whee Sammy Park and colleagues report, in a 2026 analysis of the LuDO-N trial, how absorbed radiation doses shifted between two treatment fractions in children and young patients with high-risk neuroblastoma. This tumor often displays somatostatin receptors, making it targetable by a radioactive drug, lutetium-177 DOTATATE. The trial intensified dosing across two fractions guided by dosimetry.

Fourteen patients with recurrent or refractory disease received a fixed first fraction, then a second adjusted to keep whole-body or kidney dose at target ceilings. Tumor-to-organ dose ratios fell by about forty-four percent at the second fraction, and tumors absorbed over half less dose per unit of activity, while organ doses fell less. Four patients needed stem cell rescue, and no lasting kidney toxicity appeared. The protocol now front-loads more activity into the first fraction.
pmc-13526722:
Chuanqi Zhang and others decode, in a 2026 multi omics study, how chromatin regulators connect atherosclerosis with results in lung adenocarcinoma. Artery disease often occurs with this lung cancer, yet shared mechanisms were murky. The team joined public tumor cohorts, machine learning, single cell analysis, and cell culture checks.

Chromatin regulator patterns divided patients into high and low atherosclerosis risk groups that also differed in medical results. A gene called LAIR1 emerged as an atherosclerosis related factor found mostly in M2-like macrophages, a calmer macrophage type, and tied to tumor progression. Readable machine learning and pathway work built the predictive model, with findings checked in an independent cohort. Compound screening by deep learning and docking picked quercetin, a plant flavonoid, as a possible preventive agent, and co-culture tests supported the picture.
pmc-13527922:
Wenzhen Li and five colleagues review in 2026 how computers can predict T-cell receptor cross-reactivity. That term means one immune receptor can recognize several different targets. The trait helps the immune system cover many threats. It also risks harmful off-target reactions when receptors are built into cancer therapies.

The review surveys the data banks open for modeling. It then compares methods based on sequence, on structure, on machine learning, and on mixed inputs. Each approach is weighed for how well it explains itself, generalizes, and scales. Known weak points include few confirmed cross-reactive examples and bias toward viral targets. Trustworthy negative cases are also scarce. The authors call for dedicated datasets and stricter testing before predictions guide treatment design.
pmc-13528022:
Deniz Uğur Cengiz and five colleagues study mood, falls, and dizziness in older adults with BPPV in a 2026 paper. BPPV is a common inner-ear cause of brief spinning spells. The study compared 52 patients aged sixty or more with 52 healthy peers. Diagnosis was checked with video eye-movement testing. Before any treatment, both groups completed scales on depression, balance confidence, vertigo, and fall behavior.

Depression scores did not differ between groups. Almost everything else did. Patients had lower balance confidence and higher dizziness handicap. Their fall-related behavior scores were worse across safe movement, awareness, and strategy subscales. The authors conclude that BPPV harms daily confidence and safety habits even when mood scores look normal. Care should address balance and fall risk directly, they argue.
pmc-13528122:
Rodrigo Carmona Camacho and fifteen colleagues test remote therapy for pregnant women with both mental health and substance use symptoms in a 2026 trial. Over two thousand women were screened. A total of 111 joined and were split three ways. One group got therapy by telephone. One got it through a digital tool. The third got usual care. Sessions used third-generation therapy methods over eight weeks.

Phone delivery won clearly at two and four months. Alcohol use, depression, and trauma symptoms all improved more than in other groups. The digital arm showed little gain and lost more participants. By twelve months every group had slid back to its starting point. The authors back phone-based care for this group. They say digital tools need fresh thinking before they can match it.
pmc-13529122:
Xu and colleagues used genetic methods to test whether immune traits actually cause Guillain-Barré syndrome. That syndrome is a rare immune attack on peripheral nerves and the commonest cause of sudden flaccid paralysis. Their 2026 analysis applies Mendelian randomization, a technique that uses inherited gene variants as natural experiments, in both directions between immune measurements and the syndrome.

Xu found eighteen immune traits and one inflammatory protein with causal evidence for raising or lowering Guillain-Barré risk.
