They included several features of monocytes, a type of white blood cell, such as surface markers linked to higher risk. Reverse analysis showed the syndrome itself alters eleven immune traits, and checks found no sign that the genetic instruments were biased or that the arrow of causation ran backward. The authors offer the trait list as concrete leads for biomarker and treatment research into this poorly understood disease.
pmc-13530122:
Eren Tosyali and Yesim Oniz test in 2026 whether a learning system can crack a chaos-based method for scrambling audio. Their cipher shuffles sound blocks, permutes frequencies, and hides phase details behind a structured mask driven by a chaotic signal. An attacker is assumed to glimpse only part of that hidden material.

The attacking network, an echo state model, trained only on blocks where phase hints leaked. It then guessed the missing phase values for the remaining blocks and attempted rough decryption. Speech clarity and error measures showed a sharp jump in attacker success once leaked permutation detail passed a threshold.
pmc-13530222:
Kenshiro Matsuda heads a large 2026 team tracing how eczema in mice leads to depressive behavior through a blood signal. People with atopic dermatitis often face low mood, yet the physical link stayed unclear. Attention fell on interleukin-6, an inflammatory signal that rose in the blood of affected mice.

High IL-6 plus its soluble partner weakened the blood-brain barrier and cut new neuron growth in the memory center. Blocking IL-6 with an antibody eased behavior and restored neuron growth. Mice lacking IL-6 never developed the mood changes, and cell tests pinpointed which receptor route carried the harm.
pmc-13531822:
Maëlle De Coninck and colleagues interview parents and clinicians in 2026 about pregnancy and newborn care shifting toward community services in Flanders, Belgium. Shorter hospital stays push more care onto midwives and local teams, yet midwife roles stay undefined. Thirteen parents and nineteen providers shared their experience.

Seven barrier themes emerged, spanning low awareness of pre-pregnancy care, weak mental health follow-up, fuzzy role sharing, split prenatal offers, unclear value of after-birth care, and blocked record access. Coordinated pathways, clear roles, and one shared record form the proposed fix, with more dialogue planned.
pmc-13532222:
Nadia Toumeh and co-authors report in 2026 a tick-borne parasite infection hiding at vanishingly low levels behind a runaway immune syndrome in a 51-year-old woman. She takes a B-cell-depleting multiple sclerosis drug that weakens defense against tick pathogens. Weeks of fever, weakness, low blood counts, and liver strain fit hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, an inflammatory overdrive.

A cell-free DNA blood test spotted the Babesia parasite, later confirmed with under one-hundredth of a percent of red cells infected. Anti-parasite drugs plus steroids for the overdrive brought improvement. Broad early testing matters in such masked cases.
pmc-13534222:
Maria Elaine Trevisan and colleagues test in 2026 combined breathing muscle training and light therapy in rats with type 2 diabetes. Harmful oxygen by-products drive much of the organ damage in diabetes, beyond blood sugar alone. Diabetic and healthy rats were split into treated and resting groups for six weeks of care.

Treated diabetic rats showed less oxidative damage in blood, diaphragm, lungs, and kidneys, with stronger defences in several tissues. Blood counts and protein levels also improved toward normal. Healthy treated rats gained tissue defences too, supporting this drug-free pairing for wider study.
pmc-13534522:
Zeyu Luo and colleagues examine in 2026 changeable risk factors for depression and anxiety in the UK Biobank. Which body, social, and reproductive factors matter most, and for whom, was not fully mapped. The cohort held 87,648 adults who joined between 2006 and 2010, with follow-up lasting a median of 13 years.

Psychosocial factors carried the largest population burden in both sexes, with neuroticism traits topping the list. Obesity led among body factors, while inflammation linked to both outcomes. In women, hormone therapy added notable burden, supporting sex-aware and life-stage prevention planning across adult care and public health programmes today.
pmc-13534922:
Sif Korsbaek Topsoe-Jensen, Carl Johan Wingren, and Chiara Villa test in 2026 alternate light sources for photographing bruises on deceased people under normal autopsy room lighting. Special lights may reveal bruises better, yet prior advice assumed dark rooms that real autopsy suites cannot offer. The team photographed 161 bruises under white light and three filtered light setups.

Alternate lights did not improve visibility overall versus white light in these conditions. Two setups reduced visibility, while violet light with a long-pass filter sometimes helped and showed larger bruise areas. Observer agreement ranged from moderate to excellent across measures.
pmc-13536222:
Karolewski and co-authors test a blood test for bowel cancer built on light scattering rather than stool samples, which many Australians skip despite free screening kits. Raman spectroscopy reads the molecular vibration fingerprint of blood plasma, and machine learning hunts for the cancer pattern inside it. Their 2026 exploratory study analysed plasma from 370 people: 117 with colorectal cancer and 253 controls. The controls had tested positive on the stool test but proved to have adenomas, inflammation, or healthy colons.

Split into training and validation sets, the model caught the large majority of cancers in the untouched validation group. It correctly cleared most controls, at accuracy levels the authors call high for a screening candidate. Projected onto practice, nearly all cancer patients would still reach colonoscopy, while about two fifths of stool-positive people might be spared an unnecessary one.
pmc-13536622:
Ying Zhu-ge and colleagues build in 2026 a competency scale for medical teachers who blend simulation teaching with generative AI tools. Rapid AI growth is reshaping simulation training, and schools lack a standard way to judge teacher readiness. Expert rounds and surveys with 434 learners from clinical, technical, and nursing fields shaped the scale.

The final scale holds 16 items with strong consistency and expert agreement in testing rounds. Fit checks were acceptable overall for classroom use. The scale mainly captures ethics awareness rather than full governance skill, a limit the authors note for faculty development planning.
pmc-13538322:
Habtamu Milkias Wolde and co-authors analyze seven years of measles surveillance in Ethiopia in a 2026 study of cases from 2018 to 2024. Ethiopia carries a heavy measles load despite a strong vaccine, and drivers of lasting spread stay poorly mapped. Nearly seventy thousand confirmed cases supplied age attack rates, death rates, and spread intensity estimates. Reporting delay from symptom start to confirmation was also related to outbreak size and length.

Children aged one to four years bore the highest attack rates. Typical infection age ran much younger in pastoral regions than in the capital area. Death rates peaked in infants under nine months. Spread stayed strong during epidemic peaks. Median confirmation delay reached eighteen days, longer than the usual gap between linked cases. Longer outbreaks grew larger, yet delay showed no link to outbreak length.
pmc-13538622:
Shirin Ghotboddin Mohammadi and colleagues test a marine antioxidant supplement in heart failure patients in a 2026 randomized trial. Eighty patients with advanced heart failure and weakened pumping function took astaxanthin or placebo daily for eight weeks under double-blind conditions. Blood markers of inflammation, blood fats, and body measures were checked before and after the course.

Two inflammation markers fell clearly more in the supplement group than under placebo. One blood fat fraction also dropped significantly, while total cholesterol showed only a borderline dip after adjustment. Other fats, a third inflammation marker, and body measures stayed unchanged. The authors conclude the supplement may help selected inflammation markers with limited fat effects, while body effects remain unsettled.
pmc-13540822:
Shabbir Ahmed and colleagues feed special diets to goats in a 2026 study. Each diet lacked one of two key amino acids. The team then studied a cell cleanup process called autophagy. Gut and liver tissues were the focus. Thirty goats split into three diet groups.

One group ate a normal diet. The others lacked methionine or lysine. Lysine shortage jammed cleanup flow in the small intestine. A cargo protein, p62, built up there as proof. A stress gene, ATF4, rose in the rumen and gut. It seemed to rebalance amino acids. Methionine shortage changed gut chemistry more than cleanup itself.
pmc-13540922:
Elham Davtalab Esmaeili and six colleagues pool, in a 2026 systematic review, evidence on suicidal behaviour among pregnant teenagers, many of them married early. Adolescent pregnancy and early marriage both strain mental health, so the size of this risk needed measuring.

Twelve studies covering 125,551 pregnant adolescents were combined. About fourteen percent reported suicidal thoughts and six percent an attempt. Attempt rates ran highest in Asia and lowest in the grouped India and Africa studies. Compared with pregnant women over nineteen, pregnant teenagers faced roughly sixty percent higher odds of suicidal thoughts and about double the odds of an attempt. The authors call for screening and support aimed at this group.
pmc-13542222:
Chai Jia Law and six colleagues taste-test, in a 2026 sensory study, calcium-fortified tempeh chips against ordinary tempeh chips among one hundred women of reproductive age. Tempeh's calcium absorbs as well as milk's, yet each serving carries little calcium, so fortification could turn a familiar snack into a useful source.

Panels rated appearance, colour, texture, aroma, taste, and overall liking on a seven-point scale for three fortified flavours and one plain chip. Fortified chips scored significantly higher on most attributes, though taste tied for the original flavour. The spicy fortified chip won overall, passing the acceptance threshold comfortably while delivering a solid calcium dose per small serving. Garlic and original versions fell below that threshold.
pmc-13543622:
Yue Zhao and Yuan Lin published a 2026 ethics analysis of informed consent for invasive brain-computer interfaces. The prompt was China's approval in March 2026 of the first such device for clinical use anywhere. Their worry is diachronic. A participant consents to later removal, but after years of use the device may become part of how the person acts and experiences themselves. Removal may then feel like losing a faculty rather than ending an experiment.

Change alone, the authors argue, does not void consent, since many treatments transform self-understanding. The problem is the combination of not knowing what life with the device is like, cognitive extension, and functional dependence. They propose dynamic consent with periodic re-consent, continuing ethics oversight for implanted participants, and separating research withdrawal from consent to removal, guided by a decision algorithm. Consent, in short, must be revisited as the person-device relationship evolves.
pmc-13543722:
Onofrio Davide Palmitessa and colleagues published a 2026 study of adding red-blue LED light during hydroponic growing of Scopatizzo, an Apulian melon landrace eaten unripe as a cucumber alternative. Fruit grown with and without the extra light were compared for yield, minerals, and behaviour through seventeen days of cold storage, with ordinary cucumber as a reference point in the analysis.

Supplemental light raised fruit number per plant by about twenty-nine percent, from eleven to fourteen, without changing the fruit's mineral makeup at harvest. Light-grown fruit held roughly eighteen percent more firmness by the end of storage and started with more chlorophyll and glucose. Storage time, not lighting, drove acidity and moisture changes, while cold itself boosted phenolics and carotenoids in both groups. Light management, the authors conclude, can valorise a local landrace for the fresh market.
pmc-13546722:
Khalil Khalil and co-authors tested in 2026 mineral supplements made from local Indonesian calcite rock as a cheaper option for laying quails, replacing commercial premixes that small farmers find costly or unreliable. Five local formulas varied by particle size, heating treatment, and added minerals, and 432 quails received them at 5 percent of the diet for eight weeks alongside a commercial comparison group.

Local formulas beat the commercial premix on egg production, egg mass, feed efficiency, and profit. Coarse calcite grit performed best of all, likely because its size and density release calcium slowly for shell building. Heating and enrichment raised blood phosphorus yet added no further production gain. The authors conclude that physical form matters more than extra processing.
pmc-13547222:
Aleksandra Pietrzak and a large team tested in 2026 whether Cunninghamella fungi can break down three common painkillers that pollute water, and whether the leftovers are any safer. The fungi efficiently transformed diclofenac and ibuprofen into several breakdown products, while ketoprofen barely changed. The treated mixtures then went through a battery of toxicity tests, from bacterial light assays and algae growth to human and rat cell lines.

Fungal treatment lowered the water toxicity of both transformed drugs, and cell tests showed the products harmed liver, nerve, and heart cells less than the original compounds. No sample caused mutations in the standard bacterial test. Hormone-like interference mostly vanished, though a faint estrogen-like activity appeared. The authors back fungal treatment with careful product checking.
pmc-13548522:
Meaza Alem and colleagues measure how well intensive care nurses in Tigray, Ethiopia, prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia, in a 2026 mixed-methods study. This lung infection strikes patients on breathing machines and raises deaths and costs, yet local data on nursing practice were scarce. The team surveyed all 216 nurses in adult and pediatric intensive care units at public hospitals, then followed up with interviews.

Fewer than four in ten nurses met the standard for good prevention practice. Older age, more intensive care experience, higher education, special training, and stronger knowledge each raised the odds of good practice, while short staffing lowered them. Interviews blamed thin training, heavy workloads, weak teamwork, and limited management backing. The authors recommend regular in-service training and better staffing to close the gap.
pmc-13548622:
Frédéric Paris and colleagues compare two ways of judging how crowded an emergency department feels, in a 2026 prospective study across three French hospitals. Crowding slows care and exhausts staff, yet existing scales can be hard to interpret between departments of different sizes. Twice a day over two weeks in May 2023, the team recorded operating numbers and asked frontline staff to rate their workload, then matched two crowding measures against those ratings.

A simple census rate, expressing how full the department is, tracked staff ratings strongly. The established CEDOCS scale tracked them only moderately, and the difference between the two was significant. Inside community hospitals the pair performed alike, while the census rate pulled ahead overall. The authors propose the plain rate as an easy shared signal for workload discussions, pending wider validation.
pmc-13548722:
Jinjoo Choi and colleagues review how diabetes arising in pregnancy reshapes the gut microbes of mother and newborn, in a 2026 review. This diabetes of pregnancy disturbs the mother's metabolism and gut microbes together, with possible echoes in the baby's immune growth and later disease risk. The authors gathered clinical and lab evidence on microbe change across the three trimesters and what follows for infants.

Microbe imbalance appears early in pregnancy, though studies disagree in detail. None proves mothers directly seed the baby's microbes. Birth conditions and the mother's metabolic state likely mold the newborn's microbes jointly. Diet, weight, and probiotics shift the microbes, yet their benefit for this diabetes stays uneven. The authors look toward microbe-guided diets, chosen probiotics, and care built on metabolic products, fitted to each mother. They warn that current evidence cannot support firm causal claims.
pmc-13550422:
C. S. VinodKumar and colleagues examine the docking hardware that bacteria-killing viruses use to latch onto Staphylococcus aureus, in a 2026 molecular study. Phage therapy lives or dies on these receptor-binding interactions, and bacterial surface molecules vary between strains. The team profiled four wall-teichoic-acid related receptor genes across many isolates, catalogued their single-letter mutations, and simulated docking with tail and spike proteins from four phages.

Mutations were mostly simple letter swaps, with no insertions or deletions, and many were shared across strains. Docking stayed strong throughout, with binding energies in a healthy range, and the contact hotspots were conserved despite the variation. The picture is a coevolutionary balance: receptors drift enough to blunt some phages, yet keep the shapes that leave them open to relatives. The authors use the map to argue for broad or combined phage cocktails.
pmc-13550622:
Achille Pasqualotto and Hiroto Kawarada published a 2026 experiment on whether sounds that seem to approach change how long other sounds feel. Earlier work used the moving sound itself as the timed target, which could confuse results. Here blindfolded listeners heard background motion sounds that approached, receded, or were scrambled, delivered through sensory substitution, while separate tones played in front.

Listeners who heard approaching background sound overestimated the tones' duration, measured by reproducing how long each tone lasted. Short tones tended to be overestimated and long ones underestimated, a known pull toward the average. The authors' computational model captured that pattern, supporting the idea that looming background sound speeds the internal clock through attention.
pmc-13554122:
Ui-Seob Lee leads a seven-author team rethinking wall shielding for cancer centres that treat tumours with several kinds of heavy ions in a 2026 study. Older shielding math counts particles, yet each ion type needs a different count to deliver the same dose. The team instead defined workloads by dose itself, in two forms. Computer simulations traced neutrons from helium, carbon, oxygen, and neon beams through varied shields.

By plain dose, carbon beams made the most neutrons in every shield layout. By dose weighted for body effect, carbon stayed the safest design basis overall. Fast helium neared carbon only in narrow cases involving metal targets. The authors keep carbon as the reference ion, with a caution flag for helium under those rare conditions.
pmc-13554222:
Mohamed AbdelMongy leads an eight-author team teaching computers to predict the strength of concrete made with industrial waste in a 2026 study. Their dataset held 711 mixes, far larger than most earlier work. Seven learning models competed to forecast crushing strength from mix ingredients. A method that explains each forecast showed which ingredients mattered most.

A gradient boosting model won, edging out two close rivals on every error measure. Fine sand-like material swayed forecasts most, ahead of cement, water, and curing age. The team wrapped the model in a simple screen tool anyone can run. Builders can now test waste-based mixes on a computer in minutes, skipping slow and costly lab pours for early screening.
pmc-13554322:
Yosef A Cohen leads a nine-author team testing a new heart scan mode for patients with fast or irregular heartbeats in a 2026 study. Standard triggered scans fail when rhythm is erratic, forcing a full-cycle scan with higher dose. The new mode adjusts tube power to body shape throughout the scan. Three hundred twenty patients were sorted by rhythm into the new mode or standard triggering.

The new-mode group had faster hearts and received a higher average dose. Image quality stayed high in both groups, with mean scores near the top of the scale. Shares of usable, diagnostic scans matched between groups. Body weight drove dose far more than scan mode did. The authors see the mode as a workable option for hard-to-scan patients.
pmc-13555922:
Bounika Esvanth Rao leads a ten-author team reviewing protein clues in mouth conditions that can precede cancer in a 2026 analysis. Such disorders include white patches, stiffening of the mouth lining, and lichen-like changes. From nearly thirteen thousand papers, fifteen studies passed the quality screen. The team counted repeated proteins, built interaction networks, and traced hub proteins to their pathways.

Most included work covered the stiffening disorder, with fewer studies on the other lesions. Four studies earned top quality marks. Shared and lesion-specific proteins emerged from the vote counting. Hub proteins, the most connected in each network, pointed to pathways worth drug targeting. The authors present the synthesis as a guide for biomarker hunts in these hard-to-read conditions.
pmc-13556022:
Shaimaa Mohamed Saeed Ata and Medhat Ekrami Abouseif Mohamed surveyed school students in Saudi Arabia's Qassim Region in 2026 about what they know and do for their teeth. Their cross-sectional study covered 321 primary and intermediate students aged 7 to 15. Children answered a structured questionnaire given by the researchers, and standard clinical indices recorded decay and oral cleanliness.

Students showed moderate to high knowledge, attitudes, and habits overall. Sugary food and poor hygiene were the causes of decay they named most, while regular brushing and fluoride toothpaste led the protective habits. Boys and girls answered much the same. Gaps remained around fluoride use and routine dental visits despite the generally strong awareness. The authors point to school programmes as the place to close those specific gaps.
pmc-13559822:
Benjamin Limburg, Thekla Bacharach, and Anand Dayama present a case report, published in 2026. It describes one 68-year-old woman with an infected pseudoaneurysm. This is a contained leak in the ascending aorta. It followed earlier heart surgery. Open repair is standard but risky. No approved stent device exists for this spot. The team improvised with an abdominal aortic cuff. It was soaked in the antibiotic rifampin.

The team reached the aorta through an arm artery. They placed the graft successfully. No leak remained afterwards. The patient went home on the fourth day after surgery. One-month imaging showed the leak resolved. The graft was stable. She faces lifelong antibiotics, though. The vessel wall was infected.
pmc-13560122:
Khang Leng Lee and colleagues build a human cells-on-chip system that joins blood vessel lining cells, T cells, and liver cells to judge drug effects in metabolic disease. Their 2026 paper models the liver's sinusoidal microenvironment, a setting where vessel and immune interactions shape illness. Endothelial cells grown from patients' blood seeded the chip.

Plasma from type 2 diabetes patients treated with dapagliflozin, a glucose-lowering drug, was run through the platform. The treated plasma calmed endothelial inflammation, slowed T cell migration, and reduced fat buildup in the liver cells. Interestingly, glucose uptake in the dish did not change with the drug, suggesting the benefits travel through factors circulating in plasma rather than acting on the cells directly. The authors offer the multiplex chip for personalized screening of a patient's own plasma before therapy, and for preclinical testing of vessel-protective drugs.
pmc-13560422:
Wendy Larbi and colleagues chart five years of germs and drug resistance at a mid-level hospital lab in Accra, Ghana. Their 2026 retrospective study covers 6,395 lab specimens handled between January 2019 and December 2023. Urine, vaginal swabs, and blood dominated the workload at the Cocoa Clinic Laboratory.

Growth showed in 22.2 percent of specimens. Urine supplied half the positive cultures, and gram-negative germs led overall, with Escherichia coli on top across most years. A shift arrived in 2023, when Candida species became the top isolate. Women yielded more positive cultures than men, and working-age adults supplied most isolates. Three antibiotics kept over eighty-nine percent strength, while several common agents faced resistance above sixty-eight percent in the testing. Case finding climbed from 2021 to 2023 after a quieter early COVID span. The authors urge steady watching and tighter control of drug use.
pmc-13561722:
Qian Yang and nine colleagues published this 2026 study comparing two surgical robots for pyeloplasty, the repair of a blocked junction between kidney and ureter. The da Vinci system is the established platform; the KangDuo system is a newer alternative. The authors reviewed patients treated with each robot, then used propensity score matching to create balanced groups of 66 patients per system, checking their results with sensitivity analyses.

After matching, KangDuo operations took longer, with a median of 149 minutes against 132 minutes for da Vinci cases. Hospital stay was also a day longer, at a median of five days versus four. Everything else matched closely: blood loss, kidney function at final follow-up and complication rates did not differ, and surgical success was 93.9 percent for da Vinci and 90.9 percent for KangDuo. No major complications or equipment failures occurred. The authors conclude KangDuo is comparably safe and effective, if slower.
pmc-13562222:
Hai Zhang and four colleagues devise a way to estimate the lung's static compliance during pressure support ventilation, when the patient's own breathing corrupts the standard measurement. Their 2026 bench study connects a ventilator to a programmable lung simulator set at two compliance levels and four resistance levels. Small deliberate wiggles in the support pressure reveal the system's elasticity.

The method reads the volume change produced by a one-unit pressure step, corrected through an expiratory time-constant model. At low support levels its estimates closely matched the classic occlusion measurement taken under full volume control. Error grew to roughly ten to fifteen percent as spontaneous effort joined in, a limit the authors state openly. They pitch the scheme for noninvasive, uninterrupted compliance tracking at the bedside, accepting approximate values in exchange for never pausing the patient's own breathing.
pmc-13572522:
Carroll and colleagues published a 2026 study on probiotic feed for young meat chickens. Bacillus-based feed microbes have improved growth and curbed germs in past trials. The team fed 560 male broiler chicks with or without the probiotic mix. Half the birds then received a Salmonella dose at one week old.

Probiotic-fed birds trended heavier before the germ challenge arrived. After challenge, they ate more and converted feed into weight better. Germ shedding at day four hit 70 percent in unsupplemented challenged birds. The probiotic challenged group sat midway at 40 percent shedding overall. Samples from liver and spleen tracked how far the germ spread inside. Immune cell counts in organs added a second readout of effects.
pmc-13573122:
Chih-Yin Lin, with five colleagues, reports a 2026 method for unbuilding a common acrylic plastic back into its pure monomer. Recycling PMMA, sold as Plexiglas, by heat alone wastes energy and yields dirty output. Past gentle methods leaned on chlorinated solvents, which leave corrosive waste.

The new route uses light and heat with a trace of anthraquinone, a photocatalyst, at parts-per-million levels. It runs through oxygen-centred radicals, a chlorine-free path that cuts the chain mid-way. Up to 97 percent of the monomer was recovered. Changing the catalyst dose sped or slowed the break-down on demand. Shop goods such as acrylic tubes and light guide plates broke down well too. On-off light cycles showed the process can pause and restart at will.
pmc-13573322:
Shali and colleagues evaluate a flap technique for rebuilding soft tissue around damaged knees, in 2026 reconstructive surgery research. The method swings a flap of thigh tissue, still attached to its blood vessels, backward around the knee. Blood flow to the flap's far end can falter after rotation. The surgeons therefore watched each flap for a mandatory 40 minutes using color, temperature, refill, and bleeding checks, then added blood vessel connections only where those checks showed compromise.

The retrospective series covered 23 consecutive patients treated between January 2015 and August 2025, with a mean age of 38.48 years. Defects sat before the kneecap in 9 patients, at the outer knee in 8, and behind the knee in 6, mostly after trauma. Outcomes tracked flap survival, knee function scores, and standardized scar ratings. Shali argues the structured perfusion check lets surgeons reserve extra vascular surgery for flaps that demonstrably need it.
pmc-13576122:
Yan Wu and Yang Yang link childhood hardship to a pre-dementia warning syndrome in older Chinese adults, in a 2026 nationwide study. The syndrome, motoric cognitive risk, pairs slow walking with memory complaints and flags people at higher dementia risk. Most past work looked at risks in old age itself, not at early life.

The analysis used national survey data and covered 4,937 adults aged 60 and over. Childhood neglect raised the odds of the syndrome by about 38 percent after adjustments. Each added hardship raised odds by 16.5 percent, and people reporting three hardships had roughly double the odds of those reporting none. The authors argue for screening older adults on early hardship and for support that softens its long shadow across the lifespan.
pmc-13576222:
Wei Guo leads a 2026 study checking whether maturing eggs in the laboratory leaves marks on babies' DNA chemistry. The method, in vitro maturation, offers a gentler option than standard IVF for women with polycystic ovary syndrome, since it lowers the risk of dangerous ovary overstimulation. Worry persists that lab maturation might disturb early programming in offspring.

The analysis sat inside a randomised trial and covered ten families: five with lab-matured egg conception and five with standard IVF, parents included. Cord blood DNA from the babies showed closely matching methylation patterns between groups. Only three small differing regions appeared, none at imprinted or development-critical sites. Spread of values was also similar. The authors call the results strong support for the method's epigenetic safety.
pmc-13576322:
Shubi Zhao and five colleagues study how the balance between two cholesterol-carrier subtypes shapes immune cell behaviour in sepsis, in a 2026 paper. Sepsis is a runaway immune response to infection, and levels of HDL, the so-called good cholesterol carrier, fall fast in its early phase. Its subtypes HDL2b and HDL3 also shift in mix.

Blood came from ten sepsis patients and ten healthy controls. The ratio of the larger to the smaller subtype ran lower in sepsis. In cell tests, mixes of the subtypes damped the inflammatory signals that bacterial toxin triggers in immune and vessel-lining cells. The mixes also softened the toxin's harm to two immune cell lines. The authors suggest the subtype balance could be tuned to calm inflammation during sepsis.
pmc-13578222:
Xiaoyang Duan and colleagues introduce a 2026 imaging method that picks the ring of tissue around a tumor with the most useful signal for computer diagnosis. Tissue just outside a growth is known to hold clues, yet fixed rules for how wide that ring should be often waste data or add noise.

Their method, called APASA, builds a graph from the tumor outline and grows the outer region only where it adds value. Tested inside five machine learning models on breast and thyroid ultrasound scans, the picked regions beat simple ring widening by wide margins on key scores. Which model worked best shifted with region shape and cancer type, a point the authors flag for anyone building such tools.
pmc-13578722:
Weihua Dai sets out a math method for tracking how gas spreads through an oil reservoir as it pushes oil toward wells, in a 2026 study. Gas flooding is trickier than water flooding because gas thins and squeezes with pressure, and pressure varies across the field. Most past work leaned on heavy numerical simulators rather than direct formulas.

The method starts from a classic water flood equation and solves it with a fully implicit search at each place and time step. A bundle of flow tubes with varied rock quality captures the finger like paths gas takes through uneven ground. Pressure effects on gas thickness and volume are folded in through mass balance. On a real channel shaped field case, the forecast gas arrival time at the well matched field records closely.
pmc-13579722:
Ahmet Narin and Bahadır Ezmek test when to glaze 3D printed crown resins so their color lasts, in a 2026 lab study. Two permanent crown materials were printed into 248 samples and split across four surface plans: plain polishing, glaze after final curing, glaze before curing, and glaze on both sides of curing. Samples then endured ten thousand hot cold cycles and a month soaking in fake saliva, coffee, or red wine.

Heat cycling shifted color in every group, and coffee and wine pushed change past the level patients would accept across the board. Glazing before curing beat glazing after it, above all in one material. Plain polishing fared worst of all. Microscope views showed the early glaze fused smoother, with fewer flaws. The authors advise labs to glaze before the final cure.
pmc-13579822:
Hasan Ünver and colleagues adapt a Spanish eating disorder scale for Turkish patients with bipolar disorder, in a 2026 study at an Ankara hospital. One hundred patients and one hundred twenty nine healthy adults took the translated scale alongside mania, depression, and eating measures. Eating trouble often hides inside bipolar care, and no local tool targeted it directly.

The Turkish scale held together well, with strong internal consistency and steady item links to the total. Its scores tracked a bulimia test and most parts of a Dutch eating survey, yet not the mood rating scales, a sensible split. Total eating scores did not differ between patients and controls, and healthy adults even scored higher on emotional eating. The authors judge the scale valid and ready for clinic use in this population.
pmc-13584422:
Ryota Otoshi and colleagues search for reliable risk groups in a rare scarring lung disease in this 2026 study. The disease, shortened to PPFE, stiffens the upper lobes and follows a course that varies wildly between patients. The team grouped 32 patients by lung test values, a blood marker called KL-6, and the spread of scarring on detailed scans, then checked the grouping in 37 more patients.

Two groups appeared. One carried low breathing capacity, trapped air, high marker levels, and wide scarring, and its members died far sooner than the other group. The same split showed up in the second set of patients, and a simple four-part score sorted patients into three risk bands in both sets. A measure of telomere length, a wear marker on chromosomes, added nothing to the forecast.
pmc-13586122:
Helin Yücedağ Gündoğdu, Bahattin Paslı, and Burcu Erçakmak Güneş measure a thin patch of bone in the hip that surgeons must respect. The iliac wing, the broad blade of the pelvis, often anchors screws for broken pelvis repairs, yet its center holds a translucent area where the hard outer shell thins sharply. Their 2026 study examined 51 dry hip bones, using light to find that patch and software to measure photographs.

The thin area averaged roughly five to six centimeters across each way, with wide spread between bones. The shell at its center averaged only about two millimeters thick, and in one bone it shrank to a fraction of that. A safe screw angle from a front landmark came out near seventeen degrees. The authors urge imaging and case-by-case planning before placing hardware near this zone.
pmc-13587322:
Gloria Somalo-Barranco and a large European group survey how pregnancy is handled in women with rare diseases of the blood vessels. Such pregnancies can endanger mother and baby and need many specialists working as one team. Working through a European reference network, the group sent a short questionnaire to care providers and patient representatives and read the open answers for shared themes.

Thirty-six replies came back from ten countries, most from clinicians. Five themes recurred: the need for joined-up team care, and wide swings in advice given before conception and on genetic testing. Poor access to specialist centers for monitoring also stood out, as did the value of a written delivery plan with follow-up after birth. The authors say education and shared care pathways are already being built inside their network to close those gaps.
pmc-13591222:
Nobunari Tomura leads a team mapping the faulty electrical tissue that keeps a chaotic heart rhythm going in 47 patients with lasting atrial fibrillation. A dense mapping system recorded signals from both upper heart chambers before treatment, yielding more than 48,000 points. The team measured each point for its dominant rate and regularity, then compared spots where waves spread from one focus or spun in circles.

Both kinds of suspect spots showed higher rate shifts and regularity than quiet tissue. Left chamber values topped right chamber ones, with the roof highest of all. Repeated focal spots scored higher still, while much repeated spinning spots gave a mixed picture. Tomura and the team say the pairing of mapping and spectral checks may clarify how this rhythm sustains itself.
pmc-13591522:
Haris Patail leads a 2026 report on sucking out masses from the left side of the heart through a catheter, for patients too frail for open surgery. Such masses, clots, growths, or infected tissue on the mitral valve, can fling debris to the brain and body. Seven patients at one center, with an average age near 78, had large masses over a centimeter wide. The team crossed between the heart's upper chambers to reach them.

Every case met the goal of removing at least 70 percent of the mass, and all patients left hospital alive. One case worsened valve leakage, and one patient died within a month from a non heart cause. Procedure times fell as the team gained practice. Patail and colleagues call for larger studies.
pmc-13592022:
Jahmal J Ennis, Julianne C Griepenburg, and Grace Brannigan simulate gold nanoparticles parked inside fatty membranes. Such particles shine in medical uses because clumping changes how they interact with light. Common wisdom held that the oily coat on each particle shields its core from the surroundings. Their coarse grained simulations tested several particle models that differ in how the core is treated.

Even at full coat coverage, the core's traits still shaped how particles met solvent and each other, they found. Core pull on the surroundings seems to drive clumping directly, not merely through the coat. Ennis and the team argue that modelers who ignore core physics risk missing why coated particles gather in membranes, with lessons for drug carriers and light based therapies.
pmc-13592322:
Elena Herzog and five colleagues uncover, in 2026, a bacterial iron hunter that changes jobs after an enzyme trims its fat tail. Pandoraea bacteria make these lipopeptides to grab scarce iron, yet the fresh form first serves as a soap that helps the colony swarm. Gene mining and chemical profiling found the pair of forms and fixed the true ring structure of the mature one, revising an earlier guess.

A dedicated acylase clips the tail, the ring shrinks through a bond shift, and the product drops its swarming help while gripping iron far better. Knockout strains and rebuilt enzyme tests confirmed each step. Herzog and the team link the switch to each species' niche and flag the trimming enzyme as a possible antivirulence target.

Sauban Musa Jibril leads a team reporting in 2026 how natamycin, a natural antifungal compound, attacks the fungus behind rice blast, a disease that threatens rice crops worldwide. The compound was known to fight microbes, yet how it works on this fungus was unclear. In lab tests it slowed fungal growth by 16 to 100 percent depending on dose, and the fungus became far less able to infect plants, dropping to 4.1 percent of normal.

To find the weak point, the team combined gene activity and chemical readings from treated fungus. Both lines pointed to the cell's energy-making pathway, oxidative phosphorylation, being disrupted, along with amino acid building. Forcing two genes in that pathway to work harder made the fungus resist the drug, confirming the target. The work supports natamycin as a tool against a major crop threat.
pmc-13616322:
Masoud Karimipour leads a team showing that a heat-spreading layer made from MXene, a flaky two-dimensional material, can quadruple the working life of inverted perovskite solar cells at high heat. Such cells now convert about 27 percent of sunlight at room temperature, yet real products bake in the sun and fade fast. The MXene layer sits at the cell's hole-transport interface and is treated with the same molecule used in that layer.

Cells reached an efficiency of 23.02 percent, give or take about a point. The time to drop to 80 percent of starting power at 65 degrees stretched from 141 hours to 687 hours. That is a gain near 400 percent. Fine imaging confirmed the treating molecule had slipped between the MXene flakes as designed. Heat management at one interface, the study shows, can be the difference between a lab record and a roof-ready panel.
pmc-13616622:
Lucia F. Cardo introduces an editorial collection of reviews in neurogenetics, the study of inherited disorders of the nervous system, for the journal Frontiers in Neurology. The collection spans common conditions like dementia and ataxia and rare ones such as cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis and PRUNE1 syndrome. That review found trials growing in number and shifting toward procedures and targeted gene therapy. Academia ran 91 percent of trials, while drug companies led only 9 percent. Most trials, 86 percent, aimed at treatment, yet only about a third used the strongest blinded designs. The editorial argues that the diagnostic and therapy methods proven on common diseases should now be carried to the rare disorders that research keeps leaving behind.

Lo, Mertz, and Loeb studied a quality scale for research in 2014. The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale is widely used to judge the quality of observational studies, which track people without assigning a treatment. Poor reporting of methods is known to distort quality scores in trials.

The team compared scores given by the scale's own authors with scores given by other reviewers on the same studies. Gaps between the two sets showed where the scale can be read in different ways. That finding matters because quality scores shape which studies a review trusts. Clearer use of the scale would make health evidence more sound.
pmc-4066722:
Ayala, Muñoz, and Argüelles reviewed lipid peroxidation in 2014, a form of chemical damage to fats in cells. Free radicals and other oxidants attack fats that contain double bonds, above all the polyunsaturated fatty acids found in cell membranes. Four decades of research had built a large body of work on this process.

The review centers on two products of that damage, malondialdehyde and a compound known as 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal. It covers how they are made, how the body breaks them down, and how they act as signals. Both compounds are used as markers of oxidative stress in disease studies.
pmc-4170722:
Davey Smith and Hemani explained Mendelian randomization in 2014, a method for judging cause and effect in health studies. Plain observational studies are prone to confounding and reverse causation, and many of their findings later proved unreliable. That weakness drove the search for stronger designs.

Mendelian randomization uses genes as anchors. Since gene variants are set at conception, they act like a natural random trial of a lifelong exposure. If people with a variant also have more disease, that supports a real causal link. The method helps test whether factors like blood pressure or cholesterol truly cause illness.
pmc-4383922:
Wong and Wang built miRDB, described in 2014, an online resource for microRNA research. MicroRNAs are small non-coding RNAs involved in many normal and disease processes. A central challenge in the field is finding which genes each microRNA regulates.

MiRDB predicts the target genes of microRNAs and adds functional notes to the results. Users can search by microRNA or by gene and get ranked predictions. Good predictions save months of lab work by narrowing the list of genes to test. The resource supports studies of development, cancer, and other diseases where these small RNAs play a role.
pmc-6138922:
Gherman Uritskiy, Jocelyne DiRuggiero, and James Taylor presented MetaWRAP, a metagenomics pipeline, in 2018. Shotgun sequencing of whole communities lets scientists study microbes that cannot be grown in labs. Sorting the mixed DNA into draft genomes is the hard part.

MetaWRAP wraps several leading tools into one flow, from cleaning reads to assembling and binning genomes. It refines bins by combining results from multiple methods, which raises genome quality. Users get completeness and contamination scores for each recovered genome. The pipeline lowered the skill barrier for genome-resolved studies of soils, oceans, and guts.
pmc-6447622:
Ying Zhou, Bin Zhou, Lars Pache, and coauthors presented Metascape, a web resource for gene-list analysis, in 2019. Large omics studies end with long gene lists that need meaning. Finding enriched pathways and protein groups is the critical reading step.

Metascape merges many current databases into one workflow and updates them often. It runs enrichment, builds interaction networks, and produces a polished report in minutes. The design targets working biologists rather than programmers. Its ease made it a default first pass for interpreting systems-level data sets in many labs. Results are presented as clean summary tables and plots that non-specialists can read quickly.
pmc-8008022:
Damien Bertheloot, Eicke Latz, and Bernardo Franklin reviewed in 2021 the tangled relationships among three ways cells die: apoptosis, pyroptosis, and necroptosis. Cell death is a basic process in every living organism, shaping development, keeping organs in repair, and coordinating immune defense. Each of these three pathways was once studied in isolation, as if cells simply chose one exit.

The authors show that the pathways share parts, trigger each other, and can substitute when one is blocked. That crosstalk matters in aging, autoimmunity, and the body's response to infection. Their account replaces the old picture of separate switches with one connected control board, which changes how researchers design drugs meant to steer cell death.
pound-philosophy-law-1922:
An Introduction to the Philosophy of Law, published in 1922, prints Roscoe Pound's Storrs Lectures. They made him the leading American legal thinker of his generation. Pound, dean of Harvard Law School, maps the schools of legal thought and argues for his own.

His program is sociological jurisprudence: law studied as a working system, judged by its effects on society rather than by logic alone. He calls for the study of interests, the claims law must balance, as its central task. The lectures are compact, learned, and reforming in spirit. They shaped American legal education for decades afterward.
ptolemy-tetrabiblos-ashmand-1822:
Claudius Ptolemy, Alexandria's great astronomer, also wrote the Tetrabiblos on astrology. J. M. Ashmand's English translation appeared in 1822 with notes and appendices. The work became the most important surviving ancient text on its subject.

Ptolemy sets out how planets were believed to shape weather and nations. Individual lives, births, and fortunes receive systematic treatment in later books. Appendices add extracts from his Almagest and the Centiloquy attributed to him. Believer or skeptic, readers cannot understand two thousand years of star lore without it. Ashmand's version served English astrologers and historians throughout the nineteenth century. It set the terms for all who came after it in the field.
radcliffe-brown-andaman-islanders-1922:
Alfred Reginald Radcliffe-Brown spent two years in the Andaman Islands in the Bay of Bengal before the First World War. His 1922 book reports their myths, dances, tools, and family life. It became a founding work of the school later called structural functionalism.

Radcliffe-Brown asks what each custom does to hold the group together and keep its feelings in tune. He treats ritual as a kind of social cement that renews shared bonds. His chapters on mourning and on the meaning of tales show the method at work. Later scholars built on his method, even when they argued with his claims.
reading-character-at-sight-lesson-five-1: Reading Character at Sight, Lesson Five, 1922. The fifth lesson. This book preserves that lesson. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
sandburg-rootabaga-stories-1922:
Carl Sandburg invented the Rootabaga Stories for his own three daughters, telling them at home before writing them down. The collection appeared in 1922. Sandburg wanted American fairy tales set in prairie country, not in the castles and forests of Europe.

Rootabaga Country lies past the railroad tracks, where villages have names like Liver and Onions. The Potato Face Blind Man tells stories to children who ride the Zigzag Railroad. Gimme the Ax and his children, Please Gimme and Ax Me No Questions, wander through tall tales of corn, wind, and pigs. Sandburg's playful language rolls with jokes and music. The stories remain beloved read-aloud classics.
sanger-pivot-of-civilization-1922: The Pivot of Civilization, Margaret Sanger's 1922 book. The birth-control pivot. This book preserves that classic. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. Kept for study. The library keeps the document safe for everyone.
santayana-soliloquies-england-1922:
Soliloquies in England, published in 1922 with its later companion pieces, collects short meditations Santayana wrote in Oxford during the First World War. Stranded in England by the war, the Spanish philosopher watched the English at close range and wrote down what he saw.

The soliloquies take up the English mind, liberty, weather, snobs, soldiers, and the quiet heroism of ordinary endurance. Each piece is brief, balanced, and faintly sad in tone. Santayana praises English freedom while noting its limits with an alien's precision. The book is his most charming: philosophy relaxed into conversation with itself.
shakespeare-othello-1622:
William Shakespeare's Othello first reached print in 1622. The tragedy turns on jealousy and skilled manipulation in Venice and Cyprus. Othello, a Moorish general, weds Desdemona against her father's will.

Iago, passed over and bitter, vows to wreck his general's peace. He plants a lost handkerchief as false proof of Desdemona's faithlessness. Othello trusts the lies, kills his wife, and learns the truth too late. Few plays show so plainly how words can poison a sound and trusting mind at last. Its verse music lifts the grim plot to high and lasting poetry for readers in all lands.
spr-proceedings-vol32-1922:
Volume thirty two gathers parts eighty two through eighty four, all dated 1922. Forty years after the founding, the Proceedings keep their steady form. Thought transference trials run under rules hardened by decades of dispute. The old census habit still shapes how fresh cases get weighed.

Mediumship sittings fill the volume's core, reported in close detail. Sitters' tests, false leads, and striking hits all stand on record. Apparition reports arrive in the usual checked batches. Volume thirty two belongs to the archive's late, mature phase. The evidential debate it fed had a few years left to run. Its evidence remains open to any fresh reader.
stefan-zweig-amok-1922: Zweig's 1922 Amok follows a doctor's obsessive passion in the tropics. Madness builds. The Tower library holds the full text. It traced fever. Minds snapped. Prose burned. Souls bared. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
stein-geography-plays-1922:
Geography and Plays, published in 1922, collects Stein's writing from her Paris years: short plays, portraits, and pieces that treat words as landscape. It came out a decade after much of it was written, when her fame was finally growing.

The plays abandon plot for pattern: voices repeat, vary, and build scenes out of rhythm rather than action. Portraits catch friends and artists in her circling prose. Stein called this landscape theater, drama as a place you look at rather than a story you follow. The book is difficult and playful at once, and it marks the ground later experimental theater would claim.
tagore-creative-unity-1922:
Creative Unity, published in 1922, gathers Tagore's later lectures on art, beauty, and the creative life. Written after years of travel and school-building in Bengal, it states his mature philosophy in plain essays. East and West meet in its pages without either one bowing.

Tagore argues that truth comes when the mind joins the world in love and making, not when it merely counts and owns. He writes on the poet's religion, on woman, on art, and on the unity that creation seeks. The lectures sum up what a lifetime of poems had been saying by image.
theatrum-chemicum-zetzner-1622:
Twenty years after the first printing, Zetzner's house brought out a larger Theatrum Chemicum in 1622. The new edition of the great alchemical anthology held more texts than before. It soon became the standard set for the rest of the century.

Old masters of the art stand side by side in its pages. Their tracts cover elixirs, metals, and hidden forces in nature, in dense Latin prose. Print kept their names and claims alive long after their deaths. For historians, the 1622 set shows which works still ruled alchemical thought as new science began to rise around it.
thomson-new-guide-to-health-1822:
Samuel Thomson, a New Hampshire farmer with no medical schooling, published his New Guide to Health in 1822 and shook American medicine. His system rested on heat: steam baths, cayenne pepper, and lobelia to drive out cold and disease. Thomson sold family rights to his method across the young republic.

The guide teaches lay readers to treat their own households without calling a doctor. Against the mineral drugs of regular medicine, which Thomson called poisons, he set plants and steam. His movement, Thomsonianism, became America's first mass medical following, with agents and societies in town after town.
tob-0122:
Samuel Birley Rowbotham, writing as Parallax, built the case for a flat earth in Zetetic Astronomy: Earth Not a Globe. Rowbotham spent decades performing experiments on canals and coastlines, measuring horizons he claimed stayed level. His zetetic method claimed to follow evidence alone, doubting every received theory, including Newton's.

From his readings he constructs a disc earth with the North Pole at its center and an ice wall at its rim. The book became the bible of Victorian flat-earthism and founded a movement that outlived him. Wrong about the planet, Rowbotham's work remains fascinating evidence about the psychology of dissent and the rhetoric of amateur science.
tob-10022:
Vincent Scully wrote a short account of Blessed John Ruysbroeck, the fourteenth-century Flemish priest and mystic also known as Jan van Ruusbroec. Ruysbroeck served as a parish priest and canon before withdrawing to a life of prayer and writing. His teaching on union with God shaped later Christian mysticism.

Scully traces that life briefly, then turns to what Ruysbroeck taught. At its heart is love rising above images and forms into direct communion with God. For readers who find the mystic's own medieval works difficult, a compact life-and-teaching study like Scully's offers a clear doorway into his world.
tob-10222:
Sigmund Freud published The Interpretation of Dreams in 1900, and A. A. Brill's translation carried it to English readers. Freud argues that dreams are disguised fulfillments of wishes. Decoding them, he claims, opens the royal road to the unconscious mind, where forbidden desires continue to work unseen.

Freud analyzes his own dreams alongside his patients', using free association and the study of symbols, puns, and everyday slips. He separates the dream as remembered from the hidden thoughts beneath it. Whatever readers conclude about his theory, the book launched psychoanalysis and changed how the modern West talks about minds, childhood, and desire.
tob-10622:
Shinran Shonin, the thirteenth-century founder of Japan's Pure Land school, poured his teaching into hymns known as wasan. L. Adams Beck's translation, titled Buddhist Psalms, keeps their devotional warmth in English verse. Shinran's message centers on Amida Buddha's vow to save all who trust in him.

Salvation, in Shinran's hymns, comes by grace through entrusting, not by the monk's own effort or merit. That emphasis has often been compared to faith alone in Christianity, though it grew within Japanese Buddhism. Readers hear an old man's gratitude: Shinran considered himself a foolish, bald-headed sinner saved anyway. The psalms remain sung and recited in Jodo Shinshu temples today.
tob-10822:
Reynold A. Nicholson, the great English orientalist, offered a classic short introduction to Sufism in The Mystics of Islam. Nicholson read deeply in Persian and Arabic sources, including the poets and saints he introduces. Origins, leading figures, and doctrines of divine love structure his account.

Sufi teaching on the path, the annihilation of self in God, and the lives of ecstatics and martyrs of love are explained in calm, clear prose. Nicholson neither romanticizes nor condescends, a balance harder than it looks. V1 evidence calls the book the clearest doorway into Islamic mysticism for English readers, and generations of students have entered through it.
tob-13322:
St. John of the Cross, a Spanish Carmelite friar of the sixteenth century, wrote the poem and commentary known as the Dark Night of the Soul. He composed the poem after months jailed by his own order. David Lewis's translation is the version named here.

The work describes how God purifies the soul through a night of dryness, in which prayer feels empty and all comfort fails. John maps two nights, of sense and of spirit, before union with God in love. Many judge it the summit of Christian mystical writing, and it still guides readers through spiritual desolation.
tob-4022:
George Berkeley staged Three Dialogues Between Hylas and Philonous to defend the strangest thesis in modern philosophy: matter does not exist. Philonous, Berkeley's spokesman, presses the materialist Hylas step by step. To be, Berkeley argues, is to be perceived; what we call physical objects are ordered collections of ideas in minds.

Trees in unobserved forests persist, on his account, because God perceives them always. The dialogues answer the objections readers still raise first: Are we dreaming? Does anything stay real? Berkeley writes with sparkling clarity against skeptics and atheists alike, making an outrageous conclusion feel, page by page, uncomfortably hard to escape.
tob-4222:
Algar Thorold translated Catherine of Siena's Dialogue into English in 1896, and his version long served as the beloved one. Catherine dictated the work in ecstasy near the end of her short life, in colloquy with God the Father. Providence, prayer, and the reform of the church fill its chapters.

Thorold's rendering favors the mystic's fire over literal stiffness. The evidence notes the version is not on Gutenberg and no text is attached to this entry yet. What can be said from the record is clear: of English Catherines, Thorold's carried the saint's voice to the widest circle of devoted readers.
tolstoy-war-and-peace-maude-1922:
Leo Tolstoy wrote War and Peace in Russian, and Aylmer Maude made this Oxford version in 1922. Maude worked in consultation with Tolstoy's own circle and knew the author himself in Russia. His text became the landmark English War and Peace for the century that followed it.

Pierre, Andrei, and Natasha live through Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812 and its wars. Balls, hunts, and drawing rooms alternate with Borodino and the burning of Moscow in 1812. Tolstoy asks how great events truly happen, and scorns the great-man view of past times. Essays on history interrupt the tale and dare readers to rethink war and power itself. Its human breadth makes it, for many, the greatest novel ever written.
tour-through-the-eastern-counties-of-eng: Daniel Defoe's 1722 travel account of eastern England, from London through East Anglia to the Humber. With a merchant's eye he records trade, towns, and the great storm damage of 1703, centuries before guidebooks. A vivid, ground-level portrait of England just before the industrial age.
un-ga-res-2022:
Southern Rhodesia stood on the edge of a breakaway when the General Assembly passed Resolution 2022 on 5 November 1965. The Assembly had read the reports of its decolonization team on the colony. It lists the chain of past votes. They run from the 1960 call to end colonial rule down to a text of October 1965, and a Security Council vote of May that year. None, it holds, had been put into force by Britain, the ruling power.

Fresh worry runs through the text. The chiefs of Southern Rhodesia were drawing closer to South Africa and to Portugal, in a pact to keep white minority rule in place across southern Africa. That drift, the Assembly warns, puts freedom, peace, and safety in Africa at risk. Six days later, the regime broke away.
un-ga-res-22:
Legal shelter for the United Nations itself was set down in Resolution 22, passed by the General Assembly on 13 February 1946. Annexed to the vote stands the full text of the Convention on the Privileges and Immunities of the United Nations. The Assembly approves the pact and puts it to each member state for joining.

The Charter's own words frame the pact. Under Article 104, the UN holds such legal standing in each member's land as its work needs. Under Article 105, the UN, its member envoys, and its staff hold such shelter from local law as their tasks demand. The pact spells out what that means in courts, taxes, and bags of mail. It is still in force today.
un-ga-res-a-66-222:
Family farms feed much of the world, and Resolution 66/222 gave them a year of their own. The General Assembly had taken note of a vote by the world food body in July 2011. It recalled its own 2010 text on farm growth and food safety. Smallholder farmers, many of them women, draw a named share of praise for their needs and their work.

The vote declares an International Year of Family Farming. Such farms, it holds, are a sound base for food output that can last, and a path out of poverty for the countryside. The year would fall in 2014. A later text in this same set marks how the year was kept.
un-ga-res-a-69-22:
News and public facts shape the fight over Palestine, and Resolution A/69/22, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, deals with that field. The Assembly had read the yearly report of its Palestinian rights committee, above all the part on facts and outreach. It recalls the vote of the year before on the same work.

Wide spread of true and full facts is held to be of vital weight. Civic groups and public bodies help raise grasp of the fixed rights of the Palestinian people, above all self-rule and a state of their own. The text backs a just, lasting peace built on past deals between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 2022 (XX), adopted on 5 November 1965, sharpened the Assembly's stand on Southern Rhodesia days before the minority regime's expected move to independence. The Assembly restated the people's right to freedom and backed their struggle. It condemned racial discrimination in the territory in the strongest terms.

The text solemnly warned that the United Nations would oppose any move to independence that was not based on a vote for every adult. It demanded freedom for political prisoners, and repeal of harsh and unfair laws such as the Land Apportionment Act. It demanded suspension of the 1961 constitution and a conference of all parties. It called on Britain to use all the means it needed, force included.

General Assembly Resolution 22, adopted on 13 February 1946, approved the Convention on the Privileges and Immunities of the United Nations and offered it to each member for joining. The Charter had promised the Organization the legal standing and protections it needs to do its work, and the convention spells out what those are.

The text gives the United Nations legal personality. It shields its buildings, funds, and records from search or seizure. It frees it from direct taxes and customs duties on official goods. It also grants protections to member representatives, officials, and experts on mission. It covers United Nations travel papers. It sets ways to settle disputes.

With resolution 66/222, the General Assembly declares 2014 the International Year of Family Farming. The decision rests on the view that family and smallholder farming underpin sustainable food production and food security. This holds especially for the many small farmers who are women. The Food and Agriculture Organization is invited to lead implementation. It would work with governments and other United Nations bodies. Costs beyond its existing mandate are met from voluntary contributions. Member states are encouraged to back the year through their own development programs.

Resolution 69/22 of the General Assembly keeps the special information programme going on the question of Palestine run by the Department of Public Information for 2015–2016. The programme publicizes United Nations work on Palestine. It makes and updates publications and audiovisual material. It holds fact-finding missions and seminars for journalists in the region. It trains Palestinian broadcasters and journalists each year. The Assembly treats wide, accurate public information as part of building support for a just and lasting settlement.
un-sc-res-122:
Kashmir's own assembly could not settle the state's future, the Council ruled in 1957. India and Pakistan had restated their cases that January. On 24 January 1957 the Council recalled the old United Nations plan for the state. The final shape of Jammu and Kashmir would come from a free vote of its people. That principle came from resolutions passed in 1948 and 1949. A commission for the two countries had framed the terms.

A constituent assembly chosen in the state could not replace that vote. Any act by such a body to fix the state's status would have no standing. The Council said it would keep considering the dispute. The Soviet Union abstained. The plebiscite at the heart of the text was never held.
un-sc-res-1322: Year 2000 in the catalog holds Resolution 1322, a formal Security Council decision of the United Nations. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-1422:
The International Criminal Court opened its doors on 1 July 2002. Eleven days later the Security Council acted to shield some peacekeepers from it. On 12 July 2002 it asked the court to hold off on certain cases. Cases over United Nations work by staff from states outside the Rome Statute were covered. The court should not start or proceed with such a case for twelve months. Article 16 of the statute allows that request.

The Council said it intended to renew the request each July. The renewal would run as long as needed. States had to avoid acts that clashed with the pause. The deal ended a standoff that had threatened peacekeeping mandates. Critics saw it as a carve-out for powerful states.
un-sc-res-1622: Kept under the number 1622, this Security Council resolution reproduces the official record as transcribed by Wikisource. Its paragraphs follow the body's settled grammar: verbs like decides, demands, and requests, each with a different force. Reading the grammar closely is how lawyers tell a binding order from an appeal, and the text here allows it.
un-sc-res-1722: Security Council Resolution 1722 is held in this collection as a record transcription sourced from English Wikisource. Its decisions rest on the findings stacked in its preamble, in the Council's settled order of writing. Because governments argue later over what was truly decided, the untouched full text preserved here is the reference that settles it.
un-sc-res-1822: Resolution 1822 is a Security Council decision preserved here in official-record wording through English Wikisource. The act is built like its fellows: a preamble that frames the question, then numbered paragraphs that answer it with the Council's authority. un-sc-res-1922: From 2010, Resolution 1922 is a formal Security Council decision kept in this collection through a Wikisource transcription.
